<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "bare" or "immediate" dry fires started on page 165. While the previous page likely detailed the first two grades of fire, this page begins by describing the third and strongest grade before moving into "mediated" fires and the subtle heat used for digestion.</meta>

The third is the reverberatory fire <term>Reverberir-Feuer</term>, being the strongest of all, which not only drives all moisture out of bodies but can also transform the body into ash and reduce it to cinders.

It is called a reverberatory fire because of the manner in which it acts; because this work is performed in a furnace built in such a way that the fire not only passes through and rises upward, but the flames even beat back together over the material <term>materia</term> one wishes to prepare—hence it is also called a reverberatory furnace <term>Reverberir-Ofen</term>.

## Note.

Here we speak only of the sublimation fire and every strong fire, by which one wishes to understand all of them—both dry and moist—to which certain grades can be assigned. This is as if we were speaking here only of dry fires, because other strong or moderate fires likewise take into account a specific quality of stages and numbers.

Otherwise, there is a fire—which can be either dry or moist—that has its grades no less than the aforementioned, yet its work in the process is hardly noticed (because it is almost imperceptible). This is like a tempered heat compared to an external task <note>original: "Obhaben," referring here to the specific chemical operation being performed.</note>; such is mostly the case with a digestion fire <term>Digerir-Feuer</term>, whose every effect upon the elements occurs so subtly and stealthily that one does not feel it. And yet its grades are governed, increased, and decreased in comparison to an external task—the first grade of which is compared to innate and natural heat. This is more clearly described by the sitting of a hen over her eggs when she hatches her young, or by the sun's warmth in the month of May or June; and so one rises through almost imperceptible changes up to the fourth grade.

Beyond this, it is further to be noted that this distinction of fire grades through external tasks is observed not only in the digestion fire but also sometimes in a stronger one. Hence, directions are so often and so much spoken and written of: that the fire should be so strong that you can keep your hand in the sand; or so that the lead <note>original: "Bley"</note> can be kept in flux <note>original: "im Fluß," meaning in a molten or liquid state.</note>.

A dry fire with a medium <note>This refers to indirect heat, such as a sand bath (balneum arenae) or ash bath, where a substance sits between the flame and the vessel.</note> is when the material to be prepared is placed in the first vessel, between it and the fire. This vessel is then filled with another material or is left empty.

If it is empty: Then the material <term>materia</term> is placed in its vessel, inside another empty vessel, and all joints are well luted <term>sealed with a clay-like paste</term>, or glued together with adhesive; and for this reason it is called a dry vat or dry bath. An immersion-bath, namely when the vessel is dipped into the water, and

### An essential fire.

An essential fire <term>wesentlich Feuer</term> is one that works within the fire: yet it is not a fire and is also not found to be a fire <note>This refers to internal chemical heat or biological heat that mimics the effects of fire without a flame.</note>.

However, such a thing is applied externally by means of a medium or air, directly to the material that is to be processed.

When it is placed externally to a thing, the addition works through warmth, such as horse manure <term>Roß-Mist</term> and the like.

When it is added directly to it, it works through its natural essence and its own power, like the most violent fire <note>This likely refers to caustic or corrosive substances that "burn" chemically.</note>.

But one must also take heed of the grades <term>gradus</term> in such a fire; these, however, are impossible to describe, but must be left solely to the artist’s discretion, opinion, and a perfect judgment <note>original: "Judicio"</note>.

For the same grade of fire is not required to distill water as for other substances; therefore, in and with a material fire, one must take care that the heat is increased by degrees, and thus the grades of the fire are well observed;

The chemical place is that which, either indirectly or directly, receives the materials that are to be processed, or the instrument through which they are processed.

### These places are of two kinds:
### Vessels and Furnaces.

The vessels <term>Geschirr</term> <note>While "Geschirr" means dishes today, in this context it refers to laboratory glassware and ceramic apparatus.</note> are places that contain the material itself, and do so either indirectly or directly. ### Distillation Upwards.

Distillation upwards <note>Also known as ascending distillation, where vapors rise before being condensed.</note> requires a straight flask, or as some prefer, a ceramic vessel or boiler <term>Blase</term> made of the material best suited for the substance one intends to process, with its beaked still-head <term>Helm</term> placed upon it; this assembly they call an **Alembic**.

### Distillation to the Side.

Distillation to the side requires a curved boiler (which is why it also bears the name **Retort** or **Muses' Horn** <note>original: "Musen-Horn." An archaic term for a retort due to its curved, horn-like shape.</note>), with a receiver <term>Vorlage</term> attached to it. This method is appropriate for minerals, or for processing minerals within such a vessel.

### Distillation Downwards.

Distillation downwards <note>Known as distillation *per descensum*, often used for extracting oils from wood or resins.</note> requires a pot or glass with a broad bottom and a narrow neck, with a sieve and an iron grate positioned at the mouth so that the *dead head* <note>original: "Caput mortuum." The useless solid residue remaining after distillation or sublimation.</note> cannot pass over into the receiver.

To all of these, one attaches a receiver according to the intention of the artist and the material one wishes to work with; for some [substances] necessarily require large receivers, and small ones would burst if one intended to make, for example, <term>Vitriol</term> <note>Sulfate minerals used to create "oil of vitriol" or sulfuric acid.</note>, <term>Spießglas</term> <note>Antimony or stibnite.</note>, oils, and the like. Some require only small receivers, such as common waters and various herbal mixtures.

### Sublimation.

All **Sublimations** <note>The process of heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then collects as a solid again, bypassing the liquid phase.</note> require straight vessels and an attached still-head with a beak, if one intends to catch the extracted moisture. Occasionally, such vessels are also prepared and covered with another lid made of glass or clay <term>Letten</term>.

**Calcination** <note>Heating a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air, usually to oxidize it or reduce it to a powder.</note>, which is also commonly called **Reverberation**, requires broad...

## Exhalation

**Exhalation** <note>original: "Aushauchung." This refers to the process of evaporation or the releasing of vapors.</note>, when it occurs from salts, requires a very low vessel with a wide mouth made of metal and glass; if it is another matter that is not so penetrating, one can also use any glazed vessel.

## Circulation

**Circulation** <note>A process of continuous distillation where the condensed liquid flows back into the original vessel.</note> requires a vessel called a **Pelican**; in the absence of which, one can place a **blind still-head** <term>blinder Helm</term> (so named because it has no beak or spout) upon it, and must carefully **lute** <term>lutiren</term> <note>To seal the joints of the apparatus with a paste or clay to prevent the escape of vapors.</note> the flask <term>Kolben</term> and all the air-holes.

## Casting

**Casting** <note>original: "Giessung." The pouring of molten material into molds.</note> occurs especially in the well-known goldsmiths' **crucibles** <term>Tiegel</term> or from iron spoons. These are all mostly the common vessels that a laboratory practitioner <term>Laborant</term> cannot do without.

## The Furnaces

The **furnaces** <term>Ofen</term> are the places which hold, warm, govern, and protect the matter to be processed <term>elaboriren</term>, as well as the chemical instruments, so that they do not quickly shatter.

Of all these, no extensive descriptions are necessary, and the artist may, according to his pleasure, keep the old designs or invent new ones; moreover, chemical books are here and there sufficiently filled with such reports, which, however, can be much more easily understood through what has been mentioned above. Something must still be mentioned regarding the construction of furnaces.

## Furnace Construction

A furnace actually consists of three parts, either in reality or in potentiality.

# The Apparatus-Chamber
# The Hearth
# The Ash-Grate

The **Apparatus-Chamber** <note>original: "Zeug-Lege." A designated area or structure within a laboratory where furnaces and chemical materials are arranged.</note> is the location of the furnaces which contains the materials to be processed <term>elaboriren</term>, along with their necessary vessels.

The **Hearth** is the part of the furnace that receives the fire.

The **Ash-Grate** <note>original: "Aschen-Reuter." Literally an "ash-sifter."</note> of the hearth is either an iron grate or another suitable floor with holes so that the ash can fall through, which would otherwise stifle the fire; it also allows the pressing air to blow upon the fire through the door of the ash-grate.

Since, as has been mentioned, the furnaces govern and maintain the fire, they have certain **registers** <term>Register</term> <note>Dampers or vents used to control the flow of air and heat.</note>, by means of which the heat is forced and intensified, or also diminished and eased, as the circumstances of the matter require.

## Registers

The **registers** are holes in the furnace through which the fire can be decreased and increased; namely, by removing the covers made for these holes, or by closing them.

# Explanation and Meaning of Some Chemical Words That Appear Here and There in the Preparation of Chemical and Alchemical Medicines

## Menstruum

**Menstruum**, as a chemical word, is and signifies a **dissolving and separating juice** <note>original: "Auflöse- und Scheide-Safft." In alchemy, a menstruum is a solvent capable of dissolving a solid to extract its essence.</note>; that is, such a liquid or moisture by means of which a solid body <term>Corpus</term> is opened.

All **menstrua** are watery, acidic, salty, sulfurous, or spiritual.

<meta>This page continues the glossary of chemical and alchemical terms, specifically categorizing various types of solvents (menstrua) based on their properties and defining the results of the extraction process, such as tinctures and residues.</meta>

### From Water

The solvent <term>Menstruum</term> <note>A solvent or dissolving liquid used to extract the "essence" of a substance.</note> consisting of water only dissolves watery substances, certain parts of animals, as well as juices and salts.

### Acidic Solvents

Acidic solvents <term>Menstrua</term> attack metals <term>Metalla</term> and minerals <term>Mineralia</term>, which they also do to certain parts of animals and plants.

### Saline Solvents

Saline solvents <term>Menstrua</term> are either acidic or alkaline-saline; they dissolve acidic materials, encompass what is sulfurous and oily, attack metals, and extract tinctures <term>Tincturen</term> from them.

### Sulfurous Solvents

Sulfurous solvents <term>Menstrua</term> dissolve viscous and resinous parts and extract their tincture <term>Tinctur</term>. Such solvents <term>Menstrua</term> include tartarized spirit of wine <term>Spiritus Vini Tartarisatus</term> <note>Ethanol distilled or purified with potassium carbonate (tartar) to increase its strength.</note>, or other flammable spirits <term>Spiritus</term>, as well as spirit of turpentine <term>Spiritus Terebinthinæ</term>.

### Spiritual Solvents

Spiritual and spirituous solvents <term>Spirituôse Menstrua</term> are used to extract all volatile sulfurs and salts.

### Tincture

A tincture <term>Tinctur</term> is a liquid, specifically one possessing the color and essence of the material upon which it was poured and by which it was tinted and colored.

### Capitell

Capitell <note>In early chemistry, this often refers to a strong alkaline lye or a caustic solution.</note> is a lye; it is specifically called a solvent <term>Menstruum</term> that is tinted or colored by the salt extracted from ashes.

### Dead Head (Caput mortuum)

The "Dead Head" <term>Caput mortuum</term> <note>original Latin: "dead head." A term for the useless residue remaining after distillation or sublimation.</note>, the dregs or sediment, is the body that remains after the tincture <term>Tinctur</term> or essence <term>Essentz</term> has been extracted by a solvent <term>Menstruum</term> or through distillation <term>Destillirung</term>. And in general, whatever remains after the extraction <term>Extraction</term> of any thing or material <term>Materia</term> is called a "Dead Head" <term>Caput mortuum</term>.

### A Maceration

A maceration <note>original: *Beitzung*. While this can mean pickling or etching, here it refers to a steeping process used to extract components.</note> is, as the name indicates, that which takes away or carries off from the body (from the remaining dead body <note>The "dead body" or *caput mortuum* is the solid residue left over after a substance has been processed.</note>) what was meant to be distilled or sublimated.

This is used for essential tinctures <term>Essential-Tincturen</term>, which must be distilled for the sake of greater subtlety and excellence. Its use is also necessary to distill the oils of spices, fruits, herbs, and all plants of the earth.

Thus, a maceration is actually a water or broth; however, even without that, a solvent <term>Menstruum</term> <note>A liquid used to dissolve or extract the "essence" of a substance.</note> that is separated from the tincture is called a maceration.

There is also a dry maceration that is used only for minerals: such as the "flying eagles" <note>original: *fliegende Adler*. An alchemical code name for volatile substances, most commonly sal ammoniac (ammonium chloride) or sublimated mercury.</note>.

### A Philosophical Month

A philosophical-chemical and alchemical month, as well as a medicinal one, is 40 days.

### Double Vessel

A *Diploma* <note>original: *Diploma*. In early chemistry, this refers to a double-walled vessel or a water bath.</note> is a double vessel; therefore, instead of *Diploma*, one also writes: "in a double vessel." This means a vessel that directly holds the material, placed within a bath <term>Balneo</term> <note>from the Latin *Balneum*, a bath.</note>: for by the abbreviation **B. M.** <note>original: *Balneum Mariae*, or "Mary’s Bath." A water bath used for gentle, even heating, similar to a modern double boiler.</note>, a *Diploma* or double vessel is understood.

### Process

The chemical process <term>Process</term> signifies the form of an operation, as well as its continuation and repetition.

We have diligently used and intended to retain the old words and technical terms <term>Terminorum</term> because they are not found in all books. This was done so that beginners may learn to understand them and be able to make use of—and read with understanding—old books and any manuscripts of the philosophers <term>Philosophorum</term> <note>In this context, "philosophers" refers to the "natural philosophers" or alchemists of previous centuries.</note> they might encounter.

Now we shall proceed closer to the work and come to the matters themselves.

## On Corruption (Disruption)

Corruption <note>In alchemy, "corruption" is not a negative term for rot, but a necessary stage where a substance’s physical form is broken down so its essence can be released and "reborn."</note> is a chemical operation that opens and disrupts the structure <note>original: *Gepack*, literally the way something is packed or put together.</note> of a body, its cohesion, and its compact nature in every possible way. It separates all impurity from it until it has reached that degree of perfection and purity which the artist intended as the material <term>Materiatum</term> and foundation for a new work.

But why is this spoken of in degrees? Because there are different levels and grades of medicine, such as: an extract; an oil; a sublimate <term>Sublimat</term> <note>A solid substance produced by heating a material until it turns to vapor and then collects as a solid again.</note>; flowers <term>Flores</term> <note>The fine, crystalline powder that forms on the sides of a vessel during sublimation, such as "flowers of sulfur."</note>, and the like, which do not all require the same degree of perfection. Just as corruption, according to the laws of nature, precedes generation and procreation, it does so here to provide something pure and suitable; for it is not enough to destroy the body, but the impurities and foreign matters must also be removed and separated from it, so that a purer and better medicine may be produced than the previous one, or than the raw matter <term>Materia</term> from which it is manufactured. Therefore, two kinds of instruments <note>original: *Instrumenta*.</note> are required for this.

### On the First Instrument of Corruption.

Corruption (disruption), as it is strictly understood here, includes those operations sought only for the opening of compact bodies; of these operations, there are

### Two Genera or Kinds.

The first of these contains those operations that specifically only disrupt the body, or rather prepare it and make it more suitable for the true and final disruption.

These, in turn, can be brought into two chapters; for they either divide the body into the smallest pieces, so that each piece does not retain its cohesion <note>original: *Aneinanderfatz*, an archaic term for the "stickiness" or unity of a solid substance.</note>, or they make the body fluid.

When the division into the smallest pieces occurs, these methods are: filing, scraping, pulverizing, smoothing <note>original: *Glatten*. In this context, it likely refers to a form of grinding or polishing to reduce the surface.</note>, cutting, crushing, granulating, and breaking into pieces.

### Filing.

Filing is the [disruption] of the body's cohesive existence through communal division,

### Scraping

Scraping, which is related to this, divides the body into even smaller pieces, also by means of such an iron instrument, and the prepared body <term>Corpus</term> is called scraped.

### Powdering

Powdering, which brings it into even smaller pieces, is: When one crushes something in a mortar.

### Smoothing

Smoothing or rubbing down (as the final degree to bring it to the finest powder) is a rubbing of the body against itself <note>or onto a surface</note> on a marble slab <note>original: *Marmel*</note>, using a corresponding grinding stone <note>original: *Reibe-Keihle*, likely a muller used for levigation</note>.

### Cutting

Cutting is the division of a body into the smallest pieces using a certain instrument or knife.

### Crushing

This is a crushing of the parts through pounding. It is especially used for fresh herbs and fatty substances.

### Granulating or Graining

Granulating or graining is the reduction of a body into grains: it properly pertains to metals and is performed in various ways.

1. The molten metals are poured drop by drop into water placed beneath them; by the force of which they bounce back and shatter into grains.

Flattening <term>Plättung</term> is: When a body <term>Cörper</term> is drawn into small thin plates, or beaten into the same;

When a body <term>Corpus</term> has been made fluid, it is called a general **Separation**.

## Separation.

Separation <term>Zertrennung</term> is an operation whereby that which was previously solid and held together is made fluid, and this is done either with or without heat.

If it happens with heat: then it is with either a naked or a direct fire.

If it happens with a naked fire, it pertains to metals and is properly called a casting <term>Giessung</term>, and is used in granulating or in the purification of metals;

Or, by means of minerals such as sulfur, antimony <note>original: *Spießglaß*, the common name for stibnite or antimony ore</note>, and the like; then it serves either for incorporation or purification, specifically so that the combustible sulfur may dissipate into a vapor.

In such cases, the laboratory workers <term>Laboranten</term> are accustomed to adding saltpeter, sal ammoniac <note>original: *Salmiac*</note>, or sulfur and all sorts of easily-melted things, so that they may promote the purification. Or, in the case of mineral salts such as saltpeter and others, a purification or figuring <note>original: *Figurung*, likely referring to crystallization into specific geometric shapes</note> is sought.

Or a purification of plant products <term>Erdgewächse</term> is sought: such as gums or resins <note>original: *Baum-Zähren*, literally "tree-tears"</note>; there, one is accustomed to adding something wet so that such things do not burn, and the purification happens through a strainer or through incorporation with other things, as also happens with fat and grease <note>original: *Schmer*</note>.

In all of these cases, it is called Melting: When it happens

## On Putrefaction.

Putrefaction is a separation of the mixed substance through natural rotting, occurring within a warm moisture that disrupts the essence itself and unlocks its internal "locks."

### In which work the following points are to be observed:

1. Because this operation is a work of nature aided by art (for the natural heat, awakened by an external heat, accomplishes the work), we must take great care that we do not rush ourselves in such an operation, but rather let nature have its will and pay close attention to its progress.

2. One must take care that no total dissolution occurs. Which is also not required.

3. It is to be observed and noted with all diligence that the putrefaction does not "stifle": which is to be prevented in this way; namely, by protecting the vessel in which the putrefaction occurs so well that no [outside] air can reach it.

## Of Maceration or Soaking.

Soaking is the pouring of a <term>menstruum</term> <note>original: *Menstruo*; a solvent used to extract active principles from a solid substance</note> over a body for a certain period of time. That is: until the solvent has made the body soft and suitable enough so that it can be penetrated by the solvent, and allows the tincture to be drawn out through the solvent. Thus, one cannot set a fixed time or goal for this work, but must wait until a sufficient tincture manifests itself in the solvent. For only then does the separation take place.

### Preparation for Soaking.

The preparation for soaking consists of the following:

That which one wishes to soak must first be crushed small; and then one puts the crushed material into a suitable vessel, seals it well on all sides so that no air can get to it, and then sets it aside to soak for its time. During this, it is necessary that it be stirred frequently; or, depending on the nature of the material, it is placed in a gentle heat. If they are plants <note>original: *Erdgewächse*; literally "earth-growths"</note> that one wishes to soften, this is best done using a <term>B. M.</term> <note>original: *Balneum Mariae*; a water bath used for gentle, even heating</note>. If it is something mineral, it requires a dry heat with a penetrating agent; provided, that is, that no other specific method has been prescribed by the laboratory workers. But be that as it may, it must still be shaken and agitated frequently during the soaking process.

Its use is for essences and extracts, whereby only this one thing must be observed: that one chooses the correct <term>solvent</term> <note>original: *Menstruum*</note>, for not every tincture can be extracted with every solvent.

Therefore, one must know and examine his material to see if it is compact, firm, and stiff, or if it is thin and soft, and choose his solvent accordingly.

It must also be considered what the nature of the essence one wishes to extract is, whether it is oily or watery. If it is oily, it also requires an oily solvent and cannot be extracted by any other solvent; for example <note>original: *e. g.*; exempli gratia</note>, the <term>Tincture of Sulfur</term> <note>original: *Tinctura Sulphuris*</note> cannot be brought out as easily with any other solvent as with oil of turpentine <note>original: *Terpentin-Oehl*</note>.

## Of Cohobation.

<term>Cohobation</term> <note>A process where the distilled liquid is poured back onto the solid residue and re-distilled multiple times to increase potency.</note> is a dissolution, destruction, and separation of a substance <note>original: *Cörpers*; literally "body"</note> through the frequent, repeated pouring back of the material that remains behind.

It bears a relationship to soaking, for just as soaking softens the materials and brings about separation through the constant presence of the <term>menstruum</term> <note>original: *Menstrui*; a solvent used to extract active principles</note>, so too does cohobation achieve this same result through multiple pourings, and it is utilized during distillation.

The intention here is twofold:

1. That through frequent pouring and distillation, by means of gradual heat, it finally draws the <term>essence</term> and power out of the material (which is usually a decayed matter or an <term>extract</term> or something similar) over which it is poured; and this is repeated until the <term>menstruum</term> finally passes over <note>distills</note> entirely without flavor.

2. That an oil may be produced from it; and this occurs either by transforming the entire material into an oil, as happens with the calxes <note>powders produced by heating</note> of minerals; or that through frequent pouring, the penetrating <term>menstruum</term> (which opens up the body) finally acts upon the vessels as well, and draws an oil out from the inner womb of nature. This can be seen in the distillation of oils from trees and seeds. Thus, in a proper operation, the <term>menstruum</term> must be selected according to the judgment of the artist who undertakes to work upon the substance <note>original: *Corpus*</note>, and according to the nature of the material.

## Of Calcination.

Regarding <term>calcination</term> <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its physical or chemical state, typically to oxidize or pulverize it.</note>, it is necessary to report what a "calx" is, because calcination must be described by means of it.

A calx, then, means—and is actually—a substance <note>original: *Corpus*</note> reduced to a fine powder through the power of fire. Or, it is a material that can be reduced to an incomprehensibly fine powder simply through rubbing.

And thus, calcination is the violent transformation into a calx by means of fire.

This is of two kinds, regarding the double nature of the calx:

A true and properly named calcination. And

<term>Ashing</term> <note>original: *Aescherung*; the reduction of a substance to ash through combustion.</note>.

## The True Calcination.

The true <term>calcination</term> <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to reduce it to a powder or "calx."</note> occurs when the body <note>original: *Corpus*</note>—without any loss of its <term>essence</term>—is transformed from a hard state into something active and suitable for grinding, so that it easily yields to the other prescribed operations. In every true chemical calcination, it is essential that the innate heat be intensified and the connatural moisture be preserved.

This is necessary and should be particularly observed in the case of <term>alterative medicines</term> <note>Medicines intended to gradually change the body's condition and restore health rather than causing an immediate effect like purging</note>, which are prepared through alteration or separation. Now, many and various ways of operating have indeed been invented, but all to no other end than that the body undergoes a thorough transformation; yet in such a way that nothing of its essence is lost.

Regarding the first part, the preparation of medicines that only require an alteration of the body—such as the dissolution of pearls and corals—the following must be observed: if the body one wishes to melt has subtle and volatile <term>spirits</term> <note>The active, gaseous, or "living" components of a substance</note>, one must calcinate it in a closed vessel so that the volatile parts are retained with the fixed parts. Otherwise, because every calcination (whether closed or open) produces a black <term>calx</term> <note>original: *Kalck*; the crumbly residue left after heating</note> upon the loss of moisture—which is useless for any operation—the material is <term>reverberated</term> <note>Heated in a furnace where the flame is reflected off a dome or roof back onto the material</note> with an open but tempered and graded fire, so that the <term>tincture</term> or essence does not evaporate through the force of the fire. However, for other substances that have sufficiently fixed spirits, one does not need to be so precise; as is the case with iron and <term>Crocus Martis</term> <note>original: "Saffron of Mars"; a reddish iron oxide used in alchemical medicine</note>.

In the extraction of essences and tinctures, where a separation of the spirits is sought, another thing must be noted: it is necessary to transform the body completely and thoroughly, yet in such a way that nothing of its essence is lost.

For all <term>phlegm</term> <note>In alchemy, the watery, tasteless, and medically inactive part of a substance</note> and light spirits must be separated from it, because such things can hinder the extraction of the essence.

And finally, because the essential nature is always required from this calcination, practice has invented many ways to operate; yet one must always keep an eye on what is sought and what must be separated.

For if we only desire to remove that which belongs to the separation, it is done either through distilling or sublimating.

If it is to happen through distilling, we use for open calcination a distillation to the sides <note>Likely referring to the use of a retort where the vapors travel sideways into a receiver</note>, with a fairly strong, but...

...but <note>Continuing from the previous page's discussion on the "useless" nature of certain residues</note> for a <term>grading fire</term> <note>A fire used to purify or "grade" a substance to a higher degree of strength or purity.</note>; just as when separating <term>Oil of Vitriol</term> <note>Concentrated sulfuric acid, highly valued by alchemists for its corrosive and transformative properties.</note>, one must first remove and separate all <term>spirits</term> and <term>phlegm</term> <note>The volatile "active" gases and the watery, inactive components of a substance.</note>, after which the Oil finally follows.

When a substance is to be <term>sublimated</term> <note>The process where a solid is heated until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again as a purified powder on a cooler surface.</note>, the separation is achieved through the sublimation itself: as in the case of <term>Antimony</term> <note>original: *Antimonio*</note>, before we find its white <term>flowers</term> <note>Fine powders or crystals produced by sublimation.</note>, we must first prepare the combustible parts and the yellow flowers.

In the event that one does not wish to preserve these, one calcinates with an open <term>reverberatory fire</term> <note>A furnace where the heat is reflected or "reverberated" from the roof down onto the material, rather than the flame touching it directly.</note>; in this case, however, one must take great care and regulate the fire so that what is being sought is not taken away at the same time. For if the fire is well-regulated, nothing of the <term>essence</term> is lost; as long as the phlegm or watery spirits are departing, the essence remains undisturbed.

And thus, one must pay close attention to their departure. This is recognized by the rising smoke or vapor, or even by the <term>body</term> <note>The physical matter being worked upon.</note> itself. For one will look just like the other.

Or, if such a useless matter can be easily separated—as with <term>Antimony</term> <note>original: *Spießglaß*; also known as stibnite.</note>—it is sufficient to evaporate it over a coal fire, though one must stir it often with an iron spatula until it is sufficiently processed.

It is customary in such a work to add <term>sulfur</term>, vitriol, or something similarly light to promote the process; from this it can be seen that it does not matter how or in what form it is made, provided that the medicines suffer no harm and a "true <term>calx</term>" <note>A fine, dry powder produced after a substance has been thoroughly heated.</note> is produced.

### Incineration <note>original: *Cinefactio*</note> or Ashing.

<term>Incineration</term> is an operation where the body is reduced to ash with the loss of its moisture, for which a <term>salt</term> is required.

### Its preparation is twofold:

1.  **An open preparation**, in which the matter is burned with a living flame, so that it becomes, as it were, the nourishment of the flames, until it has been reduced to a completely white and most perfect ash, from which one is to extract an elemental salt.
2.  **A closed preparation**; namely, when the matter is burned to ash in a pot or other closed vessel with a covered lid (whereby the joints are well <term>luted</term> <note>original: *lutiret*; sealed airtight with a specialized clay or paste.</note> on all sides), and thus the volatile parts are <term>fixed</term> <note>The process of making a volatile substance stable under heat.</note> with the fixed parts.

From this, an <term>Essential Salt</term> <note>A salt believed to contain the "essence" or medicinal soul of the plant or mineral, obtained after burning and leaching the ashes.</note> is drawn, which is called <term>Alkali</term>. In this regard, it differs from other substances because, although all moisture is consumed during this <term>calcination</term> <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to reduce it to a powder.</note>, certain <term>spirits</term> <note>Volatile substances or active medicinal components.</note> are "fixed" <note>Made solid or non-volatile so they do not evaporate.</note> and retained. Therefore, it is called "essential" because it keeps something of the <term>essence</term> within itself.

From this, one can now see what the <term>calx</term> <note>original: *Kalck*; the crumbly, oxidized powder remaining after a metal or mineral has been thoroughly burnt.</note> is, and in how many ways calcination occurs in regards to this calx.

It is also necessary to know the different ways of operating, or the methods of procedure. These are:

->Twofold:<-
->1. Actual, and<-
->2. Potential.<- <note>Actual calcination uses physical fire, while potential calcination uses "potential fire," such as corrosive acids that "burn" the material without heat.</note>

## On Actual Calcination.

Actual calcination occurs when the matter is brought into a calx by the force of fire. Its preparation is as follows: that which one wishes to calcinate is crushed small or, according to its nature and being, reduced into the smallest possible pieces and placed into its proper vessel. This vessel may be either open or closed, as the matter requires, either with additives that promote calcination or without additives, if the calcination can occur easily and by itself. The additives are: <term>sulfur</term>, <term>vitriol</term> <note>Sulfuric acid or sulfate minerals.</note>, <term>vinegar</term>, and many <term>salts</term>.

When it is done with additives and in a sealed vessel, one must leave air-holes open so that the steam and smoke, which usually escape in great quantities, can get out; otherwise, the vessel would burst.

If it is done without additives, and the matter is precious and contains strong spirits: then it is not strictly necessary to use a permanently sealed vessel, but rather one that is merely <term>luted</term> <note>original: *verlutire*; sealed using "lute," a specialized alchemical clay or paste designed to make joints airtight and heat-resistant.</note> with strong clay and held together with iron bands; one must then apply the fire by degrees.

Some vessels are merely wrapped with cloth and then luted afterward; however, one must let the <term>lute</term> dry thoroughly before bringing it to the fire.

In every actual calcination, it should be noted that frequent quenching with vinegar or another similar "sharp" liquid, or even sprinkling, is necessary.

**Vocabulary List:**
**Essential Salt:** A purified salt containing the plant's essence.
**Alkali:** A salt extracted from ashes.
**Calcination:** The reduction of a solid to powder via heat.
**Calx:** The powdered residue of a burnt substance.
**Spirits:** The volatile, active vapors of a substance.
**Sulfur:** A common alchemical additive for "burning" metals.
**Vitriol:** Corrosive metallic salts or sulfuric acid.
**Vinegar:** Used here as a chemical solvent or quenching agent.
**Lute / To Lute:** A sealant clay or the act of sealing a vessel.

## On Potential Calcination.

A <term>potential fire</term> <note>original: *mögentlich Feuer*; a chemical agent, such as acid, that acts like fire by breaking down substances without the use of a literal flame.</note> is one through which the matter is brought into a true <term>calx</term> <note>A dry, crumbly powder produced by heating or chemically treating a metal.</note> by an <term>essential fire</term>, but never into ash. This is the most excellent way to calcinate, and especially to extract the <term>quintessence</term> <note>The "fifth essence" or the purest, most concentrated medicinal core of a substance.</note> of metals, which cannot easily be extracted without it. This method also serves for the essential tinctures of plants and animals, as well as stony things. The lovers of chemistry <note>original: *Liebhaber der Chymie*; a common term for practicing alchemists.</note> have also found different ways to put this calcination into practice, all of which seem able to be categorized as follows:

->1. <term>Precipitation</term> <note>original: *Præcipitatio*; the process of a solid settling out of a liquid solution.</note> or falling-down.<-
->2. <term>Fumigation</term> <note>original: *Fumigatio*; treatment with smoke or vapors.<-
->3. <term>Stratification</term> <note>original: *Stratificatio*; arranging materials in alternating layers.<-
->4. <term>Amalgamation</term> <note>original: *Amalgamatio*; the process of softening or dissolving a metal, usually with mercury.<-

### Precipitation or falling-down, is a calcination by strong waters.

It is called "falling-down" <note>original: *Niederschlag*.</note> because the metal, having been dissolved with <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>original: *Scheide-Wasser*; literally "parting water," usually nitric acid used to separate silver from gold.</note> or another strong water, is struck down to the bottom with warm, pure water. For when this happens, the <term>pores</term> <note>In 17th-century chemistry, it was believed that liquids contained "pores" or tiny holes that held dissolved particles; adding water "widened" these pores, making them unable to hold the heavy metal.</note> of the aqua fortis are widened and thus, as it were, forced to strike the dissolved metal to the floor because of its weight. Therefore, this is called precipitation.

Its arrangement and preparation is as follows: The matter which one wishes to calcinate in this way is commonly a metal or something of stone; this is then filed as seen fit, or beaten into thin and subtle plates or small sheets, so that it furthers and eases the work, as the materials prepared in this way are all the sooner attacked by the strong waters. Upon the filed or plated matter, enough aqua fortis is then poured so that it rises 3 or 4 finger-breadths above it; there it immediately begins to work and does not stop until it has entirely completed the task and dissolved the matter as far as it is able. If, however, it takes too long, or one fears that the water is too weak, it is customary to set the glass containing the water and matter into warm ashes, where it is then set into motion by the external heat of the potential fire, so that it [performs] its work...

Furthermore, the practitioner must rightly know for what purpose he seeks a calx; for a different water is necessary if one wishes to use the calx for the medicine of the human body, and another if one desires and seeks such a calx for the **transmutation** of metals.

## Of Fumigation.

Fumigation and the other type of **calcination** <note>original: *Calcination*; the process of reducing a metal to a fine powder or oxide, either through heat or chemical corrosion.</note> is either moist or dry.

When the fumigation is performed with a moist vapor, the process is as follows:

Thin sheets are beaten from a metal from which one desires a **calx** <note>The powder resulting from calcination.</note> or **saffron** <note>original: *Crocum*; in alchemy, a "crocus" refers to a metal oxide, usually red or yellow, resembling the color of the saffron flower.</note>. Holes are made through these so they can be hung. Now one takes a pot or glass with a wide mouth and fills it mostly with distilled vinegar or another such liquid serving the purpose. Hang the plates inside, yet in such a way that the plates do not touch the liquid but are instead a short distance from it. Cover the vessel and then place it in warm ashes or **horse manure** <note>Used as a consistent, gentle heat source in early laboratories.</note>, so that the rising vapor may creep into the body <note>The metal.</note> and attack it. Let it stand until it has attacked the body from the outside and extracted a calx or saffron, which is then scraped off; this is repeated until one has enough of the collected matter.

### To this calcination, one can also add quenching and soaking.
### The Quenching.

The quenching is: when one makes a metal glowing hot and plunges it into a strong vinegar, a lye made of herbs, urine, or the like...

## Soaking or Moistening.

The soaking or moistening of metals occurs when one sprinkles a metal with **nitric acid** <note>original: *Scheid-Wasser*; literally "parting-water," so called because it was used to separate gold from silver.</note> or another "strong water," or pours a broth of all kinds of herbs over it and then sets it out in the air until it has been corroded and gnawed away. Then, such a calx is **edulcorated** <note>original: *ausgesüsset*; the process of washing a chemical precipitate with fresh water until it is free of all corrosive salts or acids.</note> or washed with fresh water until everything corrosive leaves it.

### Soaking of Plant Matters.
### For Medicines.

1. The **liquid** <note>original: *Feuchtigkeit*; literally "moisture," referring here to the solvent used for soaking.</note> in which the **plant matters** <note>original: *Vegetabilia*.</note> are soaked;
2. The **quality** of the same—namely, whether the liquid must be cold or warm?
3. The **quantity**: how much liquid is required for the soaking of each herb or root?
4. Also, the **time** must be taken into account: at what time or for how long must each thing soak?

### Fruits and Roots That Are to Be Preserved.

For the soaking of fruits and roots that are to be **preserved** <note>original: *condirt*; from the Latin *condire*, meaning to pickle or preserve in sugar or syrup.</note> or candied in sugar, one takes warm water and a good quantity of it, letting the things lie in it until they have drawn in enough moisture, and then they are cooked as is customary.

## Concerning Fumigation.

**Fumigation** <note>original: *Räucherung*; the process of exposing a substance to vapors to change its chemical state or create a surface oxide.</note> and other types of **calcination** <note>The process of reducing a substance to a fine powder or oxide, usually through heat or corrosion.</note> are either moist or dry.

If the fumigation is performed with a moist vapor, the process is as follows:

Thin sheets are beaten from a metal from which one desires a **calx** <note>The powdery metallic oxide.</note> or **crocus** <note>original: *Crocum*; a term used by early chemists for a deep-colored—often reddish—metallic powder, named for its resemblance to saffron (*Crocus sativus*).</note>; holes are made through these so that they can be hung up. Now, one takes a pot or glass with a wide mouth and fills it mostly with distilled vinegar or another liquid suitable for the purpose. The sheets are hung inside, but in such a way that they do not touch the liquid but are still somewhat removed from it. The vessel is covered and then placed in warm ashes or horse manure <note>Rotting horse manure was used in early laboratories as a source of gentle, steady, and long-lasting heat.</note> so that the rising vapor may creep into the **body** <note>original: *Corpus*; the physical structure of the metal.</note> and attack it. It is left there until it has attacked the body from the outside and drawn out a calx or crocus, which is then scraped off; this is repeated until one has enough of the collected material.

## The Dried Flowers, Herbs, Roots, Seeds, and Fruits that are to be Boiled.

These are soaked in a large amount of warm or cold liquid <note>original: *Feuchtigkeit*; literally "moisture," referring here to the solvent or water used for extraction.</note>, though the amount of time they are left depends on whether there is much or little of the material, until they are thoroughly saturated with the liquid so that they can afterwards be boiled all the better.

### The Seeds from which one wishes to obtain a Mucilage.

The seeds from which one desires to extract a <term>mucilage</term> <note>original: *Mucilaginem*; a thick, gluey substance produced by most plants, often used as a binder or soothing agent.</note> or slime must be soaked overnight.

### Roses and Violets.

On the evening before, one places the roses, violets, and similar flowers in very hot water and lets them lie there until morning. One then presses them out; in the expressed or remaining water, one can then soak other fresh materials. This soaking of the first material is often repeated, and then the <term>Rose-Honey</term> <note>original: *Rosen-Honig* or *Mel Rosatum*; a medicinal honey infused with rose petals used for sore throats or as a mild cleanser.</note>, the <term>Laxative Rose Syrup</term>, the simple <term>Violet Syrup</term>, and the <term>Laxative Violet Syrup</term> are made from it.

The <term>purgative medicines</term> <note>Medicines intended to cleanse the bowels; laxatives.</note> are soaked in various juices and waters, along with various other medicines, in order to remove their harmful properties <note>Early modern pharmacists believed that soaking harsh laxatives like senna or hellebore could "correct" their violent effects.</note>.

I must also mention here the soaking in which no dissolution <note>original: *Zerlassung*; the process of a solid melting or fully dissolving into a liquid.</note> occurs.

When the <term>substance</term> <note>original: *Corpus*; the physical "body" of the material being processed, such as a mineral or metal.</note> is too hard and cannot be forced by any of the above methods, or when time does not permit such a long <term>preparation</term>, it is then customary only to dip the filed substance into water and let it soak and lie there until it is eaten away like <term>clay</term> <note>original: *Letten*; a type of fatty clay or loam. The text suggests the metal becomes soft and crumbly.</note>. When the water has been gradually drawn off, the substance is dried, rubbed down, and <term>sweetened</term> <note>The process of "edulcoration," or washing a substance with water to remove any remaining corrosive salts or acids.</note> with water.

In this way, metals can also be reduced to a powder by rubbing them with salt, using the dry vapor of <term>Saturn</term> <note>The alchemical name for Lead.</note> or <term>Mercury</term> <note>The alchemical name for Quicksilver.</note>, which makes them brittle with their natural breath. Just as Mercury <term>calcines</term> <note>The process of reducing a metal to a powder (oxide) through heat or chemical action.</note> Saturn, so too does Saturn calcine Mercury.

For example: One places cast lead or warm <term>mercury</term> <note>original: *Mercurium*; also known as quicksilver.</note> into a pot with a long neck and sets it over a gentle fire. When one then places gold or silver sheets upon it, the rising vapor creeps into the "body" <note>In alchemy, the "body" (*corpus*) refers to the solid physical form of a metal.</note> and makes it brittle. This material is then rubbed with salt on a marble stone until it becomes a <term>calx</term> <note>original: *Kalck*; a powder produced by heating or chemically treating a metal.</note> or powder, and the calx or powder is then "sweetened" <note>The process of "sweetening" (*aussüssen*) involves rinsing a substance with pure water to wash away salts or corrosive agents.</note> with clean water. This, then, is a **dry calcination**.

### Stratification.
## Layering.

This, indeed, one cannot call a true calcination, yet <term>Libavius</term> <note>Andreas Libavius (c. 1555–1616), a German physician and chemist famous for writing one of the first systematic chemistry textbooks.</note>, as well as others, includes it alongside "plastering"; even though both operations do not technically constitute a calcination on their own, they are nonetheless often used to assist and promote the process! This is especially true of **layering**—namely, when layers of salts or other similar substances are mixed with the sheets or even the powders of metals. After this layering, the prepared material is placed in a calcining fire, for the salts penetrate the body with their corrosive properties and promote the calcination; sometimes, they are even worked together into a single substance.

### Plastering.

<term>Plastering</term> <note>original: *Einpflaſtrung*; likely referring to "cementation," a process where a metal is encased in a reactive paste and heated.</note> has another use beyond calcination: namely, that goldsmiths use it to separate gold from gilded silver vessels. For example: they coat the gilded vessel with a "plaster" of corrosive materials and let it sit for a time. They then wash it off with water, which takes the gold away with it, which is then further "sweetened" with water.

### Amalgamation.
## Etching Through.

**Amalgamation** is an operation used by both alchemists and goldsmiths. It is essentially a calcination of metals, whereby they are reduced into a calx or the finest possible powder.

**Amalgam** is metal struck together and prepared with <term>mercury</term> <note>original: *Mercurio*; also known as quicksilver.</note>, so that it can be spread like butter in the palm of the hand.

The purpose and use of amalgamation in **Alchemy** is varied; we shall mention only a few things from many. Thus:

1. Through this, the artist takes all that does not belong to it, such as gold and silver. <note>Amalgamation was a primary method for extracting precious metals from impurities or ore.</note>

2. It serves for the precipitation of gold with mercury in the **Golden Turpeth**. <note>original: *turpeto Aureo*; a yellow chemical compound, often basic mercuric sulfate, used in both medicine and metallurgy.</note>

3. It is of much use in gold and silver and in almost all operations occurring in <term>Saturn</term> <note>Alchemical name for Lead.</note> and <term>Jupiter</term> <note>original: *Jove*; Alchemical name for Tin.</note>, especially when one wishes to make an **oil** from them; other metals are not amalgamated because they have a completely different and foreign nature than mercury.

4. Amalgamation is used by gold-workers in the following manner:

Some place mercury in a glowing crucible, and when it begins to smoke, they add filed or leafed silver to it and stir it **well** with a stick until it is well incorporated together; then the amalgam is quickly poured into fresh, clean water and thus quenched and washed until all the blackness has gone from it, which it received from the burnt wood with which it was stirred.

Then, if one only desires a bare <term>calx</term> <note>A fine powder produced by heating or chemically treating a metal.</note>, one separates the mercury through a leather; but the ball that remains in the leather is placed back into a crucible in the fire until the mercury evaporates there, and then the calx is **sweetened** <note>original: *ausgeſüßt*; rinsed with water to remove salts or impurities.</note> or washed with fresh water. However, the fire must not be too strong, so that the metal does not melt.

But if one wants a very subtle powder, the amalgam is first rubbed with salt on a marble stone; after that, one allows the mercury to evaporate and sweetens the powder or the calx.

Since the preceding has sufficiently shown how the dissolution of the **compact body** happens, or in what way the solid essence of the body can be dissolved; so follows in order and of necessity **Separation**. For in all chemical and alchemical works, as well as in the preparation of such medicines, one can achieve nothing useful if one does not follow nature. Nature, however, performs a separation after putrefaction, when she separates the impure from the pure, which certainly gives a lover of chemistry occasion for greater and higher things, when he [observes] these lesser works...

## On Separation or Abstraction

Separation is an operation wherein the parts of a dissolved and decomposed body are laid apart and divided from one another.

This is of two kinds:

1. Superficial separation. And
2. Essential separation.

Superficial separation is that which distributes the pieces of a body that has been completely opened yet remains homogeneous <note>original: *gleich-artig*; meaning the chemical nature of the parts has not yet changed, only their physical arrangement.</note>, merely dividing them from one another without any internal or essential penetration.

This has to do with three methods:

### 1. Either with the separation of the dry from the dry.
### 2. The moist from the moist.
### 3. Or the moist from the dry.

When the separation of the dry from the dry occurs, it serves for pulverization and smoothing; it is called <term>Cribratio</term> <note>original: *Reiterung*; the process of sifting or sieving through a mesh.</note>. It is also called "removal" when we desire an even more subtle separation, such as in the <term>preparation</term> <note>original: *Præparation*.</note> of amber <note>original: *Agstein*; a historical term for amber, often used in medicinal and alchemical recipes.</note>, pearls, corals, and the like. This separation is also useful during calcination <note>original: *Räucherung*; literally "smoking," here referring to the heating of substances until they turn to powder.</note>, namely so that it gently divides the adhering lime <note>original: *Kalck*; refers to the "calx" or powdery metallic oxide left after heating.</note>, as in sugar of lead <note>Lead acetate, a sweet-tasting but toxic white crystalline substance.</note>. This is called "wiping away," and is performed with a feather or a rabbit’s foot. Alternatively, it is used to remove tough, clinging lime, which is then called "rinsing," as with copper-calx. It also serves for amalgamation, specifically so that the superfluous <term>mercury</term> <note>original: *Mercurius*; quicksilver.</note> may be separated from the calcined metal; this is called "pressing out" <note>Usually involves squeezing the amalgam through a chamois cloth to recover liquid mercury.</note>.

## Separation of the Moist from the Moist

When the separation of the moist from the moist occurs, they are either of one nature, or—

When the materials to be separated are of the same nature, they either become moist of their own accord through nature, or they are made moist by the art <note>original: *Kunst*; here referring to the practice of chemistry or pharmacy</note>.

When they are moist by nature, such as: syrups, <term>juleps</term> <note>original: *Julepe*; sweet medicinal drinks usually made with sugar and flavored waters</note>, and the like, one mixes them with well-beaten egg whites and simply strains them through without pressing.

However, if they are made moist by the art, such as <term>gums</term> <note>original: *Gummata*; resinous or gummy plant exudates</note> and fatty substances, they are strained through with strong pressing.

But when the liquids are of a different kind, such as oil and water: then for the separation of the oil from the water or spirit, distillation or evaporation <note>original: *Abrauchung*; the process of heating a liquid so the more volatile parts "smoke" away</note> sometimes serves. Or, one may scoop out the water with a glass that one calls an <term>attractorium</term> <note>original: *Attractorium*; a suction tube or pipette</note> or a suction-glass, and this is especially used with heavy oils where the water floats on top: such as cinnamon oil. Or finally, if one wants the pure, clear, and thin part separated from the thick, one is also accustomed to filtering the oil with a fine cloth.

## Separation of the Moist from the Dry.

When there is a separation of the moist from the dry (as occurs in the spirits of tinctures or the separation of oil from the thick dregs), it is the separation from the gum or some other things. If it is from gum, then a simple decanting <note>original: *Abgiessung*; the act of pouring off the top liquid layer</note> is made by tilting the vessel after the sediment has settled, and the tincture is separated from the thick material at the bottom. The latter allows no other method, for the tincture of a gum cannot be strained or filtered <note>because gums often clog the pores of a filter or cloth</note>.

If it is other things, then the separation happens through decanting, straining, pressing, or through filtering, according as the circumstances of the matter and material require.

Among all these separations, however, none is capable of drawing off spirits except distillation. And all of these are only superficial separations; such as:
->Sifting.<-
->Rinsing.<-
->Wiping.<-

## Rinsing

## Filtering

Filtering is a distillation through a chemical <term>filter</term> <note>original: *Filtrum*; in early modern laboratory practice, filtering was often classified as a form of "cold distillation" because the liquid "travels" through the medium</note>; and it is made of woolen cloth, linen, and paper.

## On Essential Separation

An essential separation <note>original: *Bestandwesentliche Scheidung*; a separation of the "essential" components or chemical constituents, as opposed to mere mechanical sorting</note> is one that not only divides the substance—that is, all parts into their homogeneous pieces—but also takes away and sets aside the impurities and the contrary natures dispersed throughout the entire substance. Thus, the essential separation is a chemical operation that not only removes external and obvious uncleanness, but also separates the hidden impurities spread throughout the entire <term>body</term> <note>original: *Corpus*; the physical matter or substance being treated</note>. Furthermore, it separates the homogeneous parts from those of a different nature, such as: the spirit <note>original: *Spiritum*; the volatile, active principle of a substance</note> from the <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: *Phlegmate*; the watery, tasteless, and inactive part of a distillate</note>, the oil from the spirit, the water from both, and then finally the essence from the salty earths.

And there are two kinds, the first of which is the essence, or that same pure substance which we have separated from the impure and desire to extract from the <term>caput mortuum</term> <note>literally "dead head"; the useless solid residue remaining after distillation or sublimation</note>. ## On Distillation.

Distillation is an operation by which all moisture of a body is separated from it in the form of a vapor or steam; this is afterwards turned into a liquid by the surrounding cold and is collected by the receiver <note>original: *Vorlage*; the vessel placed at the end of a still to catch the distillate</note>.

Thus, only moist bodies—those which have such moisture by nature, or actually, or potentially, and those which are moistened through the Art <note>Alchemical practice is frequently referred to simply as "the Art"</note>—can be distilled.

Meanwhile, distillation is of such great use that it is beneficial to almost all other operations, such as preparing the <term>menstrua</term> <note>original: *Menstrua*; solvents used to dissolve solids</note> and separating them again from the essences. Indeed, distillation seems to have been invented primarily for this reason: so that the essences may be elevated and made more subtle and penetrating, they must be distilled. However, because not all materials allow themselves to be separated in the same way, laboratory workers have invented three ways to distill. Namely:
->1. Distillation upwards (ascending).<-
->2. Downwards (descending).<-
->3. And sideways.<-

Distilling upwards is: when the moisture is driven out of the body by heat from below, so that it must rise in an airy form up into the helm <note>The "helm" or alembic is the cap of the still where vapors collect</note>, where it then congeals together and drips off through the beak. This is commonly called distillation by <term>Mary’s Bath</term> <note>original: *Balneum Mariæ*; a water bath used for gentle heating</note>, by dew-bath, by ashes <note>original: *per Cineres*</note>, or by sand <note>original: *per Arenam*</note>.

To this type of distillation may also be added distillation by the bell <note>original: *per Campanam*; using a bell-shaped glass cover</note>, by which among other things the so-called oil of sulfur is prepared; and distillation by the pan <note>original: *per patinam*</note>, which is used at the same time for the fragrant—

As the cloth captures the rising vapors, it allows them to fall drop by drop through the fabric into the oil placed below. This distillation also occurs downwards if one turns the vessel over.

## Distilling Downwards.

This occurs when, through the power of the heat placed above, the moisture is forced to fall downwards. This is used for those substances and materials that cannot withstand rising heat, but would instead be ruined by it; their strong <term>spirits</term> <note>original: *Spiritus*; the volatile essences or active chemical principles of a substance</note> would vanish if they rose through excessive heat.

## Sideways Distillation.

Sideways distillation is when the process is performed with a vessel laid on its side. And because this is commonly done with a <term>retort</term> <note>a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids</note>, this distillation is also called <term>distillatio per retortam</term> <note>Latin: "distillation by retort"</note>. It is primarily used for <term>mercurials</term> <note>substances containing or derived from mercury</note> and certain earth-growths <note>original: *Erdgewächse*; a term often used for minerals, ores, or plants found in the soil</note> that cannot easily be driven upwards. Like the previous methods, this distillation is performed with both moist and dry heat.

Finally, in all distilling, it must be noted that one must not let the fire go out. For if something interrupts the work, nothing more will rise over; or if it does, there is a great loss involved. For even if the heat is not powerful enough to lift the vapor into the <term>helm</term> <note>original: *Helm*; the cap or top part of a still where vapors collect</note>, it still consumes the moisture by drying it out. Furthermore, if the materials melt and liquefy during the operation, they will—after cooling—cling so firmly together and collapse upon themselves that they can hardly, or not at all, undergo separation without being <term>pulverized</term> <note>original: *Pulverisirung*; the process of grinding a solid back into a fine powder</note> again.

## On Rectification.

Rectification is nothing other than a repeated distillation in order to complete and perfect a work. It is only used for <term>liquors</term> <note>original: *Liquoribus*; liquid substances or solutions</note> (although repeated <term>sublimation</term> <note>the process of heating a solid to a gas and then back to a solid to purify it</note> cannot be called a rectification...

## Concerning Sublimation.

Sublimation is an operation in which the <term>body</term> <note>original: *Corpus*; the solid physical matter being worked upon</note> is driven upward in the form of a vapor by the power of the fire, where it then solidifies through the surrounding cold; it is named for the nature of the operation and is the opposite of <term>precipitation</term> <note>original: *Præcipitation*; the process where a substance settles out of a solution to the bottom</note>.

Two things are required for sublimation:

->1.<-

That the body must be ground upon a marble slab with another heavy material that can hold it back, so that it does not escape the fire too quickly before a proper and pure separation has occurred, and so that [this material] retains the dregs or the impurity of the body according to their natural affinity.

Or that [the heavy material], through its sharpness, promotes the transformation, decomposition, and finally the separation of the body, without impressing any foreign properties upon the body to be sublimated.

->2.<-

It is required that all moisture be previously removed with a gentle fire, especially if it is a substance containing excessive moisture (as with the sublimation of sulfur, salt, and <term>vitriol</term> <note>a historical name for sulfate minerals, often used as a starting material in alchemical processes</note>, where the phlegm must be drawn off); otherwise, it would not be a proper distillation, or it would at least be somewhat impure.

Now, sublimation may involve only one substance to be sublimated, or several materials together.

...tion. If there is only one material, the objective is twofold:
1. Only the cleansing of the **body** <note>original: *Cörper*; the solid matter</note> is sought, so that the body becomes pure, as in the sublimation of **sal ammoniac** <note>original: *Salmiac*; ammonium chloride, often used as a flux or cleaning agent in alchemy</note>.
2. Or, along with the cleaning, the transformation of the body into another form is required, which then necessitates more operation than the sublimation of **mercury** <note>original: *Mercurii*</note>.

If there is more than one material, then an **incorporation** into a stable substance is required, so that a sublimated compound results from it, creating a new medicine, as with **cinnabar** <note>original: *Zinober*; mercury sulfide, valued for its bright red color and medicinal properties</note>.

Or, the extraction of an **essence** is required, and then the new body that is sublimated serves only as a **conductor** <note>original: *Leitung*; a medium that carries or "leads" another substance upward</note> for the other, through which the perfected work is again drawn off. Such a body, which is here called a "lead" or "conducting-work," is commonly sal ammoniac, as in the extraction of the **tincture** from **gold calx** <note>original: *Gold-Kalck*; gold that has been reduced to a fine powder through heating or chemical action</note> with the **flying eagle** <note>original: *fliegenden Adler*; an alchemical code name for sal ammoniac when it is used to volatilize or "lift" other substances</note>.

It should be noted here that in these last two types of sublimation, no additional additive is required except for those bodies that are to be sublimated, unlike in the previous types, which retain the **dregs** <note>original: *Fæces*; the impure residue left behind</note> within themselves.

Sublimation is of two kinds:

One, where the sublimate is separated by a considerable distance from the **dead head** <note>original: *Capite mortuo*; the worthless chemical residue remaining after distillation or sublimation</note>; this pertains to dry things and minerals; although **Libavius** <note>Andreas Libavius (c. 1555–1616), a famous German chemist and physician known for his work "Alchemia"</note> describes a completely different distillation of water, which is actually nothing other than a pure **rectification** or **circulation**; however, it is best to distill water rather than to sublimate it.

### Preparation for sublimating.

When one wishes to sublimate, one should thoroughly pound together that which is to be sublimated with its proper material that retains the dregs, or with the lime whose tincture is desired; **incorporate** it with one another upon a **marble stone** <note>a flat slab used for grinding materials to extreme fineness</note>, place it in a distilling pot or glass, and after evaporating the wateriness over a gentle fire, place a cover or **alembic** <note>the "helmet" or cap of a distilling apparatus</note> upon it. Manage the fire **degree by degree** <note>gradually increasing the temperature</note> until everything has risen upward. After that, let it cool down gradually by itself; then, if necessary, pound or rub the removed sublimate again to the finest degree and distill it with fresh material that separates and retains the dregs; and repeat this until the sublimate is perfectly purified.

Another type of **sublimation** is when the sublimate only rises to the top of the glass and remains clinging to it. This is then more of an **efflorescence** <note>original: *Aufblühung*; a flowering or crystalline growth appearing on the surface</note>; in this kind of sublimation, the laboratory workers are accustomed to adding substances that promote the sublimation.

## On Extraction.

**Extraction** is the drawing out of the **essence** <note>the vital, active principle or "soul" of a substance</note> by means of a **menstruum** <note>original: *Menstruum*; a solvent used to dissolve or extract specific parts of a material</note> from a **body** <note>physical matter</note>. From this, a **tincture** arises; then, once the menstruum is removed—either through evaporation or the distillation of the body—the essence remains at the bottom, and it is then called an **extract**.

The menstruum is either a substance created alongside the body, or one brought to it, or something that comes to the body from the outside.

If it is co-created, it serves for fresh herbs, whose juice, squeezed out by a press, carries the essence of the herb along with it;

If the menstruum is brought to it, it serves for all dry plants, the **calxes** <note>original: *Kalcken*; powders produced by roasting or chemically treating minerals</note> of minerals, and prepared things from animals.

In this work, the appropriate menstruum must be chosen for each specific body.

The extract also takes on either a liquid form—and is then simply called a tincture—or it takes on a stable and solid consistency, according to the judgment of the laboratory worker or the physician who prescribes it; and it is then specifically called an **extract**, an **inspissated juice** <note>original: *inspisirter Safft*; a juice thickened or concentrated by boiling or evaporation</note>, or a tincture.

Thus, general extraction occurs **by ascent** <note>original: *per Ascensum*; rising as vapor</note>, **by descent** <note>original: *descensum*; flowing downward</note>, and **by means of an intermediary** <note>original: *Extractione ratione intermedii*; using a third substance to facilitate the process</note>.

Extraction gives the chemist much trouble, so that he may diligently separate the **formal virtue and power** <note>the essential properties and medicinal strength of a substance</note> from its own **matter or dregs** <note>original: *Materia oder Fecibus*; the useless physical waste left after the power has been removed</note>. This is because the most powerful effect comes from that which is extracted and drawn out once the bond has been dissolved by a suitable menstruum—the bond that keeps the material mass united with that same essence. This essence is the most secret and innermost substance, which is covered and hidden by nature in its very **center or midpoint** <note>the core or "heart" of the substance</note>, so that it does not easily suffer hindrance from accidents or external violence.

## On Expression.

The **expression** <note>original: *Ausdruckung*; the process of pressing or squeezing out liquids from a substance</note> mentioned here is a very different kind than that shown in the previously mentioned separation.

This [process], however, separates it from all parts of the body, both internal and external, and leaves the **dead body** <note>original: *Corpus mortuum*; a common alchemical term for the exhausted, lifeless remains of a substance after its essence or "soul" has been extracted</note> behind.

### One.

That the juices of the herbs are drawn out through squeezing and then serve, as mentioned, for **extraction**.

### The other.

Is for the drawing off of **oils**, namely when the oils are squeezed out of the seeds and grains by a press.

This concerns those operations that separate and remove impurities and foreign matter from the remaining pure essence. These consist of the following.

## On Digestion.

**Digestion**, or gentle stewing or cooking, is a process by which matter is cooked using a heat that matches natural heat. Just as the stomach consumes and cooks food with a moderate and constant heat, transforming and converting it into **chyle** <note>original: *Speise-Safft*; the milky fluid produced during the digestion of food</note>, so that once the **waste** <note>original: *Excrementa*</note> or impurities are separated and cast into the intestines, the purest and most refined substances can be sent to the liver.

Thus, **chemical digestion** also separates the subtle and fine parts from the coarser ones by means of moderate heat, making the coarse [parts]...

One takes the matter one wishes to digest and places it into a glass vessel, which is sealed very well and tightly, and places it in a warm location for as long as that which is being digested requires; (of which time one cannot actually give a fixed rule) then the coarse parts separate from the subtle ones, and the former settle to the bottom, while the latter—wherein the best power resides—are poured off; but that which is harmful separates itself or is improved.

### On Evaporation <note>original: *De Evaporatione*</note>

Evaporation is a separation in which that which is moist disperses into the air or as a vapor.

This is useful for truly moist things, such as: for extractions and watery oils, although it is occasionally also useful in **sublimation** <note>the process of heating a substance until it becomes a vapor and then solidifies again</note>, namely when the material to be sublimated contains some moisture within it.

The procedure for evaporation is as follows: The <term>menstruum</term> that is to be evaporated from the extracts—such as **tinctures**—should be allowed to evaporate to the consistency of honey or a pill, or any other consistency according to the chemist's judgment (which they call an "extract"). If it is carried out with a violent fire when it contains strong and subtle spirits, a lid pierced with several holes is placed upon it, so that the vapor has air to escape through, so that the <term>species</term> <note>here referring to the volatile essential components or medicinal particles</note> do not fly away at the same time. However, it is more advisable to distill such things with a gentle fire, because they suffer less danger or damage thereby.

Thus, one also prefers to undertake a **distillation** instead of this if the <term>menstruum</term> is expensive and worth saving.

However, in the event that the <term>menstruum</term> is only water, it is much better to let it evaporate: because water does not rise without a particularly strong fire, which often causes the extract to burn and be ruined.

### On Exhalation or Vaporization

Exhalation or vaporization is slightly different from evaporation; namely, in that the latter applies to moist things, but the former to dry things.

Exhalation is therefore the separation of a spirit or dry substance into the air, dispersed as vapor by means of heat.

Its procedure is this: One pulverizes the material, if possible, and lets it vaporize in a crucible or other suitable vessel over a fire built beneath it; for the most part, this requires constant stirring with a piece of wood or iron so that it does not burn;
