## On Coagulation or Solidification.

Coagulation <note>original: *Coaguliren*</note> is one of the most distinguished operations in chemistry, by which those things that were too soft and flowing are made thick and hard; this is achieved by the removal and consumption of the moisture contained within them.

Thus, coagulation is the transition of a body from a thin and liquid state into a solid and thick matter, regardless of whether it was previously broken down through aqueous, airy, or fiery dissolution <note>the process of "opening" or dissolving a substance into its components</note>.

Therefore, evaporation, vaporization, distillation, and sublimation are also used for coagulation, if one understands the term in its broader sense.

### Coagulation is performed in two ways.

One occurs through separation; the other, however, occurs without any separation, which is then called "total coagulation" or "coagulation of the whole," and its true purpose relates to the generation <note>original: *Erzeigung*; refers to the manifestation or formation of a new state of matter</note>.

### Coagulation through Separation.

Coagulation through separation occurs when that which made the body liquid is removed, thereby returning the body to its previous consistency.

From this, it can be seen that coagulation follows dissolution <note>original: *Zerlassung*</note>; this may occur in a <term>menstruum</term> <note>a solvent used to extract or dissolve substances</note>, such as in mercury <note>original: *Mercurio*</note>, or without a <term>menstruum</term>, such as in a salt-flux.

This coagulation has a particular use in the purification of bodies, as they shed all impurity through frequent dissolution and repeated coagulation.

One type of coagulation is established, as already mentioned, through the removal of moisture, as happens during the evaporation of extracts and sometimes of salts—though in such cases it is rarely and not properly called "coagulation."

The other occurs through the separation of the internal moisture; or in whatever way they [proceed] toward coagulation by themselves without further evaporation...

## Description of Cementation.

Cementation is a dry corrosion <note>the term "corrosion" here refers to the chemical breakdown of impurities</note> and purification of metallic bodies, which are layered with a <term>cement<gloss>in alchemy, a powdered mixture used to refine metals through heat</gloss></term>. Namely, one takes a crucible, places a layer of the cement on its bottom, and places a layer of metallic sheets upon it, continuing in this way to make **layer upon layer** <note>original: *stratum super stratum*</note> until the crucible is full. Afterward, one seals the crucible well with <term>luting<gloss>a clay or sealant used to make vessels airtight</gloss></term>; however, in the middle of it, one leaves a small air-hole (depending on the nature of the cement). Then, the crucible is placed under a chimney and given a circular fire <note>a fire that surrounds the vessel to provide even heat</note> according to the required degrees, until it is sufficiently "cemented" according to the artist's intent. When the vessel has cooled, the cement is separated from the metal, and it is then found that the metallic sheets have been purified.

The cement consists mostly of sharp, corrosive salts or other drying substances, and it is either used as a dry powder or moistened with urine, vinegar, <term>aqua fortis<gloss>original: "Scheide-Wasser"; nitric acid used to separate metals</gloss></term>, or other strong liquids.

Cementation is also a method for the corrosion of all sorts of imperfect metals, and besides their purification, it may also serve as an assay or test. Although the latter is properly called <term>cupellation<gloss>original: "Capelliren"; a refining process where ores are treated under high heat to separate noble metals</gloss></term> or refining, because it is done with lead; and since this is unknown to most, or at least many, I will also mention it here at the same time.

## Cupellation or Refining.

This process applies only to gold or silver and takes place in the following manner:

One takes the ashes of horns or animal bones—especially the bones of sheep—and <term>calcines<gloss>burns to a fine white powder</gloss></term> them. Or, if these are not available, one may take well-leached willow or beech ash and let it evaporate thoroughly. From any of these things, either alone or stirred together, one makes a soft mass like a dough, presses or puts it into the mold for the <term>cupel<gloss>original: "Capell"; a shallow, porous vessel used in assaying</gloss></term> and shapes it, then lets it dry in order to use it. If one has no molds, one takes a small round bowl or crucible, makes a hole in the bottom, and fills it with the aforementioned ash, which one [makes] into a soft...

...made into a soft dough and press it down gently; in the center, make a small round cavity with a spoon to carry the metal into it and to perform <term>cupellation<gloss>original: *capelliren*; a refining process where ores are treated under high heat to separate noble metals from base metals</gloss></term> or refining <note>original: *abtreiben*, literally "to drive off," referring to the oxidation and removal of base metals</note> in the following manner.

One takes the <term>cupel<gloss>original: *Capelle*; a shallow, porous cup usually made of bone ash</gloss></term>, which must be very dry, and places it in the middle of a furnace prepared for this purpose. Place glowing coals beneath it, then cover it well and put coals on top as well, letting it burn until the cupel is standing in full fire. Afterward, for one part of the metal that is to be cupelled, take 3 to 4 parts of lead—which must have been well-purified beforehand—and put one part of the lead into the cupel while it sits entirely in the fire. When it has melted, add the metal to it, but first let it warm up a little with a pair of tongs. Then, when the lead begins to "go off" <note>this refers to the lead oxidizing and being absorbed by the porous cupel</note>, one should add the rest of the lead in 2 or 3 portions (likewise slightly warmed). When all the lead is consumed, the work is accomplished; this can be recognized and known in two ways:

->**1.**<-

->When one no longer sees any movement in the cupellation;<-

->**2.**<-

When the gold or silver remains clean and pure in the middle of the cupel in a dry lump, which one can see rising up shortly after like flowers <note>this likely refers to "sprouting" or "vegetation," a phenomenon where oxygen escapes the cooling metal, creating a textured surface</note>, which comes from the purity of the metal. When one sees this, remove the fire, take the metal out with tongs, and quench it in cold water; thus, you will see that you have made your gold or silver entirely pure.

In this refining process, it should be noted that the fire in the cupel must always be kept equal both below and above on the lid. The lid is made with many holes, according to a size that matches the cupel.

Regarding all the operations mentioned thus far, one must know that every process has its own destruction and separation, yet in such a way that the destruction always precedes the separation. ### On
### Generation or Production, and
### Those things pertaining to it. <note>original: *De Generatione oder der Erzeugung, und Was dieser Anhängig handeln wollen*</note>

## On Generation or Production.

When the bodies are destroyed, their parts separated, and the impurities removed from them, it is necessary to bring them to perfection so that they are naturally prepared to submit themselves to generation. Now, however, we must look to how a new body and a new medicine can be brought forth and achieved from the body thus prepared. And yet, "generation" or "production" is taken here in a broad sense, meaning the creation of a new and intended <term>medicament<gloss>original: *Medicament*; a healing or transformative substance</gloss></term> from an impure and raw body. This occurs in two ways, namely **immediately** and **mediately**.

If the generation occurs **immediately**, it is nothing other than the fruit and the purpose of the destruction and separation, so that where these cease, a generation must follow.

However, this is only a generation according to the first general description, but not the **true** one.

For true generation requires not only the separation of the body but also the preparation of the material brought from there, changing it into another form and, if necessary, mixing it with others.

Moreover, this is more properly the *matter* of a true generation rather than the generation itself, because true generation always takes its beginning from that very matter.

<summary>This page concludes the metallurgical refining process and transitions into the alchemical theory of "Generation," defining it as the process of creating a new "medicine" or "body" from purified materials.</summary>

Although the intended production is of the nature of a <term>medicine<gloss>original: *Medicament*; a refined substance with transformative or healing powers</gloss></term>, which physicians use in a single form without further preparation, the remedy brought forth in this way is still too coarse and not yet sufficiently prepared to deserve or represent the status of a true <term>generation<gloss>original: *Erzeugung*; the alchemical process of "birthing" a new, perfected substance</gloss></term>. This is because it cannot yet provide a proper and complete benefit, and furthermore, it cannot be preserved for a long duration. Thus, such remedies, without further preparation, are not yet to be considered complete medicines. Therefore, it is easy to understand that these incomplete medicines must be followed by a true generation and further operations to make them perfect.

Next, we must consider how such a medicine is elevated and in what manner it may be brought to the most perfect advantage within its degree.

However, because a perfect medicine results after several means are used between true destruction and generation, it is then properly called a true generation. This is primarily dealt with and described (as it requires no further instruction):

### The introduction of a new form or quality into a prepared matter, along with the elevation of its power.

Since a new form or property cannot be brought into a matter—even if it is pure—without <term>alteration<gloss>original: *Alteration*; a fundamental change in the state or nature of a substance</gloss></term>, it is necessary to know through which operations this can happen, and how these differ from <term>separation<gloss>original: *Sonderung*; the previous stage of removing impurities</gloss></term>, which achieves this to no lesser degree.

Accordingly, five operations belong to the generation and production of a new medicinal remedy. Namely:
> <term>Digestion<gloss>original: *Digestio*; the slow heating of a substance to mature or refine it</gloss></term>.
> <term>Coagulation<gloss>original: *Coagulatio*; the thickening or solidifying of a liquid into a solid state</gloss></term>.
> <term>Incarnation<gloss>original: *Incarnatio*; the process of giving a physical "body" or substantial form to a volatile spirit</gloss></term>.
> <term>Circulation<gloss>original: *Circulatio*; the continuous distillation and condensation of a liquid in a closed vessel</gloss></term>, and
> <term>Fixation<gloss>original: *Fixatio*; making a volatile substance stable under heat</gloss></term>.

Through this <term>digestion<gloss>the process of exposing a substance to gentle, continuous heat to mature it</gloss></term>, a single operation is sought:

->1.<-

### The preparation consists of the following:

If a laboratory worker seeks to remove the excessive "cold" and the power that otherwise seizes the head and makes it dull—qualities which afflict the <term>Extract of Opium<gloss>original: *Extractum Opii*</gloss></term>, the extract of <term>Henbane<gloss>original: *Bilsen-Kraut*</gloss></term>, and <term>Poppy seed<gloss>original: *Magsamen*</gloss></term>—and if he wishes to soothe or suppress the poisonous properties of the extract of <term>White Hellebore<gloss>original: *weisse Niesewurtzel*</gloss></term>, so that it not only does no harm in the body but also proves as beneficial as possible, he should proceed as follows:

He should obtain <term>cordial tinctures<gloss>original: *Tincturen von Hertz-Kräutern*; herbal extracts used to strengthen the heart and counteract toxins</gloss></term> that have the power to dampen poisons and suppress adverse qualities. He should pour these over the aforementioned extracts and seal his <term>digestion vessel<gloss>original: *Digerir-Gefäß*</gloss></term> as tightly as possible. He must then place this in a <term>digestion furnace<gloss>original: *Digerir-Ofen*; a specialized stove designed to maintain constant, gentle heat</gloss></term> for several days. Driven by the external warmth, the moisture will rise and fall, penetrating all parts so that the tincture mixes with the extract and the extract with the tincture. They must unite so thoroughly that not the slightest bit of the extract remains that does not fully taste of the tincture.

It should be noted that if the material has a strong and coarse nature, it will easily fall to the bottom. Therefore, one must take the digestion vessel out of the furnace two or three times a day and shake it diligently to mix the contents better. After this, the <term>solvent<gloss>original: *Menstruum*</gloss></term> should be gently drawn off and the material remaining at the bottom should be dried.

And so this work is also brought to an end; if only a change in the old property is desired, it provides benefit even in a case of generation that is not "true" <note>perhaps referring to an incomplete alchemical transmutation</note>, so that their imperfect property may be altered and brought to perfection.

### Concerning Coagulation. <note>original: "De Coagulatione"</note>

Coagulation is when one brings a liquid body to a solid consistency.

This happens in two ways: either by removing the moisture through distilling or evaporating, so that what was liquid is drawn away.

Or when one gradually incorporates the same moisture into the substance of the body, until everything coagulates and is "fixed" <note>becomes stable and solid</note>.

If moisture is to be drawn off, it serves—as already reported—for digestion, and one desires either the elevation of the body or the extraction of the <term>menstruum<gloss>a solvent used to dissolve or extract solids</gloss></term>. For this reason, a distillation occurs more often and more extensively than a simple evaporation <note>original: "Abrauchung"; literally "smoking off"</note>, because much <term>cohobation<gloss>the process of repeatedly redistilling a liquid back onto its solid residue to concentrate its power</gloss></term> is necessary for it. After distillation, a drying follows over a gentle ash-fire, with the vessel kept covered and closed.

For cohobation works more powerfully upon a dry body than upon a moist one.

Therefore, if the substance is an extract or a powder, it draws the menstruum into itself more eagerly. However, if the <term>calx<gloss>the powdery residue or oxide left after a metal or mineral has been roasted</gloss></term> is to be turned into an oil—which is also frequently desired, as mentioned regarding digestion—then the menstruum penetrates the body much more strongly, transforms it, and dissolves the calx. For if the moisture within the body escapes <note>is lost to the air</note>, the power of the menstruum is weakened, and the operation fails.

Finally, drying is useful to prove the perfection and completion of the body; for when it allows no further <term>coagulation<gloss>thickening or solidification</gloss></term>, it is a sign that the work is finished.

If one wishes for all the moisture to be <term>fixed<gloss>rendered stable, solid, and resistant to heat</gloss></term> without being drawn off, then it serves for <term>inceration<gloss>from the Latin "cera" for wax; the process of softening a dry substance to a waxy consistency</gloss></term> (or "waxing")—or sometimes for the preparation of certain medicines that are naturally moist and are completed through a full coagulation.

## On Incarnation <note>original: "De Incarnatione"</note> or In-fleshing.

Incarnation or "in-fleshing" <note>original: "Einfleischung"</note> is the mixing of a moist matter with a dry one through an entirely gentle and slow soaking, until it reaches the thickness of soft wax; hence it is called a "waxing" <note>original: "Einwichsung"</note>.

This is used in the same circumstances where digestion is applied; however, here this operation requires a total coagulation.

### The preparation happens thus:

The matter to be waxed must be pulverized separately on a marble stone and sprinkled with only a few drops of the <term>liquid<gloss>original: "Liquoris"</gloss></term>, then thoroughly mixed and pounded together. Then, carefully place it in a digestion vessel and coagulate it through an extremely gentle fire until the matter appears dry; at that point, one opens the vessel again—

### Concerning Circulation.
<note>original Latin: "De Circulatione"</note>
## Of Circulation.

Circulation, as mentioned regarding extraction <note>original: "Abziehung"</note>, has such an affinity with <term>digestion<gloss>the process of heating a substance slowly to refine or mature it</gloss></term> that one is often taken for the other without distinction. And yet, circulation is distinct from digestion; for digestion always requires an extraction so that either the impurities or foreign natures are separated from the matter, in which case it is a work of destruction.

Or, so that the drawn-off substances take on another form and thickening more easily upon reunion; and this is characteristic of <term>generation<gloss>original: "Erzeugung"; the alchemical process of creating or "birthing" a new substance</gloss></term>, as already reported, but <term>circulation<gloss>a process where liquid is boiled, condensed, and dripped back into itself repeatedly in a closed vessel</gloss></term> is not.

For circulation is the elevation of a pure <term>liquid<gloss>original: "Liquoris"</gloss></term> through a circulatory distillation, and deals with nothing other than: pure waters, <term>spirits<gloss>original: "Spiritibus"; the volatile, active essences of a substance</gloss></term>, and distilled oils, so that they namely reach the highest perfection and <term>subtlety<gloss>fineness or the ability to penetrate other substances</gloss></term>:

Or it deals with <term>quintessences<gloss>the most concentrated and pure medicinal essence</gloss></term> or essential <term>tinctures<gloss>liquid extracts of a substance's transformative properties</gloss></term>; and a <term>digestion<gloss>prolonged gentle heating</gloss></term> precedes this, so that it may remove all impurities that usually either settle to the bottom or float on top.

Then only after this does a circulation follow upon the pure tincture, which completes and carries it out; for in the "ascending" <note>referring to the rising of vapors during the distillation process</note>, such a strong union of the <term>solvent<gloss>original: "Menstrui"; a liquid used to extract or dissolve substances</gloss></term> with the tincture happens that their powers are no longer distinct, but rather like a new and single body, they have a single common <term>temperament<gloss>a balanced state of qualities</gloss></term>. By virtue of this, they do not act separately, but manifest as one power in the human body and achieve such subtlety that they pass through the entire human body without any hindrance.

Circulation is also used for <term>fixing<gloss>original: "figiren"; making a volatile substance stable under heat so it does not evaporate</gloss></term>, as in the circulation of the quintessence of wine in the works of <note>Gerhard Dorn (c. 1530–1584), a Belgian philosopher and famous commentator on Paracelsus</note> **Dornæus**. This is also observed in circulatory <term>sublimation<gloss>the process of heating a solid until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again</gloss></term>, in which the sublimation vessel is turned around in a circular fashion until the <term>mercury<gloss>original: "Mercurius"</gloss></term> or the <term>flowers<gloss>original: "Flores"; the fine powder or crystals produced by sublimation</gloss></term> of the metals or the intermediate minerals, such as <term>antimony<gloss>original: "Spieß-Glaß"</gloss></term> and the like, sublimate and finally fix themselves.

In circulation, it is required that one brings the body back to a natural temperament, which perhaps was lacking in the <term>preparation<gloss>original: "Præparation"</gloss></term>; or that the body be elevated and become uniform throughout. In this process, the natural heat, excited by the external heat, passes through the whole body and <term>tinctures<gloss>permeates or imbues with its essence</gloss></term> it. Therefore, distilled waters, when circulated, also last longer and can be preserved from <term>decay<gloss>original: "Fäulung"; putrefaction or rotting</gloss></term>. And tinctures become more delicate, lighter, and more penetrating through circulation.

To fix is: to make the <term>volatile<gloss>substances that evaporate or flee the fire easily</gloss></term> and fleeting substance fixed and stable. And there are two ways.

->I.<-

When one attaches something volatile to a solid body.

->2.<-

When the entire volatile body is <term>fixed<gloss>the alchemical process of making a substance stable under heat so it does not evaporate</gloss></term>, making it stable and permanent.

Both are achieved through <term>cementations<gloss>a process where a solid is packed in a powder and heated, often used to refine metals</gloss></term> using stabilizing substances.

The purpose of fixation is to ensure that the <term>animated parts<gloss>the active, "living" essences of the substance</gloss></term> are not lost due to excessive volatility, which could introduce unwanted defects; or to produce a <term>quintessence<gloss>the most concentrated and pure medicinal extract</gloss></term>, which is then completed through <term>circulation<gloss>the continuous distillation and condensation of a liquid in a closed vessel</gloss></term>.

There is another operation related to this which makes fixed substances volatile; however, it has no specific or unique name, despite being just as useful as the former.

For unless medicines are activated by our internal body heat—which can in no way happen if they remain entirely fixed and solid—they will never be able to transform or heal the body.

Therefore, many operations have been invented to break down such fixed medicines—including gold, silver, precious stones, pearls, and coral—into the smallest particles, so that they might yield more easily to our body's heat as a <term>necessary cause<gloss>original Latin: "Causæ sine qua non"; an indispensable condition</gloss></term>. How much more powerful will they be then, if they are made light and fluid?

This process of making substances volatile is carried out using operations almost identical to those mentioned above: quenching, softening, soaking, <term>sublimations<gloss>heating a substance until it vaporizes and then solidifies again to purify it</gloss></term>, extractions, and the like.

However, one must utilize various assisting means more frequently to complete this operation.

I hope, my reader, that you will not object to my venture in providing these <term>handbooks<gloss>original: "Manuductionen"; literally "hand-leadings" or introductory guides</gloss></term>, which may perhaps be familiar to you already, or even better known to you than to me. However, what is known to you, to me, and to many, is not known to everyone. # The Fifth Treatise.
## *Aurum potabile*. Or
## Drinkable Gold.

Take gold as much as you wish, and purify it by means of <term>Antimony<gloss>a metallic element used in alchemy to purify gold by removing base metals through smelting</gloss></term> in the very best way, thereafter through a <term>Royal Cement<gloss>Latin: "Cæmentum Regale"; a dry refining process where gold is heated with salts to remove silver and other impurities</gloss></term> (which is known to all practitioners and laboratory workers), then <term>amalgamate<gloss>to soften or dissolve a metal by mixing it with mercury</gloss></term> it with <term>Mercury<gloss>Latin: "Mercurio"; quicksilver</gloss></term>. Let this mercury smoke away from it entirely again; what remains, <term>calcine<gloss>to reduce a substance to a fine powder through prolonged heating</gloss></term> and bring it into the thinnest sheets, treating it with prepared salt for three days, but pour fresh salt into the crucible or your vessel in which you calcine each time.

When you have thus prepared and calcined your gold, pour three times as much <term>altered<gloss>chemically changed or transformed</gloss></term>—that is, united with its own salt and of a similar nature—<term>Spirit of Wine<gloss>Latin: "Spiritum Vini"; high-proof alcohol or ethanol</gloss></term> upon it; and put these together into a glass vessel with a long neck, closed with the <term>Hermetic Seal<gloss>an airtight glass seal made by melting the neck of the flask shut</gloss></term>, and set it in horse-manure <note>a common alchemical method for providing gentle, steady, and natural heat through fermentation</note> for at least 14 days, so that your gold may be thinned to the highest degree. 

Thereafter, set it to distill, and distill as often as necessary until, through the repeated process called <term>cohobation<gloss>the process of repeatedly pouring a distilled liquid back onto its solid residue and re-distilling it to concentrate the essence</gloss></term> by the <term>chemists<gloss>literally "separation-artists"; those skilled in chemical analysis</gloss></term>—that is, until the <term>menstruum<gloss>a solvent used to extract medicinal properties</gloss></term> is brought into a <term>body<gloss>Latin: "Corpus"; here referring to a unified state</gloss></term> (at the end, strengthen the fire)—the material all rises into the receiver, and you thus have the gold made volatile along with the silver. Once you have achieved this, you have a magnificent medicine; for it is certain: <note>original: "Aurum qui possidet potabile secretissimum habet remedium"</note> "He who possesses drinkable gold has the most secret remedy," and whoever knows how to make the <note>original: "verum solutionem auri"</note> true solution of gold without fire can, next to Divine help, accomplish much good for the benefit of human health.

The purpose of <term>fixation<gloss>the alchemical process of making a substance heat-resistant</gloss></term> is to ensure that the <note>original: "beseelte Theile"; literally "ensouled parts," referring to the vital spirits or volatile components of a substance</note> ensouled parts are not lost due to their excessive lightness, which might cause <note>original: "Zufälle"; here meaning unintended medical side effects or complications</note> accidents; or to produce a <term>quintessence<gloss>the purest, most essential extract of a substance</gloss></term>, in which case it is completed through <term>circulation<gloss>the continuous distillation and condensation of a liquid in a closed vessel</gloss></term>.

For unless medicines are excited to our [body] heat (which can in no way happen if they are entirely fixed), they will never transform the body.

Therefore, various operations have been invented to bring such fixed medicines—such as gold, silver, precious stones, pearls, and corals—into the smallest <term>particles<gloss>original: "particulgel"; atoms or microscopic fragments</gloss></term>, so that they yield all the more easily to our heat as an <term>essential condition<gloss>original Latin: "Causa sine qua non"; a requirement without which the result cannot happen</gloss></term>. How much more powerful they become when one makes them light and fluid!

Fixation is performed in much the same way as the operation mentioned above for making things volatile; such as: <term>quenching<gloss>cooling a hot substance suddenly in liquid</gloss></term>, <term>softening<gloss>original: "Anweichungen"</gloss></term>, <term>maceration<gloss>original: "Einwichungen"; soaking to extract components</gloss></term>, <term>sublimations<gloss>heating a solid until it becomes vapor and then solid again</gloss></term>, <term>dissolutions<gloss>original: "Aufschliessungen"; "unlocking" a substance into its constituent parts</gloss></term>, and the like.

However, one must use various promoting agents more frequently to complete this operation.

## Another Way:
## To make Potable Gold.

Dissolve purified gold in <term>Spirit of Salt<gloss>original: "Spiritu Salis"; known today as hydrochloric acid</gloss></term>, and when everything is dissolved, draw the Spirit off from it again until it is dry; thus a yellow salt remains on the bottom of the flask. Turn this into a <note>subtle: meaning very fine or delicate</note> powder and keep it in a warm place, for otherwise it attracts the air to itself <note>This refers to the "deliquescent" nature of gold chloride, which absorbs moisture from the air and turns back into liquid if not kept warm and dry.</note>. Over this powder, pour <term>Spirit of Wine<gloss>original: "Spiritum Vini"; ethanol or high-proof alcohol</gloss></term> and let it extract for its proper time; thus the Spirit colors itself red-yellow and draws all the gold into itself. Then let it cool and pour the clear solution off into a glass. Drive it <note>original: "per gradus"; by degrees</note> with increasing heat as is known, for at least 6 days and nights. Everything that has risen over during that time, pour into a flask that is high enough; place a <term>helm<gloss>the top part of a still, also called an alembic</term> upon it and attach a receiver, with everything well <term>luted<gloss>sealed with airtight paste or clay</gloss></term>. Distill with a very gentle warmth, according to the eye's measure, about the 3rd part of a <term>Mass<gloss>a traditional unit of liquid volume</gloss></term> over, which is the <note>original: "Spiritus Vol."; volatile spirit</note>. In this, dissolve salt that is fine and white, and when it is dissolved, let it run through a <term>filter<gloss>original: "Filtrum"</gloss></term> so that it becomes clear. Nothing from the gold will <term>precipitate<gloss>original: "præcipitiren"; settle as a solid at the bottom</gloss></term>. Of this, one takes 20 to 24 drops.

## Liquor of Salt.

The <term>Liquor of Salt<gloss>original: "Liquor Salis"</gloss></term> is a gold dissolved in its sharp <term>menstruum<gloss>an alchemical solvent</gloss></term> and brought to the consistency of a liquor, in which 1 part of the menstruum remains. For this reason, if the menstruum is entirely drawn out, it can be <term>reduced<gloss>brought back to its metallic state</gloss></term> and returned to its previous nature.

### The Preparation is as follows.

Take the gold that has been purified to the highest degree through Antimony, make or beat it into very thin sheets, put it into a glass with a long neck, pour <term>Spirit of Salt<gloss>original: "Spiritum Salis"; hydrochloric acid</gloss></term> over it, seal your glass well, and place it for 3 or 4 weeks in horse-mist <note>original: "Pferde-Mist"; decomposing horse manure was used in laboratories to provide a constant, gentle "digestive" heat similar to an incubator</note> or a similar gentle heat. After the digestion is completed, one should draw off the Spirit of Salt by a gentle distillation, yet not entirely, but so that a little remains behind with the thickness of an oil. In this way, the gold is indeed unlocked, but not yet sufficiently thinned; therefore, this work must be repeated once more. Thus, when the essential substance of the gold has united most closely with the menstruum, one pours the last drawn-off menstruum together with the first, digests it, and finally completes it over a gentle fire entirely, leaving one part of the menstruum with it, as mentioned above.

## Flower of the Sun. Or

### The Common Red Precipitate from Mercury.

Take as much <term>mercury<gloss>original: "Mercurium"; also known as quicksilver</gloss></term> as you wish, which has been well-purified with salt and vinegar, and dissolve it in a <term>parting water<gloss>original: "Scheide-Wasser"; nitric acid</gloss></term> made from <term>vitriol<gloss>a sulfate mineral</gloss></term>, <term>alum<gloss>a potassium aluminum sulfate used as an astringent</gloss></term>, and <term>saltpeter<gloss>potassium nitrate</gloss></term>, until no more of it can be seen; after that, place it over the fire in a glass vessel that is rounded at the bottom. ### On Antimony. Or Stibnite.

That <term>antimony<gloss>original: "Antimonium" or "Spieß-Glaß"; a brittle, silvery-white metalloid often used in early medicine for its purging effects</gloss></term> is a special medicine for the human body (after its preparation) is now quite well-known and established; some even wish to conclude this from the fact that it "heals" metals and cleanses them of their impurities. Many kinds of medicines are prepared from antimony, some of which we intend to show how to make here.

### A Powder from Antimony.

Take as much of the purest antimony as you wish, crush it and make it very small, mix some well-purified saltpeter into it, and pour it into an unglazed earthenware vessel. Cover this with a lid and place it over a charcoal fire; let it stand there until the fire violently pushes off the lid; then take it out, make it very small again, and repeat this process—always with constant stirring—until the antimony has purified itself of its dross through sufficient vapor and a powder remains for you without a stench, like white ash. To this, finally add a little raw antimony, put it in a crucible, place it in the strongest melting fire and let it melt, then take it out and pour it onto a marble stone;

### Regulus of Antimony.

## The Second Method.

### These are made through calcination in the following manner.

Take <term>regulus of antimony<gloss>metallic antimony; original: "Regulum Antimonii"</gloss></term> and <term>saltpeter<gloss>potassium nitrate; original: "Salpeter"</gloss></term>, equal parts of each; <term>calcine<gloss>heat to a high temperature to oxidize the material without melting it; original: "Calcinir"</gloss></term> them together over a gentle fire for 3 or 4 consecutive hours. Put the lump that is taken out into a glass and pour common distilled water over it; leach out the salt and wash it well until sweet <note>meaning washed until the water no longer tastes of salt</note>. Once the regulus has dried, add saltpeter by weight again and mix it in; calcine it again, wash it until sweet as before, and repeat this process for a third time until it is <term>fixed<gloss>rendered non-volatile or stable under heat; original: "figire"</gloss></term>. And thus, the <term>flowers of antimony<gloss>the resulting chemical oxides; original: "Flores Antimonii"</gloss></term> remain behind, which can also be turned yellow through <term>reverberation<gloss>heating intensely in a furnace where the flames are reflected down onto the material; original: "reverberiren"</gloss></term>.

## Usage.

### A Mercurial Laudanum.

Take as much <term>mercury<gloss>original: "Quecksilber"</gloss></term> as you wish, wash it well with vinegar in which salt has been dissolved, and mix it once again with pure salt in a stone mortar with a wooden pestle until the salt turns black and has absorbed the mercury. After this, drive the salt and mercury through a <term>retort<gloss>a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</gloss></term> into a receiver that is half-filled with cold water. Then, let the mercury boil in the following lye—the longer, the better: Pour boiling hot water over <term>quicklime<gloss>original: "ungelöschten Kalck"</gloss></term> and stir it well; when it has cooled and settled, filter it. Afterward, pour this water over <term>willow ashes<gloss>original: "Weid-Aschen"</gloss></term> and stir it well; when it has settled, filter it again. 

After the mercury has boiled for its proper time in this lye, take it and wash it with vinegar and salt dissolved therein, and purify it from the salt as before through a retort until it becomes as transparent as a crystal. Then mix it with <term>burnt vitriol<gloss>a sulfate mineral, likely iron or copper sulfate, heated to remove moisture</gloss></term> and common dried salt, and pound it together with a wooden pestle in a stone mortar; finally, <term>sublime<gloss>to heat a substance until it becomes a vapor and then collects as a solid again</gloss></term> it according to the art, and repeat this several times.

Digest it with the spirit for 10 or 12 days in a <term>water bath<gloss>original: "Balneo Mariæ"; a vessel placed in boiling water to ensure gentle, even heating</gloss></term> at very mild heat. Finally, draw off the spirit of wine, then dry the substance and grind it upon a marble stone. Put it in a glass and let it dissolve in a damp place; <term>coagulate<gloss>to thicken or solidify</gloss></term> this dissolved substance once more, and thus the <term>Mercurial Laudanum<gloss>a sedative preparation containing mercury; original: "Laudanum Mercuriale"</gloss></term> is finished.

## Another Preparation of Oil of Vitriol <note>original: "Olei Vitrioli"</note>.

Take 15 pounds of the "righteous" <note>meaning genuine or unadulterated</note> and by now familiar vitriol; turn it red in a <term>calcining furnace</term> <note>a furnace used for heating a substance to high temperatures to remove volatile substances or to oxidize it</note> until nearly half of it is consumed. Prepare this as the previous one through <term>rectification</term> <note>the process of purifying a liquid by repeated distillation</note> and <term>circulation</term> <note>an alchemical process where a liquid is heated in a closed vessel so the vapors condense and flow back into the liquid, "maturing" the substance</note> into a pleasant medicine. ## To prepare the Oil of Vitriol with sulfur.

Take pure, good sulfur and pulverize it well; put it mixed with pure sand into a distilling vessel, and draw out the moisture of the <term>phlegma</term> <note>the watery, inactive part of a distilled substance</note> that comes over first. Pulverize the remaining sulfur again quite small and mix it again with pure sand, so that it comes over quite white from such a distillation. Thereupon, let the said sulfur be sublimated in a <term>subliming vessel</term> <note>a specialized apparatus for turning a solid into vapor and back to solid to purify it</note> and let it stand in the same. When it has stood, <term>calcinate</term> it well with Roman vitriol <note>likely blue vitriol or copper sulfate</note> in an earthen vessel, yet so sealed that all its moisture can smoke away through a small exit. When this has entirely smoked away and the sulfur itself is burned, take everything out and finally distill the remaining vitriol according to the art and as mentioned before, though in a different vessel. Guard yourself against tin- or lead-lined vessels during the calcination; take a wide <term>receiver</term> <note>the flask that collects the distillate</note> and change it as the condition of your material coming over requires.

## On Sulfur.

### To make Flowers of Sulfur.
<note>original: "Schwefel-Blumen"; these are a fine, bright yellow powder of pure sulfur produced when sulfur vapor is cooled suddenly against a cold surface, skipping the liquid phase.</note>

Take 1 part sulfur, and a half-part each of vitriol <note>iron or copper sulfates</note> that has been <term>calcined</term> <note>heated to a high temperature to remove moisture</note> until it is yellow, and "cast" common salt <note>salt that has been melted and solidified to remove impurities</note>. Pound them together and mix them with one another; place the mixture into a glass <term>subliming vessel</term>, and set upon it a fairly wide <term>helm</term> <note>the "head" or alembic of a still</note> with a <term>receiver</term> attached to the front. Seal all the joints well and apply heat by degrees in a <term>sand bath</term> <note>a container of sand heated by a fire, providing even, controlled heat to the glass</note>. At first, proceed slowly, then strengthen the fire more and more, so that the flowers of sulfur rise upward into the helm. The <term>sublimation</term> <note>the process of turning a solid directly into a gas and back into a solid to purify it</note> will be completed in 12 to 15 hours. These "flowers" are then taken out, rubbed off, and mixed with new materials <note>original: "Species"</note>—namely, with the aforementioned vitriol and cast salt—and sublimated as before. In this way, one obtains beautiful flowers of sulfur, which are very useful for treating chest illnesses and other conditions.

### Another way to prepare Flowers of Sulfur.

When one wishes to prepare sulfur for medicine, it must first be purified through sublimation so that its impurities and coarse <term>feces</term> <note>in an alchemical context, this refers to the solid dregs or waste matter left over after a process</note> remain behind, and only the volatile, subtle, and fiery substance rises. In this, care must be taken to use beautiful yellow sulfur and not any that is reddish, because the latter has absorbed some "smelter-smoke" <note>original: "Hütten-Rauch"; this refers to toxic arsenic trioxide or other poisonous vapors produced during the smelting of ores</note>, making it unhealthy and difficult to clean.

Therefore, take as much yellow sulfur as you wish and place it into an earthen <term>cucurbit</term> <note>a gourd-shaped chemical vessel</note>. Set it in an open fire and place a pot or another inverted cucurbit (which must not be glazed) on top of it, in such a way that the neck of one fits into the other. Every half hour, remove the top pot or cucurbit and replace it with another. Then, collect the flowers that have settled inside, and repeat this as often [as]...

## A magnificent tincture is prepared from the Flowers of Sulfur in the following manner.

Take triple-sublimed <term>Flowers of Sulfur</term> <note>pure sulfur powder that has been vaporized and recollected three times for maximum purity</note>, as much as you wish; pour over them <term>Spirit of Turpentine</term> <note>an essential oil distilled from pine resin</note> and place it in <term>digestion</term> <note>the process of steeping a substance in a liquid at a gentle, steady heat to extract its medicinal properties</note> at a mild temperature. Repeat this work as often as necessary until you have drawn all the tincture out of the flowers and nothing but the dregs remain at the bottom. Pour all the tinted spirits together and draw off [distill] the tincture in a <term>Balneo</term> <note>a water bath or "Bain-Marie," used for gentle, indirect heating</note> until it reaches a thick consistency, roughly like honey. Pour <term>Spirit of Wine</term> <note>high-proof distilled alcohol</note> over the remaining tincture and extract with this also, as before, until all the tincture has been drawn out of it. Distill the Spirit of Wine away again, and thus the Tincture of Sulfur remains behind as a noble medicine.

### Use.

This Tincture of Sulfur serves particularly well (alongside the flowers) for chest complaints and all ailments of the liver. One takes 3 to 4 <term>grains</term> <note>a historical unit of weight, approximately 65 milligrams</note> of it in hyssop-water.

Whoever desires to make such a <term>Theriac</term> <note>a famous ancient "universal" antidote and cure-all consisting of dozens of ingredients</note> correctly must gather the herbs at the right time, namely at the beginning of summer, for this composition requires nothing but select pieces gathered at the proper time, each in its proper weight.

Cordial sieve <note>original: "Cordial-Sieb"; likely referring to the specific sieve used for the heart-strengthening or "cordial" ingredients of the mixture</note>: whatever does not pass through, pound it so often and long until you have brought everything through the sieve.

The saffron must be dry, rubbed alone and mixed among the powder; when all this is done, let the opium melt in a tinned vessel, press it through a woolen cloth, and save it.

In the same way, you must also soak and melt the licorice, the juice of hypocistis <note>original: "Succum hypocistidis"; an astringent plant extract</note>, the acacia, and the gum Arabic, just like the opium, press them through a cloth, and save them.

Furthermore, take clear white honey, put it in a kettle, let it become warm and boil it over the fire two or three times; take it from the fire and skim the froth off; afterwards, weigh out as much as you need and pour one or two pounds into a large, wide kettle, or into a stone or copper mortar; stir it with a round, smooth stick, and gradually mix the powders into it so that they do not clump together.

When this is well mixed together, then pour some more honey into it and mix powder in again, likewise some of the opium and the melted juices, and thus continue until everything is finished.

If you take the pressed <term>storax</term> <note>a fragrant resin</note> and have not pounded it among the powders, this must also be added at the beginning; but you must pay close attention to mixing it in, that you proceed correctly with it; therefore, bring the storax, turpentine, and nutmeg oil together over a very gentle fire and mix everything very well together.

If the black balsam is used and it is liquid and thin, you do not need to warm it; otherwise, you may add it to the melted nutmeg oil <note>original: "Museaten-Oehl"</note>. However, let the white balsam, which is very hard, be crushed along with the other ingredients.

To give this well-mixed substance, or <term>Theriac</term> <note>A famous ancient "polypharmacy" preparation used as an antidote to poison and a cure-all</note>, its proper color, mix in the burnt and well-pulverized <term>chalcitis</term> <note>A mineral traditionally identified as a copper ore or a weathered form of iron pyrites, used here to darken the mixture</note>. Stir it well together in the sun for a good while, after which it will turn black from this small quantity of chalcitis, provided it is properly burnt. This is done with Roman vitriol <note>original: "Römischem Vitriol"; iron or copper sulfate</note>, which is boiled in a crucible as much as necessary for this purpose and blended into the aforementioned Theriac.

Finally, after the Theriac is well-blended and has its proper color, pour it into its appropriate vessel, but ensure that one-third remains empty so that the Theriac has room to ferment <note>original: "Gähren"</note> and does not overflow. You must also stir it well in the vessel every day, two to three times, for seven to eight consecutive days; thereafter, stir it once every week for two months. Place it in a warm spot so that it ferments well; for this reason, it is best to make it during the hot days of summer. Once the Theriac has fermented sufficiently, place it in a cool location so that its potency does not diminish.

### Usage

This Theriac possesses the following virtues: It maintains a person in their health and dispels existing illnesses. It keeps the human spirit in a good state, promotes all functions of the senses, dries and disperses rising vapors <note>referring to the "vapors" believed to rise from the stomach to the brain in humoral medicine</note>, brings about a good temperament <note>The healthy balance of the four bodily humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>, consumes all bad humors <note>original: "böse Feuchtigkeiten"</note>, warms the chilled limbs of the elderly, and strengthens natural forces. Taken internally, it serves against all poisonous bites and stings of animals, dispels bloating of the body, restores lost color to the complexion, promotes digestion, and is also good against weakness of sight. It prevents all pestilence and poisonous diseases and has many other virtues besides.

Some among the ancients and our ancestors used it on the first day after the new moon, while others used it only on the fourth day after the new moon, each time a dose the size of a bean, in a suitable, warmed vehicle <note>original: "Vehiculo"; the liquid medium, such as wine or water, used to administer the medicine</note>.

# Instruction
## How to extract the salt from precious stones and how it should be used.

If you wish to extract the salt from precious stones, take whichever stone you desire, grind it into a fine powder, and mix in an equal weight of sulfur. Perform a cementation <note>A process of heating a solid material in a sealed container surrounded by a powdered chemical agent (in this case, sulfur) to change its properties without melting it.</note> in a closed vessel for six hours; afterward, heat it strongly in an assay furnace <note>original: "Probir Ofen", a specialized furnace used by chemists and assayers for high-heat refining.</note> with constant stirring. Then, while the material is still glowing hot, pour it into good distilled vinegar. Carefully pour off the vinegar once it has settled well, and thoroughly wash the powder or material with water. Next, dry the powder and, while it is still somewhat moist, form it into small cakes. Pour spirit of juniper <note>original: "Spiritum Juniperi"</note> over them and let it digest for a good long time until you have extracted all the essence; filter this, and distill off the spirit, and the essence will remain at the bottom, which can be stored and used as desired.

As for what remains after this extraction, wash it well with water, pour distilled honey-water over it, and extract the salt in the proper manner <note>original: "Sal debito more"</note>. Distill off the water and thoroughly wash the remaining salt with spirit of wine <note>original: "Spiritu Vini", i.e., high-proof alcohol</note>; in this way, you will have the salt clear and pure. In this manner, one can extract the salt from any stone.

## Use of the salts extracted from precious stones.
### Ruby.

One grain of this salt taken in a spoonful of "water of life" <note>original: "Aqua Vitæ", a term for concentrated distilled alcohol or brandy used as a medicinal solvent.</note> strengthens the heart, makes one joyful, and grants a good memory.

### Emerald.

One grain of this salt, taken with spirit of wine or a spoonful of water of life, resists and expels poison from those who have been affected—one must sweat after taking it. It causes falling hair to grow back and drives away melancholy <note>original: "Melancholiam", a state of deep despondency or depression attributed to an imbalance of "black bile".</note> and epilepsy <note>original: "Epilepsiam"</note>.

### Diamond.

Half a grain in an oil of salt <note>original: "Oleo Salis", likely a solution of hydrochloric acid or a concentrated saline distillate.</note>, or two quints <note>term: "Quintlein" — a small unit of weight, roughly 3.75 grams or about 1/8th of an ounce.</note> of potable gold <note>original: "Auri potabilis", a legendary alchemical medicine consisting of gold dissolved in a liquid state.</note>

### Magnet.

# Of Trees and Herbs.

Next to the aforementioned medicines, the ancients of former times made use of trees and herbs for the healing of their diseases, successfully using the medications prepared from them both internally and externally. Among others, the following have been noted.

## Of the Apple Tree.

The leaves and blossoms of this tree are astringent <note>original: "ziehen zusammen", meaning they cause tissues to contract, often used to stop bleeding or discharge</note>.

### Sour Apples.

Sour apples cool, are astringent, and disperse the thick phlegm in the stomach; cooked in butter, they provide good nourishment during fevers, promote the flow of urine, and still vomiting.

### Sweet Apples.

Sweet apples soften the body <note>indicating a mild laxative effect</note>, provide good nourishment, strengthen the heart, take away sadness, promote the coughing up of phlegm, and drive away a cough, especially when they are cooked.

Applied externally, they still the pains of the eyes when roasted in ashes and laid over them; they alleviate side-stitches <note>often referring to pleurisy or muscular pain in the torso</note> when bound on with myrrh; they heal burns <note>original: "den Brand", which can mean burns or gangrene</note> when boiled in broad-leaf plantain water <note>original: "Wegrich-Wasser", a common herbal remedy for skin conditions</note> and applied with milk.

The wine-sour apples strengthen the heart and the stomach, create an appetite for eating, are good in hot fevers, and still the thirst.

Apples that have almost no taste and are unpleasant to eat are, on the contrary, harmful to one's entire nature. Because of their cold, watery nature, they often cause fevers and fluxes <note>original: "Flüsse", referring to an abnormal discharge of bodily fluids</note>; therefore, these should be avoided.

By means of this vinegar, the <term>Opening Tincture or Essence of Mars</term> <note>original: "Tinctura oder Essentia Martis aperitiva"; "Mars" refers to iron, used here to treat obstructions</note> is prepared, as well as a <term>Water of Life</term> <note>original: "Aqua vitæ", a distilled alcoholic medicine</note> and a <term>Comforting Cordial Water</term> <note>original: "Aqua cordialis confortans", a medicine intended to stimulate the heart and spirit</note>. The <term>Simple Syrup of Apples</term> <note>original: "Syrup de pomis simpl."</note> is a fortification for the heart and stomach and helps with afflictions of the heart arising from black bile <note>In the theory of the four humors, black bile was associated with melancholy and heaviness</note>; it is good for fainting, heart palpitations, bilious fever, thirst, melancholy, vomiting, and loss of appetite.

The <term>Extract</term> from the root of the sweet apple tree stills abdominal fluxes, ruptures <note>original: "Durchbruch", which can refer to a hernia or sudden abdominal distress</note>, dysentery <note>original: "Rothe-Ruhr", literally "the red flux"</note>, and liver flux.

## Of the Pear Tree.

As is well known, there are many kinds of both the tree and the fruit, and the ancients have utilized the tree and fruit in the following manner and left behind records of it.

The bark of the tree, boiled in wine or water and drunk, stills dysentery. Pears in general—but especially raw ones—cool and are astringent <note>original: "ziehen zusammen", meaning they cause tissues to contract</note>, but they are difficult to digest, bloat the stomach, and harm those afflicted with abdominal and kidney pain; however, when cooked, they are better.

Sweet pears are laxative; sour and bitter ones are astringent. When baked or cooked and eaten, they still abdominal fluxes; the broth drunk from them removes the heat in burning fevers. From common pears, a wine and vinegar are also prepared.

## Of the Cherry Tree.

Sour cherries are astringent and strengthen the heart and stomach. For this reason, they serve to treat heat and thirst in burning fevers and melancholic disorders of the spleen.

Black or sweet cherries soften <note>meaning they have a mild laxative or soothing effect</note>; they benefit the head and resist stroke, convulsions <note>original: "Fraiß", an old term for epilepsy or seizures, particularly in children</note>, and paralysis.

### Cherry Leaves

The leaves of this tree, boiled in milk and drunk, are good for jaundice <note>original: "Gelbesucht"</note>.

### Of the Peach Tree.

The blossom of the peach tree warms, dries, cleanses, softens the body <note>meaning it acts as a mild laxative</note>, and drains away excess water <note>original: "führet das Gewässer ab", referring to its diuretic properties</note>. Fresh peaches are laxative, provide little nourishment, and easily spoil within the body, giving rise to putrid fevers, abdominal cramps <note>original: "Leibreissen"</note>, diarrhea <note>original: "Durchbrüche"</note>, and dysentery <term>dysentery</term> <note>original: "Rothe-Ruhr", literally "red flux"</note>. Peach kernels <note>the seeds found inside the hard pits</note> promote urine, break up the stone <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>, and open the congested liver and spleen. ### The Resin of this Tree.

The resin <term>gum</term> of the peach tree, dissolved in plantain water <note>original: "Wegrich-Wasser", water distilled from plantain (Plantago) leaves, not the banana-like fruit</note> and used, is good for spitting blood. Taken with a bit of saffron, it is good for shortness of breath <note>original: "Engbrüstigkeit", often referring to asthma or congestion</note>, coughs, and the stone.

### Peach Blossom Water.

### Syrup of Sweet [Oranges].

The syrup made from the juice of sweet bitter oranges <note>original: "süssen Pomerantzen"; though the tree is the bitter variety, this likely refers to a sweeter variant or a preparation using more sugar to offset the bitterness</note> is particularly useful for inflammatory conditions <note>original: "hitzigen Gebrechen"</note> of the throat and chest, and for stitches in the side <note>pleurisy or intercostal pain</note>.

### The Syrup of the Peels.

The syrup made from the rinds or peels strengthens the stomach and the heart, and disperses wind <note>gas or flatulence</note>.

### Syrup of the Blossom.

This is a good tonic for the head and heart; it promotes sweating and is effective against the plague, pestilential fevers, and spots <note>likely referring to petechiae or skin eruptions associated with typhus or plague</note>.

### The Preserved Peels.

These <note>referring to candied or sugar-preserved rinds</note> warm and dry the body, resist poison, serve the liver and the heart, strengthen the stomach, aid digestion, create an appetite, and improve bad breath.

### The Preserved Blossom.

When preserved, these blossoms strengthen the heart, resist poison, and are occasionally included among the **Cordial Confections** <term>Cordial Confections</term> <note>original Latin: "Confectiones Cordiales"; medicinal preparations intended to stimulate the heart and lift the spirits</note>.

### Bitter Orange Oil.

Bitter orange oil warms, dries, promotes sweating, resists and expels poison, and is useful for worms and wind, weakness of the heart and stomach, and is good for fainting spells.

### Bitter Orange Salve.

This salve, when rubbed onto the temples, induces sleep.

When this salve is smeared upon the navel, it drives away worms and **heart-tension** <term>heart-tension</term> <note>original: "Hertz-Gespan"; a historical term for a sensation of pressure, cramping, or constriction in the upper abdomen/pit of the stomach, often associated with anxiety or digestive distress</note>.

### Walnut Tree.

The leaves of this tree, when applied externally, drive away milk <note>used to stop lactation in nursing mothers</note> and kill worms in wounds.

### Walnut Blossoms or Walnut Catkins.

The blossoms from the walnut trees are good for the rising of the womb <note>original: "Aufsteigen der Mutter"; a historical medical condition where the uterus was believed to move upward in the body, causing various physical and emotional symptoms</note>; they still excessive menstruation <note>original: "Monath-Zeit"</note>, as well as the flux <note>original: "Durchbruch", likely referring to diarrhea or a sudden discharge</note>, kidney pain, and colic.

### The Gum of the Walnut Tree.

This gum <note>the resinous sap secreted by the tree</note> is good for weaknesses of the kidneys.
And applied externally, it is good for inflammatory ulcers <note>original: "hitzigen Geschwüren"</note>.

### The Root.

The root, boiled in water or wine and frequently drunk, drives away fever.
The middle bark <note>the inner layer of bark</note> of the root relieves toothaches, whether applied fresh or boiled in water and held in the mouth.

### The Juice from the Root.

This juice purges <term>purges</term> <note>acts as a strong laxative to clear the body's humors</note> very strongly, but it stills headaches and is good for fever and aching in the limbs <note>original: "Reissen im Gliedern", likely referring to rheumatic or joint pain</note>.

### Fresh Walnuts.

Fresh walnuts resist poison, drive and promote the menstrual flow <note>original: "Monath-Blume"</note>, and protect against the plague.

### Applied Externally.

Used externally, they clear ulcers of the mouth and drive away the bruises <note>original: "Blau geschlagene Flecken", literally "blue-beaten spots"</note> of the skin.

### The Skin around the Walnut Kernel.

This skin <note>the thin, bitter pellicle covering the nut meat</note> is a good remedy for colic.

### Preserved Walnuts.

Preserved walnuts <note>likely pickled or candied</note> create an appetite for food, aid digestion, and strengthen the stomach as well as the fetus in the mother's womb; they protect against miscarriage and against foul, poisonous air <note>original: "böse gifftige Lufft", referring to miasmas believed to carry disease</note>.

## Elder Tree.

### Elder Buds or Young Shoots.

# Linden Tree

### The Blossom

The blossom of the linden tree thins [the humors], disperses [blockages], strengthens the head, and serves against dizziness and apoplexy <term>apoplexy</term> <note>original: "Slag-Flüsse," referring to strokes or sudden loss of consciousness</note>.

### The Seed or the Berries

The seed, used both internally and externally, stills all kinds of abdominal and blood fluxes <note>excessive discharge of fluids</note>, dysentery <term>dysentery</term> <note>original: "Rothe-Ruhr," literally "the red flux"</note>, and nosebleeds.

### The Leaves

The leaves disperse [humors] and promote the flow of urine and menstruation <note>original: "Monaths-Zeit"</note>. They are also good for cramps when the juice is expressed with wine and rubbed on; likewise for swollen feet, if the leaves are simply boiled in water and applied as a poultice.

### The Moisture from Cut Lindens

The moisture that flows from cut linden trees makes fallen hair grow back again.

### The Charcoal

The charcoal burned from linden wood, extinguished with vinegar and taken with prepared "crab's eyes" <term>crab's eyes</term> <note>original: "Krebs-Augen," small stony concretions found in the stomachs of crayfish, used historically as an antacid</note> or spermaceti <term>spermaceti</term> <note>original: "Wallrath," a waxy substance found in the head of the sperm whale</note>, disperses clotted blood resulting from a fall and also stills the spitting of blood.

### The Water Distilled from the Blossoms

Linden-blossom water strengthens the head and disperses "wind" <note>gas or colic</note> in children; it is good for convulsions <term>convulsions</term> <note>original: "Fraiß," a historical term for seizures, especially in infants</note>, heart tremors, fainting, dizziness, stroke, chlorosis <term>chlorosis</term> <note>original: "Milchsuecht," an iron-deficiency anemia</note>, stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>, abdominal cramps, and "heart-tension" <term>heart-tension</term> <note>original: "Hertz-Gespann," a term for various ailments including anxiety, spasms, or oppression of the chest/upper abdomen</note> in small children. It also serves pregnant women in difficult births and for clotted blood.

### Externally

If one washes oneself with linden-blossom water, it makes for a clear face <note>complexion</note>.

# Mulberry Tree

### The Root and Bark

These two parts of the mulberry tree cool, dry, constrict <term>constrict</term> <note>original: "ziehen zusammen," referring to astringent properties that tighten tissues</note>, cleanse, open [blockages], and act as a laxative <note>original: "laxiren"</note>. ### The Ripe Mulberries

Ripe mulberries soften the body <note>historically meaning to ease the bowels or act as a mild laxative</note>, bring an appetite for eating, and quench the thirst.

### Mulberry Juice

If someone has a swollen uvula <term>swollen uvula</term> <note>original: "der Zapfe geschossen," a historical idiom for an inflamed or 'fallen' uvula</note> or otherwise has inflammation or ulcers in the throat, mouth, or neck, they should make use of mulberry juice.

### Externally.

Externally, the white fir bark is good for ulcers and burns <note>original: "Brand," which in this context refers to injuries from "fire or water," meaning burns and scalds</note>, whether from fire or from water.

### Fir Cones.

These also constrict <term>constrict</term> <note>original: "ziehen zusammen," referring to astringent properties that tighten tissues</note> and dry when used internally.

### Externally.

### The Leaves.

If these are boiled in red wine and drunk, they miraculously still dysentery <term>dysentery</term> <note>original: "Rothe-Ruhr," literally 'the red flux'</note>.

## The Liquid Resin from the Leaves.

The liquid resin obtained from the leaves is also commonly used in place of <term>Venetian turpentine</term> <note>original: "Venetianischen Terpentins," a high-quality resin historically harvested from larch trees, prized for its clarity and medicinal properties.</note>.

## The Dry Resin.

The dry resin, however, is used in place of frankincense <note>original: "Weyrauch"</note>, which ants otherwise collect <note>This likely refers to "forest frankincense" or "ant-incense," resin droplets found near anthills where ants have gathered them for their own use, a phenomenon often noted in early modern natural histories.</note>.

### Externally.

Whoever is afflicted with a toothache should fumigate <note>original: "räuchre," meaning to inhale or expose the area to the smoke of the burning resin</note> themselves with this resin; they will find relief and the pain will pass.

## Branches.

The distilled water <note>original: "gebrante Wasser," a hydrosol created through distillation</note> made from the tender branches cleanses thoroughly and is astringent <note>original: "ziehet an," literally 'draws together,' referring to the tightening of tissues.</note>.

## Of Herbs.

### Common Wormwood.

The common wormwood grows in stony, mountainous, and uncultivated places.

It blooms in July and August, but it is at its greatest potency in June, at which time it should also be harvested.

### Womb-Herb.

Wormwood is a good <term>womb-herb</term> <note>original: "Mutter-Kraut," literally "mother-herb." Historically, herbs designated this way were used for gynecological issues or what was then called "hysteria" (ailments of the womb).</note>; it opens, disperses, and promotes the flow of urine.

It is good for the stomach, liver, and spleen; it expels worms, purges the bile, and promotes perspiration.

It serves in cases of fevers, obstructions of the liver and spleen, and for the <term>menses</term> <note>original: "Monath-Zeit," literally "month-time."</note>.

It expels poison, plague, wind <note>flatulence or gas</note>, spleen complaints, dropsy, and jaundice.

Anyone who has weak hearing and fumigates themselves with this smoke will not only find it strengthened, but will also be freed from ringing in the ears and other <term>ailments</term> <note>original: "incommodité," a French loanword common in 18th-century German to describe physical discomforts.</note> of the ears.
Wormwood smoke also stills toothaches.

### Wormwood Flowers.

These flowers alleviate many kinds of pain and are also good for <term>jaundice</term> <note>original: "Gelbesucht," literally "yellow-sickness."</note>, suppressed menstruation, the bites and stings of venomous animals, and they counteract poison.

### Wormwood Seed.

The seed stops all kinds of <term>abdominal fluxes</term> <note>original: "Bauch-Flüsse," referring to conditions like diarrhea or dysentery.</note>.

### Wormwood Water.

Distilled wormwood water is good for headaches and discharging ears; it also sharpens the eyesight.

### The Juice.

The juice creates a desire for food.

### The Extract.

The extract quenches thirst and counteracts poison.

### Wormwood Oil.

The distilled oil drives away stomach aches, <term>hiccups</term> <note>original: "Schlucken."</note>, and hard hearing.

### The Salt.

The salt derived from wormwood ash stills vomiting in cases of malignant fevers. <note>Salt of wormwood was an alkali (potassium carbonate) produced by burning the plant and leaching the ashes; it was a staple of early modern chemistry.</note>

### Roman Wormwood.

This herb is astringent, thins the humors, disperses blockages, and dries;
It is an herb for the stomach and liver, resists rot <note>original: "Fäule," referring to putrefaction or sepsis</note>, improves the bile, and expels it through the urine.
It serves in cases of liver obstruction, <term>jaundice</term> <note>original: "Gelbesucht"</note>, <term>dropsy</term> <note>original: "Wassersucht," an accumulation of fluid in the body</note>, and in bladder and stomach complaints.

### Boiled in Wine.

Roman wormwood <note>original: "Welschen Wermuth," often referring to *Artemisia pontica*</note> boiled in wine and drunk stills abdominal cramps and the <term>uterine pains</term> <note>original: "Mutter-Schmertzen"</note> that arise after childbirth. This is also effective when it is merely applied externally to the painful area. Roman wormwood is also placed beneath young children so that they may sleep much more peacefully.

### Egyptian Box-thorn.
<note>original: "Egyptischer Schatten-Dorn," likely referring to the Egyptian Acacia (*Acacia nilotica*), known for its astringent properties.</note>

#### The golden-yellow juice pressed from the seeds.

This juice is tart, astringent, and thickens the fluids.
Therefore, it is useful for excessive menstruation, <term>diarrhea</term> <note>original: "Durchbruch"</note>, and other abdominal flows, as well as for ailments of the rectum and the womb.

#### Against Hair Loss.

If someone's hair is falling out, they should coat the area where it is thinning with the aforementioned juice; thus, the lost hair will grow back and no more will fall out.

#### The Juice.

This juice is also good for <term>erysipelas</term> <note>original: "Rothlauf," a bacterial skin infection</note>, mouth ulcers, <term>cataracts</term> <note>original: "Augen-Fell," literally "eye-skin"</note>, and protruding eyes.

# Thorns.

The <term>decoction</term> <note>original: "Decoctum"; a medicinal preparation made by boiling plant material in liquid.</note> of thorns is particularly useful for dislocated limbs.

## Blackthorn.
<note>original: "Schlehen-Dorn," referring to the sloe bush (*Prunus spinosa*), known for its sharp thorns and tart blue-black berries.</note>

### The Leaves and Flowers.

These have a drying effect, are <term>astringent</term> <note>original: "ziehen zusammen"; they constrict bodily tissues.</note>, and still abdominal and uterine "flows" <note>Referring to diarrhea and excessive menstrual or vaginal discharge.</note>.

### Mouthwash.

A good mouthwash is prepared from both of these.

### The Tender Leaves.

Early, tender leaves soothe toothaches.

### The Flowers.

Blackthorn flowers <term>resolve</term> <note>original: "resolviren"; a medical term meaning to dissolve or break down blockages or "thickened" humors.</note>, stimulate the flow of urine and kidney grit, and are effective against side-stiches and <term>heart-tension</term> <note>original: "Herz-Gespann"; a historical term used to describe a range of symptoms including palpitations, anxiety, or cramping in the upper abdomen.</note>.

### The Berries or Sloes.

The berries, when added to and consumed with beer, wine, or whatever else one might drink, strengthen the stomach and still all manner of abdominal flows and excessive <term>menstruation</term> <note>original: "übrige Monath-Zeit."</note>.

### The Root.

The root (after the outer black bark has been discarded), boiled in vinegar or beer, drives away pains and other ailments of both the teeth and the gums.

### The Moss.

The <term>moss</term> <note>original: "Mooß"; likely referring to the lichens or bryophytes that grow on the bark of old blackthorn bushes.</note> from the blackthorn resists <term>hernias</term> <note>original: "Brüche," which can also refer to fractures, but in this context usually means intestinal protrusions.</note> and does not allow them to grow larger or increase.

### Water from the Flowers.

The distilled water from the flowers is good for stones, side-stiches, clotted blood, and lung ulcers.

### The Syrup.

The sloe syrup <note>original: "Schlehen Sirup"; made from the tart berries of the blackthorn bush.</note> purges very gently and is good for <term>shortness of breath</term> <note>original: "Engbrüstigkeit."</note>, coughing, side-stitches, and kidney stones.

### The Juice.

The juice from the sloes strengthens the stomach, stills vomiting, the spitting of blood, nosebleeds, and abdominal and menstrual "flows." It also returns the <term>womb</term> <note>original: "Beer-Mutter"; literally "the bear-mother."</note> and <term>rectum</term> <note>original: "Affter-Darm."</note> to their proper places; it drives away <term>Saint Anthony’s Fire</term> <note>original: "die Rose"; referring to Erysipelas, a bacterial skin infection characterized by a bright red, "angry" rash.</note> in the face, inflamed eyes, and other inflammations.

### Sorrel.

<term>Sorrel</term> <note>original: "Sauer-Ampffer" (*Rumex acetosa*); a sharp-tasting perennial herb often used in early modern medicine for its cooling properties.</note> resists poison and <term>putrefaction</term> <note>original: "Fäule."</note>, strengthens the stomach, heart, and liver, stimulates the appetite, and holds back hot abdominal "flows" <note>Referring to diarrhea accompanied by fever.</note>; therefore, it is used with benefit in common hot, <term>bilious</term> <note>original: "gallichten"; relating to an excess of yellow bile.</note>, and <term>pestilential</term> <note>Plague-like or highly infectious.</note> fevers, both internally and externally.

### Externally.

Externally, sorrel drives away all manner of skin impurities, such as the <term>itch</term> <note>original: "Kräthe"; usually referring to scabies.</note>, mange, <term>rashes</term> <note>original: "Flechten"; scaly skin conditions like eczema or psoriasis.</note>, <term>ringworm</term> <note>original: "Haarwurm"; literally "hair-worm," a historical term for various skin parasites or fungal infections.</note>, and the stings of venomous animals.

### The Flowers.

The flowers of sorrel, boiled in wine and drunk, heal the injured intestines in <term>dysentery</term> <note>original: "Rothen-Ruhr"; literally "the red flux."</note>, prevent <term>ruptures</term> <note>original: "Durchbruch."</note>, bloody urine, the spitting of blood, poisoned seminal discharge, and immoderate menstruation; these flowers are also good for worms, "bad air," the plague, and hot fevers.

### The Root.

The root of the sorrel opens blockages of the liver, spleen, and urinary tracts, and is good for <term>jaundice</term> <note>original: "Gelbesucht."</note> and kidney stones.

### The Distilled Water of the Leaves.

This water cools and takes away the heat of the liver and spleen. It also stills thirst in hot fevers and is good for head and toothaches.

### The Juice from the Fresh Leaves

The juice from the fresh leaves <note>referring to the sorrel mentioned on the previous page</note> takes away the heat in eye inflammations, cools the <term>hemorrhoids</term> <note>original: "Goldne-Ader," literally "the golden vein."</note>, resists drunkenness, and soothes and heals ulcers of the ears.

### Syrup.

The syrup quenches thirst, refreshes, and is very good for burning fevers.

### True Calmus.

<note>original: "Wahrer Calmus" (*Acorus calamus*), commonly known as Sweet Flag; an aromatic marsh plant highly valued in early modern pharmacy for its warming properties.</note>
From this plant, only the root is used; it disperses <note>An early medical term for breaking up "thick" or "stagnant" humors in the body.</note>, thins, opens [blockages], and promotes both sweat and urine. It opens the obstructions of the <term>menstrual cycle</term> <note>original: "weibliche Zeit," literally "the womanly time."</note>, as well as those of the liver and the spleen, when it is boiled in wine and drunk.

### Calmus Root Stept in Beer.

This root, steeped or soaked in beer and then consumed, serves for side-stitches, <term>shortness of breath</term> <note>original: "Engbrüstigkeit."</note>, and cramps; it disperses clotted blood and protects against dangerous oncoming diseases and all manner of malignant fevers.

The Calmus root is also good for "cold" catarrhs of the head <note>referring to an excess of phlegm or "runny" conditions attributed to a cold temperament</note> and serves to strengthen a weak stomach. This root is also good for bladder ailments, for the blockage of urine, colic, and <term>scurvy</term> <note>original: "Scharbock."</note>.

### Preserved and Candied Calmus.

The preserved or sugar-coated Calmus root warms a cold stomach, prevents belching from the same, and consumes the <term>indigestion</term> <note>original: "Cruditäten"; refers to undigested matter or "raw" humors in the stomach.</note> of the stomach.

### Extract.

The extract is good for abdominal griping and <term>intestinal colic</term> <note>original: "Darm-Gicht," literally "gut-gout."</note>, as well as for the paralysis of limbs and cold ailments of the chest, and it promotes the <term>monthly period</term> <note>original: "Monath-Zeit."</note>.

### The Juice.

The juice is used externally and, when smeared upon dimmed eyes, drives away the "mist" <note>likely referring to cataracts or blurred vision</note> within them.
