## False Calmus.

<note>original: "Falscher Calmus." Usually refers to Yellow Iris (*Iris pseudacorus*) or sometimes certain species of Galingale, which were used as substitutes for the more expensive Sweet Flag.</note>

Of this plant, likewise, only the root is used; it is good for ailments of the brain and the <term>sinews</term> <note>original: "Senn-Adern," referring to both tendons and nerves, which were not always clearly distinguished in early anatomy.</note>, heals discharges of the <term>womb</term> <note>original: "Bauch- und Beer-Mutter," archaic terms for the uterus.</note>, and stills all bleeding; therefore it is particularly useful against <term>dysentery</term> <note>original: "Rothe-Ruhr," literally "the red dysentery."</note>, excessive menstruation, nosebleeds, the spitting of blood, and blood in the urine.

### The Root Held in the Mouth and Chewed.

When used in this way, the root consumes the [excess] moisture in the stomach and promotes digestion; it is also included among the "wound-drinks" <note>Herbal decoctions intended to heal internal injuries or help close external wounds.</note>.

### Externally.

Externally, this root—along with peacock feathers—is hung upon or bound to children and pregnant women to protect against <term>the fright</term> <note>original: "das Erschrecken." In early modern medicine, a sudden shock or "fright" was considered a serious medical condition that could cause seizures in children or miscarriage in women; amulets were often used as a preventative.</note>.

## Wood of Paradise.

<note>original: "Paradiß-Holtz," also known as Aloeswood or Agarwood (*Aquilaria*). A resinous, fragrant wood highly prized since antiquity for incense and medicine.</note>

This is a precious foreign wood from a tree that is brought to us in pieces from Arabia and India; it is marked with many spots and streaked with ash-colored veins. It is heavy, has a spicy and bitter taste, is <term>astringent</term>, resinous, and when it is set on fire, it gives off a lovely scent.

When one can obtain the true Wood of Paradise or Aloeswood, it smells so strong that even without being lit—simply by being rubbed in the hand without fire—it gives off a piercing and pleasant fragrance. The Wood of Paradise grows in India, on the islands of Malacca and <term>Sumatra</term> <note>original: "Samaria," likely a transcription error or archaic variant for Sumatra.</note>, and also in a region located near China.

## The Wood.

The Wood of Paradise or Aloeswood is astringent, strengthens, refreshes, makes one joyful, and expels sweat and all poison. It guards and preserves the <term>natural balsam of life</term> <note>original: "natürlichen Lebens-Balsam." A vitalist concept referring to the body's innate healing power and warmth.</note> and strengthens the brain (either by being used as incense or by being smelled). It also strengthens the heart, the womb, the vital senses, and the <term>animal spirits</term> <note>original: "Bewegungs-Geister," literally "spirits of movement." These were thought to be subtle fluids in the nerves responsible for sensation and motion.</note>.

It is therefore held in high esteem for weaknesses of the heart, fainting, heart palpitations, side-stitches, ulcers of the intestines, dysentery, liver ailments, <term>leukorrhea</term> <note>original: "Weissen-Fluß," literally "the white flux."</note>, shortness of breath, and it expels roundworms.

### The Powder.

The powder thereof heals stomach griping or <term>colic</term> <note>original: "Bauch-Grimmen oder Colic."</note> and all diseases of the intestines, as well as stomach and <term>womb-ailments</term> <note>original: "Mutter-Kranckheiten." In early modern medicine, the uterus was often called the "mother."</note>, when such conditions arise from cold <note>Humoral theory suggested that illnesses were caused by an imbalance of heat, cold, moisture, or dryness; Wood of Paradise was considered "warm."</note>.

### Boiled in Wine.

When Wood of Paradise is boiled in wine and drunk, it stills pains in the loins and creates good breath.

### Externally.

Externally, it is taken and used for poultices and for matters intended to "strengthen the head" <note>Remedies meant to clear the senses or treat headaches.</note>.

### The Powder.

He who knows how to properly prepare and ready the powder can remove all <term>foul flesh</term> <note>original: "faule Fleisch," referring to necrotic or gangrenous tissue.</note>, in whatever sort of injury or wound it may be, without any pain at all.

## Larch Sponge.

<note>original: "Lerchen-Schwamm." This is the Larch Agaric (*Laricifomes officinalis*), a wood-decay fungus highly valued as a purgative since antiquity.</note>

This is a light, white, and loose sponge that emerges like a growth from the old, withered trunks of the larch tree. This sponge is actually of two genders, namely male and female. The former is black, hard, firm, and very <term>fibrous</term> <note>original: "fasicht."</note> when broken. The latter is white and light, loose, breaks easily, and is therefore better than the male.

### Location.

In former times, Larch Sponge was brought to Venice and other distant places from the land of Agaria (from which it also received the name <term>Agaricum</term> <note>The botanical name for the medicinal sponge.</note>), located in Samaria.

Nowadays, it is brought from the <term>Trentino</term> <note>original: "Tridentinischen Lande," the region around Trento in modern-day northern Italy.</note> and other places where many larch trees grow.

### Utility.

The Larch Sponge <term>ripens</term> <note>original: "zeitiget." In medical terms, this meant bringing a "raw" humor to maturity so it could be expelled.</note>, dissolves, thins, opens, cleanses, and <term>purges</term> <note>original: "purgiret."</note> bile and watery, thick phlegm; it carries away the impure <term>humors</term>—

## Liver-Balsam.

<note>original: "Leber-Balsam." This most likely refers to Costmary (*Tanacetum balsamita*), historically used to treat liver disorders and as a general tonic.</note>

This is a herb well-known to us but very useful; it cleanses and <term>purges</term> <note>original: "laxiret."</note>, is good for wounds, serves the liver, resists rot, and kills worms—specifically if one boils this herb in wine and drinks of it. This herb is praised above all others for ailments and diseases of the liver that arise from blockages. For this reason, it is especially useful in <term>jaundice</term> <note>original: "Gelbsucht."</note> and <term>dropsy</term> <note>original: "Wassersucht." ### The Seed.

The seed of Liver-Balsam drives out roundworms.

### Externally.

If someone cannot pass water or release their urine, let them <term>fumigate</term> <note>original: "råuchere." To expose a body part to medicinal smoke.</note> themselves with the Liver-Balsam herb; the urine will flow and the sick person will find the desired relief.

### Smoke.

The smoke from this herb softens the hard swellings of the <term>womb</term> <note>original: "Beer-Mutter." Another archaic term for the uterus.</note>.

### Syrup.

The syrup of Liver-Balsam increases the appetite, strengthens the stomach, promotes digestion, expels cold <term>phlegmatic</term> moistures <note>In the humoral system, phlegm was considered a cold, moist substance; an excess was thought to cause sluggishness and congestion.</note>, and disperses flatulence in the stomach and liver.

Chaste-Lamb grows tall like a tree and has long branches that do not easily break. The bark is whitish, and the leaves resemble those of the olive tree but are larger and more delicate; five of them hang together, as with the <term>cinquefoil</term> <note>original: "Fünffinger-Kraut," literally "five-finger herb."</note>. There are two kinds: one with notched leaves, and the other with unnotched leaves. It grows in the Netherlands, France, and—

## Holly.

<note>original: "Stech-Baum." Literally "prick-tree," referring to the European Holly (*Ilex aquifolium*).</note>

Holly has the size of a <term>hawthorn</term> <note>original: "Hage-Dorn."</note>; the leaves resemble the <term>laurel tree</term> <note>original: "Lorbeer-Baum."</note>, are brownish-green, thick and firm, but set with sharp prickles around the entire edge. The bark on the branches and twigs is green, tough, and can be bent.

It bears white and fragrant blossoms, but instead of fruit, it has round red berries the size of a pea, of an unpleasant taste, which have a split pit inside.

### Uses.

A drink made from the leaves, drunk in the evening and morning, takes away and soothes <term>stiches in the side</term> <note>original: "Seiten-Stechen." Often used to describe pleurisy or sharp pains in the torso.</note> and expels the cough.

### The Berries.

If 10 to 12 pieces of the holly berries are crushed and taken, they quiet <term>abdominal cramps</term> <note>original: "Bauch-Grimmen."</note> by softening the body <note>Acting as a laxative to "soften" the stool.</note> and purging the coarse, thick humors.

### Externally.

Externally, the bark of the root, when applied—having been previously boiled and well-crushed—heals bone fractures and softens the hardening of dislocated limbs. It also disperses hard swellings and boils.

### Agrimony.

Agrimony <note>original: "Odermennige." *Agrimonia eupatoria*, a herb in the rose family long used in traditional medicine.</note> grows on a plain <note>original: "schlechten." In this period, the word often meant simple, straight, or humble rather than "bad."</note>, woody, delicate, round, and hairy stem, one <term>ell</term> <note>An old unit of measurement, roughly the length of a man's arm.</note> high or long; its tip is like an ear of grain, covered with yellow and fragrant flowers. On every stalk hang many rough and notched leaves, which are always placed two against each other; it bears a rough and elongated seed; the root is woody, blackish, and of a sharp <note>original: "gestrengen." Harsh, bitter, or astringent.</note> taste. It grows in meadows by the roads, by fences, hedges, and in uncultivated places.

### Uses of Agrimony.

The herb, seed, and root, boiled in wine or water and drunk, stills <term>dysentery</term> <note>original: "Rothe-Ruhr." Literally "red dysentery," a historical term for severe, bloody diarrhea.</note>.

### Wound-Drink.

A wound-drink is also prepared from agrimony and used for <term>fistulas</term>, internal ulcers, and for all kinds of <term>scorbutic</term> <note>original: "Scorbutischen." Relating to scurvy, a disease caused by Vitamin C deficiency, often characterized in old texts by weakness and skin sores.</note> diseases.

### Externally.

Agrimony is used externally with great benefit:
> In the dislocation of limbs.

### Victory-Root.
<note>original: "Siegmars-Wurzel." This name was historically applied to several plants, most commonly *Malva alcea* (Vervain Mallow) or *Althaea officinalis* (Marshmallow).</note>

This root is a wild variety of the mallow family <note>original: "Pappel-Geschlechts." While "Pappel" means Poplar in modern German, in early modern botanical texts it often referred to the Mallow genus (*Malvaceae*).</note>, with which it almost corresponds in terms of the similarity of the stalks, flowers, and seeds, except that the leaves have larger notches and are divided into five parts, as in the herb Buttercup <note>original: "Hanen-Fuß." Referring to the *Ranunculus* genus.</note>; the flowers are also larger and brown in color; the root is long, white, and tough; it is primarily found in Hungary and grows in the fields on the banks of streams, next to fences and roads.

### Uses of Victory-Root.

The root of this plant is used alone; this root, boiled in wine or even just in water and drunk, stills <term>dysentery</term> <note>original: "Rothe-Ruhr." A historical term for severe diarrhea involving blood.</note> and all kinds of abdominal fluxes.

This root has the same effect as mentioned if one quenches glowing pebbles in milk or plantain juice <note>original: "Wegbreit-Safft." Juice from the common plantain (*Plantago major*), a staple of medieval wound care.</note>, adds the root to it, and drinks from it.

### Externally.

A plaster made from it and placed on hard swellings disperses and softens them.

<note>original: "Sinau oder golden Gänserich." *Alchemilla vulgaris* is commonly called Lady’s Mantle or *Sinau* in old German; "golden Gänserich" (Golden Silverweed) here likely refers to its yellow-green appearance.</note>

Lady’s Mantle has round, broad, pleated leaves, which are small-notched all around and split into 7, 8, to 9 angles, so that they form something like a star or an outspread lion’s foot; therefore, it is also called "Lion’s Foot" <note>original: "Löwen-Fuß." This is a literal translation of the Greek-derived name *Leontopodium*, though here applied to Lady's Mantle.</note> by some.

It likes to grow in wet and grassy places, especially in meadows and cattle pastures; however, it is also found on hills and mountains.

# Garlic Mustard.
<note>original: "Knoblauch-Kraut." Today commonly known as Garlic Mustard (*Alliaria petiolata*), a common woodland herb.</note>

As soon as the leaves of this herb emerge from the earth, they are round and resemble the **March Violet**; <note>original: "Merzen Viol-Kraut." Referring to the Sweet Violet (*Viola odorata*).</note> but when they are fully grown, they become saw-toothed at the edges and take on almost the shape of **Lemon Balm**; when one rubs them between the fingers, they smell like garlic. It produces a stalk two ells high; <term>ell (Elle)<gloss>A historical unit of length, usually representing the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger (roughly 24 inches or 60 cm).</gloss></term> the flower is white, the seed is small, black, and enclosed in pods. The root is white, elongated, and hard.

### Benefits.

Garlic Mustard opens [blockages], disperses [humors], loosens [phlegm], cleanses, promotes the flow of urine, resists decay, and heals the bites of venomous animals.

### Medicinal Drink.

A decoction made from it and mixed with oil is used for tightness of the chest and shortness of breath.

### In Enemas.

The herb is used in enemas <note>original: "Clystiren." A liquid medical treatment administered rectally.</note> against sciatica, kidney pains, and abdominal cramps, for it disperses wind <note>Refers to intestinal gas or "flatulence" in the humoral tradition.</note> and stills the aches.

### The Seed.

The crushed seed is made into a plaster with vinegar and placed upon the female genitals, which prevents the **rising of the womb.** <note>original: "Mutter-Aufsteigen." A historical diagnosis where various physical and emotional symptoms were attributed to the uterus "wandering" or moving upward in the body.</note>

### Powdered Seed.

The seed, when powdered and held to the nose, induces sneezing, cleanses the brain, and rouses one from **lethargy.** <note>original: "Schlaf-Sucht." Literally "sleep-sickness," a term for pathologically excessive sleep or a comatose state.</note>

## For Fatigue.

The green leaves <note>Likely referring to the Garlic Mustard or Garlic mentioned on the preceding page.</note> placed under the soles of the feet, inside the shoes, draw out the heat, pain, and fatigue.

The inner bark, boiled with a little alum <note>original: "Alaun." A naturally occurring mineral salt used as an astringent.</note> in wine or water, and rubbed upon the gums, strengthens them and prevents toothache. <note>original: "Zahn-Wehe."</note>

## Chickweed or Bird-Weed.

This is a soft and succulent herb, from whose fibrous root emerge longish round stems, pale-green leaves, and white blossoms, which are most similar to those of Eyebright. <note>original: "Hüner-Darm oder Vogel-Kraut." Scientifically known as *Stellaria media*. "Augen-Trost" refers to Eyebright (*Euphrasia officinalis*), a plant traditionally used for vision issues.</note>

## Preparation and Use.

The herb Chickweed is good to use both internally and externally for the inflammation of wounds, open sores, fistulas, and St. Anthony’s Fire. <note>original: "Rothlauff." A historical term for erysipelas, a bacterial skin infection that produces a bright red, swollen rash.</note>

## The Juice.

The juice is administered to small children to combat "tearing" pains. <note>original: "Reissen." This term was used to describe sharp, pulling pains associated with colic or rheumatism.</note>

## Externally.

This herb, roasted in chamomile oil or butter, is applied over the body of children for stomach cramps, <note>original: "Bauch-Grimmen."</note> and for women, it is applied against "mother-woe." <term>mother-woe<gloss>original: "Mutter-Weh." In early modern medicine, this referred to various uterine complaints or "hysteria," which was then believed to be caused by disturbances of the womb.</gloss></term>

## For the Itch.

Boiled in water and used for washing, it cleanses itchy hands. <note>original: "Kräze." This typically referred to scabies or other parasitic skin conditions.</note>

## For Wheezing.

This herb boiled with wine and placed upon the chest removes the wheezing thereof. <note>original: "Keichen." Refers to heavy breathing or respiratory distress.</note>

## For Feverish Eyes and Ears.

The juice pressed from this herb and dripped into the eyes and ears relieves the pains therein that have arisen from heat.

### Marshmallow Root or White Mallows.

This herb has round stems upon which grow wide, notched leaves that are pointed at the tips; it bears flesh-colored <note>original: "leibfarbene." This refers to a pale pink or peach hue.</note> flowers and produces seed pods like the mallows, and it has a large, long, and tough root. <note>original: "Eibisch-Wurzel oder weisse Pappeln." ## Use and Benefits.

### The Leaves.

These purge the bowels, dissolve blockages, soften tissues, and induce a gentle sweat.

### The Root.

The root, boiled with cinnamon in water and consumed, expels the afterbirth <note>original: "After-Bürde."</note> and cleanses the womb after childbirth.

### For Coughing.

The root, boiled in mead, <note>original: "Meth." A fermented honey drink used here as a medicinal base.</note> quiets the cough and is especially beneficial for the chest and the lungs.

### Externally.

The root, mixed with a little sugar and placed upon the breast, heals sore breasts <note>original: "bösen Brüste." Likely referring to mastitis or infection.</note> and cracked nipples.

### The Leaves.

The leaves are used in poultices <note>original: "Bähungen." Warm, moist applications used to soothe pain.</note> against colic and pain in the loins.

### Against Stitches in the Side.

The leaves, boiled with chamomile flowers in wine or water, placed in a beef bladder <note>A historical method for creating a hot-water bottle or warm compress.</note> and applied warm over the painful area, quiet the stitches in the side.

## Great Burnet.

<note>original: "Tausend-Schön." While this name is now used for the Common Daisy, the description of a tall stem with purple flower spikes identifies this plant as *Sanguisorba officinalis*, also known as Great Burnet.</note>

This herb grows on a brown stem, one ell <note>A historical unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the fingertips, though it varied by region.</note> in height. At its summit and at the nodes <note>original: "Gleichen." The joints or segments along the plant stem.</note>, simple purple-colored flower spikes emerge. The stem is covered with long, wide, and pointed leaves. Within the blossom lies a hidden black, smooth, and shiny seed. The root is white, fibrous, and has a puckering <note>original: "anziehenden." Referring to an astringent quality that causes a drawing sensation in the mouth.</note> taste.

### Preparation and Use.

The flowers are cold and dry and are slightly astringent. Therefore, a drink made from them is highly praised for all kinds of bleeding and abdominal discharges, including coughing up blood, blood in the urine, intestinal flux, ruptures <note>original: "Durchbruch." This can refer to hernias or internal tears.</note>, dysentery, excessive menstruation, and "white flux" <note>term: leukorrhea (a thick whitish or yellowish vaginal discharge).</note> in women.

### Externally.

The herb and flowers, boiled in water and placed upon crushed limbs, dissolve clotted blood <note>original: "gelieferte Geblüt."</note>. Boiled in wine and used as a warm compress <note>original: "gebähet."</note>, it is good for an excessive flow from the "golden vein" <note>term: hemorrhoids (historically referred to as the "golden vein").</note> and for bowel movements.

### The Root.

## Brooklime or Brook-Beans.

<note>original: "Bach-Bungen oder Bach-Bonen." The plant *Veronica beccabunga*, known for its use in treating scurvy.</note>

Brooklime grows a thick and branching stem, two spans <note>A span (Spannen) is an old unit of measurement based on the distance between the tip of the thumb and the tip of the little finger, roughly 9 inches or 23 cm.</note> high, with round, juicy, and thick leaves like those of beans, and purple-colored flowers from which pouches grow that become full of small seeds. It is gathered in June, early before sunrise.

### Preparation and Use.

The herb Brooklime is a good wound-healing, scurvy-fighting, pain-stilling, and diuretic <note>original: "Harn-und Steintreibendes." Literally "urine- and stone-driving."</note> herb; indeed, it is used with no small benefit for scurvy and scorbutic mouth-rot <note>original: "Mund-Fäule." Ulcerative sores in the mouth, a common symptom of scurvy.</note> (placed in goat whey with scurvy-grass <note>original: "Löffel-Kraut." *Cochlearia officinalis*, another plant high in Vitamin C.</note> and watercress <note>original: "Brunkressen." *Nasturtium officinale*.</note> and drunk therefrom). It opens the obstruction of the monthly cleansing <note>Menstruation.</note>, drives out bladder and kidney stones, and kills worms.

### Externally.

Used as a fomentation <note>original: "gebähet." A warm, moist medicinal application.</note>, it serves for swelling of the buttocks and for the "blind, hidden golden vein" <note>original: "blinden heimlichen goldnen Ader." A historical euphemism for internal hemorrhoids.</note>. It also heals scorbutic ulcers and injuries on the shins when boiled in beer and applied as a poultice. Likewise, for inflammations and "wild fire" <note>original: "wilde Feuer." Often refers to Erysipelas, a skin infection characterized by a red, spreading rash.</note> (when roasted in butter and applied warm); when applied over with saltpeter and salt, it dissolves the swelling of the thighs in cases of dropsy <note>original: "Wassersucht." Edema, or swelling caused by the accumulation of fluids.</note>.

### The Pressed Juice.

This juice dispels rashes <note>original: "Flechten."</note> and pimples in the face when one rubs it on. It also cures blue, bruised eyes and spots on the skin where blood has run underneath.

### A Bath.

A bath made from this herb is particularly useful for the hands and feet.

## Dill.

This is a well-known herb; its leaves or tips, flowers, seeds, and root disperse [blockages], ripen [abscesses], promote urine, still pains, bring sleep, drive away unchaste desires, resist poison, and are good for a cold stomach. They are proven against stones, painful urination <note>original: "Harn-Winde." Historically refers to strangury or the sensation of needing to urinate with difficulty passing it.</note>, obstruction of the urine, and the monthly time <note>original: "Monath-Zeit." A period-appropriate term for menstruation.</note>.

### Tips of the Dill.

When wine is poured over these tips and drunk, it expels wind <note>In historical medicine, "winds" referred to gas or vapors causing bloating and discomfort.</note> and relieves griping in the belly.

### Externally.

Applied externally as a poultice, it consumes swellings and hemorrhoids <note>original: "Feigblättern." Literally "fig-leaves," a historical term for hemorrhoids or genital warts, so named for their appearance.</note>.

### The Root.

The root, crushed and placed upon painful ears, stills the pain.

### The Steam.

Catching the steam from the boiled herb disperses the swelling of the womb <note>original: "Aufblähen der Mutter." Refers to bloating or "suffocation of the mother," a common historical diagnosis for various uterine and abdominal distresses.</note>.

### The Distilled Water.

Water distilled from this herb promotes [breast] milk, disperses wind in the stomach and intestines, induces sleep and urination, and cleanses the womb and bladder of stones.

### The Oil.

This warms, softens, disperses, and lessens pain; therefore, it is useful against febrile chills <note>original: "Febrilischen Schauer." The shivering fits associated with the onset of a fever.</note>, to smear upon the backbone and the tensed parts when the fever comes on.

## Angelica, or Breast- and Air-Root.
<note>original: "Angelicke oder Brust- und Lufft-Wurzel." These names refer to the plant's use in treating chest ailments and its aromatic, "airy" qualities.</note>

This grows on a knobby, hollow, and empty stem, over two ells <note>An "ell" (Elle) was a traditional unit of length, usually about 24 inches or 60 cm.</note> high, with elongated leaves that are notched at the edges and a juicy green color; it is otherwise well-known.

### Preparation and Use.

Angelica root in general: it opens <note>In historical medicine, "opening" referred to clearing blockages in the body's vessels or pores.</note>, thins the humors, promotes sweat, urine, and the expulsion of poison; it is good for wounds and benefits the stomach, the chest, the heart, and the womb <note>original: "Mutter."</note>.

A small amount of it eaten removes heartburn <note>original: "Sod."</note> and drunkenness, disperses winds <note>flatulence or gas</note>, kills worms, and serves against scurvy <note>original: "Scharbock."</note>, side-stitches, cold and damp coughs, and shortness of breath <note>original: "Engbrüstigkeit."</note>.

### The Oil.

The oil is applied externally for pains in the stomach and body. Taken internally with hyssop-water, it is used against short breath.

### The Seed.

The seed, when chewed or smelled, strengthens the stomach, aids digestion, and prevents vomiting and hiccups.

### The Seed.

It is also beneficial to those burdened with coughing, lung disease, and consumption <note>original: "Schwindsucht." ### The Oil.

The oil warms, dries, and promotes urination. It benefits the stomach and chest and is good against paralysis of the tongue; it restores lost speech if a few drops are allowed to fall upon the tongue.

# Silverweed, or Goosegrass.
<note>original: "Gänserich. Oder Silber-Kraut." Scientifically known as Potentilla anserina, prized for the silvery underside of its leaves.</note>

This herb creeps along the ground with its stems, similar to those of the mouse-ear <note>original: "Mäuß-öhrlein." Likely referring to Mouse-ear hawkweed (Pilosella officinarum).</note>. Its notched leaves are green on top and whitish underneath; its golden-yellow flowers stand on a separate stem, and the root is red on the outside but white inside. It grows in mossy places, in meadows, and along paths and fences.

# Preparation and Use.

The leaves or the entire silverweed herb are cold in nature; generally, it is astringent <note>original: "ziehet es an."</note>, stops bleeding, and is an excellent wound-herb. It stills the spitting of blood, bowel and uterine fluxes <note>original: "Mutter-Flüsse." Any abnormal discharge from the womb.</note>, diarrhea, dysentery <note>original: "Rothe-Ruhr." Literally "the red flux," a severe form of diarrhea involving blood.</note>, excessive menstruation, and the "white flux" <note>original: "weissen Weiber-Fluß." Leucorrhea.</note>. For these, one should boil the herb along with the root in red wine or steeled water <note>original: "gestählten Wasser." Water in which red-hot steel or iron has been quenched, believed to absorb the metal's strengthening properties.</note> and drink it in the morning and evening.

## Healing-Antidote.
<note>original: "Heyl-Gifft." This likely refers to *Vincetoxicum hirundinaria* (Swallow-wort) or *Aconitum anthora* (Healing Wolfsbane). These plants were historically called "Healing-Poison" because they were believed to act as a counter-poison or antidote to toxins and the plague.</note>

This herb grows a stiff, hairy, and angular stem, from which many subtle, divided branches spring; at the summit, it bears pale yellow, sweet-smelling flowers. When these have fallen away, small pods are found, which contain many black and useful seeds. The root consists of 2, sometimes 3 or 4 elongated bulbs, which almost resemble olives, having a brown skin on the outside but a white, bitter flesh within.

### The Root.

The root of the **Healing-Antidote**, powdered and taken in milk or wine, opens, cleanses, induces vomiting, drives out sweat, and resists all poison. Therefore, it is useful and good against all poisonous diseases, the plague, and all kinds of infectious, evil fevers; also for griping of the belly <note>original: "Bauch-Grimmen." ### Externally.

Applied externally as a plaster, it is useful for the blockages and swellings of milk <note>Likely referring to mastitis or clogged milk ducts in nursing mothers.</note>.

### The Pressed Juice.

This is good for poisoned wounds and plague-boils <note>The "buboes" or swellings associated with the bubonic plague.</note> when simply spread upon them.

### The Leaves.

The leaves, together with the flowers, when crushed and applied as a poultice, draw splinters and thorns out of wounds.

### Preparation and Use.

**Snapdragon** <note>original: "Dorant." Likely *Antirrhinum majus*. ## Cleavers.
<note>original: "Kleb-Kraut." *Galium aparine*, also known as goosegrass or bedstraw. It is famous for the tiny hooked bristles that allow it to cling to clothing and fur.</note>

This herb produces thin, rough, four-cornered stems set with many branches, around which narrow and rough leaves grow out in a star-shaped circle <note>A botanical whorl.</note>. White flowers appear on the stems, upon which a grey, hollowed, round seed ripens; it soon looks like a navel and, like the leaves and stems of the herb, sticks firmly to clothing. The root is delicate and has many fibers.

### Use and Preparation.

Taken internally, this herb—including its stems, leaves, and seeds—heals, opens, dispels <note>original: "zertheilet." Refers to the medicinal action of breaking up "congealed" humors or blockages.</note>, cleanses, and purifies.

Dysentery.</note>, jaundice, side-stitches, and the chest and stomach pains of children.

# Garden Parsley.

They drive out stones, gravel, and urine, and promote the monthly period. They are good for blockages of the liver, spleen, and stomach, and they cleanse the kidneys and bladder if one presses out the juice and drinks it mixed with vinegar and salt.

It serves externally for hot ulcers, black eyes, and bruises <note>original: "Mählern." Marks or spots on the skin.</note>. ### Stone Parsley.

It grows leaves like common parsley, though somewhat smaller, and has a thick, hollow, and branched stalk. At the top, it has umbels <note>A flower cluster where stalks spring from a common center, like an umbrella.</note> with white flowers, followed by a fragrant, somewhat bitter seed that resembles garden parsley. It has a single, fragrant, juicy, and sharp-tasting root.

### Preparation and Use of the Seed.

This is hot and dry in the second degree <note>The "degrees" refer to the intensity of a plant's qualities (heat/cold/moisture/dryness) according to Galenic medicine.</note>; it thins [the humors], opens, promotes urine and the monthly period, benefits the liver and resists poison, is used for theriac <note>A famous ancient "universal" antidote and cure-all composed of many ingredients.</note>, and serves against sorcery. Its remaining virtues correspond with those of common parsley.

### Mountain Parsley.

Its stalk grows from a small root to the height of an ell <note>An old unit of measurement, roughly the length of a forearm (about 24 inches).</note>, with branches and flowers. The seed is elongated and smells like cumin. It grows in mountainous, sandy, and stony places. It is also sown in gardens.

### Use and Preparation, internally.

The seed, along with the root, is warm and dry in the 3rd degree; it thins, opens, disperses, promotes sweat and urine, breaks the stone, aids the monthly period, and resists poison; it serves for those ob-

## Common Marsh Parsley.
<note>Known in modern botany as *Apium graveolens*, also called Wild Celery or Smallage.</note>

This grows in swampy places, in streams and puddles, especially among brooklime <note>original: "Bach-Bungen." Brooklime (*Veronica beccabunga*) is a succulent herb found in wet areas.</note>. It develops a hollow, striped, and knotted stem of moderate height; elongated, notched, shiny, and strong-smelling leaves; at the top of the stem, white flowers appear, followed by a small seed. The root, which resembles parsley, is surrounded at the top by many small fibers. One collects the seed when the sun enters the sign of Leo <note>This refers to late July or August, highlighting the importance of astrological timing in early modern herbalism.</note>.

### Preparation and Internal Uses.

Its root and seed are hot in the second degree and dry in the third <note>In Galenic medicine, plants were classified by degrees of "heat" and "dryness" to balance the body's humors.</note>; they open, cut through <note>meaning to break up thick fluids or phlegm</note>, and cleanse. It benefits the liver, spleen, and womb <note>original: "Mutter." Referring to the uterus.</note>, promotes urine, and breaks up stones. It is used against blockages of the liver and spleen, jaundice and dropsy <note>original: "Wassersucht." Edema or swelling caused by fluid retention.</note>, suppressed urine and menstrual cycles <note>original: "Monats-Zeit."</note>, uterine pains and afterpains, gravel, and stones—if one eats the root in the morning. When chewed, the root helps with toothaches, dim-sightedness <note>original: "blöde Gesichter." Refers to weak or clouded vision.</note>, and abdominal cramps.

### External Uses.

One crushes and mashes the herb and leaves to apply them as a poultice; this dispels blue marks <note>bruises</note> resulting from falls, bumps, and blows. It likewise helps with clotted and excessive milk in nursing women if the root and herb are boiled in spearmint water <note>original: "Krausemünz-Wasser."</note> or vinegar—adding coriander and caraway <note>original: "Kümmel."</note>—and applied. It serves against stones and urinary blockages when used in baths. The distilled water is praised for the previously mentioned ailments. The juice is used for tertian fever <note>A fever that reoccurs every three days, often associated with malaria.</note>—mixed with sage juice and wine vinegar, two *Loth* <note>A traditional German unit of weight, roughly 15-16 grams.</note> of each. It is also used for clotted blood in the stomach when taken with honey; for swelling of the throat and tonsils when used in a gargle with barley water and honey of roses <note>original: "Rosen-Honig." A medicinal preparation of honey infused with rose petals.</note>; and dripped into old, putrid wounds and sores with honey of roses. The ointment serves to soften and heal hard, swollen breasts, as well as to cleanse and cure ulcers infected by cancer and other impure, malignant sores.

### Columbine.
<note>original: "Agley." Modern botanical name: *Aquilegia vulgaris*.</note>

This herb is sown in gardens and also grows wild in damp meadows. It blooms in June and July; for <term>distilled water</term>, it is gathered in August, including both the herb and the root. It is a branchy herb with blue-green leaves that resemble <term>Greater Celandine</term> <note>original: "Schell-Kraut."</note>; it produces thin, reddish stems about one and a half <term>feet</term> <note>original: "Schuh." A historical unit of measurement roughly equivalent to a modern foot.</note> high, which bear blue flowers at the top, similar to <term>Larkspur</term> <note>original: "Ritter-Spor."</note>. When these have finished blooming, five small pods appear, containing a small black seed. Its root is long, white, and as thick as a finger.

### Use and Preparation.

The seed, flowers, and herb are hot and dry in the first degree <note>According to Galenic medicine, this mild "heat" was used to balance "cold" illnesses.</note>. Taken internally, it opens [the body], promotes sweat and urine, and expels poison; it is a good <term>vulnerary</term> <note>An herb used for healing wounds.</note>; it serves against obstructions of the lungs, liver, and spleen, and against the flow of bile, <term>asthma</term> <note>original: "Engbrüstigkeit."</note>, <term>quartan fever</term> <note>original: "viertägige Fieber." A form of malaria where fever recurs every four days.</note>, dropsy, jaundice, and <term>epilepsy</term> <note>original: "fallende Sucht."</note>, stomach ache, obstructed menstruation, and stones. If the root is consumed on an empty stomach, it is good against the plague and infectious, poisonous diseases. The seed is useful in difficult labor if it is crushed and taken in wine; it also aids in jaundice (if made into a milk), measles and smallpox, hot and poisonous illnesses, and vertigo if the liver should be obstructed, as well as in the <term>rising of the womb</term> <note>original: "aufsteigen der Mutter." A historical diagnosis for various female health complaints, often attributed to the displacement of the uterus.</note>. The flowers are a heart-strengthener, especially for those who know how to make a syrup from them.

### External Uses.

Externally, this herb is useful for wounds, <term>fistulas</term>, and ulcers of the nose and mouth if the juice is dripped into them; it treats <term>thrush</term> <note>original: "Mundfäule."</note>, inflammation of the throat, neck, and windpipe when prepared as a gargle. The distilled water is powerful for [inducing] sweat, expelling poison, and treating dangerous illnesses, pestilential fevers, measles, smallpox, heart tremors, fainting, obstructed liver and spleen, abdominal pains, and throat ulcers if one gargles with it. The tincture is used for <term>scorbutic</term> <note>related to scurvy (Scharbock).</note> mouth rot; the conserve, syrup, and honey are used to strengthen the heart in cases of malignant fevers. The wine prepared from it restores lost <term>virility</term> <note>original: "Mannheit."</note> and infertility caused by <term>evil spells</term> <note>original: "böse Beusen." Likely a reference to "Nestelknüpfen" or magical hexes thought to cause impotence.</note>. Its vinegar is also used externally for weaknesses, fainting, and hot fevers; the ointment is used against rotten...

## Tree of Life.
<note>original: "Baum des Lebens." Likely *Thuja occidentalis*, the Northern White-cedar, which was introduced to Europe from North America in the 16th century.</note>

Since this shrub was brought over to us from Canada in North America, it is also found in various gardens. The leaves, which turn somewhat pale-yellow in winter, become green again in spring; it is propagated through broken-off branches. Otherwise, it is a strong-smelling, bitter little tree, whose trunk grows straight up and is covered with a blackish bark. It has durable wood; the leaves resemble the <term>Savin Juniper</term> <note>original: "Saven-hier zu Land sieben Baum." *Juniperus sabina*.</note>, and like those, they are mostly green. At the ends of the branches, it puts forth yellowish flowers with elongated fibers.

### Preparation and Use.

The little tree is of a warm and dry nature; it thins, consumes, and cleanses <term>tartaric phlegm</term> <note>original: "tartarischen Schleimen." In early modern medicine, "tartar" referred to stony or hardened metabolic waste or deposits within the body.</note>. If the branches are tied to the nose in cases of congestion, it induces nosebleeds. The leaves, distilled water, and oil soothe external <term>gout</term> <note>original: "Podagra." Historically, this term specifically referred to gout in the foot.</note> pains.

## Strawberry Tree.
<note>original: "Erdbeer-Baum." *Arbutus unedo*.</note>

This grows willingly in fertile lands, on mountains, in forests, and meadows; it blooms from July until toward September, and finally the fruit arrives. The leaves are like the Laurel tree and the <term>Holm Oak</term> <note>original: "Stein-Eiche."</note>; the fruits are not much larger than a hazelnut, though sometimes they grow as large as small apples and resemble a strawberry.

### Preparation and Use.

The fruit is not very beneficial to the stomach. Dyers use the leaves, but the root is said to be good against the plague and poison. The water distilled from the leaves and blossoms is highly praised during poisonous and pestilential times.

The root is round, fibrous, and crinkled.

## False Hollow-wort.
<note>Likely *Corydalis cava*, also known as Holewort or Bulbous Fumitory.</note>

It likes to grow in thorn-hedges, vineyards, and shaded places; it emerges in the early spring, blooming in March and April. It grows a thin stem a span high, with pale-green colored leaves like <term>fumitory</term> <note>original: "Erdrauch." *Fumaria officinalis*, a plant often used to treat skin conditions.</note>; it bears purple-red flowers, a small black shining seed enclosed in broad pods, and a round, knotty, fibrous root that is hollow underneath.

### Preparation and internal use.

The root is hot in the 2nd degree and dry in the 3rd degree <note>This refers to the Galenic system of humors, which categorized medicines by their perceived temperature and moisture levels.</note>; it cleanses, opens, and attracts everything evil to itself like a magnet. It promotes sweat and urine: it serves the <term>womb</term> <note>original: "Mutter."</note>, liver, poison, and wounds, cleanses the blood, and induces sweat in cases of <term>the itch</term> <note>original: "Kräze," or scabies.</note>. If the powder is mixed with laurel, it stills coarse humors and the pains arising therefrom. If it is mixed with other anti-scorbutic things, it heals <term>scurvy-related shortness of breath</term>. If women consume it in wine, it promotes the monthly time, expels a stillborn fruit and the cleansing after birth, and is also good for jaundice.

### Externally.

It cleanses wounds and fistulas, heals the <term>itch</term> <note>original: "Kräze," usually referring to scabies or other itchy skin eruptions.</note> and eases <term>gouty pains</term> <note>original: "Podagrische Schmerzen." ## Hedge Mustard <note>original: "Heydenreich," likely referring to Sisymbrium officinale or a similar plant in the mustard family.</note>

It grows in fields by streams and in valleys; it blooms in June and July. It soon looks like mustard or <term>stinking-weed</term> <note>original: "Staucken," an archaic name for certain field weeds.</note> leaves; it has branching stems that are rough and hairy; it bears whitish flowers like <term>rocket</term> <note>original: "Raucken," referring to arugula or similar cruciferous plants.</note>, which are marked with blue stripes, and elongated pods, a finger long, which are shaped like a <term>scorpion's tail</term> when ripe; the root is white, single, and divided.

### Internal Use and Preparation.

The root cuts through, thins, opens, and dissolves [congested humors]; it promotes urine, breaks the <term>stone</term> <note>Refers to kidney or bladder stones.</note>, and is effective against <term>scurvy</term> <note>original: "Scharbock."</note>, the stone, <term>dropsy</term> <note>original: "Wassersucht," the historical term for edema or swelling caused by fluid retention.</note>, and <term>suppressed menstruation</term> <note>original: "verhaltene Weiber-Zeit."</note>, if the juice is taken with wine; it also softens the milk in the breasts. The seed also promotes urine.

### Externally.

The <term>spirit</term> <note>An alcoholic distillation or tincture.</note> of the root serves externally for the <term>wasting of the body</term> <note>original: "Abnehmen des Leibes," referring to muscular atrophy or general physical decline.</note>, if one has withered limbs and rubs it on diligently, covering it well with warm cloths; thus the marrow in the bones is strengthened and the nerves <note>In historical medicine, "nerves" often referred collectively to nerves, tendons, and ligaments.</note> become more supple.

## Arnica <note>original: "Wolverley," an old folk name for Arnica montana.</note>

It grows on mountains and meadows and blooms throughout the summer. It has leaves like <term>plantain</term> <note>original: "Wegrich."</note> and a stem an <term>ell</term> <note>original: "Ehlen," a historical unit of length roughly equal to the distance from the elbow to the fingertips.</note> high, upon which a round, yellow flower shaped like an eye emerges. The root is bitter and sharp.

## Internal Use and Benefit.

The herb, along with its flowers, warms, dries, and thins <note>In the humoral theory of medicine, "thinning" refers to reducing the viscosity of bodily fluids like blood or phlegm to allow them to flow better.</note>, induces sweating and urination, provokes vomiting, and dissolves the blue marks <note>original: "blaue Mähler," referring to bruises.</note> that men strike onto women's faces with their fists; it dispels fevers when boiled in beer and drunk. The root is penetrating; it promotes the flow of urine and the <term>monthly flux</term> <note>original: "Monath-Fluß," a common historical term for menstruation.</note> when boiled in wine, and, taken internally, it heals the bites of toads and worms.

## Mugwort <note>original: "Beyfuß" (Artemisia vulgaris). A staple of medieval and early modern herbalism, often associated with women's health and protection for travelers.</note>

It grows in stony land, in fields by the paths, and in gardens; it blooms in July and August, but the herb is collected in June. It has high, branching stems that are white and red, with deeply notched leaves that are green on top and whitish underneath. The flowers look almost like wormwood flowers, in which a small round seed ripens. The root is woody, a finger’s length, and <term>fibrous</term> <note>original: "zassericht."</note>.

## Internal Use and Preparation.

It opens, dissolves, and cleanses. It is a good herb for the <term>mother</term> <note>original: "Mutter." In this period, "the mother" was a common term for the uterus or womb.</note>, for promoting urine and the stone, and for stilling pains in the nerves; it also promotes the monthly flux, childbirth, and the afterbirth. If one boils **red mugwort** with lavender seeds in beer and adds the root, it expels a <term>stillbirth</term> <note>original: "todte Geburt."</note>. In the throes of labor, it is placed upon the navel; it also stills <term>pains of the mother</term> <note>uterine cramps or hysteria.</note>, <term>strangury</term> <note>original: "Harn-Winde," referring to painful, drop-by-drop urination.</note>, "stone-water" <note>likely referring to the painful passing of urinary calculi.</note>, and jaundice. For stomach ache, it is applied with bitter almond oil. For <term>gout</term> <note>original: "Gicht."</note>, the root is eaten or the person is <term>fomented</term> <note>original: "gebähet," meaning treated with warm, moist medicinal compresses.</note> with the boiled herb. For trembling of the limbs, the juice is rubbed on with rose oil. For paralyzed limbs, it is used as a fomentation with chamomile flowers, <term>agrimony</term> <note>original: "Odermennig."</note>, rosemary, and sage, having first been boiled in wine. It is good for aching limbs after a long illness. The [distilled] water promotes the "women’s time," birth, and cleansing; it warms the stomach, aids sleep, dispels coughing, and opens a congested liver, the kidneys, and the urinary tracts; it aids in dropsy and jaundice, and crushes the stone. The **Extract** and the **Syrup** stimulate the <term>women's flowers</term> <note>original: "Weiber-Blume," another euphemism for the menstrual cycle.</note>, open obstructions, and are useful for uterine complaints, <term>convulsions</term> <note>original: "Frayß," a term often used for seizures or "the fits," particularly in children.</note>, and <term>stroke</term> <note>original: "Schlag," referring to apoplexy.</note>. The **Conserve** dispels <term>green sickness</term> <note>original: "Bleich-Sucht," an old term for a type of anemia (chlorosis) that primarily affected young women.</note>. The **Oil** is good for gouty pains when rubbed on with olive oil. The **Salt** is used against pestilential, feverish diseases.

### German Ginger <note>original: "Teutscher Ingber." This refers to *Arum maculatum*, known today by many names including Cuckoo-pint, Lords-and-Ladies, or Wild Arum. Despite the name, it is not related to true ginger.</note>

This grows willingly in rich soil and shaded places; the leaves appear as early as March, the flowers in June, and it ripens in July and August. The root is dug in March. It produces broad, heart-shaped, spotted leaves, each on its own separate stalk; between them, a straight stem shoots upward, looking like a rabbit's ear, within which is the flower and eventually the seeds. From this emerges a growth resembling a cluster of grapes, full of "horns" <note>This refers to the berry-like fruit spikes.</note> which are first green and later become red. The root is white, tuberous, and fibrous.

### Internal Use and Preparation.

The root thins, cuts through, opens, and disperses <note>These terms describe the humoral action of breaking up thick or stagnant fluids in the body.</note>. It is useful for the stomach, the chest, an unhealthy body, and serves to promote urine and expel poison. It is praised for its ability to combat <term>tartaric humors</term> <note>In the medical tradition of Paracelsus, "tartar" referred to stony or gravel-like deposits in the body, similar to the scale found in wine barrels.</note>, to strengthen and warm the stomach, to aid digestion, and to stimulate the appetite. It is also used against wheezing, old coughs, and obstructions of the intestines, liver, spleen, and <term>mesenteric veins</term> <note>original: "Gekröß-Adern."</note>. It treats "windy melancholy" <note>Depression or anxiety believed to be caused by digestive gases.</note>, scurvy, a poor constitution, and the pale complexion of young women <note>likely referring to chlorosis or "green sickness," a form of anemia.</note>. It is also used for beginning stages of dropsy, quartan and lingering fevers, <term>falling sickness</term> <note>Epilepsy.</note>, the "rising of the mother" <note>original: "Aufsteigen der Mutter," a historical term for hysteria or uterine displacement.</note>, loss of speech, stones, gout, hip pain, hernias, and poison.

### External Use.

For carbuncles, <term>fig-warts</term> <note>original: "Feigblattern," referring to hemorrhoids or similar skin growths.</note>, prolapse of the rectum, the "golden vein" <note>Hemorrhoids.</note>, and facial spots. The water distilled from the root is good for the plague, hernias, unclean wounds, nosebleeds, and pits or marks on the skin; the leaves, however, are used for scurvy. The prepared root is used for ailments arising from "tough humors." **Dr. Biermann’s Stomach Powder**, for which this root is the primary ingredient, serves to treat stomach pain, <term>heart-tension</term> <note>original: "Hertz-Gespann," a term for cramping in the upper abdomen or cardiac anxiety.</note>, headaches, dizziness, spleen ailments, discoloration of the skin, stones, quartan fevers, and many other resulting complaints; anyone who wishes to be healthy can contemplate the virtues listed above to apply it further.

### Sugar Cane.

This grows in the East and West Indies, as well as in Africa and Asia; in Europe

The flower is hairy; the roots resemble the common reed but are not as salty and have much sweet juice.

## Internal Use and Preparation.

There are many kinds of sugar, such as: Madeira, Loaf [Melis], brown farin, or St. Thomas, Valerhin, or Valerh sugar. It is called fine, superfine, candy, white and red rock candy, food-mixed farin, and Cassonade <note>original: "Cassau," a type of raw or semi-refined sugar.</note> sugar, sugar-honey, and syrup—called white or black rock-candy syrup, or common syrup. All sugar is heating, yet balsamic: it serves the chest and stomach, softens, and acts as a laxative; used in clysters <note>An enema.</note>, it quenches thirst when mixed in wine. The fine kind makes humors thinner, cuts through, and cleanses; the common kind soothes, makes smooth, and is therefore good for lung complaints; both kinds of rock candy are useful for a hoarse voice, sharpness in the chest, coughs, and to promote expectoration.

## External [Use].

It is used in wounds; because of its acidification, it harms those afflicted with fevers and <term>scurvy</term> <note>original: "Scharbock."</note>. Twisted sugar is given to children for coughs; *Diapenidion* <note>An ancient medicinal confection or lozenge made of sugar, starch, and sometimes almond milk, used for respiratory relief.</note> is proven for ailments of the chest and throat, wheezing, coughs, consumption [tuberculosis], lung disease, stitches in the side, and the spitting of pus or blood. The prepared rose sugar and violet cakes also perform this; *Manus Christi* cakes <note>literally "Hand of Christ"; a traditional medicinal sugar lozenge, often flavored with rose water or containing ground pearls, used as a general tonic.</note> refresh, draw out, strengthen the heart, and expel poison. The syrup made with spirit of wine <note>alcohol</note> is powerful for ailments of the throat and lungs; the liquid made with egg white is for a rough throat and children’s coughs; externally it is for red eyes, and the essence and crystals for hoarseness and coughs. The water or spirit distilled from this is good for stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note> and is suitable for dissolving hard obstructions. The oil and salt of sugar are not highly regarded.

## Common Reed.

This grows frequently in ponds, puddles, and marshy places; it bears long, many-knotted, hollow stalks, stands on a fibrous root, and the blossom looks like ostrich feathers.

### Use and Preparation.

The root is moderately cold, thins [the humors], and cleanses; it serves to treat stones <note>Kidney or bladder stones.</note>. Externally, it is used against pock-marks <note>Scars left by smallpox.</note>, displaced limbs, hair loss, and scalp-scab <note>original: "Haupt-Grind," likely referring to crusty skin conditions like favus or seborrheic dermatitis.</note>; the ash is used by women in childbed for a foot-bath. The leaves are used externally for inflammations and <term>erysipelas</term> <note>original: "Rothlauf," a bacterial skin infection characterized by a large, raised red patch.</note>. Otherwise, an incomparable cooling ointment is made from this reed-stalk: if one burns the stalks and moistens and stirs the black ash with tree-oil <note>Usually olive oil.</note>, mixing in other cooling substances such as white lead <note>original: "Bleyweiß," a lead-based pigment used historically in ointments, despite its toxicity.</note>, it stills the burning in hot ulcers. Otherwise, the master linen-weavers know this reed very well <note>Reeds were used to make the "comb" or "reed" part of a loom that separates warp threads.</note>.

## Spanish Reed.

It is planted in Italy <note>original: "Welschland," a historical German term for southern, Romance-language-speaking lands, particularly Italy.</note> in damp vineyards; it has thick, strong, hollow, jointed stalks, ten ells <note>An ell (Ehle) was a unit of length roughly equal to the reach of an arm.</note> high, which, when cut, provide sticks and poles.

### Preparation and Internal Use.

The root is cold and dry; it is good for kidney-pain, and to promote urine and the <term>menses</term> <note>original: "Weiber-Blume," literally "women's flowers."</note>.

### External.

For scorpion stings and to draw out thorns. The burnt bark is hot and dry; it makes hair grow.

## Asarabacca.

<note>original: "Hasel-Wurtz." *Asarum europaeum*, also known as Hazelwort or Wild Spikenard.</note>
Is gladly found in shady, mountainous places near hazel-bushes. It is always green, but in spring it always gets new leaves and flowers. It has round, firm leaves similar to wintergreen, under which are many thin, jointed, crooked roots; from these, purple-brown, fragrant flowers emerge, which resemble the seed-vessels of henbane and contain an angular seed like grape-pips.

### Preparation and Internal Use.

The root together with the leaves thins, cuts through, and opens <note>Refers to "opening" blockages in the body's vessels or organs.</note>

## Asparagus.

It is grown in vegetable gardens in rich soil; it sprouts in April, the berries ripen in August, and one collects the leaves in September. From its long, round, thick shoots, a jagged stem grows up with thin leaves, like those of dill, and yellow flowers, followed by berries like coral which contain a brown seed within them. The root is white, spongy, and tangled.

### Preparation and Internal Use.

The root and seed are of a heating nature; they promote urine, break the stone <note>Kidney or bladder stones.</note>, and open the liver, spleen, kidneys, and bladder.

### Externally.

It does good in mouthwashes for toothache and loose teeth.

### White Asphodel Root.

Grows in all gardens; blooms in May and June, and is propagated by transplanting the roots. It grows a stalk one and a half feet high, with white star-shaped flowers; it has long, narrow, three-sided leaves and elongated, tuberous roots.

### Preparation and Internal Use.

The root and seeds are hot and dry in the first degree <note>According to Galenic medicine, plants were classified by degrees of "heat" and "moisture" to balance the body's humors.</note>, promote urine, break up the stone <note>Likely referring to kidney or bladder stones.</note>, and open the liver, spleen, kidneys, and urinary bladder.

### Externally.

Used in mouthwashes for toothaches and loose teeth; the shoots create an appetite for eating and promote urine, stimulate sexual desire, and serve for jaundice and the onset of <term>dropsy</term> <note>original: "Wassersucht," an old term for edema or swelling caused by fluid retention.</note>, stones, side-aches, the spitting of blood, cramps, and coughing.

### Externally.

Used for the itch <term>scabies</term> <note>original: "Kräze."</note>, goiters <note>original: "Kröpffe," a swelling of the neck or thyroid.</note>, snake and scorpion bites, <term>fig-warts</term> <note>original: "Feyg-Warzen," a historical term for hemorrhoids or skin growths.</note>, rotting sores, and frozen or chapped hands and feet; the burnt root is used for <term>proud flesh</term> <note>original: "wilden Fleisch," an overgrowth of granulation tissue during wound healing.</note> and to promote hair growth.

### Garden Orache, or as it is pronounced in other places, Melle.

This is grown in gardens and blooms in June, July, and August; it is sown annually. It grows on a straight stalk 3 ells <note>original: "Ehlen," a historical unit of measurement roughly the length of a forearm.</note> high and develops wide leaves that are pointed at the front; these are pale green on the white variety and dark green on the red variety; [the former] has yellow flowers, while the latter has dark red flowers. The root is long and jagged.

### Preparation and Use.

The herb is cold in the first and moist in the second degree; it softens, disperses, and moves the bowels <meta>catchword: bowels</meta>

## Stinking Orache.
<note>original: "Stinckende Melle." Likely *Chenopodium vulvaria*, known for its strong, fishy odor.</note>

Grows by the fences in several gardens; it bears blossoms and seeds in high summer. It produces leaves almost identical to good orache, appearing a light blue. The flowers and seeds form small clusters. The root is thin and fibrous; the whole herb stinks greatly.

### Preparation and external use.

The herb dries and cleanses; it serves externally for the <term>rising of the mother</term> <note>original: "aufsteigen der Mutter," a historical diagnosis for "hysteria" where the uterus was believed to migrate upward, causing distress.</note>, rotting and worm-infested wounds, and old injuries.

## Smooth Oats, otherwise written as Hafer.

It loves manured and moist soil; its harvest falls in August. The oats bear wide-spreading ears atop long stalks, in which many elongated seed-grains are tucked; the root is fibrous. Otherwise, there is a type of oat that bears a panicle, cob, or tuft at the top like millet; it shoots up very high, almost like rye, has a yellowish stiff stalk, and is very profitable for the farmer.

### Internal use and benefit.

The seed, which is warm and dry, when placed warm upon the body in a small bag with some roasted salt, stills the <term>griping</term> <note>original: "Grimmen," referring to sharp abdominal cramps or colic.</note> and uterine pains. Peeled and boiled, it is useful for throat inflammation, hoarseness, bad wheezing, and coughing.

### Externally.

For spots on the skin and face. The <term>groats</term> <note>original: "Gräß," likely referring to oat groats or a decoction of the grain.</note> are good and healthy for those with fevers; the flour for <term>scalp-scab</term> <note>original: "Haupt-Grind," likely referring to fungal infections or cradle cap.</note>; the straw in baths for loin-pains <note>original: "Lenden-Wehe," or lower back pain.</note>, unexpected fatigue in the elderly, scabs, mange, weeping ulcers, leprosy, etc.

### Wild Oats.
<note>original: "Taubhaber." Also known as "deaf oats" or *Avena fatua*, a species of grass that resembles common oats but is considered a weed.</note>

This grows wild along paths near barley; it thrives especially when the weather is wet, blooming and ripening during the summer. It produces very thin ears that hang down just like common oats, containing only 3 or 4 red grains, and possesses many delicate, hairy awns <note>original: "Aehren-Spitzen," referring to the needle-like bristles on the grass.</note>.

### Preparation and Use.

It dries and consumes <note>In the medical context of the time, "consuming" meant the ability of a substance to absorb or dry up excess "humors" or fluids.</note>; for this reason, it is crushed and applied as a plaster, or its juice is mixed with flour and laid over ulcers and fistulas of the eyes, known as the <term>Werner</term> <note>A historical German term for a lacrimal fistula or a specific type of inflammatory growth or stye on the eye.</note>. It is also beneficial for damaged nostrils; when boiled with pure water <note>original: "zartem Wasser," literally "tender water."</note> until it reaches the thickness of a syrup and inserted into the nostrils with soft linen cloths, it provides soothing and cooling relief.

### Bear’s Ear.
<note>original: "Bären-Oehrlein." This refers to *Primula auricula*, a mountain-dwelling relative of the primrose.</note>

Grows frequently on the mountains in Austria and Styria, and is also cultivated in gardens. It blooms in April and again in August; the leaves and yellow flowers are similar to the <term>cowslip</term> <note>original: "Himmel-Schüssel," literally "Heaven’s Keys," a common folk name for *Primula veris*.</note>; the root is very fibrous.

### Preparation and Use.

The herb is cold and dry in nature; it is astringent, heals, and is an excellent <term>vulnerary herb</term> <note>original: "Wund-Kraut," an herb used specifically for the healing of wounds.</note>. It serves both internally and externally for wounds and <term>ruptures</term> <note>original: "Brüche," which could refer to bone fractures or, more likely in this herbal context, hernias.</note>, as well as for dizziness, as does the root. The juice of the herb is used externally for frostbitten limbs, scratches on the hands and feet, and all <term>putrid sores</term> <note>original: "faulen Schäden."</note>. The water distilled from the flowers drives away all spots on the skin and makes it smooth and beautiful. From the blue Bear's Ear, a water is made that breaks <term>stones in the kidneys and bladder</term>, provided it is distilled correctly according to the art by a knowledgeable person.

This grows in shady and mountainous forests and on old walls. It blooms in July; it has a red, smooth <note>original: "glaichichte."</note>, and fibrous root, from

## The Balsam Tree.

It grew in ancient times in Arabia and in the Promised Land. Nowadays it is planted near Mecca in wealthy Arabia. It is now also cultivated in gardens in Syria and Egypt. In June, July, and August, the sap either drips from the scored trees or flows out by itself, and is collected in glasses. The trunk is three ells high and has few leaves, which resemble rue <note>A bitter herb (*Ruta graveolens*) known for its bluish-green, lobed leaves.</note>, but they are whiter, and it has small white flowers like blackthorn <note>original: "Schlehdorn" (*Prunus spinosa*).</note>. Its fruit smells strong and corresponds in size, shape, and color with the fruit of the turpentine tree <note>The *Pistacia terebinthus*, known for its aromatic resin.</note>.

## Internal Use and Preparation.

The balsam is hot and dry in the second degree <note>This refers to the Galenic system of medicine, which classified substances based on their primary qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) and their intensity (degrees 1 through 4).</note>; it opens and dissolves <note>In historical medicine, "opening" and "dissolving" meant clearing blockages in the vessels or breaking down harmful fluids (humors).</note>, benefits the stomach and heart, and serves against poison and wounds. It is used against suppressed menstruation, stomach aches, fevers, poison, snake and viper bites, and the plague, either alone or mixed with plague powders. It is also useful in the rotting of the intestines, the liver, kidneys, and lungs, as well as for ulcers and wasting disease.

## Externally.

It is smeared into the nose and onto the chest for protection against the plague, and is applied for the healing of wounds. In ancient times, dead bodies were embalmed with it to protect them from decay, which is how mummies come to us—that is, those bodies of people that [were] balfa- <note>The text cuts off mid-word as a catchword for the next page: "balfa-" refers to *balsamiret* (embalmed/treated with balsam).</note>

## Great Burdock.

It grows by paths and fences and in uncultivated places. It blooms in June and July; the root is gathered in April. It first produces large, broad, and rough leaves, between which a thick, angular stem emerges, having many small leaves and branches upon which prickly balls <note>These are the well-known "burrs" of the burdock plant.</note> hang; in their center, a purple-brown blossom can be seen. The root is strong, red on the outside and white on the inside.

### Internal Use and Preparation.

The root cleanses and is slightly astringent <note>original: "zieht ein wenig an," referring to a drying or tightening effect on bodily tissues.</note>, and in a double dose, it follows the strengths of Sarsaparilla <note>A tropical root used historically to treat skin conditions and syphilis.</note>. It serves the chest, promotes urine, sweat, and the expulsion of toxins. It is useful against shortness of breath, cold and damp coughs, side stitches, the spitting of blood, clotted blood, kidney stones, old wounds, swelling of the milk <note>Likely referring to mastitis or breast engorgement in nursing mothers.</note>, receding fevers, quartan fevers <note>A form of malaria where the fever returns every fourth day.</note>, joint pain, gout <note>original: "Podagra."</note>, paralysis, bites from poisonous animals, and the French disease <note>original: "Franzosen," a common historical term for syphilis.</note>.

### External Use.

For broken and bruised legs, dislocations, and dropsy <note>Edema or swelling caused by fluid retention.</note> when bound to the soles of the feet. For hair loss, when one washes with lye made from the ashes of the root. For toothaches, as a mouth rinse. The seed cleanses, draws, breaks and clears stones, and stops fluxes of the belly and the womb. The leaves serve externally for old and hardened wounds, dislocated limbs, gangrene <note>original: "Brand."</note>, headaches, and swollen feet. For a prolapsed womb <note>original: "Austreten der Mutter."</note>, bound upon the head; for the rising of the same <note>original: "Aufsteigen derselben," referring to "hysterical rising," an old medical belief that the womb could move upward and cause suffocation.</note>, placed under the feet. The simple water distilled from the root is good for cold and damp ailments of the chest; when compounded, it powerfully drives out sweat and provides great help in the Plague.

## Basil.

It is grown in gardens and blooms in June and July, which is also when it is gathered; it propagates by its seeds. It is a succulent herb, one foot high, with leaves like Mercury <note>original: "Bingel-Kraut" (Mercurialis), a common European plant.</note> and white, flesh-colored flowers; the root is hard and fibrous.

### Preparation and Use

It is hot in nature, like all spicy herbs; it moistens, disperses blockages, and strengthens the head and the heart. It exceptionally promotes the flow of urine, the menstrual cycle <note>original: "Weiber-Zeit."</note>, and eases difficult births. It increases the milk of nursing mothers and cleanses lungs filled with ulcerous blood. It is useful in cases of severe fainting and melancholy—which it drives away because of its pleasant scent—as well as for weak and tearing eyes, coughs, vomiting, and ruptures <note>original: "Brüchen," usually referring to hernias.</note>. ## White Behen

This herb, which is said to have originally grown on Mount Lebanon, is now also cultivated here in our gardens. It blooms during the three summer months. Its stems are thin, oblong, and round, growing up to one and a half ells <note>An "Elle" (ell) was a unit of length roughly equal to the length of a man’s arm, about 24 inches.</note> high. It has leaves similar to the Catchfly <note>original: "Lychnis"</note>, but smooth; it bears white or even purple-colored flowers that project out of the flower buds, which also contain seed pods full of seeds like the Catchfly.

### Preparation and Use

The root is moderately warm and strengthens the heart; used externally in a fomentation <note>A "gébähet" or fomentation involves applying warm, medicinal liquids to the body with a cloth.</note>, it serves to treat hardened nerves. The juice is used for weeping and painful eyes. The seed is said to expel stones <note>referring to kidney or bladder stones</note> and heal fits <note>original: "Fraiß," a historical term for convulsions or epilepsy, especially in children.</note>; if placed secretly under a sick person's bed, it is said to cause a change in the course of the illness.

## Red Behen

This is grown in gardens and sown in April in an open, airy place. It has leaves like chard <note>original: "Mangold"</note>, but narrower and longer, and on the thin, straight stems—much like lilies—it is full of red seeds. The root is reddish, split in two, and has a slightly astringent quality.

### Use and Preparation

The root is moderate in nature, leaning toward cold; it is categorized among the tempered heart-strengthening species <note>term: species/compound medicines</note>, such as the **Sweet Musk Compound** <note>original: "Diamosch. dulc." or Diamoschu dulce</note> and the **Warm Pearl Compound** <note>original: "Diamarg. callid." or Diamargariton calidum</note>, etc. In the absence of this plant, Tormentil root is used for Theriac <note>A famous "universal" medical ointment or potion used as an antitoxin.</note>. The seed stills "fluxes of the womb" <note>original: "Mutter-Flüsse," referring to excessive menstrual or uterine discharge</note>, as does the root.

## Barberry.

<note>original: "Saurach"</note>
It is cultivated along the fences in gardens; the leaves appear in April, the bloom in May, and the fruit in autumn. ### Red Mangold.
<note>Red Mangold refers to varieties of *Beta vulgaris*, such as Swiss chard or beetroot.</note>

It is planted like the aforementioned variety and looks entirely similar to the common type, except for the leaves, stems, and the root color, which is a brownish-red.

### Internal Benefits and Use.

The herb, seeds, and root cleanse and soften; they purify the body and the head when the juice is drawn into the nose or made into a <term>clystier</term> <note>an enema or liquid injection into the rectum</note>. It is eaten internally in salads and also cooked to treat a congested spleen.

### External.

Used for scales on the head <note>dandruff or seborrheic dermatitis</note>, lice, itchy skin, and abrasions on the hands and feet; it is also used in head and foot baths. The juice from the root stills earaches; when dripped into the ears, it removes scales and headaches. It is also drawn into the nose with marjoram water—a practice which some criticize, claiming it causes madness, but this is false.

### Betony.
<note>Betony (*Stachys officinalis*) was highly prized in medieval and early modern medicine as a "cure-all."</note>

It grows in gardens and meadows; it blooms in June, and the leaves are collected in May, while the flowers are gathered in the following season. It bears long, notched, white, and fragrant-smelling leaves, between which a thin, four-edged stem grows an <term>ell</term> <note>a traditional unit of measurement, roughly the length of a man's arm</note> high or more. At the summit stand purple flowers arranged like a spike, within which an elongated, angular seed is enclosed. The root is fibrous.

### Use and Preparation.

The flower dries, opens, thins, cleanses, and disperses. It serves for headaches, and ailments of the spleen, liver, and chest, and it expels poison and urine. Indeed, against everything harmful to the head, it is a faithful aid. It strengthens the stomach and removes nausea <note>original: "Eckel," meaning a loathing of food or stomach upset</note>, lung and liver ulcers, and is used against jaundice <note>original: "Gelb-Sucht"</note> and dropsy <note>original: "Wasser-Sucht," an old term for swelling caused by fluid retention</note>, for all fevers, and for all menstrual and seminal discharge...

### Birch.

This tree grows in sandy places and prefers mountains; it produces its blossoms, which are catkins, in March, and its leaves in April. ## Bistort.
<note>original: "Natter-Wurtz," literally "Adder-wort" due to the snake-like shape of its root</note>

It grows in meadows in moist and rich soil, blooming in May and June; the seeds ripen in July. The root is dug in April and when the sun enters the sign of Cancer <note>the zodiac sign associated with midsummer, roughly June 21 to July 22</note>. From the reddish root, which is wound like a snake and fibrous, long curved leaves emerge, followed by a delicate stem, one ell high with small leaves, which bears at the top a reddish flower like an ear of grain, leaving behind a triangular shiny seed.

### Internal Use and Preparation.

The root is astringent, promotes sweating, expels poison, and heals wounds; it is highly praised for "bloody flux" <term>dysentery</term>, bleeding piles <note>original: "Gülden-Ader-Fluß," referring to hemorrhoids</note>, coughing up blood, and against vomiting, miscarriage, and worms.

### External Use.

To dry up discharges, to stop uterine bleeding <note>original: "Bluten der Mutter"</note> and the bleeding of wounds, for toothache and rotting gums, and for <term>canker</term> <note>original: "Krebs," which in this period could refer to malignant tumors or persistent, "eating" ulcers</note>. The sponge-like growth <note>possibly referring to a specific preparation or fungal growth associated with the plant</note> is used for all types of bleeding; the water and syrup made from the root are useful for ruptures, dysentery, spitting blood, and excessive menstruation.

## Pigweed.
<note>original: "Meyer," a name used historically for various plants like Amaranth or Goosefoot; the description of "red Meyer" here refers to *Amaranthus cruentus* or similar species</note>

It is found in fields and gardens, blooming in the middle of summer. It produces white flower clusters on the stem and branches, in which every seed-grain is enclosed by two leaves. The white Pigweed resembles the red in every respect except for the color.

### Internal Use and Preparation.

The Pigweeds are kitchen herbs and provide little nourishment; the leaves of the red variety are cold and moist, they act as a laxative, and heal scorpion and spider bites.

### Externally.

They promote the <term>menses</term> <note>original: "Frauen-Zeit"</note>, the afterbirth, and <term>molae</term> <note>original: "Mon-Kälber," or "moon-calves," a historical term for abnormal uterine growths or non-viable pregnancies</note> if the herb is boiled and the steam is allowed to reach the womb. It stills headaches that have arisen from heat. The seed of the red Pigweed prevents <term>dysentery</term> <note>original: "Rothen-Ruhr"</note> and excessive menstrual flow.

## Cotton Plant.

It is a foreign small tree, very branched with three-lobed leaves and yellowish flowers that are somewhat purple on the inside. The fruit resembles a hairy nut, in which the seed lies covered with a soft wool.

### Use and Preparation

The seed makes [the humors] thin, softens, and serves the chest, throat <note>original: "Raichen," likely referring to the pharynx or throat</note>, and dysentery.

### Good King Henry.
<note>original: "Guter Henrich," *Blitum bonus-henricus*, a perennial herb often used like spinach</note>

It is very beneficial and grows on uncultivated, dilapidated farmsteads, in poor soil, and along fences. The stem emerges in May. ### Borage.
<note>original: "Borragen," *Borago officinalis*</note>

It grows readily in gardens, in the wild, and in uncultivated places. It blooms throughout the entire summer until September and is gathered in May and June. It develops broad leaves; the stems are likewise soft and hollow, bearing sky-blue flowers—sometimes white—which consist of five pointed petals. These surround a jagged rim at the bottom, in the middle of which appear as many points that together form a sting-like shape. Following the flowers is a black, paired seed-pod. The root is as thick as a thumb, a span long, white, and smooth.
