Effect: It is bitter, warming, drying, opening, and cleansing; it serves against blockages of the intestines and <term>mesentery</term> <note>original: "Gekröse," the membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall</note>.

### Externally.

Against inflammation of the eyes, to dye the hair yellow, and to drive moths away from clothing.

## Amaranth.
<note>original: "Meyer." While "Meyer" can refer to various plants like Pigweed (*Chenopodium*), the description of "blood-red" stems and "Amaranth-like" leaves identifies this as *Amaranthus*.</note>

It is found in fields and gardens and blooms in the middle of summer. The Red Amaranth has a long, blood-red, branched stem upon which grow broad leaves resembling the amaranth, though these are brownish-red. It produces white flower-clusters along the stem and branches, in which each little seed-grain is enclosed by two leaves. The White Amaranth resembles the Red in all respects except for the color.

### Internal Use and Preparation.

The Amaranths are kitchen herbs and provide little nourishment; the leaves of the Red variety are cold and moist, they act as a laxative, and they heal scorpion and spider bites.

### Externally.

They promote <term>menstruation</term> <note>original: "Frauen-Zeit"</note>, the expulsion of the afterbirth, and <term>false conceptions</term> <note>original: "Mon-Kälber" or "moon-calves," a historical term for uterine masses or molar pregnancies</note> when the herb is boiled and the steam is directed toward the <term>womb</term> <note>original: "Mutter"</note>. It stills headaches that arise from heat. The seed of the Red Amaranth prevents <term>dysentery</term> <note>original: "Rothen-Ruhr"</note> and excessive monthly flow.

## Cotton Tree.

This grows frequently in Cyprus, Syria, and <term>Italy</term> <note>original: "Welsch-Land," a term formerly used by Germans to refer to Italy or other Romance-speaking regions</note>; it matures in three or four months after sowing. It is a foreign little tree, very branched, with three-lobed leaves and yellowish flowers that are somewhat purple on the inside. The fruit is much like a hairy nut, in which the seed lies covered by a soft wool.

### Use and Preparation

The seed makes [the humors] thin, it softens, and is beneficial for the chest, throat, and <unclear>cough</unclear>.

<term>dysentery</term> <note>original: "thenruhr," likely "rothen Ruhr," a severe form of diarrhea involving blood</note>, kidney stones, and increases one’s vital essence <note>original: "mehret die Natur," a phrase often referring to reproductive health or libido</note>. Burnt cotton stills bleeding; the smoke from it settles the <term>rising of the womb</term> <note>original: "auffsteigende Mutter," a historical term for hysteria or uterine displacement</note>. The oil pressed from the seeds heals weeping scalp-scabs and also eliminates measles and pockmarks on the face.

### Good King Henry.
<note>original: "Guter Henrich," *Blitum bonus-henricus*.</note>

It is so good and grows on uncultivated, derelict farmsteads, in poor soil, and along fences. The stem emerges in May. This "honest man" <note>another folk name for the plant</note> has leaves that resemble <term>sorrel</term> <note>original: "Sauerampffer"</note> and <term>arum</term> <note>original: "Aron," also known as Lords-and-Ladies</note>, and they are soft and greasy to the touch. At the top of the stem, it produces yellow-brown flowers, followed by many seeds set in white clusters like grapes. The root is long and yellowish.

### Preparation and Internal Use.

The herb, together with its root, heals wounds and encourages the growth of new flesh; it is added to <term>enemas</term> <note>original: "Clystiren"</note>; it cleanses the lungs and cures ulcers within them.

### Externally.

It is good against the pains of <term>gout</term> <note>original: "Gicht"</note> and <term>hemorrhoids</term> <note>original: "Gülden-Ader"</note>; for foul and worm-infested wounds and injuries; and for <term>scabies</term> <note>original: "Kräze"</note> and spots upon the skin.

### Borage.
<note>original: "Borragen," *Borago officinalis*.</note>

It grows readily in gardens, as well as wild in uncultivated places. It blooms throughout the entire summer until September and is collected in May and June. It develops broad leaves, and the stems are likewise soft and hollow. It bears sky-blue flowers, as well as white ones, which consist of five sharp-edged petals surrounding a jagged rim at the base; in the center, just as many points appear, which together form a spike. The flowers are followed by black seeds <note>original: "Stamme," likely a transcription error for "Saamen" (seeds)</note> joined in pairs. The root is as thick as a thumb, a span long, white, and smooth.

## Use and Preparation.

The leaves, flowers, seeds, and root soften <note>original: "erweichen," referring to emollient properties that soothe tissue</note>, prepare <note>an alchemical/medical term for making "humors" ready for expulsion</note>, and purge bile; they make one cheerful, strengthen the heart, and expel poison. They are therefore praised against melancholic conditions <note>historical term for depression or low spirits</note>, ailments of the spleen and jaundice <note>original: "Gelbsucht"</note>, obstructed menstruation, heart palpitations <note>original: "Herz-Zittern"</note>, dizziness, hot and pestilential fevers, and poison. The boiled leaves soften the body <note>act as a mild laxative</note> and soothe a rough throat and coughs; the flowers drunk in wine gladden the heart. The root, when coated in sugar, moistens the body and takes away madness <note>original: "Tollheit"</note> during fevers. The seeds, when used in wine, increase breast milk; the water distilled <note>original: "gebrandte Wasser"</note> from the flowers and the herb warms, moistens, and moderates bile, and strengthens the head and heart. It is good for abdominal swelling, <term>bloody flux</term> <note>original: "Blutfluß," likely dysentery</note>, fevers, wheezing, inflammation of the eyes, pains and ringing in the ears, and scorpion or spider bites. The preserve <note>original: "Conserve," herbs preserved in sugar</note> balances the humors, drives away sadness, encourages good spirits, and is a secret for promoting the <term>flower of women</term> <note>original: "Frauen-Blume," a euphemism for menstruation</note> when dissolved in thin white wine. The syrup moistens and is proven against melancholy, madness, fainting, trembling, and weakness of the heart. The tincture made from the flowers with sorrel water and <term>spirit of vitriol</term> <note>original: "Eisen Vitriol-Geist," a preparation of sulfuric acid used as a tonic</note> is praised for hot fevers and melancholic episodes.

## Grape-Wort.
<note>original: "Trauben-Kraut," likely *Chenopodium botrys*, also known as Oak of Jerusalem</note>

It grows in gardens, vineyards, and on hills lying in the sun; it blooms in July and August; it bears seeds in August and September and is collected in July. It produces a branchy, rough stem three to four <term>ells</term> <note>an "Ehle" or ell was a unit of length, roughly 24–27 inches</note> high, and has leaves like <term>groundsel</term> <note>original: "Kreuz-Kraut"</note> that are hairy, rough, and range from sea-green to yellow, and have a pleasant scent. At the tips of the branches, it brings forth many yellow flowers clustered together like small grapes, followed by small seed grains, each enclosed in two small leaves. The root is reddish-white, woody, and fibrous.

## Internal Use and Preparation.

The herb thins <note>the humors</note>, opens, penetrates, divides, and cleanses. It resists rot <note>original: "Fäulung," likely meaning infection or gangrene</note>. It is good for the chest, for promoting menstruation, for stilling pains, and for promoting urination. It is used in chest diseases, lung ulcers, <term>shortness of breath</term> <note>original: "Engbrüstigkeit"</note>, wheezing, heavy breathing, persistent coughs, and <term>consumption</term> <note>The text cuts off at "Schwin-," referring to "Schwindsucht" or tuberculosis</note>...

### External Use.

It serves for ailments of the windpipe, and when the uvula has fallen <note>original: "Halß-Zäpflein," literally "throat-peg"; refers to an elongated or inflamed uvula</note>, used in a gargle; also in enemas <note>original: "Clystiren"</note> for diarrhea <note>original: "Bauchflüssen"</note>. To induce menstruation <note>original: "Weiber-Zeit"</note> and expel a stillborn fetus <note>original: "tode Frucht"</note>, the steam therefrom is captured; it is applied externally for uterine pains <note>original: "Mutter-Schmerzen," often referring to "hysteria" or "suffocation of the mother"</note>, and the juice is dripped into runny eyes. It is also used to embalm bodies and to repel moths when scattered among clothes. The preserve and syrup are very useful for consumption and other difficulties.

## German Hogweed.

<note>original: "Teutsch Bären-Klau," literally "German Bear's Claw," likely *Heracleum sphondylium*</note>

It grows in wet and damp meadows; it blooms in May, and the herb is collected in April. It produces long, broad leaves that are deeply notched on all sides, and a stalk one and a half cubits <note>original: "Ehlen," an ell, roughly the length of an arm</note> high, which bears crowns of white blossoms at the top, and seeds like Meadow Saxifrage <note>original: "Sesel"</note>. The root is white and fragrant. The herb and leaves serve against an obstructed liver and jaundice <note>original: "Gelb-Sucht"</note>. It is also used in enemas to still pain and as poultices. The root benefits those suffering from gout <note>original: "Podagrämern"</note>; the seed helps with shortness of breath.

## Italian Hogweed.

<note>original: "Welsch Bären-Klau," literally "Foreign Bear's Claw," likely *Acanthus mollis*, also known as Bear's Breech</note>

It grows in Italy <note>original: "Welschland"</note>, but here it is found in apothecaries' or university gardens. It bears its bloom in summer and its seed in autumn. It has leaves like rocket <note>original: "Raucken"</note>, yet broader, longer, and prickly. The stalk is two cubits high, as thick as a finger, and surrounded at the top with small leaflets, from which a white flower emerges and an oblong yellow seed. The roots are red and mucilaginous <note>original: "leimicht," meaning sticky or glue-like</note>.

### Internal Use and Preparation.

The herb and the root soften, soothe, and resolve <note>original: "verzehrt," in a medical context meaning to dissipate or "consume" morbid humors</note>; it promotes urine and heals consumption and ruptures <note>hernias</note>.

### External Use.

In pain-relieving enemas <note>original: "Clystiren"</note> and poultices; for gout, side-ache, obstruction and swelling of the spleen, gangrene <note>original: "Brand," which can mean burning inflammation or mortification of tissue</note>, tearing pains of the nerves, and dislocated limbs.

## Cabbage.
<note>original: "Kohl-Kraut," likely referring here to the common garden cabbage or kale (*Brassica oleracea*)</note>

It is cultivated in gardens, in rich and cool soil. It blooms in March and April; the seed comes in May, or in the second year after it is sown. It is a well-known plant and requires almost no description of its form; however, it is distinct from red-brown cabbage and other types of coleworts.

### Preparation and Internal Use.

The leaves are astringent <note>original: "ziehen an"</note>, laxative, and cleansing. This herb has a nitrous quality <note>original: "salpetrische Kraft," referring to the cooling or purifying properties associated with saltpetre</note>; it is a good wound-herb. When boiled twice, it stills diarrhea <note>original: "stilt es den Stuhlgang"</note> and tearing pains in the abdomen; the broth facilitates bowel movements and heals wounds, ulcers, and fistulas. Eaten in food, it protects against drunkenness; it is also praised for gout, obstructions of the liver, spleen, and lungs, hoarseness, coughs, shortness of breath <note>original: "Engbrüstigkeit," a term for asthma or respiratory distress</note>, and other lung complaints. The pressed juice is good for those who have the falling sickness <note>original: "fallende Sucht," a historical term for epilepsy</note>, for stroke, and for those who have lost their speech.

### External Use.

It serves against inflammations, pains, St. Anthony’s Fire <note>original: "Rothlauff," also known as erysipelas, a skin infection characterized by a red rash</note>, leprosy, gout of the foot <note>original: "Podagra"</note>, headache and the stone <note>original: "Stein-Weh," usually referring to kidney or bladder stones</note>, warts, wounds, hair loss, and blemishes on the face. The seed cures and kills worms, prevents drunkenness, settles abdominal griping, and has the same effect as the leaves. The pith in the stalk relieves shortness of breath, hoarseness, and a lost voice. However, cabbage eaten in excess harms those of a melancholy temperament <note>referring to the four humors; an excess of "black bile"</note> and those with spleen ailments, as well as the eyesight; for it provides poor nourishment, creates gas, and causes cancer.

## White Head Cabbage.

It is planted in cabbage fields and gardens; it requires rich soil.

## Field Cabbage.
<note>Likely referring to wild cabbage or a related brassica like *Brassica rapa*</note>

Grows readily in fallow fields and blooms in summer. The leaves look like rutabagas <note>original: "Steck-Rüben"</note> and are rough; the stem is one and a half feet <note>original: "Schuh," a historical measurement roughly equal to a foot</note> high, with pale-yellow flowers and black seeds enclosed in pods.

The juice from the leaves, when snuffed into the nose, cleanses the head of mucus. The seed expels worms.

### Externally.

It removes spots on the skin. The distilled water <note>original: "gebrandte Wasser"</note> heals the bite of a mad dog <note>rabies</note> when applied externally.

## Cauliflower.
<note>original: "Blumen-Kohl"</note>

This came to us from Cyprus and Italy <note>original: "Welschland," a term historically used by Germans to refer to Italy or other Romance-speaking regions</note> by way of its seed. It blooms in July and also towards autumn; its seed rarely ripens in our climate. It has long, broad, white-green leaves, between which the flowers emerge, standing very close together. It is a kitchen herb and is the healthiest among the cabbage varieties, provided a good drink is taken with it.

### Externally.

In pain-relieving enemas <term>Clystiren: from the Latin 'clyster,' a liquid injection into the rectum for medicinal or cleansing purposes</term> and poultices; for gout, side-aches, obstruction and swelling of the spleen, gangrene <note>original: "Brand," which could refer to gangrene or severe inflammatory "fire" in the skin</note>, tearing of the nerves <note>likely referring to neuralgic pain or spasms</note>, and dislocated limbs.

## Cabbage.
<note>original: "Kohl-Kraut," referring here to the general genus or common garden cabbage</note>

It is cultivated in gardens in rich and cool soil. It blooms in March and April, and the seed comes in May, or in the second year after it is sown. It is a well-known plant and, due to its familiar shape, requires almost no description; however, it is distinct from red-brown cabbage and other types of cabbage herbs.

### Preparation and Internal Use.

The leaves are astringent, laxative, and cleansing. This herb has a saltpetre-like power and is a good "wound-herb" <note>an herb used to promote the healing of injuries</note>. When boiled twice, it stops diarrhea and tearing in the body <term>Reissen im Leib: a historical term for sharp, "tearing" abdominal cramps or colic</term>; the broth induces bowel movements and heals wounds, ulcers, and fistulas. When eaten, it protects against drunkenness. It is also praised for treating gout, obstructions of the liver, spleen, and lungs, as well as hoarseness, coughing, shortness of breath <term>Engbrüstigkeit: literally "narrow-chestedness," referring to asthma or chronic bronchitis</term>, and other lung complaints. The pressed juice is good for those who have the falling sickness <term>fallende Sucht: an old term for epilepsy</term>, for stroke, and for those who have lost their speech.

### Externally.

It serves against inflammation, pain, erysipelas <term>Rothlauff: a bacterial skin infection characterized by a red, spreading rash</term>, leprosy, podagra <term>gout, specifically when it affects the big toe</term>, headaches, kidney stones, warts, wounds, hair loss, and spots on the face. The seed cures and kills worms, prevents drunkenness, settles abdominal gripes, and has the same effect as the leaves. The pith <note>original: "Marck," the soft inner tissue</note> in the stem relieves shortness of breath and a hoarse or lost voice. However, cabbage eaten in excess is harmful to those of a melancholic temperament <note>In the theory of the four humors, "melancholy" was associated with the spleen and black bile</note> and those with spleen ailments, as well as to the eyesight; for it provides poor nourishment, causes flatulence, and causes cancer <note>original: "Krebs," which in early modern medicine referred to any persistent, malignant-looking sore or ulcer</note>.

This is planted in cabbage fields and gardens; it requires rich soil.

## White Bryony.
<note>original: "Zaun-Rübe," literally "fence-turnip." Known scientifically as *Bryonia alba*.</note>

It grows in sandy and shaded places, among shrubbery, on hedges, and fences. It blooms in May, and the berries ripen in autumn. The root is dug in April; it produces long vines and small tendrils <term>Gäbelein</term>. The leaves resemble grape leaves but are rougher, hairier, and whitish. It bears small, white flowers clustered together like grapes, followed by berries that are initially green and later become red or black.

### Internal Use and Preparation.

The root thins and "cuts" <note>In early modern medicine, certain substances were thought to "cut" through thick, sticky bodily fluids or humors like phlegm</note>, purging mucus and watery humors through the bowels and by vomiting. It cleanses the liver, spleen <term>Miltz</term>, and womb <term>Mutter</term>; it expels fluids and promotes the menstrual cycle. It is praised against vertigo, the "falling sickness" <term>fallende Sucht: a historical name for epilepsy</term>, madness, dropsy, fever, swelling of the spleen, and blockages of the mesentery <term>Gekröse: the membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall</term> and the women's period. It is used to assist in childbirth and for the "rising of the womb" <note>original: "Aufsteigen der Mutter," a condition historically called hysterical suffocation, where the uterus was thought to move upward and cause respiratory distress</note>. Boiled in wine, it is used for impurities of the stomach, wheezing, coughing, gout, and podagra <term>Podagra: gout specifically affecting the big toe</term>.

### Externally.

It is used to disperse clotted blood, hard growths, and other swellings. It is used against cancer when crushed with ox blood. For dropsy, it is applied as a plaster mixed with goat dung. For quartan fever <note>A fever that recurs every four days</note>, it is bound to the pulse; for "the French disease" <term>Frantz: a historical term for syphilis</term> and cramps, it is fastened around the neck. It is also used for gout pain, old and putrid sores, and facial wrinkles when boiled with figs. It treats tetter <term>Flechten: a general term for various crusting skin diseases</term>, "trembling marks," and birthmarks. The distilled water <term>gebrandte Wasser</term> is good for the unnatural cravings of pregnant women, difficult labor, a retained afterbirth <term>verstandener Nachgeburt</term>, and blockages...

The salt made from the ashes is a magnificent remedy for obstructions of the liver, spleen, and womb.

## Oxtongue
<note>original: "Ochsen-Zung," also known as Bugloss or *Anchusa officinalis*</note>

It grows in fields and meadows and is also cultivated in gardens. It blooms from May and June into late summer. The leaves and flowers are gathered in May and June. Its leaves resemble Borage but are longer, hairier, rougher, and set with very small prickles. The stem is round, rough and hairy, and one and a half cubits <note>An "Ehle" (ell) was a historical unit of measurement, roughly the length of an arm</note> high. From among these leaves emerge small purple flowers, similar to Borage, from which the black seeds develop. The root is very similar to Borage, except that it has a thicker, fatty skin.

## Use and Preparation
<note>The OCR "Nuß" is a transcription error for "Nutz," meaning "Use."</note>

The flowers, leaves, and root have the same effect as Borage: they soften [the humors], prepare the bile <note>In early medicine, "preparing" a humor meant thinning it so the body could expel it</note>, strengthen the heart, and resist poison. The seed, when drunk in wine, increases breast milk. The distilled water warms, moistens, balances the bile, and benefits the heart.

### Externally.

It serves against the bites and stings of venomous animals and snakes, as well as inflammations and pains of the eyes. The conserve, syrup, and juice are excellent for melancholy <term>Melancholie: historically viewed as an illness caused by an excess of black bile</term>, madness, frenzy, trembling, palpitations, weaknesses of the heart, and fainting. They make one joyful, moisten and soothe the chest, resist hot fevers, and drive away impurities of the skin, leprosy, the "French disease" <term>Franzosen: a common historical term for syphilis</term>, ringworm <term>Flechten</term>, and the like. Wine made from it takes away sadness and the "falling sickness" <note>original: "Schwere-Noth," usually referring to epilepsy or severe distress</note>; the preserved root is very beneficial for those with spleen ailments.

## White Bryony
<note>original: "Zaun-Rübe," also known as *Bryonia alba*</note>

It grows in sandy and shady places, in thickets, and along hedges and fences. It blooms in May, and the berries ripen in autumn. The root is dug up in April. It produces long vines and small tendrils; the leaves resemble grape leaves but are rougher, hairier, and whitish. It bears small, white flowers clustered together like grapes, followed by berries that are initially green and later become red or black.

### Internal Use and Preparation.

The root thins [fluids], cuts through [blockages], and purges phlegm and watery humors through bowel movements and vomiting. It cleanses the liver, spleen, and womb <note>original: "Mutter"</note>; it expels fluids and encourages the monthly period. It is praised for dizziness, the falling sickness <term>falling sickness: an old term for epilepsy</term>, madness, dropsy, fevers, swelling of the spleen, and obstructions of the mesentery <term>Gekröse: the membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall</term>. It is used to promote the menses, to facilitate childbirth, and for the "rising of the mother" <note>a historical term for symptoms of hysteria or uterine displacement</note>. When boiled in wine, it aids impurities of the stomach, wheezing, coughing, gout, and podagra <term>Podagra: gout specifically affecting the big toe</term>.

To disperse clotted blood, hard masses, and other swellings. Against cancer, when crushed with ox blood. For dropsy, applied as a plaster with goat dung. ### Ox-Eye, or Bull’s-Eye.
<note>original: "Rinds-Auge, oder Ochsen-Auge"; likely *Buphthalmum salicifolium* or a similar composite flower like the Ox-eye Daisy</note>

This herb has thin, soft stems; the leaves resemble fennel, and the yellow flowers look like an eye, followed by seed grains that hang together in a round shape, appearing much like a mulberry. The root is fibrous and black.

### Preparation and Use of the Flowers (Internally).

These, boiled in wine and drunk, drive away jaundice <term>Gelbesucht: a yellowing of the skin and eyes, historically treated with yellow-flowering plants according to the "Doctrine of Signatures"</term>, promote urination, and soothe kidney pain.

### Externally.

The flowers, slightly crushed and mixed with melted wax and applied over hard swellings, will dissipate them.

### Shepherd’s Purse.
<note>original: "Täschel-Kraut, Säckel-Kraut, oder Hirten Tasch," referring to *Capsella bursa-pastoris*</note>

It grows long, curved, and deeply notched leaves at the root, similar to vervain <note>original: "Eisen-Kraut"</note>, which lie flat against the earth; it bears a white flower, followed by broad-edged seed-clusters <note>these refer to the plant's distinctive heart-shaped or purse-like seed pods</note>. The root is long and covered with many fibers.

### The Herb.

This herb is an excellent wound-herb <note>a plant used specifically for healing cuts and stopping blood</note>.

### Internal Use and Benefits.

Shepherd’s Purse, boiled in red wine and drunk, is good for all forms of bleeding, whether from the nose or wounds, as well as spitting blood, diarrhea, dysentery <term>Rothe-Ruhr: "the red flux," a severe form of bloody diarrhea</term>, excessive hemorrhoids <term>Guldene-Ader: literally "the golden vein," a historical term for the hemorrhoidal veins</term>, the monthly periods of women, seminal discharge, and bloody urine.

### Externally.

This herb, crushed with vinegar and placed on the back of the neck, or held in the hands, or placed under the armpits and the soles of the feet, stills nosebleeds.

### The Herb.

Boiled in wine and applied as a poultice, it heals wounds and the bites of venomous animals.

### The Herb.

Crushed with vinegar and bound upon the pulse-points <note>a common medical practice of applying cooling herbs to the wrists to lower body temperature</note> during burning fevers, it drives away the heat and the fever.

## Boxwood
<note>original: "Buchs-Baum"; *Buxus sempervirens*</note>

This is a well-known plant that is cultivated in pleasure gardens; it is evergreen, produces new shoots every year in April, and occasionally produces flowers at this time, though it never bears seed in these lands.

### Preparation and Internal Use.

#### The Leaves.

The leaves, boiled with whey and drunk, drive away jaundice.

#### The Juice.

The juice, freshly pressed with the help of a suitable liquid <note>original: "Liquoris"</note>, is administered and praised as an extraordinary remedy for side-stitches <note>often referring to pleurisy or sharp abdominal pains</note>.

### External Use.

The leaves, boiled in lye and used to wash the head, make the hair a beautiful yellow.

#### The Flowers.

The flowers, powdered and taken in the weight of one quintin <term>Quintin: a historical German unit of weight, roughly 3.7 to 4 grams</term> in wild poppy-seed water, or even just half a quintin, are said to purge the bowels very violently.

#### The Root.

If eaten, this is said to heal snake bites.

### The Wood.
<note>This continues the entry for Boxwood from the previous page.</note>

The wood dries, contracts, promotes sweating, and is used by some in place of "French-wood" <note>original: "Franzosen-Holtz," referring to Guaiacum wood, which was a standard treatment for syphilis</note>. The drink prepared from it along with the leaves is said to perform special service for skin eruptions, smallpox <note>original: "Kinder-Blättern," literally 'children's leaves,' a historical term for smallpox or similar pustular rashes</note>, the "French disease" <term>the French disease: a common historical name for syphilis</term>, and jaundice.

### The Distilled Oil.

The distilled oil made from this makes one numb <note>acting as a local anesthetic</note>, serves against the heavy ailment <term>the heavy ailment: original "schweren Gebrechen," usually referring to epilepsy or the "falling sickness"</term>, and is used externally for toothache.

### Calamint.
<note>likely *Calamintha officinalis*</note>

This herb has square stems and branches upon which grow notched, hairy, and fragrant leaves, two standing opposite each other. Beside these, purple flowers arise on special stalks, which leave behind a blackish seed.

### Preparation and Utility.

From this, one prepares a water, a salt, and a syrup. These aforementioned things thin, open, disperse, and cleanse; they serve the stomach, chest, liver, and the womb <note>original: "Mutter," meaning the uterus</note>; they are also good for wounds, abdominal cramps, shortness of breath, cough, a congested liver, and jaundice.

### Larkspur.
<note>original: "Rittersporn," literally 'Knight's spur'; genus *Delphinium*</note>

Among the many varieties of larkspur, the wild kind is the best. This has long, thin, dissected blue leaves and flowers resembling spurs, which, when they fall away, leave behind small pods that hide the black seeds.

### The Herb.

This herb, along with the flowers, promotes menstruation <note>original: "Frauen-Blume," literally 'women's flower,' a euphemism for the menstrual cycle</note> and the flow of urine, and aids in childbirth. It serves for wounds, dropsy, jaundice, and the afterpains of a woman in childbed.

# The Distilled Water.
<note>Continuing from the previous page, this refers to water distilled from Larkspur.</note>

This is effective for clotted blood <note>often referring to bruising or internal hematomas from trauma</note>, for injuries from falling, for the stone <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>, and for suppressed urine.

# Marigolds.
<note>original: "Ringel-Blumen"; *Calendula officinalis*</note>

This herb has thin, angular, hairy, and sticky stems, with elongated, fresh, rough, grayish leaves shaped like tongues without stalks, having a herb-like taste. From its hairy and many-cleft flower-buds, it produces star-like, golden-yellow flowers which have a yellow or brown disk in the center; after these, a hard, curved seed is found. The root is woody.

## Preparation and Utility.

### The Flowers.

The flowers open <note>referring to "opening" blockages in the body's channels</note>, disperse, contract slightly, and drive out sweat and poison. They strengthen the heart and the liver, promote the female period <note>menstruation</note>, and are therefore very good in times of plague, for smallpox <term>smallpox: original "Kinder-Blättern," a historical term for pustular diseases</term>, and measles. They are used against poison, for heart palpitations resulting from a blocked menstrual flow, for jaundice, and similar ailments. They also assist in childbirth and are good for shortness of breath, stroke, and paralysis.

### The Flowers and Leaves.

### Externally.

Against worms in the ears, toothaches, warts, and excessive bleeding of the "golden vein" <term>the golden vein: a historical term for hemorrhoids</term>. One can also dye the hair yellow with them.

### The Tender Fresh Shoots.

These open the bowels and promote the female period.

### The Seeds.

These drive out roundworms, as well as long-lasting and quartan fevers <note>a fever, often malarial, where the paroxysm occurs every fourth day</note>, when just 7 seeds are taken in white wine.

## Wood Bellflower.
<note>original: "Wald-Glöcklein"; the description of "thimble-like" flowers suggests a species of Foxglove, likely the Yellow Foxglove (*Digitalis grandiflora*)</note>

This herb develops long, dark green, woolly, and slightly notched leaves; a straight stem hung with elongated, hollow flowers resembling a thimble <note>the German name for Foxglove is *Fingerhut*, meaning "thimble"</note> that are yellow on the outside and saffron-yellow and hairy on the inside. From these, triangular seed pods form, which are filled with bright, fiery-red seeds.

### The Herb.

The whole herb opens <note>referring to the "opening" of blockages in the body's internal channels or vessels</note>, cleanses, and carries away biliary and dropsical humors <term>dropsical: relating to dropsy, an old term for edema or the swelling caused by excess fluid</term>; it is a good wound-herb, serves against catarrhs <note>original: "Flüsse," referring to "fluxes" or abnormal discharges of fluid</note> and dampness of the chest, and has almost the same power as Gentian root. Although this herb is not particularly used in pharmacies, and in some places not used at all, it is well worth getting to know for the sake of its virtues, and the ancients <note>referring to historical medical authorities</note> held it in high regard.

# Camphor Tree.

This is an exotic tree, as tall as a walnut or poplar tree, whose trunk and branches are covered in an ash-grey color; the wood is white and light, the leaves are whitish and almost like willow leaves. The camphor tree grows in the East Indies, on mountains situated by the sea, and also in China.

## Uses and Preparation.

From the center of this tree, a resinous, white, transparent gum sweats out, which is called camphor. This is of two kinds: the Bornean, which is rare, and the Chinese, which is commonly brought to Europe. Some is granulated, having been pushed out of the trunk by itself and by nature; some is formed into round disks by art <note>meaning by human skill or processing</note>. Those who return from the Indies nowadays say that camphor is prepared from the root of the cinnamon tree on the island of Ceylon <note>original: "Zeilan"</note>. Camphor is entirely volatile <note>meaning it evaporates easily</note>; for that reason, it is stored in flax, millet seeds <note>original: "Hirsche-Saamen"</note>, or pepper.

## Camphor.

Alleviates pains and sharp humors <term>humors: the bodily fluids that early medicine believed must be balanced to maintain health</term>, induces sweating, and dispels unchastity <note>camphor was historically used as an anaphrodisiac to reduce sexual desire</note>. It resists decay, poison, heart palpitations, anxiety, a feverish liver, sleep-inducing illnesses <note>referring to lethargy or comatose states</note>, and "rising of the mother" <term>rising of the mother: an old term for hysteria or various uterine-related distresses</term>; specifically if one ignites such camphor and often extinguishes it in larkspur or lemon balm water and takes it internally.

### Externally.

It serves in pain-relieving compresses for inflammation of the eyes, wounds and injuries, gangrene <note>original: "Brand"</note>, and pox.

### For the Plague.

Simply by smelling it; it is also used for nosebleeds.

### Worn in Clothes.

It drives away lice.

# Caper Tree.

This is a thorny shrub, covered with spines that are curved inward and lean toward the earth; it has fuzzy, round leaves, which are always placed two against each other, or opposite. At their base, elongated stalks emerge, which bear round, greening buds; when these open, they are the flowers, which resemble a small rose. These are followed by much smaller, reddish seeds enclosed in pods. The bark or roots are ash-colored, wrinkled and full of crevices, and taste bitter and astringent.

The caper tree grows of its own accord in many lands, such as in Alexandria in Egypt, in Spain, France, Italy <note>original: "Welschland"; a historical German term for Italy or other Romance-speaking regions</note>, Crete <note>original: "Candien"</note>, Cyprus, and other places. Among us Germans, it is cultivated in gardens with the greatest diligence.

This tree bears flowers until late in the summer. When they begin to open, they are plucked, pickled with vinegar and salt water, and brought to us in Germany.

## Preparation and Uses.

The bark of the root cuts through, opens, cleanses, and is slightly astringent. It promotes the flow of urine and serves the spleen; therefore, it is used against blockages of the spleen and liver, scurvy <note>original: "Scharbock"</note>, splenetic illness <note>original: "Milz-Sucht"; historically associated with melancholy and digestive issues</note>, joint pain, and paralysis.

## The Pickled Flowers.

These flowers, which are called capers, cleanse, resist rot <note>putrefaction or infection</note>, promote menstruation <term>Frauen-Blumen: literally "women's flowers," a historical term for the menstrual cycle</term> and the flow of urine, awaken the appetite, benefit those suffering from splenetic illness, and kill worms. However, they harm a weak stomach and produce watery, bilious, and melancholic humors <term>humors: the bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—that early modern medicine sought to keep in balance</term> if one consumes too many of them.

## Caper Oil.

The oil thins [the humors], opens, and softens hard swellings and boils, but it is especially beneficial for the spleen.

### Extract <term>Extractum: a concentrated preparation made by drawing out the active medicinal components of a plant, in this case using a liquid solvent.</term>

An extract is also prepared from the barks using barley water, which is useful for all the aforementioned ailments <note>Refers to the spleen, liver, and joint issues mentioned on the previous page regarding the Caper tree.</note>.

## Honeysuckle <term>Geiß-Blat: literally "Goat-leaf," the common German name for Honeysuckle (Lonicera).</term>

The stalks of this herb have green leaves on both sides, and at the very top, white and flesh-colored <note>original: "leibfarbene"; likely referring to a pale pink or creamy hue</note> flowers, and red berries that are full of hard, red seed-grains.

### Preparation and Use.

#### The Flowers.

The flowers are beneficial to the spleen and promote the flow of urine.

#### The Berries.

The berries are effectively used against dropsy <note>original: "Wassersucht"; a historical term for swelling caused by excess fluid retention, now called edema.</note>.

### The Distilled Water.

This is particularly useful for those burdened with shortness of breath, wheezing, coughing, heart palpitations, and similar illnesses; it also assists in a difficult labor <note>original: "Schwer-Geburt"; refers to prolonged or obstructed childbirth.</note>.

### Externally.

This water serves to cure old wounds, fistulas, cancers <note>original: "Krebs"; in this context, it refers to spreading or persistent ulcers/sores rather than modern oncology.</note>, and the like.

From the flowers, some make an oil. From the berries, however, they make a wound balsam.

The juice from the leaves heals wounds of the head and the skull.

## Cardamom and Grains of Paradise.

These are triangular pods of an Indian plant that grows like a reed; these are full of brownish-red, strong-smelling, bitter, and sharp seeds. They are brought to us from the East Indies.

### Use.

Both <note>referring to the Cardamom and Grains of Paradise described on the previous page</note> strengthen the head, stomach, and chest; they are good against dizziness, fainting, heart palpitations, wind <note>intestinal gas</note>, colic, coughing, cold ailments of the womb <note>original: "Mutter"; in early modern medicine, "cold" ailments were those thought to be caused by an excess of phlegm or a lack of vital heat</note>, poison, and the plague.

### Motherwort <term>Herzgespann: Leonurus cardiaca. The German name literally translates to "heart-tension," reflecting the plant's traditional use for treating heart palpitations and anxiety-induced tension.</term>

This herb develops square stems nearly 3 feet high; and divided leaves standing opposite one another in pairs, from whose base the white and purple flowers emerge from their buds; the root is yellow and fibrous.

## Preparation and Use.

### The Leaves.

The leaves or the herb serve those with shortness of breath <note>original: "Engbrüstigkeit"; often used to describe asthma or chronic bronchitis</note>, promote urine and the monthly period <note>original: "Monath-Zeit"; menstruation</note>, and are good for the liver and spleen, for bloating of the sides, "heart-tension" in children <note>original: "Herzgespann der Kinder"; likely referring to abdominal cramps or digestive distress in children</note>, wheezing, convulsive paralysis, and difficult birth.

### Externally

Externally, the leaves serve against worms, and are good for wounds, bleeding, uterine pain, and stomach ache.

### The Distilled Water <term>Gebrandte Wasser: water produced by distillation, which captures the volatile essential oils and essences of the plant.</term>

This promotes urine, the "woman's flower" <note>original: "Weiber-Blume"; a historical euphemism for menstruation</note>, and labor.

### Blessed Thistle <term>Cardobenedicten: Cnicus benedictus. Its name, "the blessed thistle," stems from its historical reputation as a cure-all, particularly during plague outbreaks.</term>

This has a delicate yet succulent root, from which emerge deeply notched, hairy, rough leaves set with small prickles, and striped, shaggy, trailing stems that look upwards, a finger thick, upon whose tips sit small scaly heads from which the yellow flower shines forth, leaving behind an elongated seed hanging in woolly tufts <note>original: "Lackenwollen"; referring to the downy pappus attached to the seeds</note>. The whole herb tastes bitter.

## Preparation and Use.

The herb or the leaves open, dissolve, cleanse, and resist...

### The Spirit.
<note>original: "Spiritus"; a distilled essence or alcoholic solution of the plant's volatile components</note>

This prevents the falling sickness <note>epilepsy</note>.

### The Salt.

The salt extracted from the ash <note>potash or fixed salts obtained by burning the plant material and leaching the ashes</note> promotes sweating in cases of toxic fevers and scurvy <note>original: "Scharbock"</note>.

### Confection and Syrup.

Both are beneficial for pestilential <note>plague-related</note> fevers, the onset of dropsy <note>original: "Wassersucht"; swelling caused by fluid retention</note>, jaundice, wheezing, stitches in the side, consumption <note>original: "Schwindsucht"; a wasting disease such as tuberculosis</note>, and the falling sickness; they also relieve abdominal cramps <note>original: "Bauch-Grimmen"</note>, prevent putrefaction, induce sweating, and kill parasitic worms.

### The Extract.

The extract drives out sweat and poison and is used against the plague, all manner of "unclean" diseases <note>likely referring to skin ailments or venereal diseases</note>, as well as for shortness of breath, stitches in the side, and various types of fever.

## Milk Thistle.
<term>Marien-Distel: Silybum marianum. Also known as St. Mary's Thistle, recognizable by the white veins on its leaves which folk tradition claimed were caused by a drop of the Virgin Mary's milk.</term>

It has broad, long, curved, white-spotted, shiny, and prickly leaves, and a striated, grayish, branched stem. It bears scaly heads as thick as a finger, which are armed with sharp thorns. The flower is mostly purple in color, followed by seeds that resemble those of wild saffron. The root is thick and is good to eat.

## Preparation and Use.

### The Herb.

The herb <note>the leafy parts of the plant</note> opens <note>refers to the "opening" of bodily blockages in the liver or pores</note>, is somewhat astringent, and promotes sweating, urine, and the monthly period; it also stills the "white flow" in women <note>leukorrhea</note>.

### The Seed.

This serves the chest and is good against stitches in the side, as well as kidney and stone pains.

### Externally.

The seed, when applied externally, drives away and heals the beginning of cancer in the breasts.

## Star Thistle.
<term>Stern-Distel: Centaurea calcitrapa. A thistle-like plant named for the star-shaped arrangement of spines around its flower head.</term>

It grows an angular, hairy stem, one ell <note>about 24–27 inches</note> high or more, with long, soft, grayish, and deeply notched leaves. At the tops of the branches hang smooth little heads, like those of the cornflowers, whose scales <note>bracts</note> end in long spines and form the shape of a star; the flower is purple, rarely white. The seed is smooth, small, and elongated. The root is long, thick, succulent, and whitish.

### Preparation and Benefits.

### The Herb and the Seed.

The herb and the seed purify the blood <note>original: "Geblüte"</note>, promote urination, and are good for the pain of stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>.

### The Distilled Water.

This opens obstructions of the liver, dispels quotidian <note>daily</note> and tertian <note>occurring every third day</note> fevers, and heals smallpox in children <note>original: "Kinder-Blattern"</note>. However, it is not commonly kept in the apothecaries; therefore, one must prepare it oneself.

<term>Weber-Distel: Dipsacus fullonum. Literally "Weaver's Thistle," so named because its dried, prickly heads were used in the textile industry to "tease" or raise the nap on woolen cloth.</term>

### There are two kinds of this plant: the Domestic and the Wild.

The domestic variety sends up a straight, striated, strong stem, two or three ells high, covered in spines. It has two wide, long, prickly leaves growing opposite each other, which are joined at the base and hollowed out so that they constantly hold water <note>these "basins" around the stem collect rainwater, a characteristic feature of the teasel</note>. The heads are the size of a fist, elongated, and provided with curved spines, between which the pale red flowers shine out like small tubes. The root is smooth and white. The wild variety differs from the sown <note>cultivated</note> kind in that its heads...

#### The Root.

The water that is distilled from the leaves heals mouth ulcers. However, the water that is contained within the leaves <note>Teasel leaves form "cups" at the stem that collect rainwater; hence its botanical name Dipsacus, from the Greek for "thirst"</note> serves for red and dark eyes, spots on the face, and freckles, if one washes oneself with it. Clothmakers use the heads, or "cards," to dress <note>original: "puzen"; to raise the nap or clean</note> their cloths, and this Weaver’s Thistle is now also sown and cultivated here and there in Germany.

The worms found within the head <note>likely the larvae of the teasel moth or similar insects</note> are good for toothache and quartan fevers <note>fevers occurring every fourth day, often associated with malaria</note> when they are tied around the neck or worn on the arm.

If these worms are crushed with oil of roses, or even placed alive upon the "worm" <note>referring here to a "whitlow" or "paronychia," a painful infection of the fingertip once believed to be caused by a tiny worm</note> and the damaged place on the finger, they kill the finger-worm.

## Carline Thistle.

<note>original: "Eber-Wurtz"; literally "Boar-root." This refers to *Carlina acaulis*, the Silver Thistle or Carline Thistle, long prized as a "panacea" or universal remedy.</note>

The common Carline Thistle grows with long, narrow leaves that are deeply cut on both sides and prickly; it has a short stem about a span long, the top of which bears a broad head that yields various blossoms resembling hyacinths, followed by a grey seed covered in down. It is supported by its long, thick root, which is blackish on the outside but yellowish and aromatic <note>original: "würtzhaffte"; having a spicy or medicinal scent</note> on the inside. The small Carline Thistle is not unlike this one. The common variety grows in the high mountains of Switzerland, Thuringia, Silesia, and other places. The small variety grows on hills, in fields, and by roadsides.

### Preparation and Use.
### The Root.

This opens [the vessels], promotes sweating, and expels poison, urine, and the monthly period; therefore, it is used with great benefit for a congested liver and spleen, and against dangerous illnesses, poison, plague, stomach cramps, worms, side stitches, fevers, convulsions, bladder stones, and dropsy <note>original: "Wassersucht"; an archaic term for swelling caused by excess fluid, often related to heart or kidney failure.</note>.

If one boils the root in meat broth and drinks it, it induces vomiting.

### Externally.

This root, when chewed and held in the mouth, drives away toothache.

Boiled with vinegar and used as a wash, it heals the itch <note>original: "Kräße"; historically referring to scabies or general itchy skin rashes</note>, scabs, and ringworm <note>original: "Flechten"</note>.

### The Resin or Mistletoe-substance.

This is collected from the roots of the white Carline Thistle in Apulia; it is called <term>Thistle Wax</term> <note>original: "Cera di Cardo"</note> and is often used in place of <term>Mastic</term> <note>A resin obtained from the mastic tree, used for its medicinal and adhesive properties.</note>.

### Wild Saffron.

<note>original: "Wilder Saffran"; this refers to Safflower (*Carthamus tinctorius*), which was widely cultivated as a dye plant and a cheaper medicinal substitute for true saffron.</note>

This is cultivated in many places, including Germany, and is sown among the summer crops.

### Preparation and Use.
#### The Seed.

The seed opens [the vessels], cleanses, dissolves [congealed humors], and expels wind; it <term>purges both above and below</term> <note>meaning it acts as both an emetic (inducing vomiting) and a laxative</note>, clearing away tough phlegm and watery fluids. It is particularly useful for jaundice, dropsy, <term>quartan fever</term> <note>a form of malaria where the fever recurs every fourth day</note>, coughs, and shortness of breath. However, it is harmful to the stomach; therefore, it must be improved by adding ginger, galangal, and mastic, as well as anise.

#### External Use.

The expressed juice expels lice and other vermin. The flowers are often used to adulterate genuine saffron.

#### The Extract.

The <term>Extract of Safflower or Thistle-Medicine</term> <note>original: "Extractum Diacarthamum sive Cnicopharmacum"</note> carries out excess fluids and cleanses the head, the stomach, and the remaining internal organs.
The <term>Safflower Extract</term> <note>original: "Extractum Diacarth."</note> purges phlegm and bile and resists joint pain, fever, paralysis, and headaches.
The <term>Safflower Blend</term> <note>original: "Species Diacarth."</note> produces similar effects.

#### Syrup.

The <term>Syrup of Safflower</term> <note>original: "Syrup de Carthamo"</note> promotes gentle bowel movements, thins and cuts through [thick humors], and is good for deep-seated third- and fourth-day fevers.

#### The Pressed Oil.

This oil serves against congestion of the chest and lungs, hoarseness, jaundice, and stomach cramps.

### Field Caraway.

<note>original: "Feld-Kümmel"; likely referring to Caraway (*Carum carvi*) or Wild Cumin.</note>

Field Caraway thrusts up many four-edged stalks from a long, simple root...

Stalks, an <term>ell</term> <note>A historical unit of length, usually the distance from the elbow to the fingertip, roughly 24 to 45 inches.</note> long in height, upon which the leaves are very delicate and finely divided, and the umbels are full of white flowers and full of oblong, angular, brown, strong-smelling seeds.

### Preparation and Use.

#### The Seed.

This disperses wind, promotes urination, is beneficial to the stomach, and is used both internally and externally for <term>strangury</term> <note>original: "Harn-Winde"; painful or frequent urination in small volumes</note>, bloody urine, stones, sand, and gravel, obstructed menstruation, the afterbirth, and after-pains; it is also used to increase milk, to promote digestion, for loss of appetite, against bloating, nausea, suppressed wind, intestinal worms, colic, <term>dysentery</term> <note>original: "Rothe-Ruhr"</note>, dizziness, <term>stroke</term> <note>original: "Schlag"; historically referred to as apoplexy</note>, melancholy, weak memory, poor eyesight, redness of the eyes, obstructed milk, and for the liver and lungs, shortness of breath, panting, and damp, cold coughs.

Held to the nose with vinegar, it stills nosebleeds and also resists poison and pestilence.

#### The Flour.

The flour made from the seed is mixed into plasters for bloating, <term>congestions</term> <note>original: "Stoffen"</note>, and bruises.

#### The Root.

The root, when boiled, is just as good to eat as <term>parsnips</term> <note>original: "Pastenath"</note>; it helps digestion and promotes urination.

The sugar-coated seeds <note>often called comfits</note>;
The preserved root;
The water distilled with wine from the whole herb—all are useful for the aforementioned ailments.

The oil distilled from the seeds warms, dries, promotes urination, serves the stomach, and is used usefully both externally and internally for bloating, colic, and all manner of pains in the belly, likewise for <term>wind-dropsy and tympany</term> <note>original: "Wind- und Drommel-Sucht"; conditions characterized by severe abdominal swelling due to gas</note>, and all the diseases mentioned above.

### Garden Carnations.

<note>original: "Garten-Nägelein"; these refer to the *Dianthus* genus, specifically the Clove Pink, highly valued in the early modern period for both beauty and medicine.</note>

These are quite well known; therefore, we will only set down here their preparation and use.

### The Flowers.

The flowers, but especially the brownish-red ones, strengthen the head, the nerves, heart, stomach, and liver, and they resist poison. They are effective against dizziness, <term>stroke</term> <note>original: "Schlag"; historically referred to as apoplexy</note>, paralysis, cramps, heart palpitations and oppression of the heart, fainting, malignant fevers, poison, plague, worms, vomiting, <term>dysentery</term> <note>original: "Rothe-Ruhr"; literally "the red flux"</note>, <term>suppressed menstruation</term> <note>original: "verhaltene Frauen-Blume"; literally "retained women's-flowers"</note>, and difficult childbirth.

### Externally.

For wounds of the head and the skull, <term>cancers</term> <note>original: "Krebs"; could refer to either the disease or spreading ulcers</note>, festering sores, and for head and toothaches.

### The Essence.

The essence or the thick juice of <term>Garden Carnations</term> <note>original: "Garten-Näglein"; Dianthus caryophyllus, also known as clove pinks</note> serves the heart, breaks the stone <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>, and cures fevers.

### The Distilled Water.

This has the same power as the above; it is used in heart-strengthening <term>juleps</term> <note>a sweet, medicinal drink</note> and poultices.

### The Vinegar.

The vinegar is used against fainting, headaches, toxic air, and infectious diseases; it is rubbed on or applied to the nose, forehead, pulse points, and heart.

### Culinary Cloves.

Root-cloves or <term>Merchant-cloves</term> <note>original: "Kramer-Nelcken"; cloves sold by grocers or spice merchants</note> are of two kinds:

### Small.

These are harvested before they become ripe.

### Large or Mother-Cloves.

These are not harvested until they are fully mature.

Both are the fruits, or rather the flowers, of a foreign tree that in size and leaves almost resembles the laurel tree. They are elongated like nails—which is how they received their name in German <note>The German word for clove, "Nelke," is derived from "Nägelchen," meaning "little nail."</note>—and each grows on its own branch. They are white at first, soon green, thereafter reddish, and finally blackish once they have been dried in the sun.

<page-num>340</page-num>
<header>❦ (0) ❦</header>

The **Clove-Tree** grows in the East Indies, on several islands such as Ceylon, Bantam, and others, but only bears fruit in the five Molucca Islands; from there the fruits are transported to other lands.

They are gathered from September 15th until January and February, but not by hand; rather, they are knocked off with a reed (after the earth around the tree has been cleaned beforehand).

### Preparation and Use.

The common cloves and **Mother-cloves** <note>original: "Mutter-Nelcken"; these are cloves that have been allowed to reach full maturity on the tree, becoming larger and starchier</note> cut through, thin out, open, divide, and also draw out slightly. They strengthen the head, heart, and stomach, and they resist poison; thus, they are very good and healthy for "cold" ailments of the brain, dizziness, headaches, weak vision and memory, fainting, heart palpitations, lack of appetite, nausea and vomiting of the stomach, wind <note>intestinal gas</note>, diarrhea, dropsy, <term>uterine ailments</term> <note>original: "Mutter-Kranckheiten"; historical term for various gynecological issues</note>, <term>suppressed menstruation</term> <note>original: "verstopften Weiber-Zeit"</note>, dangerous epidemics, poison, and the plague.

### The Resin.

The resin <note>original: "Gummi"</note> found on the cloves is said to have the same effect as turpentine.

From cloves, the following are prepared:
> The coated and preserved cloves.
> The distilled water.
> The spirit <note>original: "Spiritum"; an alcoholic distillation</note>.
> The oil.
> The extract.
> The tincture.
> The syrup.
> The salt.
> The balsam.
> The **Aromatic Clove Species** <note>original: "Species Aromaticas Caryophyllaticas"; a Latin pharmaceutical term for a dry mixture of aromatic spices used in medicine</note>.

The water strengthens the heart.

The oil warms, dries, and serves the head, heart, and stomach, as well as toothache (when dropped into the tooth). The syrup warms, dries, thins, and "cuts through" <note>referring to the ability to break up thick humors or phlegm</note>; it is beneficial for the heart, stomach, head, the womb, all sinewy parts of the body, and in those illnesses that arise from "cold" <note>in the humoral system, "cold" illnesses were treated with "hot" spices like cloves</note>.

<summary>This page describes the harvesting and medicinal applications of cloves, emphasizing their origin in the Moluccas and their use in treating a wide range of "cold" ailments affecting the heart, stomach, and brain.</summary>

The balsam is good for a moist and cold brain (when smelled); when rubbed upon the navel, it relieves <term>colic</term> <note>sharp, localized abdominal pain</note>; and it stops vomiting when the stomach is rubbed with it.

The <term>species</term> <note>original: "Species"; here referring to a specific medicinal mixture of dry ingredients</note> provide aid in the aforementioned ailments of the head, heart, and stomach.

### Wood Avens.
<note>original: "Benedict-Wurtz"; also known as Herb Bennet or *Geum urbanum*</note>

This root or herb produces rough, notched leaves; three large ones grow at the tip of each stem, with two much smaller ones below them. It has a branched, wide, delicate stalk, one and a half cubits high, and golden-yellow flowers like <term>Cinquefoil</term> <note>original: "Fünf-Finger-Kraut"</note>, followed by hairy little buds containing round, rough seed pods. It has many thin, brownish-red roots that smell like cloves.

## Preparation and Use.
### The Root.

This root is slightly astringent and "dividing" <note>a term in humoral medicine meaning it breaks up thickened fluids or blockages</note>: it strengthens the head, heart, and stomach. It opens blockages, refreshes the <term>vital spirits</term> <note>original: "Lebens-Geister"; the subtle substances believed to flow through the body to sustain life and movement</note>, aids digestion, resists poison, and strengthens the reproductive organs of both sexes, helping with conception. It is also useful against <term>rheum</term> <note>original: "Haupt-Flüsse"; a discharge of fluids from the head</note>, stroke, severe infirmities, stomach-ache, <term>griping</term> <note>original: "Grimmen"; sharp intestinal cramps</note>, and blockages of the chest, liver, spleen, and <term>mesentery</term> <note>original: "Gekröses"</note>. It treats <term>melancholy</term> <note>original: "Milzsucht"; literally "spleen-sickness," often associated with depression or lethargy</note>, clotted blood, side-stitches, the spitting of blood, ulcers and fistulas of the lungs, wind <note>intestinal gas</note>, and prolapse of the intestines. It also treats uterine ailments, <term>uterine pains</term> <note>original: "Mutter-Schmerzen"</note>, <term>leukorrhea</term> <note>original: "weissen Fluß"; a white discharge</note>, and stones.

### Externally.

Used externally for fainting (by smelling it), wounds, fistulas, cancerous sores, and <term>birthmarks</term> <note>original: "Mutter-Mähler"</note> when boiled in wine or water and applied as a poultice. Regarding the "Known Woman's Flower" <note>original: "Verstandene Frauen-Blume"; likely a colloquial name for a specific medicinal preparation or the herb's use in midwifery</note>, let the steam from the boiled herb be directed toward the womb.

### Purging Cassia.
<note>original: "Fistel-Cassien"; *Cassia fistula*, also known as Golden Shower Tree</note>

This is an exotic tree, the size of a walnut or almond tree. The leaves almost resemble Persian leaves <note>likely referring to Peach leaves</note>; the flowers are yellow or white, followed by long pods nearly a cubit in length. These are woody on the outside, but inside they are full of seeds and a blackish, heavy, sweet, yet somewhat acidic pulp.

It grows frequently in Egypt and various provinces in the East and West Indies.

### Preparation and Use.

From these pods, neither the seeds (as they are <term>astringent</term> <note>original: "zusammen ziehet"; causing the contraction of body tissues</note>) nor the outermost bark, and even less the dividing membranes, are used; rather, only the pulp, which is moderately warm, cold, and moist <note>These terms refer to the <term>humoral qualities</term> used in medieval and early modern medicine to balance the body's temperament</note>. This commonly used pulp softens, soothes, cleanses, and <term>purges</term> <note>acts as a laxative</note>; it alleviates bile and watery fluids, moderates their sharpness, and is beneficial to the liver and the chest. It is also used with benefit for ailments of the kidneys, bladder, chest, and lungs; for inflammation of the humors, the blood, and the <term>semen</term> <note>referring to various bodily "seeds" or reproductive fluids</note>; for foul and "poisoned" seminal discharge, stones, heat in the kidneys, shortness of breath, coughs (especially in children), pleurisy, cholera, and burning fevers.

### External Use.

Applied externally for <term>erysipelas</term> <note>original: "Rothlauff"; a bacterial skin infection once known as St. Anthony's Fire</note>, throat ulcers, joint pain, and <term>podagra</term> <note>gout, specifically in the big toe</note>; however, it must be used fresh and not when it has become stale or spoiled.

### From Cassia.

From this plant, the following items are prepared: Cassia Flower <note>original: "Cassiæ Flos"</note>, Extracted Cassia <note>original: "Cassia extracta"</note>, Extracted Cassia for enemas <note>original: "Cassia extracta pro Clysteribus"</note>, Diacassia electuary with manna <note>original: "Electuarium Diacassia c. manna"; an electuary is a medicinal paste mixed with honey or syrup</note>, Extract of Cassia <note>original: "Extractum Cassiæ"</note>, Cassia Water <note>original: "Aqua Cassiæ"</note>, and Syrup of Cassia <note>original: "Syrupus de Cassia"</note>. All of these are useful both internally and externally for the aforementioned diseases.

### Caper Spurge.
<note>original: "Spring-Körner"; likely *Euphorbia lathyris*, named for its seeds which "spring" or pop out of the fruit when ripe</note>

This plant produces a stem an ell high <note>a historical unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the fingertips</note> and as thick as a finger. The leaves are oblong and arranged irregularly, though those found on the branches are smaller and grow in pairs. At the tips (after the white flower has appeared) is a round fruit divided into three compartments, containing round seeds that are white and sweet inside.

The root is succulent and milky.

### Use.

The seeds or grains violently purge watery and <term>phlegmatic</term> humors along with bile; they also promote a difficult birth.

## Small Centaury.

<note>original: "Klein Tausend-Gulden Kraut"; *Centaurium erythraea*. The German name literally means "Small Thousand-Guilder Herb," suggesting its high medicinal value.</note>

From its garden-root springs a thin, angular stem, a little higher than a <term>span</term> <note>about 9 inches</note> (though in damp places it grows an <term>ell</term> <note>about 45 inches</note> high), with narrow leaves almost similar to St. John's Wort. After the purple-red flowers, longish seed-pods follow, full of small seeds.

The tips, or the herb with its leaves and flowers, when opened, is a good herb for liver and spleen fevers and for wounds. It gently carries away bile, phlegm, and watery fluids; therefore, it serves against obstructions of the liver, spleen, and <term>womb</term> <note>original: "Mutter"; literally "the mother," a common term for the uterus in early modern medicine</note>, as well as jaundice and dropsy, loss of appetite, wheezing, old coughs, <term>putrefaction</term> <note>original: "Fäule"; general decay or infection</note>, roundworms, <term>scurvy</term> <note>original: "Scharbock"</note>, three- and four-day fevers <note>malarial fevers characterized by the frequency of their recurrence</note>, suppressed <term>menstruation</term> <note>original: "Weiber-Blume"; literally "women's flowers"</note>, colic and intestinal gout, sciatica, aching in the limbs, paralysis, hernias, and poison; namely, when one prepares a drink from it with wine and drinks of it.

### External Use.

Externally, the tips, herb, and leaves are good for bad wounds and ulcers, simply by sprinkling the powder of it therein.

Boiled in pea broth and used as a wash, it is good for the bites of mad dogs and other poisonous animals, for <term>scurf and scab</term> <note>original: "Schuppen und Grind"; various fungal or crusting scalp conditions</note> of the head, and for lice.

## Chervil.

This is a well-known herb. Therefore, I only record here its:

### Preparation and Use.

The leaves, seeds, and root break up [blockages], promote urine, the stone, and <term>menstruation</term> <note>original: "Weiber-Zeit"; literally "women's time"</note>, induce sleep, heal wounds, and prove powerful against clotted blood and curdled milk in the breasts, when boiled in wine and drunk. It is used for obstructed urine and menstruation, kidney ulcers and stones, obstructions of the liver and spleen, jaundice and dropsy, the <term>pale color of virgins</term> <note>original: "bleiche Farbe der Jungfern"; also known as chlorosis or "green sickness," a form of anemia historically associated with young women</note>, three- and four-day fevers, plague, spider venom, mad dog bites, roundworms (when boiled in wine vinegar), excessive wakefulness, fainting, dizziness, shortness of breath, and <term>side-stitches</term> <note>original: "Seitenstechen"; likely referring to pleurisy or muscular pain</note>.

## Wall Germander.

<note>original: "Edel Gamanderlein"; *Teucrium chamaedrys*</note>

Its small woody and fibrous root produces reddish stems, upon which hard, fuzzy, and colored leaves always stand opposite each other in pairs; the flowers located at the tips of the branches are small and somewhat purple in color; the seed is small.

### Preparation and Use.

The leaves and flowers are good for the liver and spleen; they promote sweat, urine, and the <term>menses</term> <note>original: "Monath-Zeit"; literally "month-time"</note>; they make flesh grow <note>meaning they promote the healing of wounds and growth of healthy tissue</note>. They are therefore useful in <term>lethargy</term> <note>original: "Schlaff-Sucht"; a state of pathological sleepiness</note>, long-lasting headaches, fevers, <term>scurvy</term> <note>original: "Scharbock"</note>, and <term>splenetic complaints</term> <note>original: "Milz-Sucht"; historical term for ailments of the spleen, often linked to melancholy</note>. It is also used for clotted blood, spitting up blood, side-stitches, coughs, dropsy and jaundice, <term>wandering gout</term> <note>original: "lauffende Gicht"; arthritis or rheumatism that moves between different joints</note>, <term>leukorrhea</term> <note>original: "weissen Weiber-Fluß"; historically called "the whites"</note>, worms, and snake venom.

### External Use.

For hernias, painful <term>hemorrhoids</term> <note>original: "guldenen Ader"; literally "the golden vein"</note>, <term>corrosive ulcers</term> <note>original: "um sich fressende Geschwüren"; ulcers that spread or "eat" into the surrounding tissue</note>, scabies and rashes, <term>rheumatic discharges</term> <note>original: "Flüssen"</note>, and ear-worms.

The distilled water, conserve, essence, extract, and salt made from it likewise have the aforementioned virtues. In the absence of this herb, one may use **Wild Germander**, which is also called **Lady’s Bit**. <note>original: "Frauen-Biß"; *Teucrium scorodonia* or Wood Germander</note>

## Great Carline Thistle.
<note>original: "Groß Eberwurz"; likely *Carlina acaulis* or a related tall thistle species</note>

It has high stems with long, broad, and deeply notched fragrant leaves. At the tips of the stems are upright little heads with red and white blossoms and elongated, rough seeds; the root is thick and fibrous.

Although this herb and its root are not commonly used in pharmacies, a **gargle** <note>original: "Gurgel-Wasser"</note> prepared from the whole herb with wine or water is particularly praised for toothaches. For this reason, I would rather describe it briefly than pass over it entirely.

## Chamomile.

Two varieties are in use: the common and the Roman chamomile. The first kind is called common chamomile. The other is Roman or noble chamomile. Both sorts are well known.

### Preparation and Use.

### The Herb.

The herb of both types of chamomile, as well as the flowers, serve to disperse <note>original: "zertheilen"; a medical term for breaking up or dissolving "thick" humors or blockages in the body</note>, soften, and purge the bowels. They promote urination and soothe various pains, while also strengthening the head. They deserve great praise for obstructions of the liver, spleen, kidneys, and bladder, as well as for jaundice, **dropsy** <note>original: "Wassersucht"; swelling caused by excess fluid</note>, **scurvy** <note>original: "Scharbock"</note>, worms, fevers, **splenetic complaints** <note>original: "Milz-Sucht"; historical term for ailments of the spleen, often associated with melancholy</note>, kidney and bladder stones, and **strangury** <note>original: "Harn-Winde"; painful or difficult urination</note>. They relieve **afterpains** <note>original: "Nachweh"; pains following childbirth</note>, stomach aches, and bloating, as well as colic. They also serve at the onset of **dysentery** <note>original: "rothen Ruhr"; literally "the red flux"</note> when the flowers are soaked in vinegar and drunk.

### External Use.

Against pains of the loins, head, abdomen, and the womb, and for colic—applied in poultices, enemas <note>original: "Clystiren"</note>, and baths.

The distilled water, made from both common and Roman chamomile, promotes urine and the **menses** <note>original: "Monat-Zeit"</note>. It is effective for stomach aches, intestinal cramps, jaundice, dropsy, and **consumption** <note>original: "Schwindsucht"; a wasting disease, usually tuberculosis</note>, as well as side-stitches, when drunk with rock candy.

### External Use.

For snake bites, head and earaches, and **catarrh** <note>original: "Flüsse des Haupts"; literally "flows of the head," referring to excess mucus or discharge</note>.

Externally

The blue sapphire oil distilled from common chamomile <note>The "blue" color is a result of chamazulene, a compound formed during the steam distillation of chamomile</note>, and the yellowish oil distilled from Roman chamomile flowers, serve against stones and colic, and externally for stomach pain.

Common chamomile oil warms moderately, disperses <note>original: "zertheilet"; a medical term for breaking up or dissolving "thick" humors or blockages</note>, and lessens pain. When used externally, it serves against inflammations, swellings, head- and stomach-aches, painful and paralyzed limbs, cramps, fever, and fatigue.

### In Enemas.

For pains of the intestines, kidneys, and the womb <note>original: "Mutter"; historically used to refer to the uterus or "hysterical" complaints</note>.

### The Syrup.

This heals abdominal griping in children, **intestinal gout** <term>Darmgicht: a historical term for severe abdominal cramps or colic</term>, stomach aches, and the onset of jaundice and **dropsy** <note>original: "Wassersucht"; swelling caused by excess fluid</note>; it is also included among softening enemas that quiet griping pains.

### The Fixed Salt.

Is used not without benefit for tearing pains <note>original: "Reichen," likely a variation of *Reißen*</note>, stitches in the side, colic, fevers, stones, dropsy, and jaundice.

## Greater Celandine.
<note>original: "Groß Schell-Kraut"; *Chelidonium majus*</note>

Its golden-yellow fibrous root produces round, hairy, uneven stems, one and a half feet high; the leaves resemble those of **columbine** <note>original: "Agley"; *Aquilegia*</note>, but are larger and more numerous. After the yellow flowers—which consist of 4 small petals and many yellow threads—follow small elongated pods containing a pale seed; however, the whole plant is full of a reddish-yellow, viscous, bitter, and acrid juice.

### Preparation and Use.

The herb, flowers, and root—when cut through—open <note>original: "eröfnen"; referring to opening blockages in the body's vessels or organs</note>, cleanse, and purge bile through the bowels and urine; they induce sweat and resist poison. They are therefore good for obstructions of the liver, spleen, and urinary tracts, as well as jaundice (drunk with white wine), decay, dropsy, **scurvy** <note>original: "Scharbock"</note>, fever, and pestilence (especially the drink made from the root with vinegar).

For wounds, skin blemishes, putrid sores, and fistulas.

The vinegar, distilled from the whole herb with vinegar, is especially renowned against poison. The juice and the salt are also obtained from this.

### Chicory.
<note>Cichorium intybus</note>

Of this, there are two kinds: the tame and the wild. The tame is called **Garden Chicory**, **Tame Chicory** <note>original: "Wegwart"; literally "way-watcher," referring to its growth along roadsides</note>, or **Hindleufft**.

The other is **Wild Chicory**, **Sun-Herb**, or **Sun-Turner** <note>original: "Sonnen-Wirbel"; referring to the plant's habit of turning its flowers toward the sun</note>.

### Wild Chicory.

It has a root about the length of a finger, full of white, bitter sap; this produces crooked, juicy, and branching stems with hairy leaves similar to those of the **Dandelion** <note>original: "Pfaffen-Blat"; literally "Priest's-leaf," a common folk name for the dandelion</note>. On the sides of the stems are blue or white flowers, followed by hard and angular seeds.

### Garden Chicory.

It is quite similar to the wild variety.
The wild grows by the roads.
The tame is cultivated and raised in gardens.

# Preparation and Benefits.
## Leaves and Flowers.

The leaves and flowers (especially of the wild variety) and the roots of the cultivated ones, open, cleanse, balance <note>original: "temperiren"; referring to the early modern medical practice of balancing the four bodily humors</note>, and purge the bile. They promote urination and are beneficial to the liver and the stomach. They are thus good and useful for liver congestion, feverish illnesses, internal heat, **jaundice** <term>Gelbe-Sucht: literally "yellow-sickness," a condition where the skin and eyes turn yellow due to liver issues</term>, spleen ailments, wasting of the body <note>likely referring to atrophy or chronic weight loss</note>, and loss of appetite.

### Externally.

For the **spitting of blood** <note>original: "Blutspeyen"; often associated with tuberculosis or other lung ailments</note>, the root is held under the tongue.
For headaches, the juice is applied as a compress.

## The Distilled Water of the Flowers.
<note>original: "gebrandte Wasser"; a liquid produced by distilling the plant, often containing its volatile oils and essence</note>

The distilled water of the flowers is good for stones and gravel <note>urinary calculi</note> in children.

### Externally.

Used externally for red and yellow spots [on the skin], and for dim or weak eyes.

## The Water from the Root and Leaves.

This strengthens the heart and is useful for heat and inflammations of the liver and stomach, thirst, **heartburn** <note>original: "Sod"; acid reflux</note>, and evil, hot fevers.

The **conserve** <note>a medicinal preparation of fresh herbs preserved with sugar</note> of the flowers, as well as of the root, and the simple syrup, are good for an overheated and congested liver, for burning in the stomach, fevers, and **scurvy** <term>Scharbock: a disease caused by Vitamin C deficiency, historically common among sailors and during winters</term>.

The compound Chicory syrup draws off bile and is good for jaundice, incipient **dropsy** <term>Wassersucht: an old term for edema or swelling caused by fluid retention</term>, **convulsions** in children <note>original: "Fräß"; a historical term for childhood seizures or fits</note>, worms, and various kinds of fevers.

The extract and the salt [of the plant] provide the benefits mentioned above.
