## Poison Root.
<note>original: "Gift-Wurzel"; likely referring to Contrayerva (*Dorstenia contrajerva*), which was highly valued as an antidote to poisons.</note>

This is a foreign but increasingly popular and useful root, almost like our **Blessed Thistle** <note>original: "Benedicten-Wurzel"; *Centaurea benedicta*, a common medicinal plant of the time</note>. It is knotty and composed of scales at the top, with thick and tough fibers here and there from which other knots hang. It has no particular smell, but the taste is somewhat astringent, root-like, and a little sharp. It is brought to us from the Peruvian province of **Charcas** <note>A colonial province of the Spanish Empire, now part of modern-day Bolivia</note>.

### Preparation and Benefits.

This root opens <note>in the sense of clearing "blockages" in the body's humors</note>, strengthens the heart, promotes sweat and urine, stills pains, and resists poison, the plague, heart palpitations, **love potions** <note>original: "Liebes-Träncken"; common in early modern herbals, these were remedies thought to counteract the effects of magical philters or charms</note>, worms, spleen ailments, and melancholy. It aids digestion and disperses **wind** <note>gas or flatulence</note>. It is even better than **Bezoar** <term>a stony mass found in the stomachs of goats and other herbivores, prized as a universal antidote</term>, **Theriac** <term>a complex herbal "wonder drug" or electuary used since antiquity against poison and disease</term>, or **Unicorn** <note>likely narwhal tusk or fossilized bone, which was sold at immense prices as a detoxifying agent</note>.

## Fleabane.
<note>original: "Dür-Wurtz"; likely *Inula conyzae* or a similar species in the *Pulicaria* genus, traditionally used to drive away insects.</note>

There are three kinds, and all three sorts are used for medicine: 1. Common Fleabane. 2. Small Fleabane. 3. Medium Fleabane.

### Common Fleabane.

Grows 2 **ells** <note>original: "Ehlen"; a traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to the length of a man’s arm</note> high, smells strongly, and has rough-haired, greasy leaves that are slightly notched and similar to **Black Mullein** <note>original: "schwarzen Woll-Kraut"</note>, though they are smaller. It produces yellow flowers that finally blow away.

### Small Fleabane.

This is so similar to the common variety that whoever knows the former will recognize this one: it grows one ell high but has much more delicate, narrower, shorter, and somewhat hairy, greasy leaves. It has similar but smaller and more numerous flowers.

# Middle Fleabane.
<note>original: "Mittel-Dür-Wurtz", likely referring to *Inula* or *Pulicaria* species. The name "Dürwurz" literally means "dry-root," traditionally used to treat ailments that "wither" the body.</note>

It has a thicker and softer stem; the leaves are of a medium size—smaller than the common but larger than the small fleabane—though not fleshy, yet sharper and of a pleasant scent, with golden-yellow flowers, almost like chamomiles, which finally disperse like wool <note>referring to the "pappus," the fluffy down that allows seeds to be carried by the wind</note>.

### Preparation and Benefits.

The leaves and flowers of the common and small fleabane open [obstructions] and disperse [bad humors]; they promote urine, the monthly period, and the afterbirth when used in a bath or drunk with wine.

They are good for an obstructed liver, jaundice, strangury <note>original: "Harn-Winde", referring to painful or interrupted urination</note>, and stomach cramps, when drunk with vinegar.

### Externally.

For wounds and injuries, and snake bites, applied as a plaster.

For headaches, bound to the forehead. For delirium <note>original: "Hirn-Wüten", literally "brain-frenzy" or madness</note>, placed under the soles of the feet. For ailments of the womb, used in baths. For the enchantment <note>the belief that illnesses were caused by "evil eyes" or spells</note> and the wasting away <note>original: "Abnehmen", referring to infantile atrophy or failure to thrive</note> of children, when bathed with the small fleabane.

The common fleabane repels snakes and mosquitoes when the rooms are strewn or fumigated with it.

Middle fleabane is powerful against dysentery <note>original: "rothe Ruhr", the "red flux"</note> and the plague, when used in red-sour wine.

### The Seed.

### The Oxycroceum Plaster.

### Crosswort.

Crosswort or Golden Woodruff <note>original: "Gulden Waldmeister," likely referring to *Cruciata laevipes*.</note>, whose fibrous root produces many hairy, four-cornered stems, one ell <note>a historical unit of length, often the length of an arm.</note> high, upon each of which are joints with 4 and 4 longish, rough leaves, set in the shape of a cross, with a bitter taste; from the base of these, the cross-shaped flowers emerge, consisting of 4 yellow petals and as many same-colored filaments. This herb is not used much in pharmacies.

It is, however, a very good <term>wound-herb</term> <note>a plant used specifically for healing cuts, sores, and internal injuries.</note> and can be used for such occurrences both internally and externally with benefit.

### Cubebs.

These are well-known grains, similar to black pepper, each of which hangs on a separate stalk; they have rough shells, are ash-colored, and have a sharp, fragrant taste. They come from a foreign, wild-growing, weak plant that winds itself around nearby trees like ivy, and has leaves shaped like myrtle with fragrant flowers.

### Preparation and Benefits.

Cubebs disperse [congestion] and serve for the "cold" ailments of the head, stomach, heart, lungs, liver, spleen, womb, and kidneys; they are good for a weak memory, dizziness, melancholy <note>original: "Milzsucht," literally "spleen-sickness," thought to be caused by an excess of black bile.</note>, and wind <note>intestinal gas.</note> They increase venereal desire <note>libido</note> and make for a clear voice when one chews them in the mouth.

Sugar-coated cubebs and the medicinal powder *Diacubebae* <note>original: "Species Diacubebæ," a traditional pharmacological compound where cubebs are the primary ingredient.</note> have the same effect.

## Preparation and Benefits.
### The Seed.

This [seed] cuts through [phlegm], resolves, opens, and disperses [congested humors]. It is therefore good for the "cold" ailments of the chest, consumption <note>original: "Lungensucht," a historical term for wasting diseases like tuberculosis</note>, wheezing, coughs, urinary gas, and bloating of the womb. For bruised limbs and black eyes, it is applied with the juice of Rue and Hyssop, along with egg white or honey.

For nosebleeds, it is placed into the nostrils with vinegar.

The smoke from it creates a pale complexion. The seed prepared with vinegar, the sugar-coated seed, and the distilled water are likewise useful for the aforementioned ailments.

The <term>Species Diacymini</term> <note>A traditional medicinal powder mixture where Cumin is the primary ingredient.</note> and the tablets made from it are famous for the "cold" ailments of the chest, the stomach, the liver, and the womb; for shortness of breath, side-aches caused by bloating, belching of the stomach, griping of the belly, fever, afterpains following childbirth, and when one cannot hold their urine.

The distilled oil is good for hiccups, <term>tympanites</term> <note>original: "Trommelsucht," a condition where the abdomen is bloated with gas like a drum</note>, and the involuntary discharge of seed.

### Turmeric.

Turmeric <note>original: "Curcume"</note> is a foreign root, shaped like ginger and saffron-yellow in color; it also yields a similar dye. It is found as either long or round.

This root opens, disperses, consumes [excess moisture], and promotes the monthly period, urine, and bile. It serves the womb, liver, spleen, and the stomach.

## Hound's Tongue.

It develops long, branching, rough stems and long, gray, soft, felt-like, and strong-smelling leaves. The flowers are like those of the Bugloss <note>original: "Ochsen-Zunge," literally "ox-tongue," referring to *Anchusa officinalis*</note>, upon which four joined leaflets appear, in which the seed lies; the root is thick, black on the outside, white on the inside, and somewhat sweet.

### Preparation and Benefits.

The flowers, leaves, and root soothe, constrict, and still pains.

### The distilled water.

The juice and the powder thereof are good for wounds and malignant ulcers—especially those of the mouth originating from the "French disease" <note>original: "Franzosen," a historical term for Syphilis</note>—the bite of a rabid dog, cancer, inflammation of the breasts <note>original: "Brüste-Brand"</note>, and hair loss.

## The Pills.

The pills made from this <note>referring to Hound's Tongue</note> induce sleep, take away pains, and still fluxes <note>original: "Durchbrüche," often referring to diarrhea or dysentery</note>, the "Red Flux" <term>dysentery</term>, and excessive menstruation.

## The Ointment.

The ointment made from it lessens aching days, and serves for bruises from impacts, clotted blood, as well as stitches in the side.

## Wild Galangal.

Wild Galangal, or round Cyperus root <note>likely *Cyperus rotundus*</note>, grows a 3 or 4-sided stem, one ell high <term>a measurement of roughly 24-45 inches</term> or more. It has leaves like a leek, being long, narrow, and streaked, but smaller at the top, upon which stand pale blossoms and brown, fragrant clusters that contain a small seed. The roots hang together by fibers and resemble olives; they are round, black, bitter, and at their best when they are heavy, hard, firm, full, rough, fragrant, and sharp.

There is also a long Galangal or Cyperus root, which is in all ways equal to the round one, except for the root, which is somewhat longer and more knotted.

## Preparation and Benefits.

Both types of roots are "opening" <note>in humoral medicine, "opening" refers to clearing blockages in the vessels or organs</note>; they are good for the head, stomach, chest, and womb. They aid digestion, prevent fainting, promote urine and menstruation, and expel the birth and afterbirth <term>placenta</term>, as well as sweat. Thus, this root is good for dropsy <term>edema</term>, dizziness, gross phlegm in the stomach, and heals scorpion stings. It is also good for stomach cramps, coughing, suppressed menstruation <note>original: "verstopfte Weiber-Blume," literally "clogged women's-flowers"</note>, urine, and stones when taken with wine.

## Externally.

For dropsy, it is boiled with laurel and wine and placed upon the body.

It drives out suppressed urine when crushed and boiled in oil, then placed upon the kidneys and the genitals <note>original: "Gemächte"</note>.

For suppressed menstruation <note>original: "Frauen-Blume"</note>, it is boiled and used as a warm compress <note>original: "gebähet," meaning to foment or apply heat</note>.

For nasty ulcers, especially on the private parts <note>original: "heimlichen Orten"</note>, the powder is sprinkled therein and a bandage applied over it.

## Goat’s Clover.

Out of so many species of Goat’s Clover <note>likely referring to species of *Cytisus* (Broom) or *Medicago*</note>, we wish to take and illustrate or describe only the Horned variety; this one develops woody branches, almost 3 spans <term>a measurement of about 9 inches each</term> high. The leaves are always arranged 3 and 3 together, and are grayish; the flowers are golden yellow, followed by broad, curved sickle-shaped or half-moon-shaped pods, which contain a round, flat, and hard seed.

### Preparation and Benefits.

The leaves of Goat’s Clover cool, "consume" <note>in humoral medicine, this means to resolve or diminish a substance</note>, disperse, promote the flow of urine, increase breast milk, and counteract gout and pain in the limbs. They also settle beginning swellings when made into a plaster with breadcrumbs and applied.

For inflammations, it is used without bread, pounded together with the seed and applied.

The distilled water <note>original: "gebrante Wasser"</note> made from it possesses the same power and virtue.

## Dandelion.

This herb has elongated leaves, notched and toothed on both sides, which are almost similar to those of Endive or Chicory <term>Wegwart</term>. Between these grow hollow and milky stems, a span high, each of which bears a single flower consisting of many purely yellow petals. These finally become woolly and are scattered by the wind, leaving behind only a small white-gray button, like a shorn head <note>a common historical comparison of the dandelion receptacle to a monk's tonsure</note>. The root is long and full of milky sap.

### Preparation and Benefits.

The whole herb, along with the root, is cold and dry <note>referring to its humoral temperament</note>, bitter in taste, and has the same effect as Endive or Chicory. It thins [humors], opens [blockages], and cleanses. It serves the liver and chest, promotes urine, and is also good for blockages of the liver, spleen, and mesenteric veins <term>Gekröß-Adern</term>, as well as for dropsy <term>edema</term>, jaundice, impurity of the blood, scurvy <term>Scharbock</term>, spleen ailments <note>original: "Milzsucht," a term for melancholy or physical spleen disorders</note>, fevers, internal inflammations, bladder spasms <note>original: "Harn-Winde"</note>, and difficulty urinating drop by drop <term>strangury</term>, and

## Bishop’s Weed. <note>original: "Mohren-Kümmel," likely *Ammi majus* or *Ammi visnaga*</note>

It has leaves like fennel, though more delicate; the stem is as high as an arm; the umbels <term>umbrella-shaped flower clusters</term> are like those on coriander, with white flowers and white, hairy, sharp, and pleasant seeds.

The root is as thick as a finger and a span <term>about 9 inches</term> long.

### Preparation and Benefits.

The seed "cuts through" <note>meaning it breaks up humors or phlegm</note>, promotes the flow of urine, disperses wind <note>relieves gas</note>, and is beneficial to the womb <note>original: "der Mutter"</note>. It therefore serves for the suppression of the menses <term>Frauens-Blume</term>, difficult birth, "rising" and pains of the womb <note>hysterical symptoms attributed to the movement of the uterus</note>, retention of urine, colic, hiccups, dropsy <term>Wassersucht</term> <note>swelling caused by fluid retention</note>, chronic coughs, side-stitch, seminal discharge <term>Saamen-Fluß</term>, poison, and the bites of ground-spiders, when used in drinks and other suitable vehicles. The oil made from it is good for the stone <term>kidney or bladder stones</term>.

## White Dittany. <note>Latin: *Dictamnus albus*; also known as Burning Bush or Gas Plant</note>

The stems are nearly two ells <term>a traditional unit of length, approximately 45 inches</term> high, hairy, reddish, and filled with marrow.

The leaves, of which 7, 9, or 11 are found on one branch, are similar to ash-tree foliage.

The tops of the stems bear beautiful purple and flesh-colored <note>original: "Leibfarben"</note>, strong-smelling flowers consisting of 5 petals, with yellow filaments <term>stamens</term>, each of which leaves behind 5 rough reddish pods containing a coal-black, shiny seed, somewhat larger than sea millet <note>original: "Meerhirsche," likely referring to Gromwell or *Lithospermum* seeds</note>;

The root is white, a finger thick, and divided into many parts;

### Preparation and Use.

The root serves the head, nerves, heart, and womb <term>Mutter</term>, and expels urine, sweat, and poison; it is therefore good for ailments of the head, vertigo, stroke, severe maladies <term>epilepsy or fits</term>, venomous diseases, and the bites and stings of poisonous animals, rot, worms, stomach cramps, and venereal diseases <note>original: "Venerische Kranckheiten"</note>. It is boiled with guaiac wood <term>Frantzosen-Holtz</term> <note>literally "French wood," used historically to treat syphilis</note> and drunk. For wounds, it is used in drinks and for blockages of the womb, and can also be used externally as a uterine suppository <term>Mutter-Zäpfgen</term> <note>a pessary</note>. It promotes the fruit <term>the fetus</term> and expels the afterbirth. Therefore, this root is also used, mixed by half with malt and nutmeg, to facilitate birth and the delivery of the placenta <term>Afterbande</term>. It also draws splinters and arrows out of the skin;

The water distilled from the flowers is useful for the eyes, resists poison, and is drawn into the nose for headaches caused by cold;

The oil boiled from the flowers is smeared externally for aching limbs and side-stiches <term>pleurisy or sharp chest pain</term>.

The root preserved with sugar stills the "white flux" <term>leukorrhea or vaginal discharge</term>.

At the top, it bears a longish ear <term>spike</term>, which is composed of many [parts] similar to marjoram, and pressed together in a scale-like manner—

## Leopard’s Bane. <note>German: *Gemsen-Wurtzel*; likely referring to *Doronicum*</note>

This plant produces oblong-round, hairy, and notched leaves, a rough striated stem, and star-shaped flowers that eventually blow away <note>original: "verfliegen," referring to the dispersal of seeds by wind</note>; the seed is small and black. The root is fibrous and is found among the stone cliffs of the highest mountains in Austria and Styria <note>original: "Steurmarck"</note>.

## Preparation and Use.

This root disperses [bad humors], resists poison, prevents dizziness, heart palpitations, fainting, the severe malady <term>Bösen Gebrechen</term> <note>a historical term often referring to epilepsy or fits</note>, and bloating of the womb; it drives out belly-aches and worms.

## Dragon Arum. <note>German: *Drachen-Wurtz*; *Dracunculus vulgaris*</note>

The smooth and red-speckled stem resembles a colorful snake, and its reddish tail <note>referring to the spadix or lower stem</note> looks like a dragon.

The fruit, which grows like a cluster of grapes, is green at first, and afterwards saffron-yellow.

The leaves are bent backward and very deeply cut.

The root is bulbous, round, and white.

It grows in shady places and near fences; it is also produced in gardens.

## Preparation and Use.

The leaves and root have nearly the same power as Cuckoo-pint <note>original: "Aron"; *Arum maculatum*</note>, but are sharper and more bitter; they warm, dry, cut through [phlegm], resolve and disperse [blockages], promote sweat, and resist poison. They are good for scurvy <term>Scharbock</term>,

### Water-Snake-Herb <note>Likely Marsh Calla (*Calla palustris*), known for its serpent-like roots</note>

From its long, jointed, and fibrous root arise elongated broad leaves. The flowers, which consist of white or red dots, appear at the tip from one of the smallest leaves; these are followed by berries pressed together like a cluster, which are green at first and become red when they are ripe, containing an elongated seed within them.

### Preparation and Use.

The root, roasted in the ashes, mixed with honey and consumed, dissolves thick phlegm; it is good against catarrh <term>Flüsse des Haupts</term> <note>literally "flows of the head," referring to excess mucus or rheum</note>, for stabbing pains, asthma <term>Engbrüstigkeit</term>, and coughs.

### Tarragon <note>German: *Dragien*; *Artemisia dracunculus*</note>

This plant produces thin, hard, and somewhat angular stems, two cubits high, with long, narrow, dark-green, and shiny leaves; at the tip, however, are small clusters, like Southernwood <note>German: *Stabwurz*</note>, with very small yellow flowers and seeds.

### Preparation and Use.

The leaves are warming, consuming <note>in the sense of "dissolving" humors</note>, and opening; used in a salad, they promote the digestion of the stomach, awaken the appetite, stimulate the <term>Women’s Flowers</term> <note>a common euphemism for menstruation</note>, and create a desire for marital acts <note>original: "Lust zu ehlichen Wercken," referring to libido</note>.

### Externally.

Applied externally, they serve for toothache and swollen gums when boiled in wine and used to rinse the mouth. 
The water distilled from it induces sweat and is good in times of plague.

### Bittersweet, "The Longer the Dearer" <note>Bittersweet Nightshade, *Solanum dulcamara*</note>

This plant has woody vines, with the branches of which it fastens itself around fences and shrubs.

## Dwarf Elder <note>German: *Attich*; *Sambucus ebulus*, also known as Danewort</note>.

It is almost entirely similar to the common Elder <note>German: *Hollunder*</note>, except that it is much lower and smaller; it is also to be counted among the herbs rather than the trees, for the stems perish annually.

### Preparation and Use.

Dwarf Elder has almost the same effect as common Elder, but it purges more strongly.

### The Flowers and Leaves.

These soften, resolve, dissipate, and induce perspiration.
The flowers, consumed in food, benefit the liver, spleen, and heart, and resist dropsy.
The leaves, made into a pulp and applied as a poultice, are good for milk-pains, watery swellings, hydrocele <term>Wasserbruch</term> <note>a swelling of the scrotum</note>, and swollen feet when bathed therein. The young shoots, cooked in food with salt and oil, are useful for dropsy.
The whole root, dug in the spring, halts the excessive <term>Women's Flowers</term> <note>a common euphemism for menstruation</note>; the juice from it heals all poison.

### The Inner Bark.

This softens, dissolves <note>referring to the traditional medical practice of "resolving" or breaking up stagnant bodily humors</note>, promotes the flow of urine, discharges watery humors, and is useful for dropsy <term>Wassersucht</term> <note>edema or swelling caused by fluid retention</note> and diseases of the joints <term>Glieder-Kranckheiten</term> <note>likely referring to gout or rheumatism</note>.

## Horsetail <note>German: *Roß-Schwanz*; likely Field Horsetail, *Equisetum arvense*</note>.

It produces many knotty long leaves, or tubes, on the same stem; in place of a flower, however, it has a white-clustered head <note>referring to the spore-bearing cone or strobilus</note>; it has a long, black, and straight root.

### Preparation and Use.

This is a wind-expelling <note>carminative</note> and urine-promoting herb; it serves against wheezing, old coughs, nosebleeds, the flow of the womb <note>uterine bleeding</note>, and the "Golden Vein" <term>Goldnen Ader-Fluß</term> <note>bleeding hemorrhoids</note>, ruptures <note>hernias</note>, red dysentery <term>Rothe-Ruhr</term>, spitting of blood, bloody urine, wounds, and ulcers—especially of the small intestines, lungs, kidneys, and bladder—as well as fractures, strangury <term>Harn-Winde</term> <note>painful or difficult urination</note>, and stones.

### Externally.

For red heat-blisters, swellings, and inflammations of the genitals, and for mouth-rot <term>Mundfäule</term> <note>stomatitis or oral thrush</note>.
The distilled water made from this also serves for the aforementioned ailments.

# Heather <note>German: *Heide*; likely *Calluna vulgaris* or *Erica*</note>.

From the woody root sprout thin rods, a span high, with smooth evergreen leaves and red or white flowers.

### Preparation and Use.

The leaves along with the flowers consume <note>in the sense of diminishing or "eating away" excess fluids in the body</note>, disperse, and open <note>referring to the medical practice of "opening" blockages in the vessels or organs</note>.

### Infusion.

The drink made from it is good for blockages of the spleen, belly-ache and loin-pain, and increases breast milk;
For swellings and snake-bites, it is made into a mash and applied as a poultice.
In steam-baths, they serve for paralysis and limb-ache <note>likely rheumatism or arthritis</note>.

### The Juice.

Dispels weakness of the eyes.
The water distilled from the flowers is good for colic and the stone <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>.

# Rocket <note>German: *Raucke Ruckette*; likely Garden Rocket or Arugula (*Eruca sativa*)</note>.

Has stems one and a half feet high; long, broad, dark-green leaves that are cut on both sides; at the top of the stem are white, striped flowers, and the seeds are in elongated pods; the root is white and long.

### Preparation and Use.

The seed cleanses, aids digestion, increases semen and milk, protects against stroke <term>Schlag</term> and scurvy <term>Scharbock</term>, promotes the flow of urine, stones, and worms, and heals the bites of poisonous animals.

### Externally.

It serves for paralysis of the tongue when rubbed on with stroke-water <note>German: *Schlag-Wasser*; a medicinal distilled spirit used to treat neurological issues</note>; it is also used in baths for smelly armpits, measles, skin-marks, and scurvy or liver spots.

## Field Eryngo <note>German: *Mans-Treu*; *Eryngium campestre*, also known as Sea Holly</note>.

Has a long white root, the thickness of a small finger, and a whitish, stiff stem full of spongy white marrow, with many branches; the leaves are broad, almost grayish-blue, deeply notched, and covered with spines.

The prickly heads standing at the summit bear whitish flowers in the center; beneath these are striped, pointed, and prickly leaves arranged in the shape of a star.

### Preparation and Use.

#### The Root.

This serves the stomach, the liver, and kidneys, and resists poison. It is good for obstructions of the menses <term>Weiber-Blum</term> <note>literally "women’s flower"</note>, of the urine, the liver, gall, bladder, and spleen; for heartache, difficult birth, gravel <term>Grieß</term> <note>small urinary stones or sediment</note>, kidney and bladder stones, dropsy <note>water-sickness</note>, jaundice <term>Gelbesucht</term>, and cramps, when eaten and drunk with oak-mistletoe.

#### Externally.

Externally, it pulls out thorns and splinters; applied with lard <note>German: *Schmer*</note>, it is useful in cases of premature labor; soaked in red wine and struck <note>applied firmly as a compress</note> over the body for swellings.

#### For the poisonous seminal discharge <note>likely referring to venereal infections such as gonorrhea</note>.

The leaves crushed with wine and the juice pressed from them.

### Hedge Mustard <note>German: *Hederich*; likely *Sisymbrium officinale*</note>.

Develops tough and flexible stems, with elongated, deeply notched leaves and yellow flowers, followed by thin pods shaped like stalks, inside which sits a sharp yellow seed, similar to cress seed <note>original: *Greß-Saamen*</note>.

### Preparation and Use.

The seed and the herb thin the humors, open and cleanse the chest, and serve in cases of obstruction of the liver and spleen. They are good for jaundice <term>Gelbesucht</term>, griping of the belly <term>Bauchgrimmen</term> <note>abdominal cramps</note>, shortness of breath <term>Engbrüstigkeit</term> <note>literally "narrow-chestedness"</note>, hoarseness, and old coughs—especially the seed made into a syrup with honey. This seed is also good for a poisonous seminal discharge <note>likely referring to venereal infections like gonorrhea</note>.

### Externally.

They are good for cancer <note>historically used for various hard swellings or tumors</note> that has not yet come to an ulcer <term>schwären</term>, and also for swollen breasts.

The syrup prepared from hedge mustard is good for phlegm on the lungs, hoarseness, and coughs.

### Spindle Tree <note>German: *Spindel-Baum*; *Euonymus europaeus*</note>.

The branches of this small tree are four-angled and have green bark adorned with long, fire-red stripes; the leaves grow in pairs opposite one another. After the flower—which consists of 4 small white petals—it bears yellow berries in red, four-angled pods, each containing a small white seed. It grows in living hedges and thorn-bushes, along roadsides, in forests, and on mountains.

### Preparation and Use.

Eating 3 or 4 of the berries purges both above and below <note>acts as an emetic to induce vomiting and a laxative to clear the bowels</note>.

### Externally.

Externally, they resolve <note>dissipate swellings</note> and soften. Boiled in lye and used to wash the head, they kill vermin on the head and dye the hair; boiled in wine with "Schauer" <note>The meaning here is unclear; it may refer to "sourness" (*Sauer*), or perhaps treatment for "shivers" (*Schauer*)</note>, pressed out, and with which one <insert>washes oneself...</insert>

### Hemp-Agrimony <note>German: *Wasser-Dost*; *Eupatorium cannabinum*</note>.

Hemp-agrimony has a straight, rough, fragrant stem, upon which stand elongated, notched, and hairy leaves, almost like those of hemp; at the top of the stem, it bears spikes with light-red flowers, which mostly consist of only small threads <note>original: *Dräten*; referring to the fine, feathery florets</note> and finally blow away.

The root is fibrous, white, and bitter, as are the leaves. It is found in wet and marshy places.

### Preparation and Use.

The flowers and leaves are somewhat astringent <term>ziehen etwas an</term> <note>meaning they contract the tissues to stop bleeding or discharge</note>, serve the liver and spleen, and promote the menstrual cycle <term>Monath-Zeit</term>, urine, and sweat. They are good for a sallow complexion <term>Mißfarbe</term>, dropsy <term>Wassersucht</term>, jaundice <term>Gelbesucht</term>, scurvy <term>Scharbock</term>, feverish fluxes, venomous animals, and worms.

### Euphorbium <note>The resin of the Spurge plant, *Euphorbia resinifera*</note>.

Some hold it to be a plant whose leaves are elongated, thick, and provided with double rows of whitish thorns; others hold it to be a tree from which a sap is drawn and dried, which is incisive and very sharp, and appears white or yellow. It grows in Africa, but is mostly brought from Peru in the West Indies <note>Historical confusion: while true Euphorbium comes from North Africa, various succulent plants from the Americas were often conflated with it in early herbals</note>.

Euphorbium is hot and dry <note>referring to its qualities in the humoral system of medicine</note>; it burns and raises blisters; it very strongly purges phlegm and watery humors.

### Externally.

Mixed with laurel oil <term>Looröhl</term>, it prevents hair loss; mixed and smeared with olive oil <term>Baumöhl</term> <note>literally "tree oil," the common term for olive oil</note>, it treats pains of the spleen; it also draws out splinters from bone fractures <term>Beinbrüche</term>.

### Eyebright <note>German: *Augentrost*; *Euphrasia officinalis*</note>.

Has delicate hairy stems, a span long, with curled, curved leaves set in pairs opposite one another, and white flowers with reddish stripes; the root is thin and woody.

### Preparation and Use.

The herb along with the flowers is astringent and dispersive; it strengthens the sight and the head, and serves for internal and external use against the darkness <note>meaning dimness or cloudiness of vision</note>

### Orpine <note>German: *Fette Henne*; literally "Fat Hen," today commonly known as Stonecrop or *Hylotelephium telephium*</note>.

It develops straight stems, one foot <term>Schuh</term> high, with upright, fleshy <term>fetten</term>, gray-blue leaves; it bears white flowers consisting of five petals on the umbels <note>the flat-topped flower clusters</note>.

### Preparation and Use.

The leaves ripen <note>meaning they help "draw" or bring an abscess to a head</note>, are astringent <term>ziehen an</term>, soothe pain, serve for wounds, and stop their bleeding. They are good for dysentery <term>Rohen-Ruhr</term> <note>literally "the raw flux"</note>, damaged intestines, bad ulcers—especially of the womb <term>Beermutter</term>—dandruff of the head, skin spots, and gangrene <term>Brand</term>.

The root is worn <note>as an amulet</note> for hemorrhoids <term>Goldne-Ader</term>; the water distilled from the leaves and flowers clarifies the skin.

### Giant Fennel <note>German: *Gerten- oder Stecken-Kraut*; *Ferula communis*</note>.

It has a thick, branched stem full of spongy pith, and is five to six cubits <term>Ehlen</term> high. Its leaves are like fennel leaves; the umbels bear yellow flowers and a large, flat, and broad seed. When it sprouts in the spring, it yields a bud <term>Auge</term> or pith like a hard egg yolk. If the root is injured, a milky sap flows out of it.

It is common in Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, yet it is also cultivated in Germany in well-tended gardens.

### Preparation and Use.

The seeds, boiled in wine and drunk, dispel colic. The bud or pith is good for spitting up blood <term>Blutspeyen</term>.

### Externally.

Placed into the nose, it stops nosebleeds. This is not available in pharmacies <note>indicating it might need to be gathered fresh or grown in a private garden</note>.

# Galbanum Plant <note>German: *Galben-Kraut*; likely referring to *Ferula gummosa* or related species that produce the resin Galbanum</note>.

This plant has thin leaves, flowers on the umbels <note>flat-topped flower clusters</note>, and many broad seeds with a spicy taste; the root is thick and juicy. From this plant flows a resinous gum, which is called Galbanum, Schulbanum, and Stragenitio <note>archaic names for different grades or types of the resin</note>. The best kind is that which is lumpy, yellow, pure, fatty or oily, easily ignited, having a heavy scent and a foul taste.

Galbanum dissolves <note>original: *resolviret*; meaning it breaks down "bad humors" or swellings</note>, draws out, stills pain, strengthens the nerves, resists poison, induces the menses <term>Frauen-Zeit</term>, and promotes childbirth. It serves for head-fluxes <note>discharges or catarrh from the head</note>, wheezing, old dry coughs, and a congested spleen and liver.

### External Use.

Externally, it is good for suppressed menstruation, heavy ailments, bloating of the womb, dizziness, and for freckles. Placed upon the male member, it drives the urine.

### The Distilled Oil.

The oil distilled from this settles the "rising of the womb" <note>original: *Aufsteigen der Mutter*; a historical belief that the uterus could move upward in the body, causing various physical and emotional symptoms</note>, whether taken internally or smeared externally upon the navel; it also ripens plague boils <note>helps them reach a head so they can be drained</note>.

The Galbanum of Theophrastus <note>referring to a specific preparation described by the Greek philosopher/botanist</note> strengthens the head and the nerves, and is good for paralyzed limbs when they are smeared with it.

### Mynsicht’s Galbanum Plaster <note>Latin: *Emplastrum de Galb. Myns.*; referring to a recipe by the 17th-century physician Adrian von Mynsicht</note>.

Dispels warts and corns <term>Elster-Augen</term> <note>literally "magpie eyes"</note>.

Mynsicht’s Saffron-Galbanum Plaster <note>original: *Emplastrum de Galb. Crocatum Myns.*</note> softens, dissolves, and breaks up hard swellings, eases pain, and settles convulsions and hiccups.

# Galangal <note>German: *Galgan*</note>.

The large Galangal grows 2 cubits <term>Ehlen</term> high, has leaves like an orchid <term>Knaben-Kraut</term> which surround the stem, white flowers, and a small seed. The small Galangal is only 2 hand-widths <term>querhände</term> high and has a knotty, reddish, and sharp root. The large kind grows in India and Malabar, but the small kind grows in China.

### Preparation and Use.

The root, especially of the small Galangal <note>German: *Galgan*; *Alpinia officinarum*</note>, is good for the head, stomach, and the womb <note>German: *Mutter*; referring to the uterus or the historical condition "the mother" (hysteria)</note>; it serves against coarse humors <note>referring to the four bodily fluids of Galenic medicine</note> and bloating of the stomach, for colic, dizziness, and the vomiting of seafarers <note>seasickness</note>, lingering fevers, obstruction of the womb, and after-pains of childbirth when used with Zedoary <note>German: *Zitwer*; *Curcuma zedoaria*, a warming root similar to ginger</note>; it also aids fainting and heart palpitations.

### External Use.

Externally, it strengthens the head when drawn into the nose <note>used as a medicinal snuff</note>. Placed in a small pouch, dipped in wine, and applied to the stomach, it strengthens it excellently. The Spirits of Diagalangal <note>original Latin: *Spiritus Diagalangæ*; a distilled medicinal compound featuring galangal</note> are good for the head, heart, stomach, and spleen; they resist poison, promote the menses <term>Frauen-Zeit</term>, and serve against wind <note>gas/flatulence</note>, dropsy <note>edema or swelling</note>, wheezing, hiccups, and the excess and superfluous casting off of saliva. An extract is also made from the root; occasionally, the preserved root is also brought to us.

## Goat’s Rue.

This plant gets striated, branched stems, two ells <note>an ell is an old unit of measurement, roughly 45 inches or 1.1 meters</note> high; the leaves almost resemble vetch leaves but are longer; the flowers are white or white-bluish; the seed is enclosed in small and elongated pods. It grows in wet places, on mountains, and in forests, and is also cultivated in gardens.

### Preparation and Use.

The herb drives out sweat and poison; it serves for spotted and pestilential fevers <note>such as typhus or plague-like illnesses</note>, measles, smallpox, viper venom <note>German: *Nattern-Gift*</note>, and the bites and stings of other venomous animals, worms, and the foul ailments of small children.

### External Use.

It is applied warm as a poultice for belly-ache. The seed kills worms. The distilled water, conserve, and syrup are likewise useful in the aforementioned cases.

# Galbanum Plant.

Galbanum resolves <note>dissolves or disperses blockages</note>, draws out [impurities], stills pain, strengthens the nerves, resists poison, promotes the menses <term>Frauen-Zeit</term>, and aids in childbirth. It serves for "head-fluids" <note>catarrh or mucus</note>, wheezing, old dry coughs, and a clogged spleen or liver.

This drives away warts and corns <note>German: *Elster-Augen*, literally "magpie eyes"</note>.

### Gentian.

It has a single smooth stem, two cubits <term>Ehle: an old unit of measurement, roughly equivalent to a yard or the length of an arm</term> high and more; the leaves upon it are similar to those of the white hellebore <term>Niesswurz: white hellebore, *Veratrum album*</term>, smooth and shiny. Many of these are found near the root, but on the stem they are set two by two opposite one another. Next to the topmost leaves, individual elongated yellow flowers emerge, followed by small elongated pods <note>literally "little houses"</note> containing a thin brown seed.

The root is long, yellow, and bitter.

It grows wild in various places, in meadows and pastures situated in the mountains, in the Alps between Germany and Italy; it is also cultivated here and there in gardens.

### Preparation and Use.

#### The Root.

The root resists decay and poison, promotes urine, and is good for the stomach. It serves to treat a clogged liver and spleen, dropsy <note>edema or swelling caused by excess fluid</note>, poison, plague, Saint Anthony’s Fire <note>original: *Rosen*; typically refers to erysipelas, a skin infection</note>, and the bites of poisonous animals and the diseases arising from them. It is also used for the rising of the mother <term>hysterical suffocation or various uterine disorders</term>, weaknesses and pains of the stomach, worms, fevers, colic, ruptures, phlegm and inflammation <note>original: *Loder*; refers to a burning heat or congestion</note> of the chest, coughs, wheezing, clotted blood, suppressed menstruation <term>Frauen-Blume: literally "women's flower," a common euphemism for the menses</term>, cleansing after childbirth, gravel, and stones.

#### Externally.

Inserted externally into the nose, it draws phlegm from the brain and cleanses the head. It is also used on wounds and fontanelles <term>Fontanellen: artificial ulcers or "issues" created by physicians to drain "bad humors" from the body</term> to clean them and keep them open. It opens ulcers and drives away films over the eyes when boiled in distilled vinegar and applied as drops. It also defends against the bite of a rabid dog when applied with theriac <term>Theriac: a famous ancient polypharmaceutical "cure-all" and antitoxin</term>.

The distilled water made from it consumes the phlegm in the stomach, opens a clogged liver and spleen, promotes urine and the monthly period, and resists poison—especially that of snakes, adders, and rabid dogs. It is good for congealed blood, long-lasting fevers, and side-stiches...

[...and the] Plague. Externally for blemishes of the face and old, festering wounds; the thick juice from it serves well in subsiding fevers. The extract is useful against poison and all the aforementioned ailments.

## Cross Gentian.

This is also called Cross-wort and Heal-all <note>original: *Heyl aller Schaden*</note>; it has leaves like Swallow-wort <note>likely *Vincetoxicum officinale*</note>, with blue flowers, and is frequently found here in Germany. Its root has the same power and virtue as the true Gentian and is also to be used externally just like the other.

## Crane's-bill.

It has hairy, reddish, and branched stems, about an ell <term>Ehle: an old unit of measurement, roughly equivalent to the length of an arm</term> high, with rough, reddish leaves. It also bears five-petaled purple flowers, upon which pointed beaks appear where the seeds hang. It grows on old collapsed walls, felled hollow trees, and in shady, cool, and damp places.

### Preparation and Use.

The leaves are slightly astringent, binding and healing wounds. Used internally, they <term>resolve: to dissolve, disperse, or dissipate a physical congestion or tumor</term> clotted blood. Externally, they stop bleeding and are good for wounds, swellings, and sores in secret places <note>a common historical euphemism for the genitals</note>, as well as for torn, swollen, inflamed, and hard breasts and cancer of the same. They are also used for erysipelas <note>original: *Rothlauf*; a bacterial skin infection characterized by a red rash</note>, congealed blood, swollen feet, and bone fractures. The powder, when used, stills feverish heat if mixed with salt and vinegar and bound under the soles of the feet.

### The Distilled Water.

The distilled water <note>original: *gebrandte Wasser*</note> made from the whole herb breaks up lumpy clotted blood, promotes urine, expels sand and stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>, and opens the obstructed urinary tracts.

### Externally.

It serves to treat quinsy <term>Bräune: an old term for severe throat inflammation or tonsillitis</term> when mixed with quince seed mucilage and smeared on the tongue. It heals cracked nipples, mouth ulcers, swellings and inflammations of the breasts, St. Anthony's Fire <note>original: *Rose*; another term for erysipelas or similar skin inflammations</note>, and cancer.

### The Root.

The root of Tuberous Crane’s-bill <note>original: *Geranii tuberosi*</note> is good for bloating and swelling of the womb <note>original: *Mutter*; commonly used in this period to refer to the uterus or "hysteria"</note>, as well as for consumption <note>original: *Schwindsucht*; a wasting disease, usually tuberculosis</note>.

### The Herb.

The herb of Musk Crane’s-bill <note>original: *Geranii Moschati*; likely *Erodium moschatum*</note> warms, <term>resolves: to disperse or break up "humors" or blockages in the body</term>, and strengthens the nerves. The herb, when boiled and drunk, stills bleeding and promotes the flow of urine.

## Licorice.

Licorice <note>original: *Süß-Holtz*</note> has jagged roots that are brown on the outside but yellow and sweet on the inside, which creep far and wide beneath the earth. From these roots, shoots grow up to two <term>ells: an old unit of measurement, roughly the length of an arm</term> high, upon which the leaves stand in pairs opposite one another. It bears pale blue flowers and smooth pods containing a small seed. It grows in Germany, France, and Spain.

### Preparation and Use.
### The Root.

This soothes and softens; it serves the chest, the stomach, and the kidneys. It is good for hoarseness, coughing, tightness of the chest, lung disease, consumption, stitches in the side, heartburn <note>original: *Magen-Brennen*</note>, thirst, ulcers of the bladder, difficulty urinating <note>original: *Harn-Winde*; likely strangury</note>, and stones.

### Externally.

Used for erysipelas <note>original: *die Rose*; a bacterial skin infection</note>, mouth sores <note>original: *Mund-Blattern*</note>, and festering eyes.

## Dysentery Herb.

This herb <note>original: *Ruhr-Kraut*; likely a species of *Gnaphalium* or Cudweed, traditionally used to treat dysentery or "the bloody flux"</note> bears woolly green stems rising to a height of one and a half spans <note>a measurement based on the width of an expanded hand</note>. These are surrounded throughout with narrow, white-green, and soft leaves, and bear pale yellow flowers at the top, which are scattered by the wind.

The root is woody, white, and fibrous.

### Preparation and Use.

The herb dries, draws, and binds together <term>astringent: a property that contracts tissues to stop bleeding or secretions</term>; it is good for injured intestines in red dysentery <note>original: *Rothen-Ruhr*; a historical term for severe diarrhea containing blood</note> when boiled in red wine and drunk. The juice of the leaves, tempered with wine and milk, serves as a gargle for ulcers of the throat.

It resists cancer of the breasts.

It drives away blue bruises caused by bumping or hitting, and stills the immoderate "women’s flowers" <note>original: *Frauen-Blume*; a period term for the menses</note>. This herb is not commonly used in the apothecaries.

## Couch Grass.

Couch grass <note>original: *Quecken-Graß*; scientifically known as *Elymus repens*</note> has round, smooth stems a foot and a half long, which bear small clusters at the top instead of a blossom. The leaves are narrow and pointed; the root is long, divided into segments, and white.

### Preparation and Use.

The root promotes the flow of urine and serves for a congested liver, spleen, and urinary tracts, as well as the bladder and the womb <note>original: *Mutter*</note>. It is used for spitting blood, fevers, purple spots <note>original: *Petechien*; small red or purple spots on the skin caused by bleeding, often seen in typhus</note>, eruptions, spleen-sickness <note>original: *Milzsucht*; once believed to be a physical ailment of the spleen causing melancholy</note>, scurvy <note>original: *Scharbock*</note>, worms, stones, and colic.

### Externally.

Used externally for headaches, inflammation of the eyes, fluxes <note>original: *Flüsse*; an abnormal discharge of fluids</note>, festering ears, toothaches, and fresh wounds.

The seed stills toothache.

The water distilled from the root promotes urine, expels gravel and stones, and can be administered in those medicines used against worms. It also stills the flow of blood.

Used externally, it prevents diarrhea in small children.

### Passion Flowers.

This is a foreign plant that bears a flower on a weak stem which looks like a white rose; in the middle, several figures of the Passion of Christ <note>original: *Leydens Christi*</note> are to be seen, namely a pillar, at the base of which lie small, round, red petals like drops of blood, and at the top three branches like nails, around which a crown of thorns entwines. At the bottom of the stem grow fruits like pomegranates, the size of a goose egg, full of sweet and sour juice and filled with seeds similar to melon seeds.

It was originally brought to us from the Indies <note>historically referring to the Americas, where the Passion Flower is native</note> and is now also cultivated in many gardens in Europe.

### Preparation and Use.

The Indians suck the juice out of the fruit with the greatest delight; this opens and cleanses the entire body, and serves against heart and stomach pain and other illnesses.

### Wild Aurin.

Wild Aurin <note>likely *Gratiola officinalis*, commonly known as Hedge Hyssop</note> or Grace of God <note>original: *Gnade-GOttes*</note>, grows many stems about a span and a half high, on which two leaves always stand opposite each other; these are almost similar to those of Soapwort, though somewhat smaller. Next to these grow small branches which bear partly leaves like Hyssop, and partly elongated flesh-colored, yellow, or white flowers. The roots are divided into segments, knotty, fibrous, and white.

It grows in fields and on meadows.

### Preparation and Use.

### The Flowers.

These are bitter and purge phlegm, watery humors, and bile, both upwards and downwards <note>meaning they act as both an emetic and a laxative</note>. They serve for jaundice <note>original: *Gelbsucht*</note>, dropsy <note>original: *Wassersucht*; swelling caused by fluid retention</note>, lingering fevers, worms, hip pain, and malignant sores <note>original: *bösen Grund*; likely referring to deep-seated ulcers or necrotic tissue</note>.

### Externally.

For wounds.

### Ivy.

This plant <note>original: *Epheu*; Latin: *Hedera helix*</note> seizes whatever is nearest to it with its woody vines. It initially produces somewhat three-angled leaves, which later become rounder. After the mossy blossoms, the berries follow in clusters, appearing black when they are ripe.

### Preparation and Use.

The leaves are slightly astringent and soothe pain, but they must only be used externally.

### Externally.

They cleanse the head when the juice is drawn into the nose; they also serve for nasal ulcers, old sores, scalp scabs <note>original: *Haupt-Grind*</note>, painful and suppurating ears, hardness of the milk <note>likely referring to mastitis or congested breasts</note>, corns, gangrene <note>original: *Brand*</note>, withered breasts, and are used in fontanelles <note>artificial surgical wounds used to "drain" humors</note> to treat inflammation of the same.

### The Berries.

These purge both upwards and downwards <note>meaning they act as both an emetic and a laxative</note>. They are used for kidney stones, dropsy <note>original: *Wassersucht*; an accumulation of fluid in the body</note>, fever and plague, and for drunkenness. The gum or resin from them is used for stomach aches.

### Externally.

It drives away hair and the nits <note>original: *Nüsse*, likely a variant of *Nisse* (nits/lice eggs)</note> on the head. The oil distilled from the berries drives away pains of the ears.

### Ground Ivy.

This plant <note>original: *Gundermann*; Latin: *Glechoma hederacea*</note> grows vines a span long, with which it lies spread out upon the earth. It has rounded, notched, and crinkled leaves, and purple-colored flowers shaped like an open helmet.

## Elecampane.

This plant <note>original: *Alant*; Latin: *Inula helenium*</note> grows a straight, rough-haired, tall stem with woolly leaves similar to Mullein <note>original: *Wull-Kraut*</note>. ### Preparation and Use.

#### The Root.

This root disperses humors, promotes sweat, and the feminine time <note>original: *Fräuliche Zeit*; a euphemism for menstruation</note>. It serves for wheezing, coughing, stitches in the side, clotted blood, a cold and weak stomach, blockages of the womb, the itch <note>scabies</note>, the stone, strangury <note>original: *Harnwinde*; painful or difficult urination</note>, colic, spleen ailments, and the coughing up of blood.

#### The Leaves.

These are externally good for sciatica and pains of the nipples.

### White Hellebore.

This plant <note>original: *Weisse Nieß-Wurtz*; Latin: *Veratrum album*</note> shoots up on a stem one to two ells <note>an "ell" is an old unit of measurement, roughly 24–45 inches</note> high; this stem is set with ribbed leaves similar to those of Gentian, and at the very top, on small branches, it bears many white-green flowers consisting of seven petals, which leave behind small pods with broad, whitish seeds.
The root is white and fibrous.

The root cleanses and is almost a universal and potent purgative <term>purgantz: a strong laxative used to "purge" the body of harmful humors</term>. It serves as a remedy against poison.

It relieves toothache when boiled in vinegar and held in the mouth.

### Black Hellebore.

This plant <note>original: *Schwartz-Nieß Wurzel*; Latin: *Helleborus niger*</note> produces a firm stem, not quite an ell high; it bears leaves like those of Sanicle <note>original: *Sannickel*; a small perennial herb</note>, seven on each long stalk.
The flowers are pale, purple-colored, and shaped like roses, followed by elongated seeds in five pods standing together.
The roots are fastened together like a bulb, yet are black and fibrous.

# Noble Liverwort.
<note>original: *Edel Leber-Kraut*; *Hepatica nobilis*. The name "liverwort" comes from the three-lobed shape of the leaves, which was thought to resemble the liver, suggesting its use for liver ailments under the "Doctrine of Signatures."</note>

This bears spotted leaves on special stalks, which are cut into three parts, similar to Hazelwort <note>original: *Hasel-Wurzel*; *Asarum europaeum*</note>. Likewise, on separate stems, it bears star-shaped flowers that are blue, white, flesh-colored, or purple, and may be simple or full <note>referring to single or double-petaled varieties</note>.
The seed is elongated and white.
The root is many-branched, thin, and reddish.
The full Noble Liverwort is cultivated in gardens, but the simple variety is also found growing wild in some places among the thickets.

### Preparation and Use.

The leaves and flowers cleanse the blood <note>original: *Geblüt*; referring to the blood and the balance of the body's humors</note>, open obstructions of the liver, urinary tract, and spleen, clean the kidneys and bladder, and heal wounds and hernias <note>original: *Brüche*; can also refer to ruptures or fractures</note>.

### Externally.

Applied topically, the leaves are good for mouth-rot <note>original: *Mund-Fäule*; likely referring to scurvy, thrush, or gingivitis</note>, swelling of the uvula <note>original: *Zapfens*; literally the "peg" or "pin" at the back of the throat</note> and the tonsils, and inflammations of the throat when used in a gargle. They also heal ulcers and stem the excessive monthly period <note>original: *übrige Monats-Zeit*; menorrhagia</note>.

### The Distilled Water.
<note>original: *gebrandte Wasser*; hydrosols or waters created through distillation</note>

It makes the skin smooth. A conserve made from the flowers is good for the liver and for cleansing the blood.

# Tongue-Leaf.
<note>original: *Zungen-Blat*; likely *Ruscus hypoglossum*, also known as Horse-tongue lily or Butcher’s Broom, named for the small tongue-like leaf growth.</note>

This is a small shrub whose root is almost like Butcher's Broom <note>original: *Mäuß-Dorn*; *Ruscus aculeatus*</note>; the leaves are similarly pointed. Next to these, small leaflets sprout forth that look like little tongues, at the base of which red berries grow.
It grows in shady places in the mountains.

### Preparation and Use.

The herb serves to treat the stone <note>kidney or bladder stones</note> and urinary wind <note>original: *Harn-Wind*; a historical term for strangury or painful, difficult urination</note>.

### Externally.

In mouthwashes, it is used for a fallen and swollen uvula in the throat, mouth-rot, and ulcers in the mouth.

## Preparation and Use.

From this, the leaves, root, and seeds are used, especially those of the white variety <note>The author refers to White Henbane (*Hyoscyamus albus*), which was historically considered milder and safer than the black variety.</note>.

### The Root.

Used externally for hip pain <note>sciatica</note>, and in poultices for toothaches when boiled in vinegar or water; the mouth is rinsed with this decoction. However, if the root itself is placed directly upon the teeth, it stills their pain, but it also causes them to fall out.

It checks excessive menstruation <note>original: *Frauen-Blume*; literally "women’s flower," a common euphemism for the menses</note> when carried under the armpits, and promotes childbirth when bound upon the left thigh.

For colic, it is worn against the body.

### The Leaves.

These are also only used externally, such as for dropsy <note>edema or swelling caused by fluid retention</note> when bound to the soles of the feet. For inflammations and swellings, plague boils, and abdominal cramps, or for people suffering from scurvy <note>original: *Scharbock*; a disease caused by Vitamin C deficiency</note>, the leaves are made into a pulp with milk and applied as a dressing. If the spine has been broken, the herb together with the root is applied.

## St. John’s Wort.

This plant produces reddish, woody stems, nearly an ell <note>a historical unit of measurement, roughly 24–27 inches</note> high, with many branches and perforated leaves <note>This refers to the translucent glands of *Hypericum perforatum* which look like tiny holes when held to the light</note>. The yellow flowers, which stand at the very top, leave behind oblong seed pods containing small black seeds that smell like resin.

The root is hard and woody.

It grows in cultivated places.

## Preparation and Use.

### The Herb.

The herb together with the flowers strengthens the head and the nerves, promotes sweat and urine, and is an excellent wound-herb. It serves for stroke <note>original: *Schlag*; apoplexy</note>, melancholic spleen-sickness <note>original: *Milzsucht*; a condition historically linked to the spleen and thought to cause depression or irritability</note>, stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>, obstruction of the urine and the monthly period, all kinds of fever, hip pain, jaundice, rot, and worms...

## Hyssop.

There are two kinds: domestic and wild. The first is called Hyssop, or Cloister Hyssop. The other is Heathen Hyssop <note>likely *Gratiola officinalis*, also known as Hedge Hyssop</note>; it has a hard, woody root from which many four-edged hairy shoots sprout, about a span <note>approximately 9 inches</note> high, from whose joints the leaves grow, like those of lavender, but much shorter; at the tips stand the flowers in a long spike, and they are mostly blue, red, or white.

Heathen Hyssop grows woody, rough, and reddish stems, upon which the leaves stand in pairs opposite one another, and is almost like common Hyssop, yet broader, longer, and hairy.

The flowers consist of five small yellow petals. The seed lies in a double, elongated, and three-parted capsule <note>original: *Häußgen*; literally "little house"</note>.

### Preparation and Use.

The leaves and flowers of Cloister Hyssop break up the tartaric phlegm in the lungs <term>tartaric phlegm: a historical medical term for hardened or calcified mucus, named after "tartar" deposits</term>, and serve for shortness of breath <note>original: *Engbrüstigkeit*</note>, coughing, hoarseness, and blockages of the liver, spleen, and kidneys; they promote the monthly period, childbirth, and the retained afterbirth <note>original: *Affterbürde*</note>, and are good for dropsy <note>edema</note> and jaundice <note>original: *Gelbesucht*</note>, strangury <note>painful or difficult urination</note>, pains of the stomach and the intestines, and for worms when taken with peony root.

### External Use.

For black eyes <note>literally "blue eyes"</note>, placed in a small bag, boiled, and applied.
For ringing in the ears, used as a fumigant <note>original: *geräuchert*; the steam or smoke was directed into the ear</note>.
For impurity of the womb <note>original: *Mutter*</note>, boiled and the steam caught.
For toothache and uncleanness of the mouth, used as a gargle.
For clotted blood, made into a poultice <note>original: *Brey*; literally "porridge"</note> and applied.
For scalp scabs <note>original: *Haupt-Grind*</note>, used as a wash.
The distilled water and oil made from it, the conserve, the *Species Diahysopi* <note>original: "Species Diahysopi"; a traditional medicinal powder blend based on hyssop</note>, and the simple and compound syrups are likewise useful for the aforementioned ailments.

## Heartsease.

Heartsease <note>original: *Freysamkraut*; "Freisam" was a historical term for childhood convulsions or fevers</note>, also called Idle-Care or Wild Pansy <note>original: *Stiefmütterlein*; literally "little stepmother"</note>, produces branched and uniform stems that shoot out from a thin and fibrous root. The leaves are initially round, but later become elongated and notched; at their base, multi-colored flowers emerge on long stalks. These are composed of five petals: specifically, two violet-brown, two white, and one yellow. These leave behind many small, shiny seeds in nearly triangular little capsules <note>original: *Häußgen*; literally "little houses"</note>.

### Preparation and Use.

The herb, together with the flowers, induces perspiration and serves to treat "children's heat" <note>feverish ailments in infants</note>, viscous phlegm, inflammation of the lungs, shortness of breath, fevers, clotted blood, itchy skin, scabies, and blockages of the womb <term>blockage of the womb: a historical medical term for menstrual or uterine obstructions</term>.

### External Use.

Used in baths for wounds and injuries, and for blockages of the womb.
The water distilled from it promotes sweating and is good for the "flying heat" <note>sudden feverish flushing or rashes</note> of small children.

This is a shrub with many slender branches; from its joints emerge two small shoots, upon which five or seven leaves are found. At the tips, fragrant white flowers appear.

### Preparation and Use.

### The Oil.

Common jasmine oil prepared from the flowers warms, softens, consumes <note>in the sense of resolving or dissipating morbid humors</note>, and opens; although rarely used internally, it warms...

## Kermes Oak.

This is a low, small tree <note>original: *Kermes-Baum*; the *Quercus coccifera*, or Kermes Oak</note>, yet it has many hard shoots and branches, with elongated, strong leaves armed with sharp thorns at the edges. It bears mossy blossoms or rather shoots, and when it reaches four years of age or more, it also bears acorns that are somewhat longer than common acorns and have rougher caps <note>original: *Nägel*; literally "nails," referring to the scaly cups of the acorns</note>. While the flower is still young, three types of outgrowths <note>original: *Excrementa*; in this context, it refers to botanical secretions or galls rather than waste</note> can be found upon it:

The 1st outgrowth grows abundantly on the branches in May; it is round and black, smooth and shiny, but inside it is full of whitish sap in which small worms swim. Finally, it becomes parched and dry.

The 2nd outgrowth consists of red, round, or perhaps elongated grains that grow further out from the leaves in April or May. They are the size of peas, white inside, and somewhat acidic but pleasant in taste; in some of these, one also finds small worms.

The 3rd outgrowth, which grows from the underside of the leaves and is far better known and superior to the previous ones, is the famous kermes grain. These are red grains, provided one wipes away the whitish dust. They are filled with a beautiful red sap, from which eventually come matching-colored flying small worms <note>these are actually the Kermes scale insects, used to produce a crimson dye</note> that finally fly away. Their development can be prevented if the grains are sprinkled with vinegar.

This plant grows in Spain, France, Italy <note>original: *Welschland*</note>, Crete, Asia, and America.

### Preparation and Use.

The kermes grains <note>these are actually the dried bodies of the female scale insect *Kermes vermilio*, which live on the Kermes Oak; they were historically mistaken for seeds or grains</note> are astringent, strengthen the heart, the stomach, and the liver, promote childbirth, prevent miscarriages, and are also good for ailments of the heart, for fainting, heart palpitations, and injured nerves; they drive out measles and smallpox, still diarrhea <note>original: *Durchbrüche*; literally "breakthroughs," referring to severe bowel movements</note>, dysentery <note>original: *Rothe-Ruhr*; literally "red dysentery," so named for the presence of blood</note>, the spitting of blood, and nosebleeds.

The Confection of Alkermes <note>original: *Confectio Alkermes*; a famous medieval and Renaissance heart tonic</note>, which is made from the juice and syrup with crimson silk, warms, dries, and draws together [is astringent]. It strengthens the heart and is good for fainting, tremors of the heart, stroke, melancholy, sadness, and abdominal fluxes.

### The Extract.

The extract or essence of kermes grains strengthens the heart and preserves the innate heat <note>original: *Calidum innatum*; in ancient medicine, this was the vital heat believed to be present from birth that sustained life</note>.

Crimson silk holds back "the Rose" <note>original: *Rothlauf*; also known as erysipelas, a bacterial skin infection characterized by a bright red rash</note> if it is tied on or laid upon it.

Scarlet cloth, however—just like the silk—dyed with the juice of kermes grains, drives out smallpox and measles if a piece is laid warm over the heart along with a little of the Confection of Alkermes.

## Masterwort.

This plant has striated, hollow stems, about 1 to 1.5 feet <term>foot: an old measurement unit, usually around 30 centimeters</term> high. On the side branches, there are usually 3 stiff leaves, each of which is further cut into 3 parts and notched at the edges. At the top of the stem stand the umbels <note>umbrella-like flower clusters typical of the carrot family</note>, or flower-wreaths, which are full of white flowers, followed by a white, flat, and plump seed. The root is as thick as a thumb, roundish, fibrous, white inside, and has a sharp, spicy taste.

In Italy and Austria, it grows wild on various mountains, but here it is cultivated in gardens.

### Preparation and Use.

The root is "opening" <note>in humoral medicine, an "opening" remedy clears blockages in the vessels or organs</note>; it promotes sweat and urine, the menstrual cycle, and childbirth. It resists poison and strengthens the head, nerves, and stomach, and clears the chest. It serves to treat blockages of the liver, spleen, and mesentery <note>original: *Gekröß*; the fold of tissue that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall</note>.

## Illyrian Orris Root.
<note>original: *Illiriſche Veil-Wurtzel*; likely *Iris pallida*, prized for its violet-scented rhizome</note>

Illyrian or Dalmatian Orris Root produces a hollow, branched stem, which the leaves surround like two outspread wings. It bears many violet-blue flowers consisting of nine petals; it also has a white, hard, fibrous root that smells like March violets.

This root is brought from Illyria, which is now also called Windic March <note>original: *Windiſchmarck*; a historical border region in present-day Slovenia</note>, to Venice, and from there to us.

### Preparation and Use.

The root softens, consumes, cleanses, and promotes urine; it serves the head and the chest and resists poison. It is good for phlegm in the lungs, asthma <note>original: *Engbrüſtigkeit*; literally "narrow-chestedness"</note>, coughing, suppressed menstruation, abdominal pains and the severe ailments of small children, and also the flow of seed <note>original: *Saamen-Fluß*; likely referring to spermatorrhea or other discharges</note>.

# Sixth TREATISE.
## On Old Age,

->Its causes, nature, and properties, as well as all<-
->manner of inconveniences that it brings with it; how to<-
->avoid them for a long time, happily improve them, and how<-
->the burden it brings may be more easily borne.<-

# Preface.
### To the Reader,

There is likely no one among mortal men who does not, by natural instinct, desire old age, and who is there that does not hope to attain it? Yet, as longingly as it is wished for, and as eagerly as it is hoped for, there is still no one who, in their youth, thoughtfully seeks a staff <note>A metaphor for preparing one's health, finances, or spirit for the infirmities of later life.</note> upon which they might walk in old age. God the eternal Creator counts this itself among His gifts of grace <note>original: *Gnaden-Geschencke*; divine favors or blessings bestowed by God's mercy</note>; when He promises to reward obedience to His commandments with long life, and also grants it to His own, yet conversely threatens that the disobedient shall not reach even half of their days <note>A reference to Psalm 55:23, reflecting the early modern belief that moral conduct was directly tied to physical longevity.</note>.

<summary>This page introduces the sixth treatise of the work, focusing on the nature of aging. The preface reflects on the universal human desire for a long life and the spiritual context of longevity as a divine reward.</summary>
<keywords>old age, geriatrics, longevity, divine grace, preface, moral health, nature of aging</keywords>

--- Page 456 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface to the Sixth Treatise on Old Age. It follows the introductory remarks on longevity as a divine gift, now turning to the social and moral obligations of the young toward the elderly.</meta>

<page-num>394</page-num>
<header>->❦ ( 0 ) ❦<-</header>

Thus we also find a Divine Commandment, that we should stand up before a gray head <note>A reference to Leviticus 19:32: "Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man."</note> and honor the aged; and that God, as a righteous Judge and true Lawgiver, desires this command to be fulfilled just as He does all His others. We see this plainly in the punishments found in Holy Scripture regarding the youth who dishonored the elderly against this command. Indeed, even the heathens <note>original: *Heyden*; referring here to the pre-Christian classical world</note> have shown through the mere light of nature <note>The philosophical concept that certain moral truths are accessible to human reason without the aid of divine revelation.</note> that one must honor old age, as can be seen, among other places, in the histories of the Romans and Spartans.

Among us Germans, we find a proverb passed down from our ancient ancestors which agrees with this, as it is commonly said: **Age is worthy of honor! Age has understanding!** Although old age, my reader, deserves no small amount of fame and high esteem according to the aforementioned and many other circumstances, yet wing-swift time daily presents before our eyes what manner of burdens, displeasure, reluctance, weakness, pain, sadness, and anxious longing for one's dissolution <note>A common early modern euphemism for death or the soul's release from the body.</note> it brings with it—even upon its arrival, but even more so in extreme old age and at its sensed end. Certainly, many worthy elders provide living testimony of this, while the young can see it with their own eyes. Although the latter daily observe all these aforementioned and even more <term>plagues of age</term> <note>original: *Alter-plagen*; a term used to describe the collective chronic ailments and social hardships associated with getting old</note> in their relatives, acquaintances, and friends, many who are flourishing in the bloom of youth either laugh at the elderly who find themselves in these painful plagues, or look upon them without pity or reflection. Much less do they believe that it will also happen to them (if they are fortunate enough to reach such an advanced age). Know, however, flourishing youth in your bloom! That by your contempt for the aged, you will inevitably heap up your own plagues of old age, or you will not escape the aforementioned punishment. Therefore, flourishing youth, if you see in someone the weaknesses—

<meta>This page concludes a sentence from the previous page regarding the visible infirmities of the elderly. It shifts the focus toward a moral appeal to the youth, urging them to show compassion and to recognize their own mortality, while also acknowledging that despite classical praise for old age, its physical reality remains a heavy burden that only faith can truly lighten.</meta>

<page-num>395</page-num>
<sig>Ddd 2</sig>

...aspects <note>Completing the word "vorgenannten" or "aforementioned" from the previous page.</note> of old age, then observe them with rational eyes; seek out everything for the **consolation** <note>original: *Consolation*; a Latin-derived term for comfort commonly used in the early modern period.</note> of a distressed elder. Remember that the same can happen to you; do not sin, so that you do not one day in your own great age have to sigh in vain for help, comfort, and rescue. Consider that Death observes no order in his snatching away, and that neither your full-blooming youth nor frail old age is freed from dying. And who knows whether the wavering foot of an elder trembling today might not accompany you—a young hero who faded overnight—to the grave tomorrow?

Therefore, green and blooming youth, learn from the complaints and plagues of the elderly to think of your own old age, and even more of your inevitable end and death, which remains unknown to both you and me. Truly, many seek to prefer old age over youth and to praise it as more blessed—of which, among others, **Cicero** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman statesman whose work *De Senectute* (On Old Age) argued that aging is a period of intellectual and character growth.</note> makes much boast regarding old age—but let the scholars say and write what they will about it: age is still age, and it has no hope of perfect improvement except through reaching eternal glory through **Death**.

Otherwise, these are and remain the days of which Holy Scripture says: *When they come, we shall find no pleasure in them.* <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 12:1: "Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth... while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them."</note> It is the arduous time which made the ancient **Patriarchs** <note>The Biblical fathers, such as Abraham or Isaac, who were noted for their extreme longevity.</note> weary and tired of life, which is otherwise the most pleasant thing on earth; of which one of the heathens <note>original: *Heyden*; referring to the Roman playwright Terence and his famous phrase *Senectus ipsa morbus*.</note> says: **Old age brings no illness, but is an illness in itself.** It is certain that old age has its unavoidable plagues; the bowing head and bent back approach ever closer to the earth; the trembling hands reach out, as it were, every moment—and yet with fear—for death. The quivering feet hasten toward the grave even with slow steps. However hurried it may look here, the only wise and merciful **God** has nonetheless spoken many a glorious comfort to the elderly at all times, beyond the aforementioned promises and assigned honors, yes

# Chapter I.

## Humanity cannot always remain in the same state and being, but must finally, out of necessity, grow old and decline.

### My Reader!

It is a general law, which Nature herself has published and spread through the entire wide world: namely, that no thing which has once taken a beginning—insofar as it is of a material nature and consists of composite parts—can endure forever, but must one day dissolve and come to an end.

Thus, there is nothing under the sun, whatever its name may be, except for the immortal soul, that is not changeable and subject to alteration, indeed even to corruption and death. To this decree, all theologians, all **philosophers** <note>original: *Welt-Weise*; literally "world-wise ones," a common term for philosophers in the early modern period.</note>, all medical men, and physicians subscribe. **Hippocrates** <note>original: *Hypocrates*</note> testifies to this in his first book on the **regimen of food and drink** <note>likely referring to *De Victu* or *On Regimen*</note>; **Aristotle** in his treatise on the **length and shortness of human life** <note>Latin: *De Longitudine et Brevitate Vitae*</note>; **Galen** <note>original: *Galenus*</note> in his first book **on health** <note>Latin: *De Sanitate Tuenda*</note>. All of these, as well as the scholars of our own time, bring forth such fundamental truths in support of the above proof that no one would dare to contradict them. Indeed, we require no testimony from the learned; for experience, as the best schoolmistress, places an example before our eyes. We are convinced by the sight itself, which cannot deceive: does a single day pass when we do not see old, spent people being lowered into the tomb and the earth? Is not the passing of honest, elderly persons constantly mourned—those whose counsel, comfort, protection, and help one would gladly have used longer, if only they did not have to **pay nature's debt** <note>original: *der Natur die Schuld bezahlen*; a common idiom for dying</note> all too soon, even though they were old?

Is not everything created by the infinite Creator finite and transitory? Has not everything that has happened since the first day of creation passed by, vanished, and changed? Of these things, nothing is left to us but a dark memory. Now, I could well [mention] many...

From this, some impurity and excess arises, which must be expelled again. For if it were to remain and be retained in the body, countless diseases would inevitably arise from it.

These include fear, sadness, anger, excessive love, and the like, all of which weaken nature not a little. And although these could for the most part be avoided, many nevertheless seek, as it were by force, to ruin their otherwise good nature through all the aforementioned circumstances. And what other accidents might befall us, such as: wounds, injuries, and other harms to the body, to which human physical frailty is in many ways subject? 

And so it remains once and for all: that for the reasons mentioned above and many others—indeed, out of great, unavoidable necessity—man must decline and grow old, considering that he not only increases, nourishes, and perpetuates the causes of his death internally within his body, but is also externally subject to those which can be avoided only with difficulty or not at all.
