# Chapter II.

### Contains within it a description of high and advanced age.

It is certain and beyond all doubt that our bodies are subject to many and varied changes from the first day of their birth; therefore, some doctors <note>original: "Medici"</note> have divided the entire human life into different parts and times based on the apparent decline of the same, which we call the ages of man. The Egyptians established as many stages of life as the number seven is contained within the number one hundred, for they were of the opinion that the outermost goal of human life could extend to one hundred years. The philosophers in Italy, who were called Pythagoreans <note>original: "Pythagoricos"; followers of Pythagoras who believed numbers were the essence of all things</note>, together with their followers, fell upon the superstitious idea that one must observe ciphers and numbers; therefore they left behind in their writings that a person experiences a visible change every 7 years, concerning both the temperament <term>Temperament: the balance of the "four humors" or bodily fluids that pre-modern medicine believed determined a person's health and personality</term> of the body as well as the senses and character of the mind, and that all of this is to be attributed solely and uniquely to the number seven. We do not wish to dispute these thoughts here with those people or others who are pregnant with such ideas, but rather only show what all naturalists <note>original: "Naturkündiger"</note> find reasonable: namely, that five particularly noticeable changes occur in the human body according to the natural course of its life, which we shall also call the five ages:

1.) **Infancy** <note>original: "Infantia"</note>, childhood, which extends to the thirteenth year.

2.) **Adolescence** <note>original: "Adolescentia"</note>, the age of youths, from the thirteenth to the twenty-fourth or twenty-fifth year.

3.) **Youth** <note>original: "Juventus"</note>, from 25 to 40.

4.) **Manly or stable age** <note>original: "Virilis sive constans ætas"</note>, which lasts until the fiftieth year.

5.) **Old age** <note>original: "Senectus"</note>, the so-called age, which lasts from the 80th year <note>This "80th" is likely a printing error for "50th," as the previous stage ends at 50 and the author notes things do not improve from this point onward.</note> until the end of life, for things do not get better from there. Now we will consider the properties of each in particular.

**Infancy**, childhood, is by nature warm and moist, although the

**Adolescence** <note>original: "Adolescentia"</note>, here follow the young men, who are also of a warm and moist nature, but the heat here gradually gains the upper hand and reveals itself throughout the entire body. In young men, the voice becomes somewhat coarser and rougher, the passages and veins in the body expand, and what we might call the "first wool" <note>a metaphorical reference to the first growth of facial or body hair</note> begins to sprout; in daughters, one notices that their breasts visibly grow, the blood moves throughout the whole body, seeking to relieve itself, and does not rest until it has found its exit <note>a reference to the onset of menstruation</note>.

**Youth** <note>original: "Juventus"</note>, youth begins, as mentioned, at the 25th year; it is warm and dry, hot and joyful, for now the body has reached its perfection until the 40th year.

**Manhood** <note>original: "Virilitas"</note>, then the masculine or "constant age" begins, which is the most perfect among all others, because the four qualities <term>the four qualities: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness, which were believed to govern health and temperament</term> are at this time almost equal and at their highest degree.

**Old Age** <note>original: "Senectus"</note>, high age begins at the 50th year, and this tends to consume the remaining time of our lives.

However, this age, specifically and particularly called "old age," can be divided into three parts: the first, second, and third. (We are by no means speaking here of when one grows old before their time, which scholars call **aging from disease** <note>original: "Senium ex morbo"</note>). Rather, the first kind is called: **Green Old Age** <note>original: "Senectus Viridis"</note>, where one is certainly advanced in years, yet possesses more understanding than the young; at this time, one is cautious, wise, full of experience, and fit to rule others and preside over the common good.

The second kind begins at the 62nd year and is subject to all sorts of inconveniences, being mostly cold and dry. And especially regarding the cold, such obvious signs are found that there can be no doubt of it. For if one only touches such elderly persons, one can feel the cold even with the hand; the lively red color of the face and cheeks has vanished, all senses are weakened, and many and various ailments occur which stem from cold.

Regarding the dryness of this age, there are many who call it into doubt, saying rather that this age is more moist than dry,

...dry, because one sees that the eyes of old people are always too wet and flow with tears, and much moisture reveals itself in the nose; moreover, the mouth is full of saliva <note>the original "Speigel" is likely a transcription error for "Speichel" (saliva)</note>, and in most of them there is nothing but coughing and—pardon the expression—spitting. However, as far as the living and healthy moisture is concerned—which is the very root of life—they have little of it. Thus, despite all their abundant useless moisture, they are still to be esteemed as dry. 

And in the first book on the *Maintenance of Human Health*, this same author states that those very parts of the body which are moist in the young become dry in the old—namely, the solid and dense parts of the body, from which the **complexion** or **temperament** <term>complexion/temperament: in early medicine, this referred to the specific balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determined a person's health and personality</term> is named. This is a well-founded opinion that one must reasonably agree with. We have no reason to doubt this, as we are sufficiently convinced by the fact that such elderly people are generally thin, as well as full of wrinkles; the skin and the "nerve-veins" are hard, and the joints of the limbs are stiff—all of which are marks and indications of a dry complexion. Many of the aged are also plagued by a constant itching and stinging of the skin, or even scabs and scales on the head, from which we can infer that their brain is filled with a sharp, salty moisture, rather than a pleasant and natural one.

**Decrepit Old Age** <note>original: "Decrepita Senectus"</note>, or the third stage of advanced age, is—God have mercy!—the time when one walks on the edge of the grave. At this stage, as the wise King says, there is nothing but weakness and pain. The entire body, along with the spirit, is weakened in all its functions; the senses are very dull, the memory is gone, the understanding is weak, and it is rightly said of such elderly people: **Old men become children for the second time** <note>original: "Bis puerii senes," a common proverb in the Renaissance suggesting that the very old return to a state of dependency and mental simplicity like that of a child</note>. This proverb was common among the Greeks. 

We have one of the most beautiful descriptions of this in the 12th or final chapter of **Ecclesiastes** <note>original: "Prediger Salomonis"</note>, in which old age is depicted with such beautiful allegories and metaphors that hardly anything more excellent can be found. Yet this is not to be wondered at, for the author of this description is the greatest philosopher and the most learned and experienced **naturalist** <note>original: "Naturkündiger"</note> the world has ever known. It is well enough known when I mention that it is King Solomon, to whom all the **secrets** <note>original: "Secreta"</note> and mysteries of...

Remember! says the aforementioned king <note>referring to King Solomon, traditionally credited with the authorship of Ecclesiastes</note>, your Creator in your youth (in the 12th chapter of his book of *Ecclesiastes*), before the evil days come and the years draw near when you will say, "I have no pleasure in them"; before the sun and the light, the moon and the stars grow dark, and the clouds return after the rain; at the time when the keepers of the house <note>an allegory for the hands and arms</note> tremble, and the strong men <note>the legs</note> bow themselves, and the grinders <note>the teeth</note> stand idle because they have become so few, and those who look through the windows <note>the eyes</note> grow dark, and the doors on the streets are closed, so that the voice of the grinding-woman becomes soft, and one wakes when the bird sings, and all the daughters of song <note>likely referring to the ears or the voice itself</note> are brought low; when they are also afraid of heights and fear the way, when the almond tree blossoms <note>traditionally interpreted as the hair turning white</note>, and the grasshopper becomes a burden, and all desire vanishes; for man goes to his eternal home, and the mourners go about the streets; before the silver cord is removed, and the golden fountain runs dry, and the pitcher is shattered at the spring, and the wheel is broken at the cistern; for the dust must return to the earth as it was, and the spirit back to God who gave it.

See there: this is the wonderful and ingenious description of old age, which is well worth us "anatomizing" <note>the author uses this term to mean a step-by-step examination or "dissection" of the text</note> and going through piece by piece, if it is to be understood rightly. Initially, the wise man says the lights—sun, moon, and stars—grow dark; these are the eyes, which are noticeably darkened in their glow and luster, and almost entirely lose their light.

When he says: *Clouds return after the rain*, it means that elderly people commonly have eyes full of water, and when they have shed enough tears, something hovers before their eyes like a cloud through which they see; but it is nothing other than thick vapors or mists that settle over the membrane of the eye <note>a historical description of what we might now call cataracts or blurred vision caused by fluid</note>, just as clouds themselves are nothing else.

**The keepers of the house tremble**; these are the arms and hands, which are given to man to protect the entire house, or the structure of his life.

**The strong men bow themselves**; these are the upper and lower legs, in which a young man possesses great strength, and which are nothing other than the pillars of our entire upper structure.

**The grinders stand idle** because they have become so few; this signifies the loss of teeth, by which food is chewed and, as it were, ground, for the sake of better digestion <note>The author uses the image of a mill to explain the mechanical process of mastication</note>.

**Those who look through the windows grow dark**; for in the eyes there often arises a defect (<note>original: "Suffusio vel Cataracta"</note> <gloss>clouding or cataract</gloss>), whereby the black part or the "apple" <note>the pupil</note>—which is not unfairly called the window of the eye—becomes dark, because one sees obscured through it and a great loss of vision is felt.

**The door to the street is closed, and the voice of the grinder becomes low**; from this it appears that in old people, the mouth is commonly kept firm and tight; the joints of the jawbone or lower jaw near the tonsils can only open and close with great difficulty to chew hard foods, just as the voice also becomes quiet, for old people can no longer call out very loudly because both the windpipe and the esophagus <note>literally "air- and food-tubes"</note> close up and become narrower.

**One wakes when the bird sings**; for the dear elderly sleep little and wake when the rooster crows at night, or the house swallow sings in the morning during springtime.

**The daughters of song are brought low**; for the voice, which was previously high, pleasant, and lovely, becomes rough and unpleasant, and the desire for music and singing begins to fade.

**The almond tree blossoms**; the hair on the head becomes white, like the almond blossom in spring.

**The grasshopper becomes a burden**; although the meaning of these words is obscure, it suggests that the thighs or legs, which once made many a good, joyful leap, become sluggish, weak, and tired, and the ankles may even flare up and swell, which is certainly no small weight or burden.

**The silver cord is loosed**; this is the beautiful white marrow <note>the spinal cord</note>, which runs the long path down through the backbone. This becomes long and stretches, whereby the vertebrae in the back masterfully bend forward, and the entire back and upper body hang down and become hunched.

**The golden spring runs out** (or the small golden vessel fails); this is the heart, which, as a very noble and golden vessel, contains within itself the blood of the arteries <note>original: "Lufft-Adern," literally "air-veins," following the ancient anatomical belief that arteries carried vital spirits or air</note> and is their golden source. It then moves very slowly and beats very softly; it can no longer propel such lively spirits, nor retain the blood of its arteries—which is called heart-blood—no differently than if this golden vessel or cup had received a crack or were even broken.

**The pitcher is shattered at the fountain**; by this is understood the largest blood vein <note>the vena cava</note>, which distributes itself through the whole body. This can no longer draw the prepared blood from the liver—which is and is called the <term>workshop of blood</term> <note>original: "Officina sanguinis"</note>—and water all the limbs of the body with it. Therefore, this vein is of no more use than a leaky pitcher at a well.

**The wheel is broken at the cistern**; by this are understood both kidneys in the loins, which draw the urine out of the blood like a wheel at a spring, along with the bladder, which can no longer hold the urine well, but sometimes must let it go against the will of the elderly.

When all this happens, then the dust—that is, our body which is of the earth—must return to dust and earth, and the spirit return to God who gave it.

Thus we have now described the five parts or stages of human life and divided each into its certain number of years. However, it is by no means the intention that one should bind oneself so strictly to the number of years, as if age and youth depended solely on or consisted within them; rather, one must look more at the <term>complexion</term> <note>the "humoral" makeup or physical constitution of a person</note> or temperament of human life than at the years. For a person who is by nature cold and dry <note>the melancholic temperament</note>, I can rightly call old, regardless of how long ago they were born. One finds people of 40 years who must be counted among the elderly, and conversely, 60-year-old persons who must be placed among the young. Some are of such a nature that they soon become grey and old, while others age slowly. Those who possess good, pure blood <note>original: "Geblüte," referring to the constitution of the blood according to the theory of the four humors</note> do not age prematurely; they mostly appear healthy and young even into their high old age because they possess a great deal of natural heat and moisture. The Melancholics <note>those with a "cold and dry" temperament, often thought to be prone to sadness or deep thought</note>, on the other hand, because they are of a cold and dry nature, grow old before their time. As for what otherwise concerns the two sexes, man and woman, we know from daily experience that women grow old sooner than men. And this was very well observed by Hippocrates <note>the famous physician of Ancient Greece, often called the Father of Medicine</note> in his book *On Seven-Month Birth* <note>original: "De Partu Septimestri"</note>, where he writes: Although young girls, while they still lie in their mother’s womb, are formed later and grow more slowly than boys, yet when they come into the light of day and are born into the world, they grow up much faster and reach understanding sooner; but they also grow old sooner than boys or men, due to the fragility <note>original: "Blödigkeit," here meaning physical delicacy or weakness</note> of their bodies and the way of life they lead. This fragility and weakness contributes much to the fact that they both grow sooner and age sooner.

Trees and plants that do not have a long duration grow up quickly; and in the very same way, those bodies appear to me which are not meant to remain long in their perfection—they reach their full size quickly, but also quickly reach their end. The lifestyle of the ladies <note>original: "Frauenzimmer"</note> is well known, and because most live only comfortably and without particular movement or effort, they must grow old before their time; for there is nothing that makes one old sooner than having little movement <note>original: "Motion," referring to physical exercise</note> and nothing to do. To be sure, I by no means wish to write here against the comfort <note>original: "Commodité"</note> and pleasant stillness of those ladies who love such things and are able to enjoy their desired rest, as if they should abandon it and bring their pleasant bodies and tender feet into more movement; however, I would ask this of them: that I be allowed to report once more how an all-too-great comfort brings after it an all-too-early old age.

# Chapter III.

### On the order one must lead in life, namely if one seeks to preserve and maintain their life for a long time.

There are actually, as has been mentioned, three natural, though unavoidable causes why we humans must grow old. Namely:

> I. The adversities of the elements <note>referring to the four classical elements—earth, air, fire, and water—which were believed to make up the human body and often conflict with one another</note>, along with their properties, from which we are composed.
>
> II. The destruction of natural heat and moisture <note>the "radical moisture" and "innate heat" thought to be the fuel of life; aging was viewed as the gradual drying out and cooling of the body</note>, both of which are the roots of our life.
>
> III. That which the nourishment and food we enjoy separates out as impure and allows to remain in the body.

To prevent this and to keep the body in good condition so that we do not grow old too early, we must maintain such order in these three matters so that the accord and agreement of the elements—which we call our temperament, or by the common name, complexion <note>in early modern medicine, "complexion" referred to the specific balance of the four humors in an individual</note>—is properly maintained; that the natural heat and moisture, which decrease every hour, are replaced and restored; and that we see to it that the impurities excessively retained in the body are carried away and driven out.

And all of this can be accomplished through a good regimen <note>original: "Regiment," referring to a disciplined lifestyle or medical "rule of life"</note> and order in living.

Now, although this name "order and regimen in life" encompasses many things, the physicians and scholars name only six.

These they call *Res non naturales*, or things not natural <note>Latin: *Res non naturales*. These are factors external to the body's nature—such as air, food, and sleep—that affect health depending on how they are used</note>, and this is because these very things, when they are used rightly and in the proper manner, and

# Chapter IV.

### Which kind of air to choose in order to preserve one's life, and which is most beneficial for the elderly.

Among all things that can bring about a change in our bodies, nothing is more necessary, nor concerns us more closely, than the air.

This necessity is proven all too clearly in those dangerous bodily infirmities through which the breath is blocked.

For if it happens that one of those instruments <note>referring to the organs of respiration, such as the lungs and windpipe</note> which Nature has ordained either as a door and entrance for the air, or for its dwelling or preparation, is injured, the human—or indeed any other animal living on the earth—must immediately suffocate and die, and

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Six Non-Naturals," specifically focusing on the first element: the Air. The previous page ended with the thought that if the organs of breath are injured, a creature must suffocate.</meta>

It almost appears as if air and life in perfect living creatures are so bound together that neither can be separated from the other. For the natural heat <note>original: "natürliche Wärme"; early medicine taught that a "vital heat" resided in the heart and needed constant regulation</note> is maintained by moderate cooling. If one takes the air away from a fire, it must immediately be extinguished. The lively spirits <note>original: "lebhaffte Geister"; these were thought to be subtle, air-like substances (spiritus) that acted as the "engines" of the soul to move the body and process thoughts</note> within us, which are the most noble instruments and tools of the soul, are created and sustained by the air alone, for they are purified by the inhalation and exhalation of breath.

And this very thing is the reason why Nature has made our body porous throughout and full of passages, so that the air—or pulse-veins <note>original: "Puls-Adern"; an early term for arteries, which were once believed to carry air or "spirit" throughout the body</note>—beat back and forth, and one moves into the other in such a skillful, special, and wonderful way. In the consideration and contemplation of these things, one might almost say that air is as necessary to a human's life as the soul itself.

How swift the element of air is, we experience every day and hour.

In an instant, it rises through the nose to the brain, and through many hundreds of crooked passages found in the wondrous networks within the head; it wanders through all the cells and chambers of the brain and visits its secrets, then immediately descends with equally unbelievable speed through the mouth and throat to the lungs, and from there to the heart. It divides itself into all the pulse-veins of the entire body, searches through it, and finally penetrates in a most imperceptible and subtle way through the sweat-pores of our body, or out through the skin.

Thus, the air is something that is very common and close to us, surrounding us on all sides and never leaving us for a single moment; we must draw and breathe it in without ceasing, whether it brings us pleasure or pain. Indeed, the entire condition of our internal lively spirits depends upon the condition of the air, just as the moistures <note>referring to the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note> in the body align themselves according to it.

In this regard, for the sake of our health, we should observe and take heed of two things:

1. The substance or essence of the air, and
2. The qualities or properties of the same.

Concerning the substance and essence of the air, we must investigate and see whether it perhaps secretly contains a wicked, strange nature within

There are also some trees and plants whose inherent natural properties are contrary to our lively spirits <note>vital energies or "spiritus" that were thought to drive bodily functions</note>; such as the walnut tree, fig tree, all sorts of caper and cabbage herbs, danewort <note>original: "Attich"; also known as dwarf elder</note>, or wild elder, wild rocket, spurge <note>original: "Hunds- oder Wolffs-Milch"; literally "dog's or wolf's milk," referring to the milky sap of the Euphorbia plant</note>, and many more of the like; these we should keep far from our houses and dwellings.

The smoke and vapor from iron smithies and ore or smelting mines is also very unhealthy for the heart, for it causes an unnoticed fading and withering.

However, if the air in a place has become unclean and we cannot easily escape or change it, one should endeavor to have good fires and fumigations in the rooms, such as: rosemary, juniper wood, berries, and shrubs, cypress, laurel and its leaves, aloe wood, and fragrant spices.

Vinegar has a special power to improve the bad qualities of the air.

### 2. On the Qualities or Properties of the Air.

By this one means to ask: is the air warm? cold? moist? or dry? For all excess and abundance in anything is harmful, as is the case here.

Therefore, one should strive to choose a temperate air that keeps to the middle path in this regard, for which the following are signs:

When the air becomes warm soon after sunrise and cool again soon after sunset. But if one cannot have such a temperature and middle state, it is better that the air be a little too dry rather than too wet and moist, for dry air is generally healthier for us than wetness and moisture.

Warm air will suit elderly people best; therefore, their rooms and chambers should never be without a bright fire in their stove. Experience teaches that they always feel better in summer than in winter; because, according to the well-known proverb, they already "carry the winter around with them" <note>an allusion to the Galenic medical theory that the elderly have a "cold and dry" temperament and thus require external heat</note>. The site of their dwelling should be fairly high,

# Chapter V.

### Some rules on how those who desire to live long, or seek to preserve their old age through a good regimen <note>original: "Ordnung"; here referring to a disciplined lifestyle or medical regimen</note>, should conduct themselves in eating and drinking.

Among the six items mentioned above <note>The "Six Non-Naturals" of Galenic medicine: air, food/drink, sleep/waking, movement/rest, excretion/retention, and passions of the mind</note>, eating and drinking hold the second place; for the latter replaces what nature loses in moisture, while the former maintains the solid matter.

### The 1st Rule.

No one should eat unless they have hunger, whether it be great or small: for the stomach does not take particularly well to food unless it has an <term>appetite</term> <note>original: "Appetit"</note> for it, and experience shows that even poor and humble foods, if the stomach craves them, are digested much sooner and better than the most tender and finest <term>delicacies</term> <note>original: "Delicatessen"</note> for which one has no desire or longing.

## The 2nd Rule.

One should not swallow food until it has first been well-chewed with the teeth, crushed, or cut into the smallest pieces. For if this does not occur, two kinds of inconveniences arise from it.

The first: that in this way one eats more than one should, whereby the stomach is burdened far too much.

The second: That the stomach receives much trouble and labor to digest the food that is not well-chewed; for the teeth serve the stomach by preparing the food for <term>digestion</term> <note>original: "Dauung"</note>, just as the cook uses a knife to make small that which is necessary. Therefore, many have come to the opinion that those who have a mouth full of good teeth usually reach a long life, because they can chew their food well, and consequently can digest it well.

## The 3rd Rule.

One should take care not to overload the stomach with food, but rather it is much better to rise from the table and the meal in such a way that one could still eat more: the reason is plain as day, for when the stomach is overfilled, its natural heat is weakened, so that it must finally fail entirely. As both the <term>doctors</term> <note>original: "Medici"</note> and <term>philosophers</term> <note>original: "Philosophi"</note> say: every thing that acts and works must also, in turn, suffer something; and he provides well for his health who does not overindulge in food, and is not lazy toward work, or seeks to engage in good <term>exercise</term> <note>original: "Motion"; referring to physical movement or light activity</note>. Elderly people also do well to drink a good old wine at the table, or in the absence of that, to give the stomach some "fire" through a good glass of <term>sundew liqueur</term> <note>original: "Ros solis"; a popular early-modern cordial or spirit made with sundew, brandy, and spices</note>, <term>mead</term> <note>original: "Meth"</note>, or <term>brandy</term> <note>original: "Brantewein"</note>. A good mead is a particularly good drink for elderly people.

## The 4th Rule.

It is also not advisable, nor beneficial to nature, to eat of many kinds of food at once; rather, if one wishes to <term>preserve</term> <note>original: "conserviren"</note> their health, they should be satisfied with one or at most two dishes. For many and varied foods harm the stomach and destroy its strength. For the many dishes are not all of the same kind and nature, but have different properties; therefore the heat and fire of the stomach, which contains no more than one degree in itself, is not sufficient or capable...

### The 5th Rule.

One should maintain a certain order in eating: foods that spoil easily should be consumed first, for if they were to enter the stomach last, they might infect the others and cause them to spoil along with them. Thus, foods that "cook" <note>In early modern medicine, digestion was viewed as a form of "concoction" or internal cooking driven by the body's natural heat</note> easily and are easy to digest should be enjoyed first; coarse foods, on the other hand, which do not cook easily and are hard and heavy to digest, should be given to the stomach last. And so, one should enjoy all soft foods first and all hard foods last.

it is not necessary to provide many reasons, as it is known to everyone: that the time between the evening meal and the morning meal is much longer than the time from noon until the night meal; from which it must necessarily follow that in the longer period, the food is better <term>digested</term> <note>original: "verdauet"</note> and distributed than in a short time.

Furthermore, it is certain that the heat of our body is much more powerful when we sleep than when we are awake, because during sleep it moves inward toward its center or innermost part. For if the distribution of nourishment in the body is to happen well, rest is highly necessary. Although the soul never rests, its ordinary functions and operations—which it conducts through the external senses during the day—cease and rest at night; there is then nothing else to consume the natural heat or lead it elsewhere. Therefore, it follows that <term>digestion</term> <note>original: "Däuung"</note> can then be performed all the better. The most prominent of the <term>physicians</term> <note>original: "Medicis"</note> of their time, such as Hippocrates, Galen, Avicenna, and others, have agreed with this and prescribed this very rule, which our ancestors also observed quite accurately, governing their meals accordingly.

The strong fighters and wrestlers in Greece never used to eat meat at noon, but rather in the evening, as Galen writes in the fifth book of *On the Preservation of Health* <note>original: "Erhaltung der Gesundheit," referring to Galen's Latin work *De Sanitate Tuenda*</note>.

The Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, known for specific dietary restrictions</note> ate nothing at noon except a little bread with honey; but they ate meat in the evening and held a hearty meal. Similarly, the Greek soldiers during the Trojan War took bread and wine more than once during the day, but never more than that; in the evening, however, they always ate meat. These, then, are the rules we should observe and take heed of when eating. To this I also add: the best hour to take food is the one that is most temperate during the day—when it is warmest in winter and coolest in summer.

## The VI. Chapter.

### Of the Four Human Complexions.

At the very beginning, we mentioned something regarding the elements—their union and qualities—which constitute the <term>temperament</term> or <term>complexion</term> <note>In early modern medicine, a "complexion" refers to the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) in a person's body</note> of a human being. Now, however, we wish to conduct a more precise investigation and describe each complexion individually.

There are, according to the four elements, also four distinct **complexions** <note>In historical medicine, a 'complexion' (or temperament) was the specific balance of the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that determined a person's health and personality.</note> or elementary qualities in human nature. Generally, one of these holds the upper hand over the other three, so that a person is natured either according to the element of **Air**, which gives the **Sanguine** or blood-rich complexion;

Or according to **Fire**, from which a **Choleric** or bile-rich temperament arises.

Or according to **Water**, which causes the **Phlegmatic** temperament;

Or according to **Earth**, which generates the **Melancholic** nature.

Those who are of a **Sanguine**, airy complexion are rich in blood, warm and moist—yet tempered or equally mixed in warmth and moisture. They correspond most closely with the quality of Air and enjoy living in high places where there is healthy, pure, tempered air; they also love nourishing food and drink, specifically those which produce healthy blood.

But those who are of a **Choleric** temperament correspond with the nature of Fire; they are hot and dry and possess a very strong **bile-making ferment** <note>original: "Gallmachende Ferment"</note> within them. This daily produces much bitter bile from their nourishment, making them very prone to all kinds of hot, violent illnesses. This must be prevented and countered by frequent purging of the bile and with cooling things.

As for the **Phlegmatic** nature, it compares itself to Water, which carries the mastery over the other elements in phlegmatic people. It creates a character that is too moist and cold, so that all ailments and infirmities—both internal and external—stem from an excess of moisture and fluid, and must be cured with drying and warming things.

Finally, concerning the **Melancholic** complexion, it is like the element of Earth: excessively cold and dry. Those of such a temperament must expect all their attacking illnesses and defects to come from too much dryness and coldness. All remedies applied against these, whether for internal or external damage, must involve warming and moistening. One can also easily recognize those of this complexion by their color and overall circumstances; for they are of an earthy, dark color and behave in every way very **fantastically** <note>In this context, 'fantastically' (original: "Phantastisch") means being prone to strange imaginings, eccentricities, or delusions.</note>, even though they consider themselves exceptionally witty and wise. This occurs because the **Saturnine** <note>Refers to the influence of the planet Saturn, which was traditionally associated with the element of Earth and a gloomy, cold, or restrictive disposition.</note> drying quality constricts their brain and constantly darkens their thoughts.

These, then, are the four primary **complexions** <note>In historical medicine, a 'complexion' or temperament was the balance of the four bodily fluids—blood, yellow bile, black bile, and phlegm—which were thought to determine a person's physical and mental character.</note>, which are governed by the four elements; yet they are rarely or almost never found in such a pure state, but are instead mostly mixed with one another. For instance, one person may be **Choleric** and **Sanguine**, while another is **Phlegmatic** and **Melancholic**, and so on in various other ways.

Furthermore, we can also include here the many times of day and the seasons, with which, among other things, the four ages of man are compared.

The course of time is divided according to the four elements into four distinct main parts: specifically, in every day and night, into the morning, midday, evening, and midnight.

In every year, however, it is divided into the spring, summer, autumn, and winter.

The morning and spring take after the element of **Air**, and according to the human age, they represent **youth**. <note>In the systems of the time, the 'Air' phase usually represented childhood and early adolescence.</note>

Midday and summer correspond to **Fire**, and in man, also to **youth**. <note>The author uses the word 'Jugend' (youth) for both phases, likely distinguishing between the 'spring' of early childhood and the 'summer' of vibrant, heat-filled young adulthood.</note>

The evening and autumn correspond to **Water**, and in man, represent **manhood** <note>original: "Männliche Alter," referring to the age of maturity and established strength.</note>.

Midnight and winter correspond to **Earth**; they represent **old age** and grey hair in man.

And just as man rises from his sleep in the morning, so too in the spring do all creatures rise as if from sleep: the trees bud, herbs and flowers grow forth anew, and the birds pair up, build nests, lay eggs, and hatch their young.

The fish in the water spawn and migrate, and other such things known to us; all of this occurs according to the true quality of **Air**, which is at its most tempered during this time, namely in the spring. In the same manner, the remaining main divisions of time can be compared with the elements assigned to them. Just as man leaves his work at midday to take his meal, so too do most fruits of the summer cease their growing and prepare themselves for ripening; most birds cease their singing and fly out. The element of **Fire** also reigns most powerfully at this time, creating great heat, stirring up lightning and thunder, and drying out the earth according to its nature so that it becomes parched and dusty. It also generates or hatches many hot-natured **vermin** <note>original: "Ungeziefer," a general term for pests.</note>, such as gnats, flies, wasps, fleas, and the like, which sting and plague both man and beast.

But just as man returns to his work after the midday meal until the evening—at which point he finishes his labor for the day <note>original: "Feyer-Abend," referring to the time when work stops.</note> and takes his supper—so many things continue to grow until the autumn, when then

## On the refrigerating, or cooling diet, and how it is to be arranged in all kinds of heated conditions.

The cooling diet must indeed be arranged according to the nature of the illness—because one requires more cooling and another less—and it must mostly be continued throughout the entire illness. However, it generally consists in first choosing a suitable room which, if possible, is on the ground floor or in the lower story of the house, and which has its windows facing <term>North</term> <note>original: "Mitternacht" — literally "midnight," the traditional German orientation for North</note> or toward the <term>West</term> <note>original: "Abend" — literally "evening," the traditional term for West</note>. For if the windows face <term>South</term> <note>original: "Mittag" — midday</note> or <term>East</term> <note>original: "Morgen" — morning</note>, such a room is much warmer, not only because of the sunlight it receives (especially if it also lies on the upper floor of the house), but also because of the sun's and moon's rays. Should these be able to shine upon the patient, they are sometimes not a little harmful, as one can observe even in irrational animals, which by nature flee the bare radiation of the sun and the moon; for the rays of the moon in particular are exceedingly harmful to the human brain. 

It also helps noticeably to soothe restlessness and sleeplessness if a room is so situated that a watery sound from a flowing brook or a springing fountain may be heard nearby. If nature does not provide this, it may in some cases—such as in <term>mania</term> <note>original: "Mania" — a state of intense excitement or madness</note> and <term>frenzy</term> <note>original: "Raserey"</note>—be imitated to some degree: namely, one places a vessel with cold water on high and, by means of a small hole, arranges things so that from time to time a drop of water falls from the height into a copper or brass basin placed below. Through such a sound, the patient is drawn away from his <term>fantasies</term> <note>delusions or racing thoughts</note>, so that he thinks upon this sound until he finally falls into a slumber. However, the chamber must also be completely dark, and everything else otherwise quiet; it also exhales from such

# Chapter VII.
## On the Choleric Diet in Particular.

Those of a choleric nature are, as we see clearly every day, very hot, fiery, and full of bile; this bile is also inclined toward agitation and turmoil every hour. It is very easily provoked by hot weather, the slightest adversity, or indeed often by a single word. When it is brought into a rage, it awakens very sharp, hot, and fierce diseases, such as: <term>jaundice</term> <note>original: "Gelbesucht"</note>, tertian and burning fevers, <term>gout</term> <note>original: "Gicht" — here referring to general joint pain</note>, colic or griping, brain-frenzy, <term>mania or madness</term> <note>original: "Maniam oder Dollheit"</note>, spasms, <term>podagra</term> <note>gout specifically in the foot</note>, fever blisters, shortness of breath, pulmonary consumption, violent "melting" sweats, stones, stabbing and tearing pains, paralysis, vomiting sickness, wasting disease, and many other ailments that frequently beset those prone to bile and wrath. For when the bile is ignited by intense anger and heat, it immediately sends its fiery power through the entire body—as can be observed clearly enough in such people, for all their limbs tremble as if in a frenzy, and with such violent force and impetuosity that they strike and tear with almost superhuman strength. Such is the nature of quickly ignited fire, an example of which is found in ignited <term>gunpowder</term> <note>original: "Büchsen-Pulver"</note>, which strikes and tears with unnatural force.

It requires little questioning as to how the bile brings its ignition so quickly to all the limbs. Since heat, or fire, penetrates everything rapidly—so much so that even thick, sealed glass, where air can neither enter nor exit, is visibly penetrated by heat—how much more easily might this occur in a body that is permeable throughout and already permeated with fiery matter? For everything we consume is hot and flammable, and in the case of the choleric, it is undoubtedly also embittered and sulfurized. Just as every <term>sulfurous ignition</term> <note>original: "Sulphurische Anglimmung"</note> is very sour and sharp, as is recognized by the eye-stinging smoke of sulfur and all other fumes, so too it happens in a choleric body: upon the ignition of the bile, one can expect nothing but stabbing, tearing, raging, anxiety, and woe. This is due to the sharp <term>acid</term> <note>original: "Acidi"</note> that comes from the ignition, alongside <term>tartaric coagulation</term> <note>A term from Paracelsian medicine referring to the hardening of waste products in the body—like the "tartar" or sediment in a wine barrel—which was thought to cause stones and gout.</note>

And because bile tends to collect in them by nature, it must occasionally be expelled through vomiting; for the bile desires the nature of fire and wishes to rise upward, though it can also be carried out through the stool. Because the Choleric nature dries out violently—as can be felt during hot weather and dry times, when even large puddles dry up, the earth turns to dust from dryness, and herbs and grass wither—we also wish to deal specifically here with the **moisturizing diet**.

## On the Moisturizing Diet.

It is true that not all great dryness comes from heat; rather, cold also makes things dry by nature, as can be felt in the hard winter and in <term>Saturnine things</term> <note>Refers to things associated with the planet Saturn, which in traditional medicine were considered cold, dry, heavy, and melancholic.</note>. Therefore, a distinction must be maintained in the moisturizing diet, since the overly heated drought as well as the cold **Melancholic Complexion** both require moisturizing, but with this difference: the one also requires cooling, while the other requires warming.

Indeed, there is almost such a distinction between them as there is between summer and winter. The dryness of summer arises from <term>evaporation</term> <note>original: "Evaporation"; the breathing out or vanishing of moisture</note>, whereas in winter it comes from <term>congelation</term> <note>original: "Congelation"; the freezing or stiffening of moisture</note> of the moisture still present. The former is remoistened with fresh wateriness, but the latter is thawed out again through spiritual warmth. Thus, the **Choleric moisturizing** proceeds from the **Phlegmatic property**, which...

Regarding the **moistening diet** in general, it is achieved, firstly, by means of air blowing from moist regions—namely from the West and South-west, and also partly from the South—especially if the windows of one's room face such winds. ### The Phlegmatic Dry Diet.

Since the **Phlegmatic temperament** <note>The Phlegmatic temperament was one of the four humors, associated with the element of water. People of this nature were thought to be naturally cold and moist, making them prone to sluggishness and fluid-based illnesses.</note> mimics the element of water in every way, and is thus of a moist and cold nature, it follows that over time—either of its own accord or due to other causes—this coldness and moisture increases. From this arise such diseases that fill the body with far too much wateriness, easily flooding and extinguishing the faintly glowing **life-wick** <note>The "life-wick" refers to the "innate heat" or vital flame that early modern physicians believed sustained life; excess "moist humors" were thought to drown this internal fire.</note> unless one knows how to prevent it in good time with a drying diet. We likewise observe in the Phlegmatic nature that they are prone to all moist diseases, such as: <term>head-fluxes</term> <note>original: "Hauptflüsse"; a general term for discharge or mucus running from the head</note>, colds, coughs, wheezing, **catarrh**, rattling breath, dizziness, stroke, epilepsy, deep sleep <note>Somnolence or lethargy.</note>, deafness, watery eyes, swelling, <term>dropsy</term> <note>Edema or the accumulation of excess fluid in the tissues.</note>, weeping sores, fistulas, diarrhea, intestinal and genital hernias, infertility, uterine disorders, prolapse of the rectum, blockage of semen, a tendency toward miscarriage, breast ailments, mouth ulcers, and the like.

Therefore, in all conditions of excess moisture, it is necessary to prescribe a drying and warming diet. This consists of ensuring the living quarters—with their windows facing East or South-East if possible—can receive the air blowing from the morning sun. The room should also be located on the upper floor of the house. Furthermore, it is helpful if the dwelling-place is in a dry, sandy, or mountainous area, far removed from foul, stinking, marshy regions, puddles, stagnant lakes, and fish-ponds, as well as waters that drive mill-wheels. 

Where such a dwelling is lacking, however, one must be diligent in compensating with drying means; namely, with frequently lit juniper brushwood, rosemary, and lavender branches, and by heating the room more often whenever cold and moist weather prevails. This should be accompanied by <term>fumigation</term> <note>The practice of burning aromatic substances to "purify" the air and balance the humors.</note> using cloves, mastic, frankincense, myrrh, **amber**, and juniper berries. If the moist air should also carry some rot or poisonous plague within it, one must be recommended the use of common sulfur and **gunpowder** for fumigation. For just as the smoke and flame of sulfur corrects and preserves the air of empty wine barrels so that they do not become moldy and musty over time, it does the same with its ignited flame to the air that one must draw in with every breath. With its sharp acidity, it consumes and bites away the rot; likewise, with its material substance and warm properties, it dries out the remaining moisture of the body when it is used in baths and ointments, and

However, dogs must not be given any of this, because coriander bread easily makes them rabid. One must also add a little salt; such bread dries the body best if it has sat for several days and is somewhat stale. Likewise, fully dried bread or zwieback, as well as bread toasted and rubbed with nutmeg, is very drying.

For kitchen meals, all kinds of easily digestible meat are useful, though they should be roasted rather than boiled. These include mutton, veal, capons, roosters, pigeons, and other poultry. However, the meat of pigs, geese, and ducks—as well as various types of fish, especially those without scales like eels and lampreys—is very phlegmatic and watery-slimy, and thus not beneficial for those of a phlegmatic temperament. Yet, if one keeps the body busy with daily work, or if those not accustomed to labor otherwise exercise well, the excess moisture is consumed; in such cases, all kinds of fish prepared with sufficient spices, wine, and vinegar may be enjoyed.

Smoked meat may also be included from time to time, for through such resistant foods, the stomach becomes accustomed to work, so that in time the **internal organs** <note>original: "Viscera"</note> generate a strong and lasting blood. However, coarse things with little nutrition, such as mushrooms, pumpkins, melons, and raw fruit, are not very useful.

For vegetables and for cooking in broths, one should use cabbage—especially the brown and curly varieties—chard, chervil, watercress, fennel, mugwort, wild thyme, sage, caraway, parsnip, and parsley roots and leaves. Garlic may also be tucked into meat and eaten roasted. If it is necessary to purge the body, one can also use mercury-herb, mallows, and orach...

## The Beverages.

Regarding beverages in such cases, the best is a good white wine that is not too strong and does not possess too much "fire," for such a wine otherwise easily inflames the liver if one drinks too much of it, so that instead of good blood, the liver produces a cold, watery blood. Next to wine, however, is a good, clear, well-boiled and well-aged beer, especially if it is brought to a boil—as is the custom in some places—by throwing in glowing **pebbles**. For the pebbles, when quenched, leave behind a <term>diuretic</term> <note>original: "Urin treibendes Saltz"; a salt that promotes the production of urine to flush the system.</note> salt therein, which makes these beers healthier and useful for carrying off the remaining wateriness through the urinary tracts, despite the fact that they do not taste as pleasant as those boiled in brewing pans.

Instead of beer and wine, one can also make a very healthy drink from honey, which is called **mead** <note>original: "Meth".</note>. To drink plain water, however, is altogether unhealthy here, for it chills and spoils the stomach and the blood, and forcefully increases the phlegmatic conditions.

But whatever the drink may be, if consumed in large quantities it increases the watery states, and in such a case nothing is better than to restrain oneself in drinking, and rather to suffer thirst than to drink much.

Likewise, much sleep and idleness are very harmful, and in such cases, one must abstain from excessive sleeping just as much as from excessive drinking; one must cut back on sleep and seek to undertake all kinds of moderate work or physical exercise daily, according to one's strength.

One must most carefully avoid the **cooling emotions**, such as: fear, sadness, greed, faint-heartedness, anxiety, terror, bashfulness, hate, envy, and grieving.

However, those emotions which set the blood and <term>vital spirits</term> <note>original: "Spiritus"; in historical medicine, these were subtle fluids or vapors believed to circulate through the body to sustain life and regulate the mind.</note> into a state of warming are beneficial, such as: cheerfulness, joy, merriment, and love; however—

### The Melancholic, or Warming and
### Moistening Diet.

Just as the **melancholic constitution** <note>In the system of the four humors, the melancholic temperament was associated with the element of Earth and was characterized as cold and dry.</note> corresponds in its nature with the element of Earth and is of a terrestrial, dry quality—and while the Earth receives its dryness from the "cold fire" of **Saturn** <note>original: "Saturno"; planetary influences were central to medical theory; Saturn was seen as the source of cold, restrictive, and melancholic energy.</note>, yet the hot material fire is also mixed therein, and often even **predominates** <note>original: "prædominiret"</note>—it produces pebble-hard and transparent **solidified matter** <note>original: "Concreta"</note>. However, when the cold, freezing fire predominates, things become as clear as water, such as ice, crystals, diamonds, alum, beryls, **rock salt** <note>original: "Sal Gemmæ"</note>, and the like. Exactly such a quality is found in the melancholic constitution: it is in every way of a dry, terrestrial nature, but not always of a cold quality. Rather, it often derives its excessive dryness from too great a heat, as such a melancholic temperament is very common in hot countries like Italy, Spain, and others. 

But just as a "hot gangrene" <note>original: "heiße Brand"</note>, when it takes hold, is finally transformed into a "cold gangrene," so it goes with extreme **melancholy** <note>Historically, "melancholy" referred to "black bile," a physical substance that could become "burnt" or "adust," leading to severe illness.</note>: whether it comes from heat or cold, it ultimately amounts to the same thing. From this arise very evil conditions that are difficult or impossible for a **physician** <note>original: "Medicus"</note> or the patient himself to **cure** <note>original: "curiren"</note> if he does not know how to make a distinction in the manner just mentioned. Daily experience teaches us this through **leprosy** <note>original: "Aussatz"</note>, deep-rooted **scurvy** <note>original: "Scharbock"</note>, **cancer** <note>original: "Krebs"</note>, **the wolf** <note>original: "Wolf"; a historical term for lupus or other "devouring" skin ulcers.</note>, **scalled head** <note>original: "Erbgrind"; a fungal infection of the scalp.</note>, **milk-crust** <note>original: "Milchsucht"; likely referring to crusty skin rashes or cradle cap.</note>, **quartan fever** <note>A fever that reoccurs every fourth day, traditionally associated with black bile and the spleen.</note>, madness, wind, **dropsy** <note>original: "Waßersucht"; an accumulation of fluid in the body tissues, now called edema.</note>, and other such diseases. All of these stem from an excessive dryness of the blood, but not always from the same kind of bodies; in their better state, some were partly hot, some cold, and some were even **temperate** and **sanguine**.

Despite such a uniform outcome, a distinction must nonetheless be maintained in the **preventative** <note>original: "præservirenden"</note> and curing diet. The temperament of every person belonging to this category must be well-investigated to see whether it originally comes more from **Saturn** <note>original: "Saturno"</note> and the cold impression, or from **Mars** <note>original: "Marte"</note>, which is hot...

Additionally, one should frequently make use of **stream and tub baths** <note>Hydrotherapy was a common treatment to balance the humors by absorbing moisture through the skin.</note> infused with herbs of a tempered juice, such as **daisies**, **chamomile**, **violet**, **mallows**, **melilot** <note>Also known as sweet clover.</note>, and **primroses**. The beneficial foods are cooked hulled barley and oats, shelled peas, and the broth and soups of all kinds of young, domestic meat, such as: **capons**, chickens, calves, and lambs, cooked together with the following herbs: **lettuce**, **borage**, **bugloss** <note>original: "Ochsen-Zungen"; literally "ox-tongue," an herb used to treat melancholic affections.</note>, and **chervil**. # Chapter VIII.

## What kinds of food serve elderly people in particular, and how they should be nourished.

The foods with which elderly people are to be maintained and nourished must be directed and ordered according to the degree of their age, as was mentioned above.

If they still find themselves quite fresh and lively despite their age, it is not necessary to prescribe a special **diet** <term>Diæt: In historical medicine, this refers to a total lifestyle regimen—including food, environment, and behavior—rather than just food restriction</term>. The rules already noted and cited can be enough for them to follow. However, for the last two degrees of high old age <note>Early modern medicine often divided old age into stages, such as "green" old age and "decrepit" old age.</note>, it is a completely different matter. These individuals must be warmed and moistened at the same time, considering that their **temperament** <term>Temperament: The physical constitution or nature of a person; here, elderly people were considered naturally "cold and dry"</term> is cold and dry. Accordingly, their dwelling should be elevated, but in warm air, and their rooms must always be kept warm. Regarding the food with which one wishes to nourish them, one should consider:

1. How much should be given to them.
2. The nature and quality of such foods.
3. How they should use or consume them.

Firstly and generally, they should not burden themselves with too much food <note>original: "Kosten"; here referring to meals or provisions</note>, because their **natural heat** <term>natürliche Wärme: The innate vital heat believed to reside in the heart and drive digestion and all life processes</term> is very weak in old age. Otherwise, this heat could easily be smothered and suppressed, much like when one puts too much wood on a fire, causing it to be choked so that it cannot burn. Even young people have enough trouble digesting when they have overeaten.

<summary>This page concludes the regimen for the dry complexion and begins a chapter on the dietary needs of the elderly, emphasizing that aging bodies require warmth and moisture. It warns that overeating can "smother" the dwindling vital heat of an older person, much like too much wood can extinguish a small fire.</summary>

Regarding the nature of the foods, they should be of good **juice** <note>original: *Saft*; in early modern medicine, this refers to the nutritive fluids or "chyle" produced during digestion that eventually becomes blood.</note>, and easy to digest; on the other hand, they should guard against all tough, slimy food that is hard, coarse, and **phlegmatic** <term>Phlegmatisch: Relating to phlegm, one of the four humors. An excess of this cold, moist humor was thought to cause sluggishness, congestion, and "dullness" of the senses.</term>, which causes winds <note>gas</note> or **melancholy** <term>Melancholey: Black bile, the humor associated with cold and dryness. In excess, it was believed to cause sadness, anxiety, and physical blockages in the veins.</term> and black blood, and brings with it the blockage of the passages and veins. The manner of nourishing them consists in giving them a little to eat often, especially those who, as is commonly said, are already walking upon the grave; those who are still somewhat more spirited can take food three times a day. In this way, several very old, aged men have been kept alive and healthy for a long time, of whom *Galen* <note>Claudius Galenus (c. 129–216 AD), the most influential physician of the Roman Empire whose theories on the four humors dominated medicine for over 1,500 years.</note> makes mention of two in his *Book of Fruits* <note>original: *Früchten-Buche*; likely referring to Galen's work *On the Properties of Foodstuffs*.</note> concerning the preservation of good health: one was *Antiochus*, a physician, and the other was *Telephus*, a grammarian.

Their bread should be made of wheat flour, well-baked, and a little salted; however, this should not be eaten warm, because it is difficult to digest, brings all kinds of changes to the body, causes blockages, and sends various wicked **vapors** <note>Physicians believed that certain foods released "fumes" or vapors in the stomach that rose to the brain, causing headaches, confusion, or "clouded" thinking.</note> to the brain. Their bread should be at most two days old, for if it sits longer than three days, it becomes too dry and remains sitting in the stomach for a long time. All cakes and tarts prepared with cheese, milk, and much butter, as well as unleavened bread, should be entirely avoided as harmful.

Meat is a good food; it gives much nourishment and is soon transformed into blood. Yet one also finds meat which is very difficult to digest, tough, and slimy—as has already been mentioned to some extent above—which is completely unhealthy and contrary for elderly people.

The meat of birds can be digested sooner than the meat of four-legged animals, just as among the birds themselves, those are better and healthier which seek their pasture in dry places, rather than those which stay and feed in marshes and watery places.

Otherwise, as concerns the meat with which one should feed and nourish elderly people, it is best to have livestock of middle age slaughtered for them, for the very young have too much moisture, and the too old are too dry. The best meat for them and the best nourishment, if they are otherwise able to have it, is from good **capons** <term>Capaunen: Castrated roosters, prized in historical diets for their tender, succulent meat which was considered more balanced and easier to digest than regular poultry.</term>, hens, pheasants, partridges, pullets and pigeons, hazel grouse, mutton, and large calves. The meat of a turtle dove is also not unhealthy. Some praise pork, but it is better that elderly people abstain from it, because it brings much superfluous moisture.

The brain of all animals, whatever they may be called, is a friend to the stomach.

---

The liver of animals is not very healthy, because it produces thick blood; likewise, the extremities of animal bodies, such as the head, tail, and feet, are difficult to digest and provide little nourishment. Lamb, as well as beef, wild boar, and waterfowl, are not suitable at all for the stomachs of elderly people.

Fresh and soft-boiled eggs, on the other hand, are very beneficial to them, for they provide good and rapid nourishment; hard-boiled or fried eggs are not as good, for they produce thick moisture <note>original: *dicke Feuchtigkeit*; likely referring to phlegm or a sluggish humor</note> and remain in the stomach for a long time. However, no matter how one prefers to eat eggs, one should always add salt and consume it with them so that they settle better; the white of the egg has little nourishment and gives the stomach much work to do.

The elderly should not eat fish often, as they are not very beneficial to them; however, when they do enjoy them, they may salt them well and have them prepared with sage, fennel, and wine. Foods that have a sharp taste and are a bit biting <note>pungent or spicy</note> serve the elderly very well to awaken their appetite, to encourage their natural warmth, and to consume the coarse **phlegmatic** <term>Phlegmatisch: Relating to phlegm, the cold and moist humor. In the elderly, an excess was thought to cause congestion and slow digestion.</term> moisture that collects in their stomachs. Therefore, it is advisable to season their food with pepper, ginger, and cinnamon; they may also occasionally make use of mustard. Prepared onions and garlic are also not unhelpful for those who like to eat them and whose nature is accustomed to them.

Cheese is of no use to them, but butter is healthy, for it moistens moderately, warms, and softens the chest—though pure, sweet **olive oil** <note>original: *Baum-Oehl*, literally "tree oil," a common historical term for olive oil</note> does this much more effectively.

It has also been found in the natures of some elderly people that milk is beneficial to them, although for those who are "stopped up" <note>constipated or having blocked vessels</note> in their internal limbs or parts of the body, milk is harmful. The Greeks and ancient Romans thought highly of honey in their old age, which they ate with bread for that reason and used in almost all their foods.

Raw tree-fruits are not good, because they carry much watery moisture with them and can easily spoil in the stomach.

Large and small raisins <note>likely referring to raisins and currants</note> serve the liver, the stomach, the kidneys, and the bladder.

Almonds induce relaxation <note>original: *schlaffen*; can mean to relax the body or aid sleep</note>, increase the substance of the brain, and cleanse the urinary tracts; preserved items <note>original: *eingemachte Sachen*; such as fruits in syrup or honey</note> are beneficial to the elderly.

## After meals, the question is: what kind of drinks benefit the elderly best?

Just as drinking is harmful to childhood, it is conversely necessary and useful for old people; for because they cannot enjoy food as perfectly in their old age as they did in their youth, those of a dry nature especially must rely on drinking (though not excessively).

In wine consists their greatest strengthening and refreshment; therefore, when it is truly good, it is called **the milk of the elderly**, because they delight in a good glass of wine just as children do in their mother's milk. As the saying goes: *Old men are twice children* <note>original: "Bis pueri Senes"</note>. Old people become children twice over through this "milk"; the wine warms the internal parts of the body, cleanses them, and carries away watery fluids through the urine.

Wine warms the bodies of the elderly and refreshes the spirit. The wise heathen **Zeno** <note>Zeno of Citium (c. 334 – c. 262 BC), the founder of the Stoic school of philosophy.</note> had a proverb about wine: wine removes the melancholy and sad expressions from sour-faced old people.

One of the ancient Arabic physicians, namely **Rhazes** <note>original: "Rhosis"; referring to Abu Bakr al-Razi (865–925 AD), a Persian physician and philosopher.</note>, writes that young people should abstain from wine, but as soon as they have reached their fortieth year, they should thank Almighty God as often as they see and enjoy wine, for He has created such a noble and magnificent juice. Every person should indeed partake of this drink with such rightful thanksgiving.

The elderly should drink good, old wine; new wines that are still thick and sweet are not good for them, for they clog the liver, spleen, and urinary tracts, which results in a frail old age burdened with **dropsy** <term>Wassersucht: An old medical term for edema, or the swelling caused by excess fluid trapping in the body's tissues.</term>, **kidney stones** <note>original: "Lendenstein," literally "loin-stone."</note>, and other serious ailments.

Drinking wine on an empty stomach is not good, nor is drinking it when one has become too overheated; for the vapors and fumes of the wine rise too quickly to the brain, whereby the nerves are weakened and **cramps** are caused, along with severe headaches and finally **stroke** <note>original: "der Schlag," referring to apoplexy or a sudden loss of consciousness/paralysis.</note> itself.

Old people should drink often and in small amounts. **Mead** <note>A fermented beverage made of honey and water.</note> is a very healthy drink, and the elderly can use it in place of their daily beverage.

## Chapter IX.

# On the Exercises that Old People Should Use.

Among all the foods, fare, and nourishment that people use, and through which they seek the maintenance of their bodies, it is well known that nothing can be found—no matter how clean and pure it may be—that does not contain something within it that is unlike our nature, burdensome, and not entirely beneficial. Therefore, it is inevitable that in all digestion <note>original: "Däuungen"; refers to the physiological process of "concoction" or breaking down food in the stomach.</note> something impure must remain behind. If this is retained in the body and not driven out or purged, it causes countless diseases.

The coarser *excrementa* <note>waste products or excrement</note>, or impurities, pass away in such a manner that one can visibly perceive how the body rids itself of them. However, as for the more subtle and delicate impurities, these must be driven out through the movement and exercises of the body. Indeed, it is almost impossible for a person to live in good, perfect health unless they are as diligent in exercise—to train the body and keep it in motion—as they are in nourishing it with food. For while food replaces what has been lost, exercise disperses and carries away what is superfluous.

Exercise preserves the human body, whereas idleness <note>original: "Müßiggang"; refers to a lack of physical activity or sloth.</note> ruins and destroys it. A moderate amount of exercise, when undertaken with proper and orderly movement of the body, prevents the internal parts of the human frame from becoming overfilled. This overfilling is the mother of countless diseases.

Exercise increases natural warmth, keeps both the perceptible and imperceptible passages <note>likely referring to the pores and the circulatory channels</note> of the body open, makes the body quick and nimble, prepares the superfluities so that they may be better carried out, strengthens the nerves wonderfully, and firms the joints and the bones of the limbs. For just as sleep generally benefits the internal organs, so a moderate, industrious exercise serves the joints.

Cornelius Celsus <note>Aulo Cornelius Celsus (c. 25 BC – c. 50 AD), a Roman encyclopedist known for his medical work *De Medicina*.</note> writes the following on this subject: Standing still and laziness make the body weary and heavy, but labor and exercise make it strong and quick; idleness makes us old before our time, but exercise and labor preserve a long-lasting youth.

One must also know what kind of order should be observed in the exercise of the body. First, bodily exercises should take place before eating, so that the natural heat, which is to perform the <term>digestion</term> <note>original: "Dauung"; in Galenic medicine, this refers to "concoction," the process by which food is "cooked" or transformed by the body's heat.</note>, may be awakened; thus, the food we take in finds the stomach well-warmed and not "sleepy."

Even <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>The famous physician of Ancient Greece, often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> gives this teaching when he writes: *Labor precedes food.* <note>original Latin: "Labores cibos præcedunt."</note> Work and exercise should go before the meal.

Beyond this, exercise should also be arranged in accordance with one's eating.

Those who are accustomed to taking in much food should also exercise more than others; those who eat little should also not engage in so much movement, and thus not exceed the goal of exercise. Therefore, moderate and steady movement and exercise are the best. "Moderate" means that one does not become exhausted by it; and by "movement," understand one where all parts of the body are exercised at the same time, but not fatigued.

For an uneven and violent movement can ruin even the strongest bodies, because it weakens the joints of the limbs and makes the <term>muscles</term> <note>original: "Mäußlein," literally "little mice," an archaic German term for muscles.</note> long and lax, when it is upon these that the body’s nimbleness and agility most depend.

Morning exercise is always best, or when the first two <term>concoctions</term> <note>original: "Dauungen"; referring to the stages of digestion in the stomach and the liver.</note> are completed. Exercise undertaken immediately after eating causes countless blockages, fills the veins with raw, "uncooked" juice <note>referring to the humors or fluids of the body that have not been properly processed by the liver</note>, and causes the food to move far too quickly from the stomach down into the intestines.

In winter, one should exercise with vigorous walking, but in summer with gentle and slow riding; however, one should mostly stick to one's own habits and see what nature can bear. Thus, there are also some ordinary and common movements, and some extraordinary and special ones. The common ones are likely the best when they are available, such as: playing ball, walking up and down, or riding to and fro on horses.

The special exercises consist of rubbing the limbs, by which the heat is wonderfully awakened to draw nourishment through to that same limb, and to break up and carry away the impurities remaining from the <term>third concoction</term> <note>original: "dritten Kochung"; in traditional medicine, the third stage of "digestion" happened within the individual tissues and limbs themselves.</note>, which sometimes linger between the muscles in the subtle membranes.

Old, aged people should be content with moderate exercise, so that the natural heat—of which they do not have much left—is not entirely consumed...

Rubbing the limbs is very beneficial for them, but one should begin early in the morning as soon as they have woken up, and continue and pursue this until the parts of the body begin to become reddish and warm. ## Concerning Sleep, and how one should behave in these matters.

Sleep is also one of the most distinguished parts that belong to a good <term>regimen of life</term> <note>A traditional medical system of rules regarding diet and lifestyle to maintain health.</note>. For this reason, we wish to set down some rules here, which those who wish to prevent themselves from growing old before their time must observe.

The best thing regarding sleep is to become accustomed to sleeping and resting at night, and being awake during the day.

For the afternoon nap is very harmful and makes the entire body heavy and bloated.

After supper, one should wait 2 to 3 hours before taking rest, and beforehand walk a little in one's room before going to bed.

A proper and natural sleep should not last longer than seven hours, and in doing so, one must not cover oneself too warmly, so that the vapors have room to escape through the <term>pores</term> <note>original: "Schweiß-Löcher," literally "sweat-holes."</note>.

During sleep, one should lie with the head somewhat higher than the rest of the body, so that the food does not rise back out of the stomach into the throat or <term>esophagus</term> <note>original: "Speise Röhren," literally "food-pipes."</note>.

Lying and sleeping on the back is not good because, in this case, the waste of which the brain unburdens itself through the nose and mouth falls backward onto the spine; furthermore, one would thereby so overheat the large <term>respiratory vessels</term> <note>original: "Lufft-Adern," literally "air-veins." In early medicine, it was believed certain vessels carried air rather than blood.</note> together with the blood vessel called the <term>vena cava</term> <note>The "great hollow vein" that carries blood to the heart.</note>—which have their seat upon the loins—that the kidneys would be heated by it and would not only gather matter for <term>gravel and kidney stones</term> <note>original: "Grieß- und Lenden-Stein." "Gravel" refers to small urinary deposits.</note>, but would also send many harmful vapors to the brain.

The first part of sleep should take place on the right side; otherwise, one is to fear that the liver would lie upon the stomach and press upon it, since

## On Sleep, and how one should behave in these matters.

Sleep is also one of the most excellent parts that belong to a good **regimen of life** <note>A "regiment" or "regimen" was a prescribed way of living—including diet, exercise, and rest—to maintain the balance of the body's humors.</note>. For this reason, we wish to set down some rules here that those must observe who desire to prevent themselves from becoming old before their time.

The best thing regarding sleep is that one accustoms oneself to sleep and rest at night, and to stay awake throughout the day.

For the **midday sleep** is very harmful and makes the entire body heavy and bloated.

After the **evening meal**, one should wait 2 to 3 hours before taking rest, and beforehand walk a little in one's chamber before laying down in bed.

A proper and natural sleep should last no longer than **seven hours**, and therein one must not cover oneself too warmly, so that the **vapors** <note>In early modern medicine, "vapors" were gases produced by digestion that needed to be released through the pores to prevent illness.</note> have room to escape through the **pores** <note>original: "Schweiß-Löchern," literally "sweat-holes."</note>.

During sleep, one should lie with the head somewhat higher than the rest of the body, so that the food does not rise back out of the stomach into the **gullet or esophagus**.

Lying and sleeping on the back is not good because, in this case, the **waste** <note>The "unrath" or impurities that the brain supposedly discharged during rest.</note> which the brain discharges through the nose and mouth falls backward onto the spine; furthermore, one would thereby so greatly overheat the large **arteries** <note>original: "Lufft-Adern," literally "air-veins." Ancient medical theory held that arteries carried "vital spirit" or air.</note> along with the large vein called the **Vena Cava** <note>Latin: "hollow vein." The primary vein carrying blood back to the heart.</note>—which have their place upon the loins—that the kidneys would be heated by it. This would not only collect matter for **gravel and kidney stones**, but would also send many harmful vapors to the brain.

The first sleep should occur on the **right side**, otherwise one must fear that the liver would lay itself upon the stomach and press upon it...
