For the **spleen** <note>In the humoral system, the spleen was associated with black bile and melancholy; here, its physical weight is the concern.</note> would come to lie under the stomach and would have to suffer a double burden, which does not happen if one lies on the **right side** while sleeping. In this way, the **liver** comes under the stomach and warms it to promote **digestion** <note>original: "Dauung"</note>, in no other way than if one were to place a **brazier** <note>original: "Kohl-pfanne"; a portable heater filled with glowing coals.</note> with glowing coals under a dish of food.

When the first sleep is over, one may lie on the **left side**, so that the **vapors** <note>original: "Dämpfe"; digestive gases believed to rise to the head and affect health.</note> that have gathered on the right side may be dispersed and evaporate.

Finally and lastly, one should turn back again to the **right side**, so that the food digested in the stomach may sink more easily and pass into the intestines.

During sleep, one should not stretch the limbs out too far, but rather keep them moderately positioned and drawn toward oneself.

These, then, are the **remarks** <note>original: "Remarques"</note> and rules that one should use before and during sleep, although it is somewhat difficult for **elderly people** to always follow them. Therefore, one must certainly look at the circumstances and conditions found among them before prescribing rules in such a matter. For it is well known that aged people often spend the whole night awake because their entire **temperament** <note>In early modern medicine, health was determined by the balance of the four "humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile). Old age was considered naturally "cold and dry."</note> is very dry and many sharp vapors are present in them, which commonly arise from a **salty moisture**; these people must certainly sleep a little after the midday meal.

Because time also generally becomes long for the elderly, since they can no longer perform anything and must abandon all their otherwise usual **actions** <note>original: "Actiones"</note> and duties for lack of strength—and therefore sit in a state of **unquiet rest**—one must reasonably be intent on **relieving** <note>original: "soulagiren," from the French "soulager," meaning to soothe or comfort.</note> them in this regard as well.

### On shortening the time and boredom for elderly people, and on driving away displeasure and melancholy, take the following advice and instruction.

**Plato** writes in a **dialogue** <note>original: "Dialogo"</note> or conversation to which he gave the name ***Charmides***, that the swiftest and most harmful diseases that the human body must endure originate from the **soul** or the **mind** <note>original: "Gemüth"</note>; which is indeed found to be so in deed and in truth.

For the soul, because it has the supreme command and highest mastery over the body, can change the same in a moment, as often as it pleases.

Und do we not see daily how many various illnesses arise suddenly, and indeed solely from the <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "Imagination" or "Einbildung"; in this period, the imagination was considered a powerful internal sense that could directly affect the body's physical health.</note>? Have we not examples of those who have died from excessively great and unforeseen joy? Do not displeasure, heartache, and mourning plunge countless people into heavy melancholic illnesses? These are so stubborn and wicked that they may well be called the <term>scourges of physicians</term> <note>original: "Geisseln der Medicorum"; diseases that are so difficult to treat they become a punishment for the doctors attempting to cure them.</note>.

We also do not lack for histories in which certain and credible examples are presented, showing that some people, out of pure fear and the expectation of death, have turned ice-gray <note>i.e., their hair turned white from shock.</note> within twenty-four hours.

Therefore, anyone who wishes to live long and in constant health is advised to abstain as much as possible from all melancholy, anxiety of the heart, and heavy <term>affects</term> <note>original: "Affecten"; strong emotions or passions that "affect" the body's balance.</note>. This is especially directed at elderly people, who are otherwise more subject to such <term>passions</term> <note>original: "Passionen"; emotional states that the soul "suffers" or undergoes.</note> than the young, since the former and the aged are <term>ordinarily</term> <note>original: "al' ordinaire"</note> ruled by fear, displeasure, melancholy, and sadness, because they are by nature and <term>temperament</term> <note>The "temperament" was the unique balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) in an individual. The elderly were believed to be naturally "cold and dry."</note> cold, and possess a weak brain.

For this reason, every opportunity for fear, mourning, and suffering should be removed from them as much as possible; it can also do no harm—provided they are not naturally inclined to anger—if they are occasionally provoked to a little anger, because through this the natural heat within them is encouraged and awakened <note>In the medical theories of the time, anger was "hot" and could help counteract the "coldness" and sluggishness of old age.</note>.

Yet it is better to seek out all means by which one may make them cheerful and set them free from complaining and mourning.

However, since everything in which our mind finds either pleasure or displeasure must be received through the external senses—because the stimulated senses are true spokesmen and faithful messengers who <term>report</term> <note>original: "referiren"</note> and display the conditions of external things to the internal senses and thus to the soul itself—necessity requires, if we wish to provide pleasure to old people and keep them in a good <term>humor</term> <note>original: "Humeur"; referring to both their mood and the literal balance of their bodily fluids.</note>, that we above all things flatter and coax their external senses, which are: Sight, Hearing, Smell, Taste, and Touch, and present to each of them something that will make it well satisfied.

The eyes delight themselves wonderfully and particularly in the sight and contemplation of beautiful and well-formed <term>ladies</term> <note>original: "Frauen-Zimmer"; a collective term for women, often used here to suggest the aesthetic and social pleasure of their company.</note>, and I believe that many who are aged and old find themselves satisfied with this and concern themselves with nothing further.

Beautiful flowers of many kinds of colors, lovely paintings and the like, can likewise delight the eyes of others.

The wealthy are also able to contribute to this by keeping precious jewelry and gems before their eyes; among these stones, sapphires and emeralds refresh the eyes the most, because sight is preserved by no colors more than by green and violet-blue.

The ears also have their pleasure, and indeed it penetrates through hearing even deeper into the heart and mind, so that even the soul is <term>affected</term> <note>original: "afficiret"; in early modern psychology, this meant the soul was physically moved or changed by sensory input.</note> by it.

**Music**, whether it consists of the voices of living men or of instruments, can by its virtue cheer up and gladden melancholy and mournful spirits. we find examples of this even in Holy Scripture <note>Likely referring to David playing the harp for King Saul to soothe his "evil spirit."</note>, which I will not list here as they are not unknown.

A certain Greek named **Elimias**, whenever he noticed that adversity and sorrow of the heart were about to befall him, would quickly seize his stringed instrument. Through its harmony and unanimous sound, he brought his <term>humor</term> <note>original: "Humeur"; referring to the bodily fluids or temperament that governed one's emotional state.</note>—which was already beginning to stir and become rebellious—back to its proper state.

The <term>discourses</term> <note>original: "Discurse"</note> or conversations with which we wish to pass the time for old people and keep them occupied should be pleasant to them. We must praise them, give them kind words, speak everything with love, never contradict them, and present nothing to them except what pleases them well—speaking of things from which they came and in which they were raised.

For example: with a merchant, one should speak of trade, commerce, and profit.

With an old soldier, of matters of war, storms, and battles.

With a scholar, of good books and the <term>liberal arts</term> <note>original: "freyen Künsten"</note>, and so forth.

For such conversations keep them alert, so that they listen gladly, enjoy themselves, and are well-satisfied.

We have an example of this in the wise lawmaker of Athens, **Solon** <note>original: "Salone"</note>. When he was already on his deathbed and saw that some of his good friends, standing not far from him, were whispering something secretly to one another so as not to disturb the <term>patient</term> or rather the dying man, he sat up quite briskly. He begged them to speak loudly, thinking that he would be happy if, even in his final hour, he might experience something—yes, that he might learn something even in death itself.

The sense of smell should be aided with lovely and fragrant things, because beyond all doubt the heart is refreshed and gladdened by this, and the <term>vital spirits</term> <note>original: "lebhafften Geister"; the subtle substances thought to inhabit the blood and nerves, responsible for life and consciousness.</note> are purified.

Whenever they wash their face and hands, some fragrant water should always be used.

The sense of taste depends on the diet, and there one should endeavor to ensure that (whenever possible) good, delicate, savory foods are presented and given to them. These should have a sharp, penetrating taste to replace and awaken the diminished and lost appetite and desire for food.

From all the above, it is now clear what the <term>regimen of life</term> <note>original: "Lebens-Regiment"; a set of lifestyle rules covering diet, exercise, and environment to maintain health.</note>—which old people should employ—consists of. In conclusion, we wish to remind everyone to apply themselves with all earnestness to recognizing their own nature; for experience will best tell them what is harmful or useful, so that they can best become their own master and physician.

### Furthermore, we shall see what kind of medicines are most useful for old people.

Beloved old age brings so many burdens and inconveniences with it that several of the ancient <term>authors</term> <note>original: "Scribenten"</note>, as mentioned before, have said: "Old age has more the character of a disease than of health," while others say that old age in and of itself is disease enough. Of these ailments, we will mention only a few, particularly those most commonly felt.

Daily experience shows that old people are generally constipated in the body and have difficulty going to the stool. They possess many <term>phlegmatic humors</term> <note>original: "phlegmatische Feuchtigkeiten"; in the medical theory of the time, phlegm was cold and moist, becoming more dominant as one aged.</note> and a watery sharpness; therefore, when they pass urine, there is often a stinging and burning sensation.

They are also plagued with much wind <note>intestinal gas</note> and are subject to a constant tiredness, living in pure weakness because they have a faint stomach and the natural warmth of the entire body is greatly impaired. You will hardly find one in ten who is not burdened with constant <term>catarrhs and head-fluids</term> <note>original: "Catharren und Hauptflüssen"; terms for the excessive drainage of mucus believed to flow from the brain into the respiratory system.</note>, so that they can often do little more than cough and spit—if indeed they are even capable of doing the latter.

### 3.

Take fresh pig fat <note>original: "Schweine-Fett"; high-quality lard was a standard base for historical ointments due to its similarity to human skin oils.</note>, melt it in a new glazed vessel over a gentle fire, then press it through a cloth, and pour the pressed liquid into another similar vessel. Pour onto it 5 or 6 pounds of proper, fragrant rose water, but add to every pound of said fat 2 <term>Loth</term> <note>A unit of weight roughly equal to 15-16 grams or half an ounce.</note> of clove oil. Stir everything well together, rub it, and crush it until your salve becomes entirely white and looks like milk. This salve protects the face and hands from sunburn, from the discomfort of the air and the winds, as well as from the cold, and consistently creates a beautiful skin.

### 4.

Take 40 Paradise apples <note>original: "Paradieß-Aepffel"; depending on the region and era, this could refer to tomatoes (then called "love apples") or a specific variety of small pomaceous fruit used in cosmetics.</note>, clean them well, and cut each one into 4 pieces. Place one clove in each piece. Once you have prepared them thus, pour good and proper rose water over them and let it stand for 8 days. After that, take fresh pig fat from a <term>barrow</term> <note>original: "Barck"; a castrated male pig, often preferred in pharmacy for having a milder scent than a boar.</note> or a boar, clean it well, and add as much of it as your material can support. Rub it well together with the prepared apples. Once it is well-rubbed, set it over a gentle fire and let it simmer until everything is well mixed together and until everything has dissolved. Then press it through a clean linen cloth. To this pressed juice, add some sweet almond oil mixed with camphor, stir it together, and keep it for your use.

### 5.

Take 6 Loth of raw pig fat.
->1 Loth of camphor.<-
->10 Loth of white wax.<-
->Musk.<-
->Civet.<-
->Ambergris, 2 <term>grains</term> <note>original: "Gran"; a very small unit of weight, approximately 0.06 grams.</note> of each.<- <note>original: "aa. 2. Gran"; the "aa." is an abbreviation for "ana," meaning an equal amount of each listed ingredient.</note>

First, divide the fat into small pieces, put it in a new glazed pot, set it over a gentle fire, and let it simmer or melt. Then pour it into rose water. When this is done, crush the camphor and add it along with the melted wax. Stir it well together until everything has dissolved and become thoroughly mixed.

...and finally, also add the musk, ambergris, and civet <note>original: "Bisam, Ambra und Zibeth"; these are animal-derived fixatives and perfumes—musk from deer, ambergris from whales, and civet from the civet cat—highly valued in early modern pharmacy for their lasting scents.</note>.

This salve heals wrinkles on the hands and the lips in a wonderful way.

The moisture that grows within elm leaves <note>original: "Ulmen-Blättern"; this likely refers to the "elm water" found inside galls on elm leaves, which was historically used as a cosmetic wash.</note> makes a beautiful face when one washes with it.

### 6.

## On distilled water for beautifying the face.

The simple herbs from which one distills water to preserve the face are:
Silverweed <note>original: "Genserich" (Potentilla anserina).</note>.
Plantain.
Water lilies.
Large nettle root.
Tormentil root <note>original: "Stück-Wurzel"; historically associated with tormentil or masterwort, used for its astringent properties.</note>.

Their leaves should be pounded, fermented, pressed, and distilled in a <term>water bath</term> <note>original: "Balneo" (Latin: balneum); a method of gentle heating using a container of water to ensure even temperature.</note>. However, once the said waters have been prepared, they must be set in the sun to preserve them.

The flowers must be gathered while completely fresh, then placed in a <term>flask</term> <note>original: "Kolben"; a round-bottomed glass vessel used in distillation.</note> and distilled in <term>Mary’s Bath</term> <note>original: "Balneo Mariæ" (Bain-Marie); a double-boiler setup named after Mary the Jewess, an ancient alchemist.</note>.

It is not strictly necessary to add a <term>solvent</term> <note>original: "Menstruum"; a liquid used to dissolve or extract active principles from a substance.</note> to them; it is enough if one bruises them slightly. One commonly takes the flowers of rosemary, almond tree, peach tree, beans, elder, lily of the valley, linden, lilies, and marshmallow.

The waters that are otherwise distilled and prepared for this use from fruits are green walnuts, strawberries, lemons, melons, cucumbers, watermelons, and pumpkins. The strawberries are pounded, but the others are cut into pieces and then distilled in a water bath. Each of these waters has its own particular property; one uses them as they are deemed useful.

### 7.

## A water for strengthening the face.

Take one pound of almond blossoms—but these must be dried in the shade, not in the sun—and a half pound of pumpkin flowers,

Take one pound of white lilies and six lemons; cut the lemons into pieces. Take the whites and the shells of two dozen fresh, newly laid eggs and a quarter of a measure <note>original: "das 4. von einer Maß"; a measure or 'Maß' varied by region but was roughly equivalent to a liter or quart.</note> of white wine. Let all of this soak together for one night or longer, then distill it all together in a <term>Mary’s Bath</term> <note>original: "B. M." (Balneum Mariae); a gentle heating method using a water bath.</note> until the <term>residue</term> <note>original: "Fæces"; the solid remains or dregs left after distillation.</note> remains dry on the bottom. This water makes the face clear and the skin beautifully white; one should wash with it in the evening upon going to sleep and dry oneself gently in the morning.

Since teeth are also counted among the graceful parts of the human body, we wish to include here a few small but effective instructions for keeping them clean and pure.

### To make the teeth white.

Take oil of sulfur <note>original: "Schwefel-Oehl"; in this period, this often referred to a diluted spirit of sulfur (sulfuric acid) used as a whitening agent, though it was quite abrasive.</note> and rub them often with it, then wash them again with fresh water.

->Or<-

Take rye bread that has been well-baked, dry it, and turn it into a powder. Rub your teeth with this powder; it does not only make them white but also strengthens the gums. If you wish to add red powdered coral to it, it is even better.

### A good tooth powder.

Take well-burnt hartshorn <note>original: "Hirsch-Horn"; the antlers of a stag, calcined (burnt to ash) and used as a cleaning abrasive.</note>, Venetian tartar <note>original: "Venetianischen Weinstein"; a high-quality potassium bitartrate collected from wine barrels.</note>, and white prepared coral, as much as you like. Add also some burnt alum, fine choice grains of mastic <note>original: "Mastix-Körner"; a resin from the mastic tree used for its pleasant scent and gum-tightening properties.</note>, and some crushed violet root <note>original: "Viol-Wurzel"; likely Orris root (the root of the Iris flower), which smells like violets and was a common tooth-powder ingredient.</note>. Powder and mix everything well together and rub your teeth with it twice a week. However short this little treatise may be, it will hopefully bring pleasure from beginning to end to its readers, both men and women, and especially to those who make use of its contents.

## The Eighth
# TREATISE.
## How one shall make
### all sorts of colors;

-> Which every House-Father and House-Mother may <-
-> use, and dye their wool and linen, or linen <-
-> cloth and yarn themselves. <-

---

-> Concerning all sorts of colors, to dye cloth, cords, and all <-
-> manner of things. <-

-> Number I. <-

### To dye linen a beautiful Sulfur-Yellow.

One takes <term>Dyer’s Rocket</term> <note>original: "Gilb-Kraut"; likely *Reseda luteola*, also known as Weld, the most common source of yellow dye in Europe at the time.</note>, as much as is needed, and boils it in good <term>lye</term> <note>original: "Laugen"; an alkaline solution made from wood ashes, used here to extract the pigment.</note>, for such a solution extracts all colors; then the herb is strained out, and a little <term>verdigris</term> <note>original: "Grünspan"; a green pigment and mordant made from weathered copper.</note> and <term>alum</term> <note>original: "Alaun"; a mineral salt used as a mordant to fix the dye to the fibers.</note> are added to it; then the yarn is dyed in it until it is yellow enough.

-> Number II. <-

### To dye linen yarn Silver-colored.

One takes blue <term>logwood</term> <note>original: "blau Priesilgen-Holz"; a corruption of "Brazilwood" or "Preseil," often referring to logwood, which produced blues, purples, and silvers.</note> and <term>copperas</term> <note>original: "Kupfer-Waßer"; also known as green vitriol or ferrous sulfate, used to darken or "sadden" colors.</note>; let them boil together in clean water; after that, one takes <term>oak galls</term> <note>original: "Gallus-Aepffel"; abnormal growths on oak trees rich in tannins, used for making ink and dark dyes.</note>, crushes them small, adds them to the dyes, and lets it boil again for a little while together—

boil, and then pour off the dye cleanly; with this, one can dye a beautiful silver-color.

->Number III.<-

### To dye linen yarn a beautiful red.

One takes, for 1 pound of linen yarn, 2 <term>Loth</term> <note>original: "Loth"; a historical unit of weight, approximately 14 to 17 grams.</note> of <term>alum</term> <note>original: "Alaun"; a mineral salt used to fix dyes to fabric.</note>, places it in lukewarm water, puts the yarn in, and lets it lie therein for a few hours; then take it out and let it dry. Afterward, take a quarter-pound of <term>Brazilwood</term> <note>original: "Priesilgen"; referring to wood from the *Caesalpinia* genus which produces red and purple dyes.</note>, let it boil well in water, and add about a knife-tip full of <term>saltpeter</term> <note>original: "Salniter"; used here to brighten the red color.</note>, and dye with it; in this way, it will become a beautiful red.

->Number IV.<-

### To dye linen yarn a beautiful gold-yellow.

One takes <term>yellow dye-wood</term> <note>original: "gelben Prisilgen"; likely referring to Fustic or a similar yellow-producing heartwood.</note>, boils it in <term>lye</term> <note>original: "Lauge"; an alkaline solution made from wood ashes</note> until all the color is extracted, then stirs in a little alum and dyes the yarn with it.

->Number V.<-

### To dye linen yarn a beautiful purple color.

One boils red Brazilwood in a good lye, puts a little <term>lime</term> <note>original: "Kalck"; the addition of an alkaline substance like lime shifts the red of Brazilwood toward a purple or violet hue.</note> into it, lets it boil together, and dyes the yarn with it until the color is pleasing.

->Number VI.<-

### To dye linen yarn a beautiful raisin-color.

One does exactly as with the red, and likewise uses lye for it, but no lime; the yarn is placed beforehand in alum-water, let it dry again, and then dye with it. <note>"Raisin-color" (Rosinfarb) refers to a deep, dark reddish-purple similar to the skin of a dried grape.</note>

->Number VII.<-

### To dye linen yarn blue from dye-wood.

One takes <term>logwood</term> <note>original: "braune Priesilgen"; literally "brown Brazilwood," which refers to logwood (*Haematoxylum campechianum*), used for blues and blacks.</note>, boils it in lye until enough is extracted; then one adds some <term>verdigris</term> <note>original: "Grünspan"; a copper-based pigment.</note> and alum to it, according to whether one wants to dye much or little, until the color is blue enough; afterward, pour it off and dye with it until it is blue enough.

### Number VIII.

## To dye linen yarn an orange color.

If one wishes to dye the yarn thus, one must first dye it sulfur-yellow; afterward, take <term>soot</term> <note>original: "Ruß"; used in historical dyeing to darken or "sadden" colors, shifting bright yellow toward orange or brown.</note>, let it boil for 2 hours, and dye the yarn with it until the color is sufficient.

### Number IX.

## To dye linen yarn a liver-color.

One takes the above-mentioned red dye, puts <term>alum</term> <note>original: "Alaun"; a common mineral mordant used to fix dye to fibers.</note> into it, and dyes the yarn from the cold dye.

### Number X.

## To dye linen yarn an "Isabella" color.

One boils <term>annatto</term> <note>original: "Orlean"; a natural orange-red dye derived from the seeds of the achiote tree (*Bixa orellana*).</note> in <term>lye</term> <note>original: "Laugen"; an alkaline solution made from wood ashes used to extract certain pigments.</note> until it is fully boiled down, stirs in a little alum, and dyes with it until the yarn is beautiful enough. <note>"Isabella" (Isabellen-Farb) refers to a pale, dingy yellow or parchment color, which was highly fashionable in the 17th century.</note>

### Number XI.

## To dye linen yarn a lily-green.

The yarn is first dyed sulfur-yellow, and afterward in the blue dye, until it is green enough. <note>original: "Arissel-Grün"; likely a corruption of "Iris-Grün" (lily or iris green). Creating green by layering blue over yellow was the standard practice before stable green dyes were discovered.</note>

### Number XII.

## To dye linen yarn a violet-brown.

One dyes the yarn first blue, and then pulls it through the red dye.

### Number XIII.

## To dye linen yarn a clove-brown.

One takes brown <term>Brazilwood</term> <note>original: "Prisilgen"; heartwood from various tropical trees used to produce red and brown shades.</note>, boils it in lye, puts a little alum into it, stirs it well, and dyes with it until the color is sufficient.

### Number XIV.

## To dye linen yarn a "Triestienne" color.

One takes yellow dye-wood and dyes the yarn yellow with it; afterward, take <term>copperas</term> <note>original: "Kupfer-Wasser"; typically refers to iron sulfate (green vitriol), which reacts with tannins to create dark, muted tones.</note> and <term>oak galls</term> <note>original: "Gallus"; abnormal growths on oak trees rich in tannic acid, used here to darken the yellow into a brownish-grey "Triestienne" shade.</note> well-crushed, boil them in water, pull the yellow yarn through it, and wash it afterward in cold water until it is finished.

<summary>This page provides recipes VIII through XIV for dyeing linen yarn in shades of orange, liver, Isabella, green, violet-brown, clove-brown, and Triestienne. The methods rely on layering primary colors (yellow and blue for green) and using mordants like alum and copperas to modify wood-based dyes.</summary>

### Number XV.
## To dye linen black.

One takes <term>copper-water</term> <note>original: "Kupfer-Wasser"; despite the name, this usually referred to green vitriol (ferrous sulfate), which reacts with tannins to create black.</note>, crushed <term>oak galls</term> <note>original: "Gallus"; tannin-rich growths used to create deep blacks and permanent inks.</note>, and oak sawdust; let them boil together. Add <term>metal filings</term> <note>original: "Schliff"; the fine dust or "grindings" from a whetstone, providing iron to darken the dye.</note> and dye the yarn until it is black enough, then wash it out.

### Number XVI.
## To dye linen yarn a beautiful flesh color.

When one wishes to dye linen yarn a <term>flesh color</term> <note>original: "Leibfarbe"; a pale, pinkish-beige or "nude" tone fashionable in the Early Modern period.</note>, take for 4 pounds of yarn: 2 <term>loth</term> <note>A historical German unit of weight, approximately 14–15 grams or half an ounce.</note> of <term>tartar</term> <note>original: "Weinstein"; cream of tartar, used as an assistant to help the dye penetrate fibers.</note> and 14 loth of <term>alum</term> for the decoction. For the dyeing itself, one needs 6 loth of <term>brazilwood</term> <note>original: "Fernebock"; a red dyewood imported from South America.</note> and 12 loth of <term>madder</term> <note>original: "Röthe"; a common European root used for red dyes.</note>. Let this boil thoroughly for half an hour, then let it cool and dye with it.

### Number XVII.
## To dye linen yarn a crimson color.

Take for 4 pounds of linen yarn: 8 loth each of white tartar and alum, 1 loth of <term>sumac</term> <note>original: "Schmack"; a plant high in tannins used as a mordant.</note>, and 1 pound of soaked brazilwood. This will make the color quite vivid.

### Number XVIII.
## To dye linen yarn a beautiful red.

The linen yarn is first boiled with 4 loth of alum and 4 loth of tartar, and then cooled. Afterward, soak 6 loth of brazilwood with a handful of <term>bran</term> <note>original: "Kleyen"; used to soften the water and help regulate the fermentation or acidity of the dye bath.</note> in warm water, add 3 loth of madder, and let it heat over a small fire, gradually bringing it to a full boil.

### Number XIX.
## To dye three pounds of linen yarn red.

Crush 4 loth of alum finely and put it in water. Place the yarn inside and let it sit for a while; afterward, wring it out and let it dry. Then pour pure water over 16 loth of <term>brazilwood</term> <note>original: "Priesilien"; another spelling for brazilwood.</note>, let it boil for half an hour, pour off the dye liquid, and let it cool slightly. Add a little <term>quicklime</term> <note>original: "ungelöschten Kalck"; used to shift the pH of the dye bath, which changes the color of brazilwood from red toward purple.</note> and some saltpeter, then put the yarn in, let it sit for a bit, and dye it.

->M m m 2<-

### Number XX.
# To dye linen yarn gray.
One heats up black dye, places the yarn inside, and lets it lie there until one sees that it is gray. <note>This is a simplified method of using a weakened or "exhausted" black dye bath to achieve a lighter shade of gray.</note>

### Number XXI.
# To dye blue.
For 4 pounds of linen yarn, take 1 pound of <term>alum</term> <note>original: "Allaun"; a mineral salt used as a mordant to fix dye to the fibers.</note>, crush it small, put the yarn and alum into the kettle, let them boil together, and let it lie therein for one night. Afterward, wash it out and let it become dry. Then take 1/2 pound of <term>blue brazilwood</term> <note>original: "blaue Priesilge"; likely referring to logwood (Haematoxylum campechianum), which produces blue and purple tones, unlike standard red brazilwood.</note>, soak it in water, then boil it well for an hour and a half. Then pour it into a vessel and add 2 <term>loth</term> <note>A historical unit of weight; 2 loth is approximately 1 ounce or 30 grams.</note> of red <term>verdigris</term> <note>original: "rothen Grünspan"; verdigris is typically green copper acetate, but "red" may refer to a specific prepared form or a related copper pigment.</note> to it, stir it well, and place the yarn inside. One must, however, turn it over often so that it does not become spotted, and cover it well during the process.

### Number XXII.
# How one should dye "rust-thread."
In <term>sourdough-water</term> <note>original: "Sauer-Teig-Wasser"; the acidic environment of fermented dough water helped dissolve iron to create a dye.</note>, place old iron; take the iron out of the water every day, set it up, and let it dry so that it becomes quite rusty. Then place it back into the sourdough-water. When it is ready <note>meaning the water has become saturated with iron acetate</note>, put your thread or cloth into it and let it lie therein overnight. Then hang it in the air, ensuring the sun does not shine upon it; let it dry, then put it in again, and hang it in the air. Do this as often as needed until it is a proper <term>rust-work</term> <note>original: "Roß-arbeit"; while "Roß" means horse, the context of iron and rust strongly suggests "Rost-arbeit" (rust-work), a common method for creating permanent dark browns and blacks.</note>.

### Number XXIII.
# To dye yarn and laces violet-brown.
Take <term>brazilwood</term> <note>original: "Priesilien Spähne"; shavings of the brazilwood tree.</note> chips, put them in a glazed pot, soak them in a good <term>lye</term> <note>original: "Lauge"; an alkaline solution made from wood ashes, used to extract color.</note>, and after soaking, let them boil well. When they are sufficiently boiled, add finely crushed verdigris to it, and test it to see if the color is to your liking.

### Number XXIV.
# To dye yellow.
Take gold-colored shavings from the <term>wild apple-heart</term> <note>original: "wilden Aepffel-Kern"; likely referring to the yellow-dying heartwood or inner bark of the wild apple tree (Malus sylvestris) rather than the seeds.</note>; soak them for one night in lye, boil them well, and after boiling, add alum to it. Place the cloth therein, wring it out a little, and let it dry in the shade; thus you will have a beautiful gold-yellow color.

->Number XXV.<-

### To dye red.

To one <term>maaß</term> <note>original: "Maaß"; a historical liquid measure roughly equivalent to 1 to 1.5 liters depending on the region.</note> of water, take 2 <term>loth</term> <note>A unit of weight roughly equal to 15 grams or half an ounce.</note> of good <term>brazilwood</term> <note>original: "Priesilgen"; ground wood from various tropical trees used to produce red and purple dyes.</note>, soak them, then let it come to a boil. Afterward, pull it from the fire and put a little <term>alum</term> <note>original: "Allaun"; a mineral salt used as a mordant to fix the dye to the fabric.</note> into it; set it back on the fire and let it come to a rolling boil. Then take it away, and when it is mostly cooled, dye whatever you wish with it.

->Number XXVI.<-

### To dye red twine.

One takes alder bark, bark from a plum tree, and bark from <term>sloes</term> <note>original: "Schlehen"; the fruit-bearing blackthorn bush (*Prunus spinosa*).</note>. Grind these barks well together, boil the twine therein, and when it has boiled, lay it in fresh oat straw.

->Number XXVII.<-

### To dye black sendal.

Take alder bark, <term>grindstone sediment</term> <note>original: "Schlief"; the sludge or fine dust produced by grinding metal, rich in iron which reacts with tannins in bark to create black.</note>, and <term>hammer scale</term> <note>original: "Hammer-Schlag"; the iron oxide flakes that fall from hot iron when struck by a blacksmith.</note>. Boil it very well and dye with it. <note>"Zendel" or Sendal was a thin, fine silk fabric popular in the medieval and early modern periods.</note>

->Number XXVIII.<-

### To dye linen cloth blue.

Take a quarter [pound] of <term>logwood</term> <note>original: "blau Holz"; literally "blue wood," referring to *Haematoxylum campechianum*, used for blues and purples.</note> and only a very little <term>verdigris</term> <note>original: "Grünspan"; a green copper acetate pigment and mordant.</note> for 6 or 8 <term>ells</term> <note>original: "Ellen"; a unit of length usually representing the distance from the elbow to the fingertip, roughly 24–27 inches.</note> of unbleached cloth, which must first be washed out with lukewarm water. One lets the logwood boil in 9 or 10 maaß of water and pours the dye into a clean vessel. Divide the clear dye into 3 parts and stir one-third of the half-portion of verdigris well into it. Press the soaked cloth into it and wet it thoroughly therein, wring it out, and pour that broth away. Then take the second third of the still-warm dye and stir into it the [next] third of the half-portion of verdigris; pull the cloth up and down [through the dye], wring it out, and throw the dye away.

In the event that the cloth is not yet blue enough, one takes the remainder of the dye and the verdigris and does with it as was done the previous two times.

->Number XXIX.<-

### To dye green.

The same must first be dyed from the blue dye. Afterward, one must take a good portion of <term>dye-flowers</term> <note>original: "Farbeblumen"; likely referring to Dyer's Broom (*Genista tinctoria*) or similar yellow-producing flowers.</note> and boil them well in water. Put a portion of verdigris into the boiled dye-flower water. That which was dyed blue is then pressed into this boiled broth, and so it becomes a beautiful green. <note>Dyeing green was traditionally a two-step process: first dyeing the fabric blue with woad or indigo, then "over-dyeing" with a yellow dye.</note>

It highlights the multi-step chemical processes required for linen and silk, including the use of mordants like alum and verdigris.</summary>

->Number XXX.<-

# To dye woolen yarn in all sorts of ways.

Make a fresh <term>decoction</term> <note>original: "Sud"; the liquid produced by boiling dye materials in water.</note> warm, and for every pound of yarn, put half a <term>loth</term> <note>A historical unit of weight, roughly 15 grams or half an ounce.</note> of <term>verdigris</term> <note>original: "Grünspan"; a green pigment and mordant made from weathered copper.</note> into the warm water. Stir it well so that it becomes a good green; then place the yarn inside and let it lie there for a good hour. Fill the kettle again with water and add 1 pound of <term>blue brazilwood</term> <note>original: "blaue Priesilge"; while Priesilge usually refers to red brazilwood, "blue" refers here to logwood (*Haematoxylum campechianum*), used for blues and purples.</note>, and let it boil for half an hour. Wring the yarn out of the verdigris, and dye it in this [blue] color; the color will take hold quickly, and the yarn will become a beautiful blue. Wash it clean and <term>finish</term> <note>original: "meiſtre"; to treat the dyed fabric with a final bath to set the color or change the tone.</note> it in lye.

->Number XXXI.<-

# To dye woolen yarn lemon yellow.

Take 20 pounds of woolen yarn and boil it with <term>alum</term> <note>original: "Allaun"; a mineral salt used as a mordant to fix dyes.</note>. Afterward, let it cool. Empty the kettle and make a new decoction; put a good portion of <term>yellow flowers</term> <note>Likely dyer's broom or weld (*Reseda luteola*), the most common historical sources for bright yellows.</note> inside and let it boil for an hour. Then add verdigris to it; stir it well together in the warm water until the verdigris has completely dissolved. When the water now looks beautifully greenish, put the yarn inside and <term>mordant</term> <note>original: "beizet"; the process of preparing fibers to accept dye.</note> it therein. Let it lie for a little while, then take it out, let it dry somewhat, and now make it yellow. Empty the kettle and fill it with fresh water; add 1 pound of <term>logwood</term> <note>original: "Blau-Holz"; used here to adjust the shade of the yellow.</note> and let it boil together for half an hour. Afterward, dye the yarn in it. One must work quickly with this, otherwise it will become too dark.

->Number XXXII.<-

# To dye woolen yarn red.

One must first boil the yarn in alum. Afterward, mix <term>Breslau red</term> <note>original: "Breßlauer Röthe"; a high-quality variety of madder root from the Silesia region.</note> and <term>madder</term> <note>original: "Krapp"; the root of *Rubia tinctorum*, the primary source for red dye in Europe.</note> together and boil them. Then put the yarn inside and proceed with it in the manner mentioned above.

->Number XXXIII.<-

# To dye woolen yarn violet.

For 1 pound of woolen yarn, take half a pound of brazilwood. But boil it in alum beforehand, and when this has boiled, put the yarn inside. Then boil them together again for a quarter of an hour. When it has boiled for that long,

### Number XXXIV.

## To dye woolen yarn orange color.

One dyes the yarn red first, and afterward makes a new <term>decoction</term> <note>original: "Sud"; the liquid produced by boiling dye materials in water.</note>, puts into it one and a half <term>loth</term> <note>A historical unit of weight, roughly 15 grams or half an ounce.</note> of <term>yellowwood shavings</term> <note>original: "Gelbspähne"; likely fustic shavings (*Maclura tinctoria*), used to produce yellow and orange tones.</note>, and lets them boil well; when it has boiled, one dyes approximately 10 loth of woolen yarn with it, one skein or one piece after the other, until it has reached its color; then one washes it clean.
